en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Sagāthāvagga of the Saṃyuttanikāya.
Introduction to the Work:

I pay homage to the Sugata, who is free from all states of existence, who is honored by the world of humans and gods, whose heart is cooled by compassion, and whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.
I pay homage to that unsurpassed Dhamma which the Buddha— having both developed and realized the state of Buddhahood— has attained, having gone where the stains have vanished.
I pay homage to the legitimate sons of the Sugata, the destroyers of Māra’s army.
I bow my head in reverence to the Noble Saṅgha, the assembly of all eight [types of noble ones].
Thus, by the power of this merit consisting of my homage to the Triple Gem—
may it, through its influence, ensure that my obstacles are thoroughly dispelled as my mind becomes serene.
For the purpose of elucidating the meaning of this excellent *Saṃyutta Āgama*,
which is adorned by the *Saṃyutta Vagga*, praised by those awakened after the Buddha (*Buddhānubuddha*),
and which generates the various distinctions of knowledge— an *Aṭṭhakathā* was [composed] from the beginning by the [Vasī] Sages.
That which was chanted at the five councils, and subsequently recited again,
was brought to the Island of Siṃhala by the great Mahinda, who possessed mastery [of the Dhamma];
it was established in the Sinhalese language for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island.
Then, having set aside the delightful Sinhalese language,
I composed this work in a faultless style suited to the method of the canonical tradition,
without transgressing the principles established by the Elders who are the lamps of the lineage of the Theras.
Having abandoned the matter that has been repeatedly approached by those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra who possess subtle discernment,
I shall clarify the meaning for the sake of the satisfaction of virtuous people and for the long endurance of the Dhamma.
The description of the cities beginning with Sāvatthī was already provided below by me while explaining the meaning of the two Saṅgītis; likewise,
the specific instances (vatthu) that were recounted therein have been told in detail.
There is nothing further here regarding them; I shall provide a detailed exposition.
However, as for the meanings of the suttas which are not clearly revealed without their underlying narratives (vatthu), I shall also present those narratives for the purpose of elucidating them.
The discourse on virtue, the ascetic qualities, and all the meditation subjects;
the detailed exposition of the jhānas and attainments together with the methods for conduct;
all the higher knowledges, and the compendium of the calculation of wisdom.
The aggregates, elements, bases, and faculties; the four noble truths;
the teaching on the mode of conditions with its perfectly pure and subtle methods;
the lineages of liberation and the paths; and the cultivation of insight.
Since all this has been very thoroughly explained by me in the *Visuddhimagga*, I shall not analyze it further here. Indeed,
this *Visuddhimagga* stands in the midst of the four Āgamas.
"Having stood [there], he will reveal the meaning exactly as it was spoken.
Since it was composed thus, you should understand that the meaning connected with the *Saṃyutta* is to be known by taking both this [work] together with its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
1. Devatāsaṃyutta 1.
Naḷavagga 1. Commentary on the Oghataraṇa Sutta (The Crossing of the Flood)
Therein, the Saṃyutta Āgama consists of five sections: the Sagāthāvagga, the Nidānavagga, the Khandhakavagga, the Saḷāyatanavagga, and the Mahāvagga.
As for the number of discourses: "Seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two discourses—this is the compendium of the Saṃyutta."

From one recitation-section (*bhāṇavāra*) there are a hundred recitation-sections. Among its chapters (*vagga*), the Chapter Containing Verses (*Sagāthāvagga*) is the first; among its discourses (*sutta*), the Discourse on Crossing the Flood (*Oghataraṇasutta*) is the first.
Even for that, the introduction beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam me sutaṃ*), spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council (*Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāla*), is the first.
Furthermore, this First Great Council has been explained in detail at the beginning of the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.
Therefore, that [exposition] should be understood there according to the method already detailed.
As for this introduction beginning with "Thus have I heard": therein, *evaṃ* (thus) is a particle;
*me* (by me) and so forth are nouns; in the phrase "dwells at Sāvatthī," *vi* is a prefix; and *harati* (dwells) is a verb.
By this method, first of all, the analysis of the word (*padavibhāga*) should be understood.

As for its meaning (*attha*), the term *evaṃ* has many distinct senses, such as comparison (*upamā*), instruction (*upadesa*), encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*), censure (*garahaṇa*), acceptance of speech (*vacanasampaṭiggaha*), manner (*ākāra*), illustration (*nidassana*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
For instance, in such passages as “By one born as a mortal, much wholesome [deed] should be done,” it is used in the sense of comparison.
In such cases as “You should approach thus; you should withdraw thus,” it is used in instruction (*upadesa*).
In such cases as “So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata,” it is used in encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*).
In such cases as “In this very way, O outcaste woman, she praises that shaveling ascetic, whoever he may be,” it is used in reproach (*garahaṇa*). [And in] “Yes, venerable sir.”
In such passages as "Those monks replied to the Blessed One," it refers to the acceptance of speech.

In such passages as "Thus, venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One," it refers to a manner of expression. In such passages as "Come, young man, go to where the ascetic Ānanda is;
having approached him, in my name [inquire after] the ascetic Ānanda’s freedom from illness... it refers to a command.

Inquire after his freedom from illness, his lightness of body, his strength, and his well-being, saying: “The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, inquires after the venerable Ānanda’s freedom from affliction, freedom from illness, lightness of body, strength, and well-being.
And say this as well: “It would be good, indeed, if the venerable Ānanda would come to the residence of the young man Subha, son of Todeyya.”
“...let him approach [him], out of compassion”—in such cases, it is used as an illustration.
“What do you think, Kālāmas: Are these states wholesome or unwholesome? “Unwholesome, venerable sir. “Are they blameworthy or blameless? “Blameworthy, venerable sir.
“Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise? “Censured by the wise, venerable sir. “When fully undertaken and practiced...”
“Whether they lead to harm and suffering or not, what do you think about this? “Venerable sir, when they are fully undertaken and observed, they lead to harm and suffering;
such is our view in this matter. In such passages, the word *evaṃ* (thus) is used in the sense of emphasis. Here, however, it should be understood in the senses of manner, indication, and emphasis.
Therein, by the word *evaṃ* in the sense of manner, he illustrates this meaning: [the Dhamma] which is skillful in various methods and originates from many underlying tendencies.

Who is capable of understanding in every way the word of that Blessed One—endowed with both meaning and phrasing, possessing manifold wonders, profound in its teaching of the Dhamma and its realization, and reaching the ear-canal of all beings according to each one’s own language—even by exerting every effort to generate a desire to hear, [one can only say]: "Thus have I heard; it was also heard by me."
"In one way it is 'heard' (sutaṃ)":

by way of illustration, avoiding self-exaltation by saying "I am not self-become; this was not realized by me," he indicates the entire discourse that is now to be spoken with the words "Thus have I heard; thus too have I heard.
By way of emphasis: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are learned..."
"Namely, Ānanda, among those who possess wisdom, mindfulness, steadfastness, and who are attendants— namely, Ānanda. Thus,
in accordance with his state of being praised by the Blessed One as "the Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in the terminology,
and skilled in what precedes and follows," and likewise by the General of the Dhamma, he displayed his own power of retention.
By declaring this, he generates in beings a desire to hear: “Thus have I heard; and that is neither deficient nor redundant in meaning or in phrasing;
it should be regarded exactly thus and not otherwise.
The word *me* (by me) is seen in three senses. For instance, in such passages as “Gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyaṃ” (“What is sung to the accompaniment of verses is not food for me”), and so forth.
The meaning is "by me. In passages such as, "It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief," the meaning is "to me.
In passages such as, "Be heirs, monks, to my Dhamma," the meaning is "my.
But here, both of the two possible meanings—"heard by me" and "heard from me"—are appropriate.

The word *suta*—this term *suta*, both with and without prefixes—has a manifold variety of meanings, including: going, renowned, moistened, accumulated, application, cognizable by the ear, and that which is known by following the door of the ear.

For instance, in such cases as “one who has set out (*pasuto*) with an army,” the meaning is “going. In such cases as “of one who sees the Dhamma heard (*sutadhammassa*”), the meaning is “of one whose Dhamma is renowned (*vissutadhammassa*”).
In such cases as “the lustful (*avassutā*) toward the lustful (*avassutassa*”), the meaning is “moistened (*kilinna*) toward the moistened (*akilinna*).”
In such passages as “A great mass of merit has been accumulated by you,” the meaning is “accumulated. In such passages as “The wise who are intent on jhāna,” the meaning is “devoted to jhāna.

In such passages as “Seen, heard, and sensed,” the meaning is “to be cognized by the ear-faculty. In such passages as “One who retains what is heard, one who stores what is heard,” the meaning is “one who retains what is cognized by following the door of the ear. But here, by means of following the door of the ear—
The meaning is either "retained" (*upadhārita*) or "retention" (*upadhāraṇa*). For when the word *me* has the sense of *mayā* ("by me"), it is appropriate to say:
"Thus have I heard; it was retained by me following the path of the ear-door. When it has the sense of *mama* ("my"), it is appropriate to say:
"Thus have I heard; it is my retention following the path of the ear-door."

Thus, among these three terms: *evaṃ* (thus) indicates the function of consciousness, such as ear-consciousness and the rest; *me* (by me) indicates the person possessing the aforementioned consciousness;
*sutaṃ* (heard) indicates the grasping of an object that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor perverted, by way of negating the state of not hearing.
Likewise, *evaṃ* (thus) proclaims the state of the occurrence of that stream of consciousness proceeding through various modes of objects by following the ear-door.
“Me” (by me) is a declaration of the person; “sutaṃ” (heard) is a declaration of the Dhamma. This is the summary here:
“By means of the stream of consciousness proceeding toward various kinds of objects, nothing else was done by me; rather, this was done, and this Dhamma was heard.

Likewise, “evaṃ” (thus) is a declaration of the manner in which the exposition is to be shown; “me” is a declaration of the person; “sutaṃ” is a declaration of the person’s function. This is what is meant: “The discourse that I shall explain, that was heard by me thus.”

"Thus" (*tathā*) means that for a stream of consciousness (*cittasantāna*) which, through its occurrence in various modes, has the grasping of various meanings and phonemes, there is a description of those various modes.
For "thus" (*evaṃ*) is a designation of mode (*ākāra-ppaññatti*). "Me" (*me*) is a designation of the agent (*kattuniddesa*). "Hearing" (*sutaṃ*) is a designation of the object (*visayaniddesa*).
At this point, by means of the stream of consciousness occurring in various modes, the determination of the grasping of the object by the agent possessing it is established.

Alternatively, *evaṃ* is a designation for the function of the person; *sutaṃ* is a designation for the function of consciousness; and *me* is a designation for the person endowed with both functions.

Herein, this is the summary: "It was heard by me—a person possessing the function of hearing through consciousness—by way of that consciousness, using the conventional expression 'heard' which has acquired its function through consciousness."
In this context, "thus" (*evaṃ*) and "mine" (*me*) are designations of non-existence according to the true and ultimate sense (*saccikaṭṭhaparamattha*).
For what is there here that exists in the ultimate sense which could receive the designation "thus" or "mine"? "Hearing" (*suta*) is a designation of existence.
For that which is apprehended here by the ear exists in the ultimate sense. Likewise, "thus" and...

It is a "designation by dependence" (*upādāpaññatti*) because it is expressed in dependence upon this or that [condition], such as "mind. It is a "designation by comparison" (*upanidhāpaññatti*) because it is expressed in comparison with what has been seen and so forth, such as "heard.
Herein, by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), he demonstrates non-delusion; for one who is deluded is not capable of various kinds of penetration.
By the word "heard" (*suta*), he demonstrates the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard; for one whose hearing has been forgotten...
He does not claim, "I heard this at another time. Thus, through non-delusion, wisdom (*paññā*) is established;

through non-forgetfulness, however, mindfulness (*sati*) is established. In that regard, there is the capacity to grasp the phrasing through mindfulness preceded by wisdom, and the capacity to penetrate the meaning through wisdom preceded by mindfulness.
By virtue of the conjunction of these two capacities, [one attains] that which is endowed with both the meaning and the phrasing.
The status of being a custodian of the Dhamma is established because of his capacity to preserve the treasury of the Dhamma.
According to another method: by the word "thus" (evaṃ), he illustrates wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), for one who attends unwisely lacks various kinds of penetration.
By the word "heard" (suta), he illustrates non-distraction, for there is no hearing for one whose mind is distracted. For it is said that one whose mind is distracted...
Even when being told of every success, a person says, "I have not heard it; say it again.

And herein, through wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), one accomplishes right self-application and prior merit-making; for these are absent in one who is wrongly applied or who has not previously made merit.
Through non-distraction, one accomplishes hearing the true Dhamma and reliance upon a true person (*sappurisa*).
He accomplishes it. For one whose mind is distracted is unable to hear, and there is no hearing for one who does not rely upon a true person (sappurisa).

Another method: since it has been said, "The term 'thus' (evaṃ) is a description of various modes for that continuum of consciousness in which the apprehension of various meanings and phrasing occurs through the manifestation of diverse aspects," and yet such a noble aspect as this is not properly [realized] by one whose self is without aspiration (appaṇihita);...
"Or for one who has not performed merit in the past"—therefore, by the phrase "thus," he demonstrates his own attainment of the latter two wheels in this auspicious manner.
"Hearing" (*suta*) refers to the attainment of the former two wheels through the application of listening;
for there is no hearing for one dwelling in an unsuitable place or one devoid of reliance upon a true person (*sappurisa*). Thus, for the sake of accomplishing these latter two wheels...
Purity of disposition is established through the accomplishment of the first two wheels; through that purity of disposition, there is the accomplishment of proficiency in realization (*adhigama*);
and through purity of practice (*payoga*), there is the accomplishment of proficiency in scripture (*āgama*).

Thus, the speech of one whose practice and disposition are pure, and who is perfected in both scripture and realization, is like the dawn preceding the rising of the sun, and like wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) preceding wholesome action (*kusala-kamma*).
Thinking, "He ought to be the precursor to the Blessed One’s word," he spoke the words beginning with "Thus have I heard" while establishing the introductory setting (*nidāna*) for the occasion.

According to another method: by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), which indicates penetration in its various modes, he demonstrates the presence of his own perfection in the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*) and of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).

By the word "heard" (*sutaṃ*), which indicates penetration into the various things to be heard, he demonstrates the presence of his perfection in the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*) and of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*).
And by speaking these words which illustrate wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), he demonstrates: "These states have been examined by me with the mind and thoroughly penetrated by insight.
By speaking this word which illustrates application to hearing (*savana-yoga*), namely "heard," he demonstrates:
"Many states have been heard by me, retained, and mastered by speech. And by both of these, he demonstrates the perfection of both the meaning and the phrasing.
By illuminating [the text], he generates respect for hearing it.

For one who does not listen with respect to the Dhamma, which is complete in both meaning and phrasing, becomes excluded from great benefit; therefore, having generated respect, the Dhamma should be heard with careful attention.
By this entire phrase, "Thus have I heard," the Venerable Ānanda [establishes] the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
By not withholding [the teaching] from himself, he transcends the plane of the unworthy person; by professing discipleship, he enters the plane of the worthy person.
Likewise, he draws his mind away from what is not the true Dhamma and establishes it in the true Dhamma.
By declaring, "This has been heard by me only as such, yet it is the word of that Blessed One," he liberates himself and [honors] the Teacher.
He refers back [to the source], applies the word of the Conqueror, and establishes the guide of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, without claiming for himself the state of having produced [the teaching] by his own effort, he explains the preceding words thus:
"This was received by me directly from that Blessed One, who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence and who possesses the ten powers."

This is the word of the Perfectly Enlightened One— the one who stands in the bull’s place, the roarer of the lion’s roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Excellent Wheel-Turner of the True Dhamma; herein,
no doubt or perplexity should be made regarding the meaning, the doctrine, the phrases, or the syllables.”
It destroys lack of faith in this Dhamma among all gods and humans, and it generates the perfection of faith. Therefore, this is said:
"It destroys the faithless and increases faith in the Teaching;
Thus have I heard—so saying, the disciple of Gotama."
This is the exposition of the delimitation by number. "At one time" (ekasmiṃ samaye) is an exposition of a delimited [occasion]. "At one time" (ekaṃ samayaṃ) is an indication of the indefinite.
In this context, the word *samaya* is seen to be used in the sense of: "conjunction, moment, time, collection, cause, view, acquisition, abandoning, and penetration."
For instance, in such passages as, “Perhaps tomorrow we might visit, taking into account the time and the occasion,” the meaning is *samavāya* (conjunction).
In such passages as, “Monks, there is indeed but one moment and one occasion for living the holy life,” the meaning is *khaṇa* (moment).
In such passages as, “The time of heat, the time of feverish distress,” the meaning is *kāla* (time). In such passages as, “A great assembly in the forest,” the meaning is *samūha* (multitude).

“Bhaddāli, you had also failed to discern this circumstance: that the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One would have known of me—‘The bhikkhu named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s Dispensation.
This, too, Bhaddāli, was a circumstance you had failed to discern. In such passages, it is the cause (*hetu*). “Now at that time... [and so forth].

In such passages as, “The wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇa Muṇḍikā, was residing at the Mallikā Park in the single-sālaka tinduka-grove of Samayappavādaka,” it refers to *diṭṭhi* (view). [And it is said:
“Whatever benefit there is in this present life, and whatever benefit there is in the future life...”
In such passages as, “The steadfast one who has the realization of the goal (attha) is called wise,” it refers to acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
In such passages as, “Through the right realization of conceit, he made an end of suffering,” it refers to abandoning (*pahāna*).

In such passages as, “The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of realization (*abhisamaya*),” it refers to penetration (*paṭivedha*).

But here, "time" (kāla) is the meaning. By this, he indicates one specific occasion (*samaya*) among the divisions of time, such as the year, the season, the month, the half-month, night, day, the morning, midday, evening, the first, middle, and last watches of the night, and the moments (*muhutta*), etc.
In that regard, although among these occasions such as the year and so forth, whatever discourse (*sutta*) [was spoken] in whichever year...

Whether it was stated [to have occurred] in a particular season, month, fortnight, during the portion of the night, or the portion of the day—all that is well-known and well-determined by the Elder’s wisdom.

However, if one were to say, "Thus have I heard: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight, during such-and-such a portion of the night, or such-and-such a portion of the day," it would not be easy to remember.
Whether to recite it oneself or to cause it to be recited, much would have to be said; therefore, having condensed that meaning into a single phrase, he said, "At one time.
Or else, [it refers to] these times:
the time of descent into the womb, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency, the time of the Great Renunciation, and the time of practicing austerities.

The time of victory over Māra, the time of full enlightenment, the time of dwelling in happiness in this very life, the time of teaching, and the time of final Nibbāna—such are the various types of *samaya* (occasions) of the Blessed One, which were exceedingly well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
Among those *samayas*, he indicates one specific *samaya*, namely that designated as the "time of teaching. Furthermore, regarding these times for the functions of wisdom and compassion:
The time for the function of compassion; the time for the practice of benefiting others among the two practices of benefiting oneself and others;
the time for discourse on the Dhamma among the two duties of those who have assembled;
and the time for teaching among the two practices of teaching and practice—it was with reference to one such occasion that he said, "at one time."
But why, in this case, has the description not been made by means of the locative case— as it was done in the Abhidhamma with the words, “At whatever time,
pertaining to the sense-sphere,” and in other Sutta passages with the words, “At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures,” and in the Vinaya with the instrumental case,
“At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One”— but rather [by using] “one”?

The term "samaya" is explained here by means of a word expressing an instrument (*upayoga*). This is because the meaning can be understood both in that way [in the Abhidhamma] and in another way [here].

For in that context—the Abhidhamma—as well as in other Sutta passages, the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the sense of characterizing a state by means of a state (*bhāvena bhāva-lakkhaṇa*) are possible.
Indeed, in those cases, "samaya" has the sense of time and the sense of a collection (*samūha*); [it refers to] the phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth that are spoken of therein.
Furthermore, their state is characterized by the state of "time," which is designated as the cause consisting of the convergence of moments (*khaṇa-samavāya-hetu*).
Therefore, the locative case is employed there in order to indicate that meaning.

And in the Vinaya, both the sense of cause (*hetu-attha*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa-attha*) are possible; for that time at which the formulation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-paññatti*) occurred was [also] [known] by Sāriputta and others.

Because it is difficult to understand, the Blessed One dwelt here and there at those various times, acting as both the cause and the instrument for the proclamation of the training rules (sikkhāpada), while also having regard for the reasons for proclaiming those training rules. Therefore, for the purpose of illustrating that meaning,
the description is made there by means of the instrumental case.
Furthermore, in this and other similar instances, the sense of absolute conjunction (*accantasamyoga*) is possible.
For at whatever time the Blessed One taught this or another discourse, he dwelt in that very moment exclusively in the abiding of compassion.
Therefore, the use of the accusative case is employed here for the purpose of illustrating that meaning.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Having regard for various meanings, [the case endings] are expressed through the locative and the instrumental;
except for the 'time' (samaya), which here is expressed by the accusative."
The Ancients, however, explain: “‘At that time,’ ‘on that occasion,’ or ‘at one time’—this is merely a difference in expression;
in all cases, the meaning is simply the locative case. Therefore, even when “at one time” is said, it should be understood to mean “at one [particular] time.”

"Bhagavā" means venerable (*garu*). For in the world, one who is venerable is called "Bhagavā. And because he is distinguished by all virtues, he is venerable to all beings; therefore, he should be understood as "Bhagavā. It has also been said by the ancients:
"Bhagavā" is the best of words; "Bhagavā" is the supreme word.
He is venerable and worthy of reverence; for that reason, he is called "Bhagavā."
Furthermore:

"He is fortunate, he has overcome [defilements], he is intent, he is possessed of the [eight] fortunes, he is the master of what is to be mastered, he has vomited out [all taints], and he has gone beyond all states of existence; therefore he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā)."

The detailed meaning of this term should be understood according to this verse; it has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha (*Buddhānussati-niddesa*).
To this extent, by the statement "Thus have I heard," the Blessed One, showing the Dhamma as he heard it, makes his Dhamma-body manifest. By this, [he shows]:
"This teaching is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this is your Teacher."
He consoles the people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher.
By the phrase "at one time the Blessed One," he indicates that at that time the Blessed One was absent, thereby establishing the parinibbāna of the physical body (rūpakāya). By this, [he shows]:
"Even such a teacher of the noble Dhamma as this—one who possesses the ten powers, whose body is like a vajra-strike..."

"The Blessed One has attained final nibbāna; by what other means could hope for life be generated?"—thus he inspires those intoxicated with the pride of life and arouses their zeal for the True Dhamma.
By saying "Thus," he points out the excellence of the teaching (*desanā-sampatti*). By "heard by me" (*me suta*), he points out the excellence of the disciple (*sāvaka-sampatti*).
By "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*), he points out the excellence of the time (*kāla-sampatti*). By "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*), he points out the excellence of the teacher (*desaka-sampatti*).
"At Sāvatthī" means in the city of that name. This locative case is used here in the sense of proximity.
"Dwells" (*viharati*) is a general indication of being endowed with any one of the modes of dwelling—whether postures, divine, brahma, or noble.
Here, however, it indicates association with any one of the specific bodily postures, distinguished as standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One dwells even when standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
For he carries and maintains his personal existence without it falling, having interrupted one bodily posture with another;
thus he is said to "dwell" (*viharati*).
"At Jeta’s Grove" means in the grove of Prince Jeta. For it was planted, nurtured, and protected by him;
therefore, it became known as "Jeta’s Grove. In that Jeta’s Grove.

"In Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery" means in the monastery belonging to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, which he offered to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha at a cost of fifty-four crores of gold.
In the monastery that had come to be known as "Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery" because it had been handed over [to him]. This is the summary here;
the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, in the exposition of the *Sabbāsava Sutta*.
Therein it might be asked: if the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, then it should not be said that he was "in Jeta’s Grove."
If he were dwelling there [in Sāvatthī], it could not be said that he was "in Sāvatthī," for it is impossible to dwell in two places at one and the same time.
However, this should not be viewed in such a way.

Have we not already stated that "the locative case is used in the sense of proximity"? Therefore, just as herds of cattle are said to be "on the Ganges" or "on the Yamunā" when they are near those rivers, so too is it here.
Just as when fish are moving about in the vicinity of the Gaṅgā or the Yamunā, one says, "They are moving in the Gaṅgā" or "They are moving in the Yamunā," so too here,
although he was dwelling at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, he is said to be "dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jetavana. For the mention of Sāvatthī is for the purpose of indicating the village of his alms-round,
while the remaining words are for the purpose of indicating a place of residence suitable for one who has gone forth.
"A certain deity" means a single deity who is not well-known by name or clan.

However, in the passage: "Does the Blessed One, venerable sir, recall having spoken in brief to a certain well-known and highly influential *yakkha* regarding liberation through the destruction of craving?", even the well-known Sakka, king of the gods, is referred to as "a certain one. And the term "deity" (*devatā*)...

This term "deva" is a common designation for both gods and goddesses. However, in this context, "deva" is intended in its primary sense, referring to a particular deity among those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
Regarding the phrase "when the night has advanced," here the word *abhikkanta* is used in the senses of excellence, beauty, loveliness, and appreciation, and so forth.
It is seen [in various senses]. Therein, in such passages as, “Venerable sir, the night has advanced; the first watch has passed; the community of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time;
let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus,” it is seen in the sense of *destruction* (khaya).
In such passages as, “This person is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons,” it is seen in the sense of *beautiful* (sundara).
“Who is it that worships my feet, shining with supernatural power and glory, illuminating all directions with a most excellent complexion?”—in such passages as these, it means “beautiful.
In such passages as “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! it means “excellent.”
In the case of approval (*abbhānumodana*), it refers here to the moment of destruction (*khaye*). By this, it is meant that "the night has passed" or "the night has been fully spent.
In this context, it should be understood that this son of the gods arrived immediately following the middle watch of the night.
For this is indeed the custom of deities who come to attend upon Buddhas or the disciples of Buddhas.
They arrive immediately after the middle watch of the night.

Regarding the phrase *abhikkantavaṇṇā*: here, the word *abhikkanta* refers to what is beautiful, while the word *vaṇṇa* is seen used in the sense of skin complexion, lineage, cause, shape, size, the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), and so forth.
Among these, in such passages as “The Blessed One has a golden complexion,” it refers to the skin. [In the passage] “But when were they gathered together?”...
“Householder, these are the praises of the ascetic,” in such passages it refers to praise. “There are these four castes, Master Gotama,” in such passages it refers to the class of families.
“Now by what quality is one called a ‘scent-thief’? in such passages it refers to a cause.
“Having manifested the form of a great king elephant,” in such passages it refers to shape. “Three [marks] of the bowl... [and so forth].
In such passages as "complexions," it refers to measure. In such passages as "color, fragrance, taste, and nutritive essence," it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
Here, however, it should be understood as the skin. By this, "exquisite complexion" means a beautiful skin;
what is meant is a desirable complexion, a pleasing complexion. For when deities come to the human world, they abandon their natural complexion and natural psychic power (*iddhi*).

Having assumed a gross physical form and manifested an extraordinary beauty and extraordinary psychic power, they arrive with a contrived body, like people going to theatrical performances and the like.

Among them, those belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are able to come even without such contrivance, but those belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are not able to do so; for their physical form is exceedingly subtle, and they cannot [come] by means of it.
There is the assuming of a posture. Therefore, this son of the gods has come by means of a specifically prepared [form]. Hence it is said:
"With surpassing beauty. Regarding the word *kevalakappa*:
here the term *kevala* has many meanings, such as "without remainder," "for the most part," "unmixed," "excessive," "firm," "separation," and so forth.
For instance, in such passages as “the holy life that is entirely complete and pure,” the meaning is that of being without remainder (*anavasesattha*).
In such passages as “the entire region of Aṅga and Magadha, taking abundant hard food and soft food, will approach [him],” the meaning is that of being for the most part (*yebhuyyatā*).
In such passages as “there is the arising of the entire mass of suffering,” the meaning is that of being unmixed (*abyāmissatā*).
In such passages as “Surely this venerable one has only mere faith,” the meaning is “nothing more than.
In such passages as “Venerable sir, Bahiya, the co-resident of the venerable Anuruddha, has stood for the schism of the Saṅgha throughout his entire life,” the meaning is “firmly.
In such passages as “The consummate one, who has lived the holy life, is called the supreme person,” the meaning is “disjunction.”
In this context, however, its meaning is intended to be "without remainder.
Furthermore, this word *kappa* has many meanings, such as: conviction, conventional usage, time, designation, cutting, alternative, a small portion, and totality.
For instance, it is used in the passage: "This is worthy of the venerable Gotama, as it is for an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha."
In such instances as these, the meaning is "firm conviction. In such instances as, "Monks, I allow you to consume fruit according to the five ascetic conventions," it means "convention" (usage).
In such instances as, "By which indeed I dwell constantly throughout the kappa," it means "time.
In such instances as, "Thus spoke the Venerable Kappa," it means "designation. In such instances as, "Adorned, with hair and beard trimmed," it means... [the sense of "arranged" or "adorned"].

*Chedanaṃ* (cutting). In such expressions as “the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted,” it means *vikappa* (adaptation). In such expressions as “there is the possibility of lying down,” it means *leso* (a trace).
In such expressions as “having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana,” it means *samantabhāvo* (all-pervasiveness).
Here, however, its meaning of all-pervasiveness is intended. Therefore, regarding the phrase “the entire Jetavana,” it means “without remainder.”
"Throughout the Jeta Grove"—this is how the meaning should be understood.

"Illuminating" means having pervaded [the area] with the radiance issuing from his robes, ornaments, and body; the meaning is that he made it a single expanse of light and a single blaze, like the moon and like the sun.
"Whereby" is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative. "He approached the Blessed One whereby" means: "to where the Blessed One was."

In this context, the meaning should be understood as: “He approached him. Or, the meaning should be understood here as: “For whatever reason the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans, for that reason he approached him.
And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached? It is with the intention of attaining various distinguished qualities, and with the intention of enjoying the fruit of sweetness.

Like a great tree that is constantly bearing fruit through the hosts of deities. "Upasaṅkami" (he approached) means "he went. "Upasaṅkamitvā" (having approached) indicates the completion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, it may also mean that having gone thus, he then proceeded to a place even closer to the Blessed One, which is to say, his immediate vicinity.

Now, desiring to ask about the purpose for which she had come to attend upon the Supreme Person in the world, she placed her hands joined in reverent salutation—resplendent with the ten nails touching—at her head and stood to one side.
The term *ekamantaṃ* is a neuter locative designation, as in such expressions as “the moon and sun move unevenly. Therefore, she was standing in the manner of one who stands to one side.
"He stood" (*aṭṭhāsi*)—thus the meaning should be understood here. Alternatively, this accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.
"He stood" means he took his place. For wise gods and humans, having approached one who is worthy of reverence, stand to one side out of skill in etiquette regarding seats;
and this deity was one of them, therefore he stood to one side.
But how does one stand "standing to one side"? By avoiding the six faults of standing. Namely:
too far away, too near, upwind, on high ground, directly in front, or directly behind.
For if one stands too far away and wishes to speak, one must speak in a loud voice. If one stands too near, there is physical jostling.
He does so. Standing in the wind, he is troubled by the odor of the body. Standing on high ground, he manifests disrespect.
Standing too close in front, if he wishes to see, he must look with eye meeting eye.
Standing too far behind, if he wishes to see, he must turn his neck to look. Therefore, this too—
Having avoided these faults of place, he stood. Therefore it is said: "He stood to one side.

"Etadavoca" means "he said this. "Kathaṃ nu" is an inquiry into the reason. For the Blessed One’s state of having crossed over the floods (oghā) was manifest throughout the ten-thousandfold world system;
therefore, that deity had no doubt regarding that point. However, for the following reason, [the deity asked] why he was called "one who has crossed": [text continues].
Knowing this, she asked about that reason and spoke thus.
"Mārisa" is a term of endearment used for deities; it means "one free from suffering. If it is so, [she said]:
"When, O Mārisa, one peg meets another peg in your heart, then you would know it."
This contradicts the statement: “I have been boiling in hell for a thousand years. For a being in hell is never without suffering.

Although he is not without suffering, he is nevertheless spoken of in this way by means of a conventional term (*ruḷhīsadda*). Indeed, this was formerly a designation for those of the first eon who were free from suffering and endowed with happiness;
later on, whether there was suffering or not, it was used as a conventional term.
This is a conventional expression; even a lotus pond that has no lotuses or water is still called a "lotus pond.

Regarding the phrase "one who has crossed the flood," there are four floods here: the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*), the flood of existence (*bhavogha*), the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*).

Among these, the desire and lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is called the flood of sensual desire. Desire and lust for the realms of form and formlessness, as well as attachment to meditative absorption (*jhānanikanti*), is the flood of existence.
The sixty-two views are called the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*). Ignorance regarding the four truths is called the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*).

Among these, the flood of sensuality (*kāmogha*) arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed; the flood of existence (*bhavogha*) arises in the four types of consciousness accompanied by greed but dissociated from the [wrong] views;
the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*) arises in the four types of consciousness associated with the [wrong] views.
The flood of ignorance arises among all unwholesome states.

This entire flood should be understood as such in the sense of "carrying away" (*avahana*) and in the sense of a "heap" (*rāsa*). "In the sense of carrying away" means in the sense of going downwards.
For this [flood] carries beings who have come under its power downward; it causes them to be reborn only in the miserable destinations, distinguished by the hells and so forth.

Alternatively, the meaning is that it does not allow one to go to the higher state or to Nibbāna, but instead causes one to go downward through the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings. "In the sense of a mass" means in the sense of something great;
for this mass of defilements is indeed great, spread out from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence, namely, throughout the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Chandarāga" means desire and lust. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Thus, this should be understood as a "flood" (ogha) in the sense of a mass. "Atarī" means:
"By what cause, O Blessed One, have you crossed over these four kinds of floods?
Thus he asks. Then the Blessed One, answering his question, said: "Appatiṭṭhaṃ khvāhaṃ... and so forth. Therein, "appatiṭṭhaṃ" means...
"Not standing. "Not exerting" means not making an effort. Thus the Blessed One spoke the question by making it cryptic and concealed.

Having heard this, the deity thought: "Those crossing an external flood indeed stand in the place where one should stand and exert themselves in the place where one must exert oneself to cross; but this [flood] spread from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence—"
"He crossed over the flood of defilements, the mass of defilements, without finding a foothold and without exerting effort," so it was said. "What indeed is this?
How indeed is this? Having fallen into such doubt, they did not understand the meaning of the question.
But why did the Blessed One fulfill the perfections and attain omniscience for the sake of speaking in a way that beings would not understand?
"Is it penetrated? It was not penetrated for that purpose. However, there are two modes of the Blessed One’s teaching:

by way of censure and by way of favor. Among these, for those who are conceited in their wisdom—perceiving what is unknown as known, like the five hundred brahmin renunciants—it was taught in a manner such as the *Mūlapariyāya* and other discourses, so that their pride might be censured and they would not know [the truth].
He teaches the Dhamma. This is teaching by way of refutation. For it has been said:
“Pressing hard, Ānanda, pressing hard, I shall speak; threshing out, Ānanda, threshing out, I shall speak; that which is the essence will remain.
But for those who are upright and desirous of training, he teaches the Dhamma—such as the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta and others—making it easy for them to understand.
“Delight, Tissa! Delight, Tissa! [I am here] with my exhortation, my assistance, and my instruction,” he thus reassured him.
This is the teaching by way of assistance.
But this son of the gods was stiff with pride and conceited; for it occurred to him: “I know the flood.”
“I know that the Tathāgata has crossed over the flood, but I do not know by what specific cause he has crossed.
Thus, much is known to me and little remains unknown; I shall understand that merely by his speaking.
For what indeed could the Blessed One say whose meaning I would not understand? Then the Teacher [thought], “This one...”

“Just as dyed cloth that has become soiled is incapable of receiving the dye without first having its pride subdued, I shall explain this to him once he asks again with a humble mind,” he thought; thus, concealing the answer, he spoke the question.
He too became one whose pride was humbled, and that state of his being humbled was evident through his very act of asking further questions.
This must be understood. Now, the meaning of that question is as follows: "But how, dear sir, did you cross the flood which has no standing place and no effort?
Tell me according to how I understand it.
Then the Blessed One, explaining to him, spoke the words beginning with "When indeed I... (*yadāsvāham*). Therein, "when indeed I" (*yadā svāham*) means at whatever time I.
*Sukāra* is a mere particle. And just as it is here, so it is in all the phrases.

"I sink" (*saṃsīdāmi*) means that, having concealed [my efforts], I do not cross over but rather settle down right there. "I am swept away" (*nibbuyhāmi*) means that, being unable to stand firm, I drift along.
Thus, seeing the fault in both standing still and exerting effort, [the Blessed One] stated the question thus: "By neither standing nor exerting effort, one crosses the flood."
This has been penetrated even by the deities, yet it is not clear; seven dyads are shown for the purpose of making it clear.

For one who stands still through the influence of the defilements (kilesa) is said to "sink," while one who exerts effort through the influence of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) is said to "be swept away.
Alternatively, one who stands still through craving and views is said to "sink," while [one who exerts effort] through the remaining defilements and volitional formations [is said to be swept away].
By means of craving, one who exerts himself is said to "sink"; by means of craving, one who stands still is said to "drown.
By means of views, one who exerts himself is said to "sink"; by means of views, one who stands still is said to "drown.
For the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) is an adherence characterized by sluggishness, while the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*) is an adherence characterized by over-exertion.
Or, by way of being sluggish, one who remains stationary is said to "sink"; by way of restlessness, one who exerts effort is said to "float.
Likewise, by way of devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure, one who remains stationary is said to "sink";
by way of devotion to the pursuit of self-mortification, one who exerts effort is said to "float. By way of all unwholesome volitional formations, one who remains stationary is said to "sink."
By means of all mundane wholesome volitional formations, one who exerts himself is said to "float upwards. And this has been said:
"Just as, Cunda, whatever states are unwholesome, they all lead to the downward direction; whatever states are wholesome, they all lead to the upward direction."
Having heard this answer to the question, the deity—established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala)—was delighted and inspired with faith.
Manifesting her joy and confidence, she spoke the verse beginning with "At long last. Therein, "cirassaṃ" means after the passing of a long time.
It is said that this deity, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, [had waited] since his parinibbāna...
Since she had never before seen another Buddha after that time, she spoke thus upon seeing the Blessed One today.
But was this deity not previously acquainted with the Teacher? Whether she had seen him before or not, it is appropriate for her to speak in this way based on her present sight of him.
"Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) refers to one who has cast out evil—the Brahmin whose taints are exhausted.
"Parinibbuta" means extinguished by the extinction of the defilements (*kilesanibbāna*). "In the world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*).
"Visattikā" refers to craving (*taṇhā*); it is called *visattikā* because of its reasons such as being attached to and clinging to objective bases like form and so forth.

"One who does not stand upon that *visattikā*, one who does not exert toward it, one who has crossed over, gone beyond, and emerged"—the meaning is: "Ah, for a long time indeed do I behold this Brahmin whose taints are exhausted."
"The Teacher approved" means he mentally rejoiced in the words of that deity; he shared the same intention (*ekajjhāsaya*).

"He vanished" means that having abandoned his constructed body (*abhisaṅkhata-kāya*) and remaining in his own natural, acquired body (*pakati-upādiṇṇaka-kāya*), having obtained hope and found support, he worshipped the One of Ten Powers with perfumes and garlands, and then—his own...
"He went to Bhavanā itself.
The commentary on the Oghataraṇa Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Nimokkha Sutta.
2. Now, beginning from the second sutta, we shall set aside what has already been encountered and what is obvious, and explain only that which is not yet clear.
"Jānāsi no? means "Do you know? Terms such as "liberation" (*nimokkha*) and so forth are names for the Path (*magga*) and other factors.
For it is by means of the Path that beings are liberated from the bonds of the defilements; therefore, the Path is called the "liberation" of beings.
At the moment of fruition (*phalakkhaṇa*), however, they are liberated from the bonds of the defilements (*kilesa*); therefore, it is said that "fruition is the liberation of beings.
Having attained *nibbāna*, the suffering of beings is entirely removed; therefore, *nibbāna* is called "seclusion" (*viveka*).
Or rather, all these are simply names for *nibbāna* itself. For having attained *nibbāna*, beings are released and completely liberated from all suffering.
They are secluded; therefore, that very state is called "liberation," "emancipation," and "seclusion. "Jānāmi khvāham" means "I indeed know.
The word *kho* has the sense of emphasis: "I certainly know. He thus utters a lion's roar, declaring:
"It was precisely for the sake of knowing the liberation and so forth of sentient beings that I fulfilled the thirty perfections and realized omniscient knowledge."
It is said that this discourse is named "The Buddha’s Lion’s Roar.
"With the destruction of delight and becoming" means by the destruction of kamma-becoming rooted in delight; it is also appropriate to understand it as "of delight and of becoming.

For in that regard, according to the former method, the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is included under "delight and becoming" by way of the threefold formative activity of kamma.
It is grasped by perception and consciousness, as well as the two aggregates associated with them.

However, since feeling associated with those three aggregates is already included by the grasping of them, Nibbāna with residue remaining is described here by way of the non-arising of the four unclung-to (anupādiṇṇaka) immaterial aggregates.
"With the cessation of feelings comes peace" refers to the cessation of clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) feelings.
And by cessation and by peace. In that context, by the mention of "feeling" (*vedanā*), the three aggregates associated with it are already included;
and by way of their basis and object, the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is also included.
Thus, Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa*) is described as the non-occurrence of these five appropriated aggregates. However, in the second method, by the mention of "delight" (*nandi*)...

The aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is included; by the mention of "existence" (*bhava*), the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*)—which is comprised of rebirth-existence—is included;
and the three aggregates beginning with perception (*saññā*) are included in their own form.
Thus, it should be understood that Nibbāna is described here as the non-occurrence of these five aggregates. And this very method is favored by the Elder Bhaṇḍika of the Four Nikāyas. Thus...
The Blessed One brought his teaching to its conclusion precisely by way of Nibbāna.
The commentary on the *Nimokkha-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Upanīya-sutta*.
3. In the third [verse], *upanīyati* means it is exhausted, ceases, or approaches; the meaning is that it gradually approaches death.
Or, just as a herd of cattle is led by a cowherd, so too is life led by old age into the presence of death—this is the meaning.
*Jīvitaṃ* refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). *Appaṃ* means limited, small, or trifling. Its limitation is twofold: [in duration and in quality].
It should be understood through both the brevity of its essence and the brevity of its moment. For it is brief by way of the brevity of its essence, because of the statement:
"Bhikkhus, whoever lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more. It is also brief by way of the brevity of its moment;
for in the ultimate sense, the life-moment of beings is extremely brief, being merely the duration of a single occurrence of consciousness. Just as...

Just as a chariot wheel, even while rolling, rolls upon only one portion of its rim, and even while standing still, stands upon only one portion, even so is the life of beings momentary, lasting for only a single thought-moment;
as soon as that thought has ceased, the being is said to have ceased. As it is said: "In the past thought-moment he lived, he does not live now, nor will he live."
In a future moment of consciousness, one will live, but has not lived, nor did one live; in the present moment of consciousness, one lives, but has not lived, nor will one live.
“Life and the personal existence, and all pleasure and pain—”
When joined with a single state of mind, the moment passes swiftly.
All those aggregates (khandhas) that have ceased for one who is dying or living here are alike; they have gone without reconnection (appaṭisandhika).
“Not born by what is unborn, he lives by what is present;
with the breaking of the mind, the world is dead—this is the supreme designation.
“Of one led away by old age” means one who has arrived at old age, or one who has been brought near to death by old age. There are no refuges.
There are none whatsoever capable of being a protection, a shelter, or a refuge. "This fear" means this threefold fear:

the fear of the life-faculty's transition into death, the fear of the brevity of the lifespan, and the fear of the lack of protection for one led by old age; the meaning is that these are the objects of fear and the causes of fear.
"A wise person should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness" means that a discerning person [should perform] those things which bring happiness and bestow happiness.

"One should perform meritorious deeds. Thus, referring to the fine-material-sphere jhāna, the deity spoke of "meritorious deeds" (*puññāni*) using the plural form to include the prior volition, the subsequent volition, and the volition of release.
Referring to the gratification of the jhāna, the attachment to the jhāna, and the bliss of the jhāna, she said, "they bring happiness. It is said that for this deity, in her own long-lived abode...
Because he was reborn in the Brahma-world, whenever he passed away from or was being reborn among the lower devas of the sense-sphere who were in short-lived positions,
he saw beings resembling heavy downpours of rain and thought: "Oh, how these beings, having developed jhāna and died without losing their jhāna,
pass away to be reborn in the Brahma-world for the duration of one kappa, two kappas, four kappas, eight kappas, sixteen kappas, thirty-two kappas, or sixty-four kappas!"
"May they endure for a long time. Therefore he spoke thus.

Then the Blessed One, perceiving that "this deity is speaking a discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) which does not lead to liberation," spoke the second verse to show her the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).
Therein, "worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) refers to two kinds of worldly bait: the figurative and the literal.
In a figurative sense, the "worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) refers to the cycle of existence in the three realms; in a non-figurative sense, it refers to the four conditions.

Here, the figurative worldly bait is intended. However, the non-figurative worldly bait is also applicable. "One who looks toward peace" means one who looks toward, desires, and aspires for the ultimate peace known as *nibbāna*.
The commentary on the Upanīyasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Accentisutta.
In the fourth [sutta], "accenti" means they pass over. "Times" refers to times such as before the meal and so forth. "They cross through the nights."
As the nights pass away, they hasten a person toward death, causing them to go ever more swiftly.
"The qualities of age" (*vayoguṇā*) refers to the qualities of the first, middle, and final stages of life; the meaning is "accumulations.

For in the passage, "I allow you, monks, a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) made of unwashed cloth," the word *guṇa* has the sense of a "layer" (*paṭala*). [In contrast,] "A gift possesses a hundredfold merit... [here it means "fold"].
In the phrase "to be expected," it has the sense of benefit (*ānisamsa*). In the phrase "the end and the intestinal coil," it has the sense of a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*).

In the phrase "one might make many garlands of strings," it has the sense of a heap (*rāsa*). In the phrase "the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañca kāmaguṇā*), it has the sense of a bond (*bandhana*).

Here, however, it has the sense of a heap and the sense of a string (*guṇa*). Therefore, "strings of age" (*vayoguṇā*) should be understood as heaps of age. "They abandon in succession" means in regular order.
They abandon the person. For one established in middle age, early age abandons him; for one established in late age, both the first and middle ages abandon him;
but at the moment of death, all three stages of life abandon him indeed. "This is fear" means this threefold thing:
the passing away of the times, the state of having transcended nights and days, and the state of abandoning the qualities of the life-stages.
Fear. The remainder is exactly as before.
The commentary on the Accent-sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Kati-chinda-sutta*.
5. In the fifth [verse], how many does he cut? While cutting, how many would he cut? The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

And here, "cuts" (*chinde*) and "abandons" (*jahe*) are one in meaning; however, for the sake of the smoothness of the verse composition, this deity spoke thus, avoiding the repetition of the same word.
"How many has he transcended the fetters? (*kati saṅgātigo*) means how many fetters has he gone beyond, has he transcended?
This is the meaning. *Saṅgātikoti* is also a reading, and it has this very same meaning. "He cuts five" means that while cutting, he would cut the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
"He abandons five" means that while abandoning, he would abandon the five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*). Here too, cutting and abandoning are identical in meaning;
however, the Blessed One spoke thus in accordance with the words attributed to the deity.
Alternatively, it is said that the five lower fetters (pañcorambhāgiya-saṃyojana) have the characteristic of pulling downward, like a bird bound by a snare at its feet;

these should be severed by the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga). The five higher fetters (pañcuddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) have the characteristic of pulling upward, like tree branches grasped by the hands;
these should be abandoned by the path of arhatship (arahattamagga). [The five] beyond...

"Bhāveya" means: one who cultivates a further, superior distinction for the purpose of cutting off and abandoning these fetters (*saṃyojana*) should cultivate the five faculties, with faith as the fifth; this is the meaning. "One who has gone beyond the five attachments" (*pañca saṅgātiga*) means one who has transcended these five attachments:
attachment to lust, attachment to hatred, attachment to delusion, attachment to conceit, and attachment to views. "One who has crossed the flood" (*oghatiṇṇa*)...
"Is called" means it is spoken of as "one who has crossed the four floods. Furthermore, by this verse, the five faculties—both mundane and supramundane—are explained.
The commentary on the *Katichinda Sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Jāgara Sutta*.

6. In the sixth [verse], "of those who are awake" (*jāgarataṃ*) means of those who are awake. However, in the response verse, "the five who are awake" refers to the five faculties (*indriya*), beginning with faith (*saddhā*).
When these five are awake, the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are called "sleep. Why?
Because a person endowed with them—whether sitting or standing anywhere—even while the dawn is breaking, due to negligence and being possessed of unwholesome states...
It is called "asleep. Thus, when the five hindrances are asleep, the five faculties are called "awake.
Why? Because a person possessing them, even while lying down and sleeping anywhere, is called "awake" due to their heedfulness and possession of the wholesome.
However, it is by means of the five hindrances alone that one takes up, grasps, and clings to the dust of the defilements.

For since the preceding factors, such as sensual desire and so forth, serve as conditions for those that follow, it should be understood that this meaning is expressed by the phrase "it is purified by means of the five faculties. Here too, the five faculties mentioned are both mundane and supramundane.
The commentary on the *Jāgara Sutta* is concluded.

7. Explanation of the Discourse on Not Penetrating (Appaṭividitasuttavaṇṇanā) In the seventh [verse], "phenomena" (dhammā) refers to the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. "Not penetrated" (appaṭividitā) means not pierced through by knowledge. "In the doctrines of others" (paravādesu) refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views.
For these are called "the doctrines of others" because they are the doctrines of other sectarians (titthiya) besides ourselves. "Are led away" (nīyare) means...

They proceed either by their own nature or they are led by another. In this context, those who grasp at eternalism and so forth on their own are said to "proceed," while those who grasp at them through the words of another are said to be "led.
"The time has come for them to awaken" means that this is the time for those individuals to awaken; for in this world, a Buddha has appeared and the Dhamma is being taught.
"The Saṅgha has practiced well; the path is auspicious; yet these great masses of people, asleep within the cycle of existence, do not awaken," so said the deity.
"Sambuddhā" means those who have awakened through the correct cause and reason. For there are four types of Buddhas:

the Omniscient Buddha (sabbaññubuddho), the Private Buddha (paccekabuddho), the Buddha of the Four Truths (catusaccabuddho), and the Buddha by Learning (sutabuddho). Among these, having fulfilled the thirty perfections (pāramīs), [one attains] Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhiṃ)..."

One who has attained the state called an omniscient Buddha (sabbaññubuddha) is so named after fulfilling the perfections (pāramiyo) for two incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya) plus one hundred thousand aeons.

One who has attained self-enlightenment (sayambhuta) and is called a Paccekabuddha is so named [after fulfilling them] for two incalculable eons. The remaining ones who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) are called those enlightened in the Four Truths (catusaccabuddha). One who is learned is called a "Buddha through learning" (sutabuddha).
In this context, all three of the former types are applicable. "Sammadaññā" means "by way of the correct cause."

Having understood by means of the cause: they walk evenly upon the uneven—whether on the unevenness of the world’s habitation, or the unevenness of the classes of beings, or the unevenness of the arising of defilements; thus they walk evenly.
The commentary on the *Appaṭividita-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the Susammuṭṭhasutta. 8.

Regarding the eighth [verse], "well-forgotten" (*susammuṭṭha*) means "completely lost" (*sunaṭṭha*) precisely because it has not been penetrated by wisdom (*paññā*). For example, it is like two fields that have both been plowed;
after sowing in one, a great deal of grain is obtained. With reference to what was not obtained from the unsown field, [it is called "lost"].

When one says, "Much of my grain is lost," one speaks of what has not even been obtained as "lost. In the same way here, those things that have not been fully penetrated are said to be "completely forgotten" (*susammuṭṭha*).
They are "not forgotten" (*asammuṭṭha*) precisely because they have been penetrated by wisdom (*paññā*). The rest is exactly as before.
The commentary on the *Susammuṭṭha-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Mānakāma-sutta* Regarding the ninth [verse], "one who desires pride" (*mānakāma*) means one who desires or seeks pride.

"Tamed" (*dama*)—he says that for such a person, there is no taming belonging to the side of concentration (*samādhipakkhika*). As it is said: "Tamed by truth, endowed with self-mastery, having reached the end of wisdom, he has lived the holy life."

For here, restraint of the faculties is called "taming" (*dama*). In the passage, “If there is truth, taming, and generosity, is there anything found here superior to patience?,” it refers to wisdom (*paññā*).
In the passage, “Through giving, taming, self-restraint, and speaking the truth, there is merit;
there is an acquisition of merit,” it refers to the observance of the Uposatha. [And] in the passage, “Punna, being endowed with this taming and tranquility, you will indeed be able...”

In the phrase "to dwell in the Sunāparanta country," there is the patience of acceptance (*adhivāsanakhanti*). However, in this sutta, "taming" (*dama*) is a name for the factors belonging to the side of concentration (*samādhipakkhika-dhammā*).
For this very reason it was said: "There is no sagehood (*mona*) for one who is unconcentrated.
In that context, *mona* refers to the knowledge of the four paths; for it "makes one silent" (*munāti*), meaning it knows the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths.
"Of the realm of Death" means of the round of existence consisting of the three planes. For that is called the "realm of Death" in the sense of being the abode of Death.
"The further shore" is the further shore of that very realm, which is Nibbāna. "One should cross over" means one should penetrate or reach it.
This is what is meant: a person who dwells alone in the forest but is heedless would not cross over to the further shore of the realm of Death.
"He would not penetrate, he would not reach" means this.
"Having abandoned conceit" means having abandoned the ninefold conceit by means of the path of Arahatship.

"Well-composed in mind" means one whose self is well-composed by means of access concentration and absorption concentration. "Of beautiful mind" means one whose mind is excellent due to its association with knowledge (*ñāṇa*). [This is] not by a mind dissociated from knowledge.
For one is not called "one of pure mind" merely by that [term]; therefore, the meaning is:

having become one of pure mind through association with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*). "Completely liberated in every respect" means being liberated from all aggregates, bases, and so forth. Regarding "he would cross":
here, it is called "crossing by penetration" because he crosses by transcending the cycle of existence in the three realms and penetrating *nibbāna*. Thus...
By this verse, the three trainings are explained. How so? This thing called conceit is a destroyer of virtue;

therefore, by the phrase “having abandoned conceit,” the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is explained. By the phrase “well-composed in self” (*susamāhitatto*), the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*) is explained.

In the term “pure-minded” (*sucetaso*), wisdom is indicated by the word “mind”; therefore, by this, the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*) is explained. And [this includes] higher virtue...
When virtue exists, there is higher virtue; when the mind exists, there is higher mind; when wisdom exists, there is higher wisdom.
Therefore, it should be understood that "virtue" refers to the five or ten precepts, while the restraint of the Pātimokkha is called "higher virtue.
The eight attainments are the "mind," and the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight is "higher mind. The knowledge of the ownership of kamma is "wisdom," and insight is "higher wisdom."

For even when a Buddha has not appeared, the five precepts and the ten precepts continue to exist; thus, they are simply "virtue" (*sīla*). However, the virtue of restraint according to the *Pātimokkha* exists only when a Buddha has appeared;
thus, it is "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*). The same principle applies to the mind and wisdom as well.

Furthermore, even the five precepts or the ten precepts undertaken by one aspiring for Nibbāna are indeed "higher virtue. So too are the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) once they have been entered.
Higher mind alone [is higher training]. Or else, all mundane virtue is simply virtue (*sīla*), while the supramundane is higher virtue (*adhisīla*).
This same method applies to mind and wisdom as well. Thus, by bringing these together through this verse, the three trainings are said to constitute the entire teaching.
The commentary on the *Mānakāma-sutta* is finished.

10. Commentary on the Arañña Sutta In the tenth [verse], "of the peaceful" (*santānaṃ*) means of those whose defilements are stilled, or of the wise. For in such passages as, "The peaceful indeed proclaim [the truth] among the virtuous;
the peaceful shine even from afar," the wise are also called "peaceful. "Of those who live the holy life" (*brahmacārinaṃ*) means of those who walk in the highest conduct.
"Of those dwelling in the holy life of the path. "By what does the complexion become serene?"—he asks this question meaning, "For what reason does the color of the skin become clear?

But why does she ask thus? It is said that this earth-deity, a resident of the forest grove, [observed] the forest-dwelling bhikkhus after they had returned from their almsround following the meal, as they entered the forest to stay for the night-vigil or the day-vigil.
He sees them sitting having taken up their primary meditation subject (mūlakammaṭṭhāna). As they sit in this way, powerful one-pointedness of mind arises in them.
Thereupon, the dissimilar continuity subsides, the similar continuity sets in, and the mind becomes serene.
When the mind is serene, the blood becomes serene, and the derived material phenomena originating from the mind become purified.
The color of his face became like that of a palm fruit stripped of its stalk. Seeing this, a deity reflected:

"This complexion of the body belongs to those who obtain choice foods endowed with excellent flavors, garments and coverlets pleasant to the touch, beds, comfortable weather, palaces of various kinds such as those belonging to the three planes, and garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth."
"But these monks, having wandered for alms, eat mixed food; they prepare their beds on sparse couches, or on wooden planks, or on rocks;
or they dwell at the roots of trees and so forth, or in the open air.
For what reason, then, does their complexion become so serene? Thus he asked.
Then the Blessed One, explaining the reason for this, spoke the second verse. Therein, "In the past" means:
"In the past, there was a certain righteous king; he gave us excellent requisites, and thus our teachers and preceptors became recipients of gain.
Then we ate such foods and wore such robes"—thus some [thought].
Like those who are obsessed with abundance, these bhikkhus do not grieve for the past. They do not long for the future, thinking:
"In the future there will be a righteous king; the countryside will be prosperous; plenty of ghee, butter, and so forth will appear;
people will say here and there, 'Eat! Feast!'—at that time we shall [enjoy] such foods."
"We shall eat; we shall put on robes"—thus they do not long for the future.
"By the present" means they subsist by whatever is obtained at that very moment. "By that" means by those three kinds of causes.
Having thus shown the perfection of their complexion, he now spoke the following verse to show the destruction of that very complexion.
In this context, "longing for the future" means a yearning for what is yet to come. "By this" refers to these two reasons.
"Like a green reed cut down" means that just as a green reed, once cut, withers when thrown onto a hot stone, so too do they wither.
The commentary on the Arañña Sutta is finished. The first chapter, the Naḷavagga, is concluded.
2. Nandanavagga 1.
Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā 11.
In the first [sutta] of the Nandanavagga, "there" (tatra) means in that monastery. "Kho" is used for the sake of euphony in the phrasing.
*Nipātamattaṃ* means "merely a particle. *Bhikkhū āmantesīti* means he made known [the address] to the monks who were the leaders of the assembly.
*Bhikkhave* is an indication of the manner in which they were addressed. *Bhadante* is the response given by them.
*Te bhikkhū* refers to those monks who were present there as recipients of the Dhamma. *Bhagavato paccassosuṃ* means they listened back to the word of the Blessed One.
"Facing [them], they heard and accepted"—this is the meaning. "He said this" means he spoke these words that are now to be stated, beginning with "In the past...
In this context, "belonging to the Tāvatiṃsa host" means those reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
The Tāvatiṃsa realm is called the second heavenly world. Together with the young brahmin Magha, [he passed away] in the village of Macala.
It is said that this designation for that divine world arose from the thirty-three sons of the gods who were born there;
however, since the six sense-sphere heavens also exist in other world-systems, as it is stated:
"A thousand [world-systems] of the Four Great Kings, a thousand of the Tāvatiṃsa [gods]," therefore this is merely a conventional designation.
This should be understood as referring to that world of the gods. For in this way, the phrase becomes faultless.
Regarding "in the Nandana grove": it is called Nandana because it gladdens and satisfies those who have entered it again and again.
Indeed, when the five signs of death have appeared, even the deities, lamenting, "We shall fall away, abandoning our prosperity," [are comforted] by Sakka.
The Lord of the Devas, having exhorted them, saying, "Do not lament; for conditioned phenomena are by nature subject to dissolution," causes them to enter there.

Even for those who are led in by other deities by grasping their arms, as soon as they behold his splendor, the sorrow of death subsides and only joy and gladness arise. Then, while they are thus sporting, he becomes heated with passion.
It is called "Nandana" because whatever enters within it causes delight and satisfaction, just as a lump of snow melts away or a lamp-flame struck by the wind is extinguished; in that Nandana.
"Surrounded by a host of accharās": *accharā* is the name for celestial nymphs (*devadhītā*); she was surrounded by a multitude of them.

“Dibbehī” means reborn in the world of the devas. “With the five strands of sensual pleasure” means with the five fetters of sensual desire, or the five divisions of sensual desire, consisting of agreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.
“Endowed” means possessed. The other term is a synonym for that same word.
“Sporting” means enjoying themselves, or alternatively, moving their sense faculties among those various forms and so forth. “At that time.”
At that time of his attendance, it should be understood that this was the period when the son of the gods had just been reborn.
For at the very moment of his rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), a physical form (*attabhāva*) measuring three *gāvutas* appeared, shining like a mass of red gold.
He was clothed in celestial garments, adorned with celestial ornaments, and wore celestial garlands and ointments.
Being scattered with divine sandalwood powder, surrounded, enclosed, and enveloped by the fivefold divine strands of sensual pleasure,
and being overcome by greed, he— failing to see Nibbāna as the escape from greed— uttered a bold proclamation and,
singing this verse with a great voice in the Nandana Grove: "They do not know happiness."
He wandered about. Therefore it was said: "At that time, he spoke this verse.
Those who do not see Nandana are those who do not see the Nandana Grove there by way of experiencing the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
"Of men and gods" (*naradevānaṃ*) means of gods and men; the meaning is "of divine beings. "Of the Thirty-three" (*tidasānaṃ*) means of the thirty [gods] three times over.
"Yasassīnan" means those endowed with fame (yasa) in the sense of a retinue.
"A certain deity" refers to a certain noble female disciple (ariyasāvikā). "She replied" [with the underlying intention]:
