"This foolish deity imagines this prosperity to be permanent and immovable; she does not know its nature of being subject to cutting, breaking, and destruction."
Turning [the bowl] to show it, she spoke this verse to her husband: "You do not know, O fool. This means:
"You do not know it in the same way that the words of the Arahants are [understood].

Having thus rejected her intention, she now spoke the words beginning with "Impermanent" in order to show the words of the Arahants. Therein, "Impermanent indeed are conditioned things" (aniccā vata saṅkhārā) [means...].

All conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) of the three planes are impermanent in the sense of having ceased after having come to be. "Subject to arising and passing away" (*uppādavayadhammino*) means having the inherent nature of arising and passing away.
"Having arisen, they cease" is a synonym for the preceding [term]. Alternatively, because they arise and then cease, they are therefore "subject to arising and passing away.
Furthermore, by the mention of "arising and passing away," the intermediate stage immediately following them is also implied.
It is indeed grasped. "The stilling of these is bliss" means that for those formations, Nirvana—which is termed their stilling—is itself bliss.
This is the word of the Arahants.
The commentary on the Nandana Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Nandatisutta 12.
In the second [verse], "rejoices" means he is satisfied and becomes glad. "Mother of sons" means one who has many sons.
For some of his sons, having performed agricultural work, fill the granary with grain; others, having engaged in trade, [acquire] gold and bullion.
Some, by attending upon the king, obtain vehicles, mounts, villages, market towns, and so forth.
Then, experiencing the glory (*śrī*) consisting of their power, either the mother or the father rejoices.
Or, on festival days and the like, seeing his son adorned and well-attired while enjoying prosperity, he rejoices; thus it is said: "One who has sons rejoices because of his sons."

He said: "By means of cattle" means: just as one who has sons rejoices because of his sons, so too the owner of cattle, seeing a prosperous herd of cattle and experiencing the abundance of dairy products dependent upon those cattle, rejoices by means of cattle. Regarding the phrase "for acquisitions are a man’s delight," here "acquisitions" (*upadhi*) refers to the four acquisitions:

the acquisition of sensual pleasures (*kāmūpadhi*), the acquisition of the aggregates (*khandhūpadhi*), the acquisition of defilements (*kilesūpadhi*), and the acquisition of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārūpadhi*).

For sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) are called "clinging" (*upadhi*) in the sense of the verbal definition "that wherein pleasure is clung to," because they serve as the basis for the pleasure described thus: "Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification (*assāda*) of sensual pleasures.
Likewise, the aggregates (*khandhā*) are so called because they serve as the basis for the suffering rooted in the aggregates, and the defilements (*kilesā*)...

Because the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*) is the basis for [the clinging to] existence, and because even volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) are the basis for the suffering of existence;
however, here it is the "substratum of sensual desire" (*kāmūpadhi*) that is intended.

For the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*), when manifested through palaces of the three planes, magnificent beds, clothing, ornaments, theatrical performances, retinues, and so forth, bring joy to a person by inducing rapture and gladness. Therefore, just as sons...
And just as with cattle, it should be understood that these acquisitions (*upadhi*) are likewise the source of a person's delight.

"For he who is without acquisitions does not rejoice"—that is, one who is destitute, lacking the attainment of the strands of sensual pleasure, and having food and clothing difficult to obtain; such a person does not rejoice.
The Blessed One said: "How could one such as this—a human ghost (*manussapeta*) or a denizen of hell—rejoice?"
Having heard this, the Teacher thought: "This deity takes a cause for sorrow and makes it a cause for joy; I shall demonstrate the true nature of her sorrow.
Like one striking fruit with fruit, he shattered her argument by means of that very same simile, and having reversed that very verse, he said:
"He grieves because of his sons. In this context, "he grieves because of his sons" refers to [sorrow] arising from their departure to foreign lands and so forth.
He grieves even when things have been lost, are being lost, or will now be lost;
likewise, he grieves by being apprehensive of death when others have died, are dying, or have been seized by thieves or royal officers, or have fallen into the hands of enemies.
He also grieves when things have been broken—such as by falling from trees or mountains through the crushing of hands, feet, and so forth—or while they are being broken.
Even when one is merely suspected of a transgression, one grieves. And just as a father of sons [grieves], so too does an owner of cattle grieve in nine ways because of his cattle.
"For acquisitions are a man's sorrow"—just as with sons and cattle, so too are the five strands of sensual pleasure acquisitions.
"If for that person who desires, who has conceived a longing..."
“Those desires fall away, and one is tormented as if pierced by an arrow.”—In the manner thus stated, people grieve for a man.
Therefore, it should be understood that a man’s grieving has its very basis in the object of grief itself.
For he does not grieve who is “without acquisitions” (nirūpadhi); indeed, he for whom these four kinds of acquisitions do not exist is one without acquisitions.
"How could one who has great taints destroyed grieve? He does not grieve, O deity.
The commentary on the *Nandati-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Natthi-puttasama-sutta*.
13. Third: "There is no love equal to that for a son. For even toward their own deformed sons, they regard them as if they were golden images;
carrying them about on their heads and other parts of their bodies like flower-garlands, they experience joy even when soiled by them, covered in filth, or smeared with scents and ointments.
Therefore it was said: "There is no love equal to that for a son. There is no love equal to the love for a son.
It is said that there is no other [wealth] called "cattle-wealth. "Cattle-wealth" means wealth equal to cattle, wealth similar to cattle;
the Blessed One said that there is no other wealth like this. "Light equal to the sun" shows that there is no other light equal to the radiance of the sun.
"The ocean as the limit": whatever other lakes there may be, they all have the ocean as their limit.
"The ocean is supreme among them; there is no other reservoir of water equal to the ocean," said the Blessed One.

For indeed, there is no love equal to self-love. For even if they abandon their mother, father, and so forth, and even if they do not nourish their sons, daughters, and so forth, sentient beings nourish only themselves. And there is no wealth equal to grain. (When...)
For indeed, there are times when beings face famine;
at such a time, people go to the owners of grain to obtain gold, silver, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, solely for the purpose of acquiring food. Furthermore, there is no radiance equal to wisdom.
For the sun and other luminaries illuminate only a limited portion, and they dispel only the darkness of the present moment.
They dispel [darkness]. Wisdom, however, is capable of making even ten thousand world-systems a single illumination, and it disperses the darkness that conceals the past and so forth.
There is no flow of water equal to the rain from a cloud. Whether it be rivers, lakes, or reservoirs, there is no flow of water equal to the rain.
For when the rain from a cloud has ceased, the great ocean does not decrease even by as much as the tip of a finger or a mountain.
There is no water; however, when rain is falling, even as far as the Ābhassara realm, it becomes one vast expanse of water.
Therefore, the Blessed One, speaking the verse in response to the deity, said: "There is no love equal to that for oneself," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Natthiputtasamasutta* is concluded.
4. Commentary on the *Khattiya-sutta* 14.
In the fourth [verse], “The khattiya is the best of bipeds” means he is the king, the most excellent among those with two feet. “A maiden” (*komārī*) refers to one taken while she was still a girl;

this [khattiya] is said to be the most excellent among his other wives. “The first-born” (*pubbaja*) means one born first; even if he is blind, he is superior to those who are maimed in their hands and so forth.
Or whichever one was born first is indeed called the "best" in the speech of this deity.
However, because among bipeds and the rest, the Buddhas and others are the best, the Blessed One spoke the following verse.
In that regard, although the Blessed One is indeed the best of all beings, including those classified as "footless" and so forth, he is the best of all beings when he appears.
He arises only among bipeds; therefore, the Fully Enlightened One said, "The Buddha is the best of bipeds. And for one arisen among bipeds, his status as the best of all beings is indeed unimpeded.
Whether it be an elephant or any other among horses and so forth, he who understands the cause is truly a *ājānīya* (a well-bred thoroughbred);
this is the meaning of "the best of quadrupeds. [Regarding] King Kūṭakaṇṇa...
Like a horse the color of molasses. It is said that the king, having departed by the eastern gate with the intention of going to Cetiyapabbata, reached the bank of the Kalamba River.
The horse stood on the bank and did not wish to descend into the water.
The king addressed his trainer, saying, "Alas! Though you have trained this horse well, it does not wish to descend into the water. The trainer—
“Your Majesty, the horse has been well-trained; for its thought is this:
‘If I enter the water, my mane will get wet, and if my mane is wet, it might splash water upon the King’s limbs. Thus, out of fear of splashing water on your body, it does not enter.
Have them seize its mane. The king did so. The horse descended with speed and reached the other side.

*Gato*: gone. *Sussūsā*: desiring to hear. Whether she was taken [as a wife] during her maidenhood or later, whether she is beautiful or ugly, she who desires to hear her husband, serves him, and pleases him—that woman is the best among wives. *Assavo*:
one who listens. Whether he is the eldest or the youngest, he who listens to the words of his parents, accepts them, and acts upon their advice.
"O Devata, this is the best of sons; what need have you for other sons who are thieves such as those who break into houses?
The commentary on the *Khattiya-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Saṇamāna-sutta*."

15. “When the midday has arrived” means when the time for the midday meal has come. “While they are sitting quietly” means while they have settled down to rest, having reached a comfortable place. This time of the midday meal is a time when the physical postures of all beings become weak;
however, here it is shown specifically with reference to birds. “It seems to cry out” means it emits a great, piercing shriek as if crying out.
And here, it is said that "it rustles" (*saṇatevā*) even while it is being rubbed (*saṇamāna*).

This is a metaphorical expression. For at the time of midday during the summer season, when herds of quadrupeds and flocks of birds are settled together, hollow trees filled with wind and bamboo joints with perforations rub trunk against trunk and branch against branch.
And among the trees in the middle of the forest, a great noise arose; it was with reference to this that it was said.
"That fear appears to me"—meaning that at such a time, as I was wandering through the great forest, that fear became manifest to me.
It is said that this deity was of dull wisdom; at that moment, she spoke of her own comfort in sitting and her comfort in conversation, seeking a companion.

Not obtaining it, he spoke thus. For at such a time, when a bhikkhu has returned from his almsround and is seated in a secluded forest dwelling having taken up his meditation subject, no small measure of happiness arises; with reference to this it was said:
“For the bhikkhu who has entered an empty place, whose mind is peaceful;”
“Supernatural delight arises for one who clearly sees the Dhamma with right insight,” and:
“Whether in front or behind, if no other person is found,
there is exceeding ease for one living alone in the forest.”

Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the second verse. In that context, "that delight appears to me" means: "In such a time as this, the sitting alone—which is called 'sitting alone'—that delight presents itself to me. The rest is exactly the same.
The commentary on the *Saṇamāna-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Niddātandi-sutta*

16. Regarding the sixth [term], *niddā* (sleep): it refers to the *thīnamiddha* (sloth and torpor) that arises in the minds of both trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) during the preliminary and subsequent stages of a prompted unwholesome consciousness (*sasaṅkhārika-akusala-citta*), such as when one says, "Aggivessana, I recall falling asleep in the last month of summer.
*Tandī* (lassitude) refers to adventitious sloth arising during times of excessive hunger, excessive cold, and so forth.

And this has also been said: “In this context, what is lethargy (*tandī*)? That which is lethargy, being lethargic, the state of being lethargic, indolence, being indolent, the state of being indolent—this is called lethargy.
Yawning (*vijambhitā*) is the stretching of the body. Discontent (*arati*) is a state of weariness belonging to the side of the unwholesome.
Drowsiness after a meal (*bhattasammada*) is intoxication from food or exhaustion from food. Their detailed explanation, however, is as follows:
“In that regard, what is yawning? It is the stretching of the body, the yawning of the body,” and so forth;
this is exactly how it is presented in the Abhidhamma. “By this” means by this defilement such as drowsiness, being defiled and having its manifestation obstructed.
“Does not shine” means it does not gleam; the meaning is that it does not become manifest. “The noble path” refers to the supramundane path. “Here” means in this world.
"Of beings" means of living creatures. "By energy" means by the energy that arises together with the Path. "Having expelled it" means having removed this collection of defilements.
"The Noble Path" refers to both the mundane and supramundane paths. Thus, by means of the path itself, having expelled the secondary defilements, the purification of the path is described.
The commentary on the Niddātandi-sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Dukkarasutta. 17.
In the seventh [verse], "difficult to endure" means difficult to bear or difficult to patiently accept. "By the unskilled" means by the fool. "Asceticism" (sāmañña) means...

The duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). By this, the deity shows this: that which wise sons of good family make into true recluseship—by clenching their teeth and pressing their tongue against the palate, by restraining mind with mind, and by subsisting on a single meal at a single sitting, practicing the holy life (*brahmacariya*) to the end of life for ten years, twenty years, or even sixty years.
"The Blessed One said that a fool, being incompetent, is not able to do it. Regarding the phrase "for there are many obstructions therein":

this shows that within this Noble Path known as *sāmañña*, there are many obstructions; that is, for one practicing for the attainment of the Path, there are many dangers (*parissaya*) in the preliminary stage.
"If he does not restrain the mind": if he does not restrain the mind that has arisen through improper attention (*ayoniso*), how many days will his state of *sāmañña* last?
Should he practice? He should not practice even for a single day. For one who is under the sway of the mind is unable to perform the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
"At every step" means at every object (*ārammaṇa*); for here, "step" is intended to mean "object.
Indeed, in whatever object defilement arises, therein the fool is said to "sink. The term "step" also refers to the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
It is appropriate. For in walking and other such activities, wherever defilement arises, there one is said to "sink.
"Of intentions" means of intentions such as sensual desire and so forth.
"Like a tortoise" means like a turtle. "Limbs" refers to the limbs including the neck as the fifth. "He draws together" means drawing them together.
"Or having withdrawn them. "Thoughts in the mind" means thoughts arisen in the mind. By this much, he shows this:

just as a tortoise, withdrawing its five limbs—including its tail—into its own shell, gives no opening to a jackal and, having withdrawn them, becomes unassailable, even so the bhikkhu [withdraws] the thoughts arisen in his mind into the shell of his own object.
Having comprehended [the mind], he gives Māra no opportunity; having comprehended it, he reaches a state that is difficult for him to overcome.
"Independent" means being independent of the dependencies of craving and views. "Non-injuring" means not causing harm. "Parinibbūta" means parinibbūta through the nibbāna of the defilements.
"He would not reproach anyone" means any person whatsoever regarding any failure in conduct or the like.

One should not speak with the desire to humiliate another; rather, having established within oneself the five qualities beginning with, “I shall speak at the proper time, not at an improper time,” one should speak out of compassion, with a mind characterized by a nature of uplifting others.
The commentary on the *Dukkarasutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Hirīsutta* 18.
Regarding the eighth verse: "One who restrains by means of shame" (*hirīnisedho*) means one who restrains unwholesome states by means of shame (*hirī*).
"There exists someone in the world" means he asks whether such a person exists. "He who wards off blame" means he who drives away censure.

He awakens. "As a noble horse [awakens] to the whip" means: just as a noble thoroughbred horse, when avoiding the whip, awakens—as if stirred by the mere shadow of the goad—and does not allow the whip to fall upon itself;
even so, that bhikkhu who does not allow the ten grounds for abuse directed at him to fall upon himself awakens to and wards off censure.
He asks this because he wonders if there exists anyone such as this who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*). However, there is no one who is truly "freed" by means of false accusation.
"Tanuyā" means "slender"; the meaning is that those who have destroyed the taints—who walk having restrained unwholesome states through a sense of shame—are few in number.
"Always mindful" means endowed with the fullness of mindfulness at all times. "The end of suffering."
"Attains" means having reached Nibbāna, which is the limit and the end of the suffering of saṃsāra. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Hirī-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Kuṭikā-sutta*.
19. Regarding the ninth verse, "Is your hut well?": this deity, having made her mother a "hut" in the sense of being the place where she dwelt for ten months in the womb, [speaks thus].

Just as birds, though they spend the day seeking food, return to their nest at night, even so do beings, despite going here and there, come back to the presence of a woman; out of a sense of attachment, they return to their wife.
Having made [the Buddha] his family nest; having made his sons the continuation of the family lineage in the sense of a biological succession; having made craving his bond;
and having combined these questions by means of the structure of the verses, he questioned the Blessed One. The Blessed One, answering her, spoke the words beginning with "Taggha" (Truly).
In that context, *taggha* is a particle used as an emphatic expression. Regarding the word "natthi" (there is not), it is because she has gone forth after having abandoned [worldly attachments].
Furthermore, because there is no longer dwelling in a mother’s womb within the cycle of existence, nor the bearing of a wife, nor the procreation of children, [he is free].
The deity thought: "I bound on my armor and asked these hidden questions, yet this ascetic has answered them as soon as they were asked.
Does he speak knowing my underlying intention, or does he speak whatever comes to his mouth without knowing it?"
Having thought, "She has spoken," he asked again, "What do you say to me? and so forth. Therein, "What do you say to me? means "What do you have to say to me?

Then the Blessed One, explaining to her, spoke the verse beginning with "A mother. Having expressed appreciation with the verse "Well done for you," and having comforted her, she paid homage to the Blessed One, worshipped him with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and departed for her own celestial abode.
The commentary on the Kuṭikāsutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Samiddhisutta: 20.
"In the Tapodārāma" means in the monastery that had received its name from the *tapoda*, a pool of boiling water.

It is said that beneath Vebhārapabbata there is a nāga-abode for the earth-dwelling nāgas, five hundred yojanas in extent, resembling the world of the devas, with a floor made of jewels and provided with parks and gardens. There, in the place where the nāgas sport, is a great lake;
from it flows a river called Tapodā, which is hot and carries boiling water. But why is it such as this?
It is said that the great world of the petas stands surrounding Rājagaha;
there, between two great hell-pots of molten iron, this Tapodā flows, and for that reason it flows hot. And this has been said:
"Monks, wherever this Tapodā flows, that lake is clear, cool, sweet, and white."
"It is well-established, delightful, and abundant with fish and tortoises; lotuses as large as cartwheels are in bloom.
Moreover, monks, this Tapodā River flows from the space between two great hells; it is because of that heat that this Tapodā flows warm.
Furthermore, at the spot facing this monastery, a great lake arose, and by virtue of that, this monastery is called "Tapodārāma" (the Hot Springs Monastery).
"Samiddhi": it is said that this elder’s physical form was perfected (*samiddha*), handsome, and pleasing;
therefore, he became known by the name "Samiddhi. "He bathed his limbs": this elder was one devoted to striving (*padhānika*);
rising from his seat at the break of dawn, he would warm his body and walk back and forth on a large walking path (*caṅkama*) sixty cubits long outside, until his sweat was absorbed.
Thinking, “If I enjoy myself with my limbs, the lodging will become defiled,” he approached for the purpose of bathing his limbs and washing his body.
He stood there wearing only a single robe; that is, having put on his lower garment, fastened his waistband, and held his upper robe in his hand, he stood there.
"Making his limbs like boiled rice" means making his limbs as clean as boiled rice or water.
For a robe worn on a wet body becomes soiled and foul-smelling, and this is not the proper conduct (*vatta*). But the Elder was perfect in his conduct;
therefore, remaining steadfast in his conduct, he bathed, stepped out, and stood there. In this regard, the following is the rule for bathing at a water-crossing:
Having gone anywhere and deposited the robes there, one should not descend with haste while still standing;
rather, after surveying all directions, knowing the place to be secluded, identifying stumps, thickets, creepers, and so forth, and having cleared the throat three times,
one should stand facing downwards, remove the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), spread it out, and unfasten the waistband.

It should be placed on top of the robe-closet. If there is no bathing-robe, one should sit in the squatting posture at the water's edge, remove the lower garment, and if there is a place where it will not get wet, spread it out;
if not, it should be folded up and set aside. When entering the water, one should descend slowly to the depth of the navel, without causing waves.
Without making a sound, one should turn back and submerge oneself facing the direction from which one came; in this way, the robe is protected.
When emerging, one should also emerge slowly without making a sound.
At the conclusion of the bath, one should sit in the squatting posture at the water's edge, put on the lower garment, stand up, and having dressed in a perfectly rounded manner, fasten the waistband.
"One must stand having tied up one's robe and without having put it on.
The elder, having bathed in that manner and stepped out, stood watching his body as the water drained away.
He was naturally handsome, and at that time of dawn, his food had been properly digested, and he had bathed in warm water.
His facial complexion shone exceedingly; like a palm fruit released from its bond, he was endowed with radiance.
His face became beautiful like the full moon or like a lotus blossoming at that very moment, and the color of his body also became serene.
At that time, the earth-deities dwelling in the forest grove gazed upon the pleasing bhikkhu and [honored] the ascetic.
Unable to restrain herself, overcome by the fever of passion, and thinking, "I shall seduce the Elder," she adorned her body with magnificent ornaments.
Like a thousand-wick lamp blazing forth, or like the rising moon, she illuminated the entire monastery with a single radiance;
then, approaching the Elder, she stood in the air without bowing and recited this verse:
He spoke. Therefore it was said: “Then a certain deity... addressed him.
“Without eating” means without enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇa*). “You beg” means you wander for alms. “Let not time pass you by”:
here, “time” refers to the period of youth and vigor capable of indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure. By one who is worn out with old age...
Indeed, one who is afflicted by illness, dependent on a staff, trembling, and overcome by coughing and shortness of breath, is unable to enjoy sensual pleasures.
It was with reference to this time that the deity said, "Let not the time pass you by. In this context, "let it not pass" means "let it not elapse.
Regarding the phrase "I do not know the time," the word *vā* is merely a particle. "I do not know the time" is said with reference to the time of death. For regarding beings—
“Life, disease, time, the laying down of the body, and destiny—these five in the world of the living are signless and do not move.

In this context, life is first signless because there is no fixed determination such as, “It shall be exactly this much and no more. Even at the stage of the *kalala* (the embryo), [there is no such certainty].
Indeed, beings die at every stage: during the *abbuda*, *pesī*, *ghana*, half-month, one month, two months, three months, four months, five months...
and so on, up to ten months; they die at the very moment of emerging from the womb, and thereafter they continue to die within or beyond even a hundred years.
Furthermore, regarding disease, there is no fixed determination such as, "Beings die only from this specific disease and not from another."
It is signless (*animitta*). For beings die from eye-disease, or from any one of the diseases of the ear and so forth.
Time, too, is signless because there is no such fixed determination as, "One must die at this very time, and not at another. For beings die in the morning, or at any other time such as midday.
Even the laying down of the body is signless, as in: "For those dying right here..."
It is signless because there is no such fixed determination as "the body must fall [in this place] and not elsewhere.

For the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of those born inside a village may fall outside the village, and that of those born outside the village may fall inside it. Likewise, one should expand upon this in many ways:

for those born on dry land, it may fall in the water, and for those born in the water, on dry land. As for the destination (*gati*), there is no such rule as "one who has passed away from here must be reborn right here."

Thus, because there is no fixed determination, it is signless (*animitta*). For those who have passed away from the world of the gods are reborn even among humans; and those who have passed away from the human world are reborn anywhere among the worlds of the gods and so forth.
In this way, the world revolves through the five destinations like a yoked ox on a waterwheel.
As it thus revolves, [one cannot know] "at this specific time death will occur."
"I do not know this time of death.
This time is hidden and does not appear" means that this time is concealed and unmanifested, and thus it is not perceived by me.
Therefore—because this time is hidden and not perceived—I wander for alms without even partaking of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "Let not time pass me by," the word "time" (*kālo*) is used here with reference to the time for performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).

For this so-called duty of a recluse cannot be performed in one's final period of life, when one has transgressed the three boundaries of age, is leaning on a staff, is trembling, and is overcome by coughing and labored breathing;
for at such a time, it is no longer possible to do whatever one desires.

Whether it be to memorize the word of the Buddha, to observe the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), to dwell in the forest, to attain meditative absorption (samāpatti) whenever one desires, or to perform recitations, expositions, Dharma discourses, and expressions of appreciation—all of these can be accomplished during the period of youthful vigor;
therefore, this is the time for practicing the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). Do not [let this time pass].
"He has surpassed me; as long as he does not pass me by, I shall practice the duty of a recluse without even enjoying sensual pleasures," he said.
"Having established himself upon the earth" means that, thinking, "This bhikkhu speaks of what is the right time for practicing the duty of a recluse and what is the wrong time;
he speaks with reason and with benefit," the deity, at this very point, [honored] the Elder.

Having established a sense of shame and regarding him as if he were Mahābrahmā or a mass of fire, she descended from the sky out of reverence and stood upon the earth; it is with reference to this that it was said.

Although she was standing on the earth, because of the purpose for which she had come, he again addressed her by that same title, saying, "O young woman," and so forth. In that context, *susū* means...
"Young" means one whose hair is very black. "By the auspicious" means by that which is fortunate.
For some, even though they are young, may be one-eyed or suffer from some other deformity such as a crooked limb; such a person is not said to be endowed with auspicious youth.
But he who is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and possessed of every excellence—whatever ornaments and refinements [he may apply]...
He moves about adorned here and there like a son of the gods; this is what is meant by being "endowed with noble youth.
And since the Elder was possessed of the most excellent beauty, he addressed him thus.

"One who has not played with sensual pleasures" means one who has not sported with sensual pleasures, one who has not enjoyed them, one who has not engaged in the play of desire—that is the meaning. "Do not [neglect] that which is visible in this life..."

"Having left behind" means that for the most part those deities—having not yet seen the Truths, being not free from lust, and unable to read the minds of others—see monks practicing the pure and unbroken holy life for ten years, twenty... [and so on]... up to sixty years, and think:
"These monks, having abandoned the five human strands of sensual pleasure, are aspiring after divine pleasures."
They give rise to the perception: "We are practicing the duty of a recluse. He too gave rise to that very same perception there.
Therefore, having treated human sensual pleasures as immediate (*sanditthika*) and divine sensual pleasures as temporal (*kālika*), he spoke thus:
"Indeed, friends, I do not—having abandoned immediate sensual pleasures, friends—I run after temporal sensual pleasures."

"I do not long for them, nor do I crave them. But as for 'timely,' friend," said the Elder, "I have abandoned time-bound sensual pleasures (*kāma*) and am pursuing the supramundane Dhamma, which is directly visible.

Thus, the Elder designated the five strands of sensual pleasure—both divine and human—as 'time-bound' because they cannot be obtained immediately after a thought; he designated the supramundane Dhamma as [untimely] because it can be obtained immediately after a thought."

"Visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*): Even for one who possesses all desires and is infatuated with the five strands of sensual pleasure, the experience of whatever object they desire does not occur immediately following the thought.

For instance, by one wishing to experience a desirable object through the eye-door, painters, book-illustrators, sculptors, and so forth must be summoned and told, "Prepare such-and-such [an object]."
In the interval between these two moments, many hundreds of thousands of millions of consciousnesses arise and cease. Only afterwards does it reach that object.
This same method applies to the other sense doors as well. However, immediately after the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), only the fruit of stream-entry arises;
there is no opportunity for any other consciousness in the interim. This same method applies to the remaining fruits as well.

Taking that very meaning, he said: "For it is timely, friends," and so forth. Therein, "timely" means that even by one who has attained success through the method described, it is to be attained at a later time.
It is "full of suffering" because of the abundance of suffering to be experienced in dependence upon the five strands of sensual pleasure.
It is "full of despair" because of the abundance of distress rooted in that very same basis. "The danger here is greater" means:
The meaning is that the danger is greater than the pleasure obtainable by relying on the five strands of sensual pleasure; suffering alone is more abundant.

"This Dhamma is visible here and now" (*sanditthiko*) means that this supramundane Dhamma, by whichever person it has been realized, is to be seen by oneself through the knowledge of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), having abandoned the need to rely on the faith of others; thus it is "visible here and now."
"Non-timely" (*akāla*) means there is no [fixed] time for it with respect to its giving of fruit; thus, being non-timely, it is "timeless" (*akālika*).
The meaning is that the noble path-dhamma herein gives its fruit immediately after its own occurrence.

It is "inviting one to come and see" (*ehi-passika*) because it deserves the method of "come and see" (*ehi-passa imaṃ dhammaṃ*), such that one would even disregard a burning cloth or head [to investigate it].
It is called *opanayika* because it leads one’s own mind toward [the goal] by way of cultivation.

It is said to be "to be personally realized by the wise" because it is to be experienced individually by each wise person—whether they be those who understand through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*) or others—thinking: "The path has been cultivated by me; the fruit has been attained; cessation has been realized. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is in the *Visuddhimagga*.
This was stated in the commentary on the *Dhammānussati* (Recollection of the Dhamma).
Now, that deity—like a blind man unable to perceive the excellence of forms—did not understand the meaning of what the Elder had said, and so she spoke the words beginning with "And how, O Bhikkhu...
In this context, regarding the phrase "And how," [the Elder replied]: "And how, O Bhikkhu, were the time-bound sensual pleasures (*kālikā kāmā*) spoken of by the Blessed One?"
“How are they full of suffering? How are they full of despair?”—thus the connection with all the terms should be understood.
A “new” [monk] (*navo*) is one who has not yet completed five years of seniority;

from five years onward he is “middle-aged,” and from ten years onward he is an “elder” (*thero*). According to another method: one who has not yet completed ten years is “new”; from ten years onward...
The one of middle standing is a senior from twenty years onward; he says, "I am new among them.

Even some who are new, having gone forth at seven or eight years of age, have passed twelve or thirteen years in the state of a novice and are thus long-ordained, yet they say, "But I am newly ordained. "This Dhamma and Discipline..."
"This Dhamma and this Vinaya"—both of these are names for the Teaching (sāsana) itself. Here, by "Dhamma" the two Piṭakas are meant, and by "Vinaya" the Vinaya Piṭaka;
thus he says, "I have now come to the practice revealed by means of these three Piṭakas.
"Of great influence" means having large retinues; for each king of the gods has a retinue of a hundred or even a thousand crores.
Having established themselves in a great place, they behold the Tathāgata.
By this he shows: "How could there be room for those like us—women of little influence?
When she says, "We too would come," that deity means: "Even if the assembly were seated filling the entire world-system..."
Knowing that he could go into the presence of the Teacher by way of the great path of the Buddhas, he spoke thus. "Ask, monk!
Ask, monk!"—this repetition was made for the sake of providing stability. Regarding the phrase "perceiving what is expressible":
here [it refers to] "a god, a human, a householder, one gone forth, a being, a person, Tissa..."
By way of the method beginning with "Phussa," the five aggregates are called "the expressible" (*akkheyya*) because they are the basis for all expressions and all discourses.
Those who possess such notions as "being," "man," "person," "individual," "woman," or "male" are "possessors of notions" (*saññino*);

those who possess notions regarding the expressible objects themselves are "those possessing notions of the expressible" (*akkheyyasaññino*), [referring to] those [who hold such views] regarding the five aggregates.
The meaning is: "perceiving [them] as seven persons, etc. "Established in the expressible" means established in the five aggregates in eight ways:
for one who is lustful is established by way of lust; one who is corrupt by way of hatred; one who is deluded by way of delusion;

one who is misapprehending by way of views; one who is entrenched by way of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*); one who is bound up by way of conceit (*māna*); and one who has gone to what is undesirable...
Through the influence of doubt, one becomes distracted; through the influence of restlessness, one becomes unsettled.
"Without fully understanding the expressible" means without having comprehended the five aggregates by means of the three types of full understanding (*pariññā*).

"The bond of death" means they come within the reach, the application, the casting down, the throwing down, the assault, and the interior grasp of death; the meaning is that they fall under the power of death.
Thus, by this verse, sensual pleasures are described as being "timely" (kālika).

"Having fully understood" (*pariññāya*) means having fully understood by means of these three kinds of full understanding: full understanding as knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and full understanding as abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*).
In that regard, what is full understanding as knowledge? One fully understands the five aggregates: "This is the aggregate of form; this is the aggregate of feeling... [and so forth].
“This is the aggregate of perception; this is the aggregate of mental formations; this is the aggregate of consciousness;

these are their respective characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes”—this is full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*). What is full understanding through scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*)? Having thus known them, one scrutinizes the five aggregates in forty-two aspects as impermanent, suffering, a disease, and so forth. This is full understanding through scrutiny. What is full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*)?
Having thus investigated, one abandons desire and lust for the five aggregates by means of the supreme path. This is the full understanding through abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*).

"He does not conceive of a speaker": having fully understood the five aggregates through these three types of full understanding, a monk whose taints are destroyed does not conceive of a person as a "speaker.
Here, "speaker" should be understood as the cause by way of karma—that which is to be spoken.
He does not conceive of, nor does he perceive, a person who should be spoken of—this is the meaning. How should he be described?
He should be designated by whatever name or clan, such as "Tissa" or "Phussa. For that [designation] does not belong to him;
it does not belong to that one whose taints are destroyed. By which he might be blamed, such as "he is stained by lust," [that too does not apply].
Or if someone were to say, "He is corrupted by hatred" or "He is deluded by ignorance," there is no such cause for that one whose taints are exhausted.
"If you know him, speak"—if you recognize such an one whose taints are exhausted, say "I know him.
If you do not know him, then say "I do not know him. He addressed the deity as "yakkha. Thus, by means of this verse—
The ninefold supramundane Dhamma, which is directly visible, has been explained. *Sādhu* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation.
"Whoever conceives" means whoever conceives of himself as "equal," or "superior," or "inferior.
By this, the three types of conceit beginning with "I am better" are indeed included. When these are included, all nine types of conceit are included.
"Thus one would quarrel with him": by means of that very conceit, that person would quarrel with any other person, saying, "How do you measure up to me?
Do you measure up by birth, or by clan, by family lineage, by physical beauty, by great learning, or by the ascetic virtues (dhutaguṇa)?
Thus, by this half-stanza as well, sensual pleasures pertaining to the present life (kālika-kāmā) are described.
“In three ways” means in three types of conceit (*māna*). For in such passages as “the grouping of form is of one way,” the term “way” (*vidhā*) refers to a category or division (*koṭṭhāsa*).
In such passages as “In what way do they say one possesses virtue? In what way do they say one possesses wisdom?
it refers to a mode or manner (*ākāra*). [And] “Bhikkhus, there are these three ways. Which three? ‘I am superior’ is a way; ‘I am equal’ is a way... [and so forth].
In such passages as “the notion ‘I am inferior’ is a *vidhā*,” the term *vidhā* refers to conceit (*māna*). Here, too, it is conceit. Therefore it is said:
“in the three *vidhās* means in the three types of conceit.
“Unshakable” means that person does not waver or move regarding these, which are three in brief and nine in detail. “Neither equal nor superior” applies to him.
This shows that for one who has abandoned conceit and whose taints are destroyed, there is no thought of being "equal," "superior," or "inferior.
The final phrase is exactly as previously explained. Thus, by this half-verse as well, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma that is directly visible is described.
In the phrase “He abandoned reckoning (*saṅkhā*)”, wisdom is what is meant by “reckoning,” as in such passages as, “He partakes of food with wise reflection (*yoniso paṭisaṅkhā*)”.
In the passage, “Do you have any accountant, calculator, or reckoner (*saṅkhāyaka*) who is able to count the sands of the Ganges?”, it refers to calculation.

In passages such as, “For conceptual proliferation and reckoning (*papañca-saṅkhā*) have perception as their source”, it refers to a constituent part. [And] in the phrase, “Whatever [is the reckoning] of those various phenomena...”
In the phrase "a designation (saṅkhā) is a conventional term (samaññā)," it is the conceptual description (paṇṇatti) that is referred to as "designation. Here too, this very same sense is intended.

For the meaning of the expression "he abandoned designations" is precisely this: the one whose taints are destroyed has abandoned, relinquished, and cast off this conceptual description—namely, [the labels] "lustful," "hateful," and "deluded."
“Na vimānamajjhagā” means he did not enter into the ninefold threefold conceit (*māna*). Alternatively, in the sense of a dwelling place, the mother’s womb is called a “palace” (*vimāna*);
the meaning is that he did not enter it again in the future by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). This is an expression in the past tense used for a future sense.
“Acchecchi” means he cut. “Chinnaganthaṃ” means one who stands having cut the four ties (*gantha*).
"Free from distress" means free from suffering. "Free from longing" means free from craving. "Searching" means looking about.
"They did not find" means they did not attain, did not discover, and did not see; this is a past tense used in the sense of the present.

"Either here or beyond" means either in this world or in the other world. "In all abodes" refers to the three realms of existence (*bhava*), the four modes of birth (*yoni*), and the five... [aggregates].

The meaning is: "In all these abodes of beings—namely, the destinies, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings—they do not see such a one whose taints are exhausted, whether he is arising at the breaking up of the body or already arisen.
With this verse, he spoke specifically of the supramundane Dhamma that is visible here and now (*sanditthika*).
Having heard this verse, that deity also discerned its meaning; for that very reason, she said, "Therefore, venerable sir," and so forth.
Regarding the verse "One should not do evil," it is appropriate to explain it both by way of the ten courses of wholesome action and by way of the eightfold path.
First, by way of the ten courses of wholesome action, [the phrase] "by speech" refers to the fourfold...
"Virtuous conduct of speech" includes the threefold good conduct of speech. "By mind" includes the threefold good conduct of mind.
"Or by body anything in the whole world" includes the threefold good conduct of body. These, first of all, are the ten factors of the wholesome courses of action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).

By the phrase "having abandoned sensual pleasures," the pursuit of the pleasure of sense-desires (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*) is rejected. By the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending," [the pursuit of self-mortification is rejected].

Mindfulness and clear comprehension are included as the cause for the ten courses of wholesome action. By the statement, "One should not practice suffering that is unbeneficial," devotion to self-mortification is prohibited.

Thus the deity says: "O Blessed One, I understand that you have explained the factors of the ten courses of wholesome action together with the causes of mindfulness and clear comprehension, having avoided both extremes."
According to the method of the Eightfold Path, however, this is the sequence: it is said that at that place there was a great teaching of the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the deities, while remaining in their respective places, directed their knowledge according to the discourse;
having established themselves in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), they spoke thus, showing the Eightfold Path they had attained. In that context, "by speech" means:
Right speech (*sammāvācā*) is included; however, since the mind (*mano*) is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*), "mind" (*manasā*) refers to the consciousness associated with the Path.
By "or by body anything in the whole world," right action (*sammākammanta*) is included, while right livelihood (*ājīva*) is already included because it belongs to the side of speech and action.

By the term "mindful" (*satimā*), energy (*vāyāma*), mindfulness (*sati*), and concentration (*samādhi*) are included. By the phrase "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*), right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) and right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) are included.
"Having abandoned sensual pleasures, one should not pursue suffering"— by these two lines,
there is the avoidance of the two extremes. Having said, "I understand, Blessed One, that this Middle Way has been taught by you,
avoiding these two extremes," he worshipped the Tathāgata with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, circumambulated him, and departed.
The commentary on the Samiddhi-sutta is finished.
The second chapter, the Nandana-vagga.
3. The Satti-vagga.
1. Commentary on the *Sattisutta* 21.
In the first [sutta] of the *Satti-vagga*, the phrase "with a spear" (*sattiyā*) is merely a heading for the teaching; it means with a weapon such as a single-edged blade (*ekato-khāra*).

"Struck" (*omaṭṭha*) means hit. For there are four kinds of blows: struck (*omaṭṭha*), struck upwards (*ummaṭṭha*), rubbed (*maṭṭha*), and rubbed all over (*vimaṭṭha*). Among these, "upwards" (*upari*)...
A blow delivered while standing face-downward is called *omaṭṭha*; one delivered from below while facing upward is called *ummaṭṭha*;
one that passes through like a door-bolt is called *maṭṭha*; and all other remaining types are called *vimaṭṭha*.
In this context, however, the *omaṭṭha* is taken [as the example], for it is the most cruel, its arrow is difficult to extract, and it is hard to treat.
It becomes filled with pus and blood; the pus and blood remain without flowing out, completely covering the opening of the wound.
Those wishing to remove the pus and blood must tie him down to a bed with his head hanging downward;
he then encounters death or suffering equal to death. "Should wander forth" means he should live as a renunciant.
What does he say with this verse? Just as a man struck by a spear exerts effort, applies means, and strives for the purpose of extracting the shaft and treating the wound;
and just as one whose head is burning, with his head aflame, exerts effort, applies means, and strives for the purpose of extinguishing it—even so...
"A bhikkhu, having abandoned sensual lust, should dwell mindful and vigilant," he said.
Then the Blessed One thought: "This deity has brought a very firm simile, yet she has grasped only a limited meaning;
for even though she speaks again and again, she refers only to the suppression and abandonment of sensual lust."
One would speak [thus]. As long as sensual lust has not been eradicated by the path, it remains persistently attached.
Thus, taking that very simile and turning the teaching back to the perspective of the first path, he spoke the second verse while teaching.
Its meaning should be understood in accordance with the preceding [explanation]. First.
2. Commentary on the Phusati Sutta 22.
In the second [verse], "that which does not touch does not touch": the result does not touch that which the karma did not touch;
or rather, the karma itself does not touch that which the karma did not touch. For karma is not performed by one who has not acted. And it touches that which it has touched.
When karma touches [an object], its result (vipāka) touches it, or else the karma itself touches it. For karma is performed by one who performs it.
Therefore, it touches that which touches; it does not touch that which does not touch. And since it touches that which touches, this is the natural law (dhammatā) of karma and its result.
Therefore, regarding the one who says: "He who offends a man who is unoffending, who offends a pure person..."
“...of a person who is without blemish”—thus it is said. Such a person is one who harbors malice without having committed an offense;
that very person is touched by the deed as soon as the deed is performed, or else they are touched by its result.

For whether or not he is able to inflict injury upon another, he has effectively placed himself in the four states of misery. Therefore the Blessed One said: “It is that very fool who comes to grief...”
“Evil is like fine dust thrown against the wind. Second. 3.
Commentary on the Jaṭā Sutta. 23.
Regarding the third verse, “Internal tangle,” *jaṭā* is a designation for craving (*taṇhā*), which is like a net. For it [craving] [entangles one] in regard to forms and so forth.

It is called a "tangle" (*jaṭā*) because it arises repeatedly upon objects in a manner that alternates between lower and higher levels, thus having the sense of being entangled like the network of branches in a bamboo thicket or similar growths.

Furthermore, because it arises with respect to one’s own requisites and those of others, with respect to one’s own personal existence and that of others, and with respect to internal and external sense bases, it is called an "internal tangle" (*antojaṭā*) and an "external tangle" (*bahijaṭā*). By means of that...

"Thus entangled by the arising of the tangle": just as bamboos and other plants are entangled by bamboo-tangles and the like, so too this entire generation—comprising the various classes of beings—is entangled, ensnared, and interwoven by that tangle of craving (*taṇhājaṭā*); such is the meaning.
And because it is thus entangled, "I ask you that, O Gotama"—therefore I ask you that. "Gotama" refers to the Blessed One.

He addresses him by name: "Who would disentangle this tangle? He asks who, having disentangled this tangle that stands entangled within these three realms, would be able to disentangle it—who is capable of disentangling it.
Then the Blessed One, answering that matter for him, said: "Having established oneself in virtue," and so forth. Therein, "having established oneself in virtue" means:

"Standing firm in the virtue of the fourfold purification. And here, when the Blessed One, being asked about the "unraveling of the tangle," began by speaking of virtue, it should not be understood that "he is answering one question with another. For virtue is spoken of here for the purpose of showing the foundation for one who would unravel the tangle.

"A man" (*naro*) means a sentient being (*satto*). "Possessed of wisdom" (*sapañño*) means one who possesses wisdom through the rebirth-linking wisdom born of kamma and the roots [of goodness]. [He develops] the mind and wisdom...

They cultivate both concentration and insight; for one who is cultivating them, the eight attainments are spoken of here under the heading of "mind" (*citta*), while insight is designated by the name "wisdom" (*paññā*).
"Ardent" (*ātāpī*) means possessing energy (*vīriya*); for energy is called "ardor" (*ātāpa*) in the sense of burning up and tormenting the defilements, and one who possesses that is "ardent.
"Discerning" (*nipaka*): "discernment" (*nepakka*) is a term for wisdom; one who is endowed with that is [discerning].
Meaning: By this term, he shows *pārihāriyapaññā* (practical wisdom).
*Pārihāriyapaññā* is the wisdom that must be maintained and applied everywhere according to the method: “This is the time for recitation; this is the time for questioning,” and so forth.
In this exposition of the question, wisdom is presented three times. Therein, the first is *jātipaññā* (wisdom of birth), and the second is *vipassanāpaññā* (wisdom of insight).
The third is the wisdom of practical accomplishment (*pārihāriyapaññā*), which guides one in all duties.
"He shall disentangle this tangle"—this refers to a bhikkhu endowed with these qualities, such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest.
Just as a man, standing firmly on the ground, might lift a well-sharpened sword and disentangle a great thicket of bamboo;
In the same way, having established oneself in virtue, one should lift up the weapon of insight-wisdom— well-sharpened on the whetstone of concentration— and,
wielding it with the hand of functional wisdom gripped by the strength of energy, one should disentangle, sever, and utterly shatter all that tangle of craving fallen within one’s own continuum.
Having thus far explained the stage of the trainee (*sekhabhūmi*), he now speaks the verse beginning with "Of whom...

to show the Great One whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) standing with his tangle disentangled. Having thus shown the one whose taints are destroyed standing with his tangle disentangled, he again speaks the verse beginning with "Wherein name... to show the scope for disentangling the tangle.
Therein, "name" (*nāma*) refers to the four formless aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*). "Resistance" (*paṭigha*)...

Regarding the phrase "and perception of form": here, sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is included by way of the perception of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*), and fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) by way of the perception of form.
When these two are included, immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) is also effectively included by way of the summary of existence (*bhavasaṅkhēpa*).
"Here this tangle is cut" means that at this point—the place where the round of the three realms is exhausted—this tangle is cut upon reaching Nibbāna.
The meaning "it is broken, it ceases" is thus shown. Third. 4.
Commentary on the Discourse on Restraint of the Mind (Manonivāraṇa-sutta). 24.
In the fourth [verse], "from whatever"—whether from evil or from what is wholesome. It is said that this deity [thought]: "Whatever there may be, distinguished as wholesome and so forth..."
"Whether it be worldly or supramundane, the mind must indeed be restrained; it must not be generated"—such was their view.
"Sabbato" means "from all. Then the Blessed One, thinking, "This deity speaks a discourse that does not lead to liberation;
there is indeed such a thing as the mind that must be restrained and that which must be developed; I shall teach her by analyzing it," reflected thus.
He spoke the second verse. Regarding that, as for the statement "the mind has not attained restraint," if one asks:
"Which is that mind which should not be restrained from everything?"—it is the mind that has attained restraint.
That mind which has attained a state of being restrained [by thinking], "I shall give a gift, I shall guard my virtue," and so forth.
That which has arisen by way of the right method, this mind should not be restrained; rather, it should be fostered and increased.
And from whatever [source] evil arises—that is, from whatever unwholesome state arises—from that very source it should be restrained. This is the fourth [sutta].
5. Commentary on the Arahanta Sutta.
25. "One who has done what was to be done" (*katāvī*) means one who has completed his task by means of the four paths. "'I say'": this deity dwells in a forest grove;
having heard the conventional speech of the forest-dwelling bhikkhus—such as "I am eating," "I am sitting," "my bowl," "my robe"—she thought:
"I consider these bhikkhus to be 'those whose taints are destroyed' (*khīṇāsava*); yet for those whose taints are truly destroyed, such [speech]..."
He asks in this way for the purpose of knowing whether there is talk based on the apprehension of a self, or whether there is not.
"Sāmañña" means worldly terminology, worldly convention. "Skilled" (kusala) means skilled in the aggregates and so forth. "By way of mere conventional expression" (vohāramattena):

having set aside talk based on apprehension, if one were to speak "I" or "mine" without making a distinction in conventional usage [regarding the aggregates], [then it would be so]. "The aggregates..."

For if one were to say, "The bowl eats," "The aggregates sit down," "The bowl belongs to the aggregates," or "The robe belongs to the aggregates," there would be a confusion of conventional usage and no one would understand it.
Therefore, instead of speaking in that way, he speaks according to worldly convention.
Then the deities thought: "If he does not speak by way of [metaphysical] views, does he perhaps speak by way of conceit?"
He asked again, "Who is it that speaks? Therein, "Is it out of conceit? means: has that bhikkhu, having fallen into conceit, spoken thus out of a sense of pride?

Then the Blessed One, thinking, "This deity treats one who has destroyed the taints as if he were still possessed of them," spoke the counter-verse to show that "even the ninefold conceit has been abandoned by one whose taints are destroyed. In that context, "blown away" (vidhūpita) means...
"Dispelled. "Of the fetter of conceit" (*mānagandhassa*) means: he has [both] conceit (*māna*) and the fetters (*gantha*). "Conceiving" (*maññana*) is the act of conceiving.

He has transcended—that is, gone beyond—all three kinds of conceiving: craving, views, and conceit; this is the meaning. The remainder is of plain meaning. Thus ends the fifth [sutta]. 6. Commentary on the *Pajjota-sutta*.
26. "Chaṭṭhe puṭṭhun" means to ask. "Kathaṃ jānemu" means how we might know. "Divārattiṃ" means by day and by night.
"Tattha tattha" means wherever it is ablaze, right there. "Esā ābhā" means this radiance of the Buddha. But what is that?
It may be the light of knowledge, or the light of joy, or the light of confidence, or the light of the Dhamma-discourse.
Or rather, all the light that has arisen through the manifestation of the Buddhas is called "Buddha-light. This is unsurpassed, the most excellent, and peerless.
This is the sixth [section]. 7.
Commentary on the Sara Sutta.
27. Regarding the seventh [verse], "From where do the lakes turn back?": this means from where do these lakes of *saṃsāra* turn back; having come from what do they no longer flow?

"It does not find a footing" means it does not establish itself. "From there" means from there, from *nibbāna*. The rest is of plain meaning. This is the seventh. 8. Commentary on the *Mahaddhanasutta*.
28. They possess great wealth such as pearls, gems, and so forth, which has been stored away;

thus they are "of great wealth" (*mahaddhana*). They possess great enjoyments such as vessels of gold and silver; thus they are "of great enjoyments" (*mahābhoga*). "They covet one another" means they greedily long for and desire one another.

"Unsatisfied" means not having reached satiety or contentment. "In regard to various tasks that have arisen" refers to various duties that have come about. Regarding those things that have not yet arisen...

Regarding those who strive for the arising of form and so forth, and for the experiencing of what has arisen; "following the stream of existence" means following the stream of the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
"Unconcerned" means not being occupied with such things. "The household" refers to a home together with a wife. "Having stripped of its splendor" means having made it devoid of beauty.
The rest is self-evident. Thus ends the eighth [chapter].
9. Commentary on the Catucakkasutta 29.
In the ninth [verse], "four wheels" (*catucakka*) refers to the four postures (*iriyāpatha*). For here, "posture" (*iriyāpatha*) is intended by the term "wheel.

"Nine gates" (*navadvāra*) means having nine openings due to the nine wound-like apertures. "Full" (*puṇṇa*) means filled with impurity. "Bound by greed" (*lobhena saṃyuta*) means conjoined with craving (*taṇhā*).
"How will there be a journey?"—he asks this, meaning: "How will there be an exit for such a body?
How will there be liberation, complete release, and transcendence? *Naddhi* means resentment (*upanāha*);
the sense is that it is a powerful anger which occurs as anger in the first instance and as resentment in the subsequent instance. *Varatta* means "having cut... [the strap].
In the verse, "The leather thong and the tether, together with the halter," craving (taṇhā) becomes the leather thong and view (diṭṭhi) becomes the tether.
However, here, setting aside the defilements specifically indicated in the text, the remainder should be understood as the "leather thong";
thus, the meaning is "having cut the leather thong of defilement. Desire and greed (icchā-lōbha) are one and the same state in the sense of desiring.
Desire (*icchā*) is called greed (*lobha*) in the sense of being greedy. Alternatively, desire is the initial, weak arising [of craving], while greed is the subsequent, powerful arising.
Or, desire is the longing for what has not yet been obtained, whereas greed is the attachment toward an object already obtained.

"Craving with its root" means craving together with its root, which is ignorance (*avijjā*). "Having uprooted" means having torn it out by means of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). The rest is self-evident. Thus ends the ninth [chapter].
10. Commentary on the Eṇijaṅgha Sutta 30.
In the tenth [verse], "eṇijaṅgha" means having legs as well-rounded as those of the eṇi deer. "Kisa" means not thick, with a body of even proportions;
or alternatively, it means withered by the heat, or a body not nourished by garlands, perfumes, and ointments. "Vīra" means...
"Endowed with energy. "Eating little" means one who eats in moderation due to knowing the proper measure in food, or one whose food is limited by way of the rejection of eating at improper times.
"Free from greed" means devoid of craving for the four requisites; this is a rejection of craving for flavors.
"Like a lion walking alone, like an elephant walking alone" means like a solitary lion, like a solitary elephant—as opposed to those who live in a group.
For those who are negligent wander about in company, whereas those who are diligent wander alone; therefore, it is the solitary ones who are taken here.
"Proclaimed" means made known or spoken. "In this" refers to this name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). For here, form is taken by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure, and name by way of the mind;
however, having taken the inseparable phenomena by way of both, the locative case should also be applied here by way of the five aggregates and so forth. The tenth [chapter].
The Third Chapter on Powers.
4. The Chapter on the Satullapa Host. 1.
Commentary on the Sabbhi Sutta.

31. Regarding the first [sutta] of the Satullapakāyika-vagga: "The Satullapakāyikas" refers to those who, having proclaimed the Dhamma by means of undertaking it, were reborn in heaven; thus they are called Satullapakāyikas. Herein is the story:
It is said that a number of sea-merchants set out upon the ocean in a ship. On the seventh day, as their ship was proceeding with the speed of a discharged arrow—
In the midst of the ocean, a great portent appeared; mighty waves arose and filled the ship with water.
As the ship was sinking, the great multitude wailed, calling upon their respective deities by name and offering prayers for protection.
In their midst, one man thought: "Is there indeed any refuge for me in such a terror?"
Reflecting thus, and seeing that his own refuge and precepts were pure, he sat down cross-legged like a yogi.
The others asked him about the cause of his fear. He explained to them: "Friends, on the day I boarded the ship, I gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and undertook the refuges and the precepts."
"Therefore, I have no fear. "But, Master, do these [precepts] apply to others as well? "Yes, they apply," he replied.
"In that case, give them to us too. He then divided those men into seven groups of one hundred each and bestowed upon them the five precepts.
Among them, he first took hold of the first hundred legs while they stood in water reaching only to the ankles.
The second he took up at the height of the knees; the third at the height of the waist; the fourth at the height of the navel;
the fifth at the height of the breasts; the sixth at the level of the throat; and the seventh, as the salt water entered through his mouth, he grasped it.
Having bestowed the precepts upon them, he proclaimed: "You have no other refuge; you must attend only to the precepts. These...
Seven hundred people also died there and, owing to the virtue they had undertaken at the time of their death, were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
their celestial mansions (vimānas) came into being by means of water-jars alone.
In the midst of them all, for the teacher, a golden mansion one hundred yojanas in size appeared, while the others became its attendants, with the very lowest [mansion] belonging to him.

It was twelve yojanas in extent. At the very moment of their rebirth, reflecting upon their past karma and realizing that their attainment had been achieved through reliance on a teacher, they thought, "Let us go now;
we shall speak in praise of our teacher in the presence of the One of Ten Powers.
Thereupon, immediately following the middle watch of the night, those deities approached the Blessed One for the purpose of proclaiming the praises of their teacher.
They each recited a verse.
Therein, "with the good alone" (sabbhireva) means with the wise, with the true persons (sappurisa). The letter *ra* is used for the purpose of euphonic junction (*padasandhi*).
"One should sit together" (*samāseyya*) means one should sit in company. This is merely a stylistic convention of the teaching; in all postures, one should act together with the good alone.

The meaning is as follows: "One should cultivate" means one should perform. "Familiarity" refers to friendship; however, familiarity with craving should not be cultivated with anyone at all, whereas friendship should be cultivated with Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha.

It is with reference to this that it was said. "The virtuous" refers to true persons such as the Buddhas and others. "The True Dhamma" refers to the various divisions such as the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the four foundations of mindfulness.
The true Dhamma; here, however, the five precepts are intended. "It becomes better" means there is progress. "It does not become worse" means nothing base occurs.

Or, "not from another" means that wisdom is not obtained from an ignorant fool—just as oil and such are not obtained from sand and such—but rather, by knowing the Dhamma of the virtuous and associating only with the wise, it is obtained just as oil and such are obtained from sesame seeds and such.
"By honoring [the Dhamma], one obtains": "In the midst of sorrow" means that, having entered into the midst of those who possess grounds for sorrow or of beings overwhelmed by sorrow,

one does not grieve— just like the female lay follower of Bandhula the Malla general, or like Saṅkicca the novice, the co-resident disciple of the General of the Dhamma, in the midst of five hundred thieves.
"He shines in the midst of kinsmen" means that he is resplendent in the midst of the assembly of relatives, like the novice Adhimuttaka, who was the co-resident pupil of the Elder Saṅkicca.
It is said that he was the Elder’s nephew; then the Elder said to him, "Novice, you have grown old;
go, ask for the years [of seniority], and then come back, and I will ordain you. Saying "Very well," he [responded to] the Elder.
Having paid homage and taken his bowl and robes, he went to the village of his sister on the far side of the Cōra forest and wandered for alms.
Seeing him, the sister paid homage, seated him in her house, and fed him. When he had finished his meal, he asked about the years [of his absence].
She said, "I do not know; my mother knows. Then he said, "Stay here; I shall go to my mother's presence."
“I shall go,” he thought, and entered the forest. A bandit saw him from afar and informed the other bandits.

The bandits gave the order, “A novice monk has entered the forest; go and bring him here! Some said, “Kill him! while others said, “Release him. The novice thought: “I am still a learner (sekha) with duties yet to be performed; [what will happen] with these men?”
“Having recited this, I shall ensure my own safety. Thus addressing the chief of the bandits, he said, “Friend, I shall give you a parable,” and spoke these verses:
“In the past, in a vast forest in the wilderness;”
Having set his snares, he then killed a hare.
Seeing the hare dead, the birds and wild animals were terrified;
they departed for the night, thinking, "An evil deed is being committed here."
“Just so, having slain the ascetic who is liberated and possesses nothing, travelers will not return, and there will be a loss of wealth.
“The ascetic has indeed spoken the truth; he is liberated and possesses nothing.”
“Travelers will not arrive; there will be a loss of wealth.
‘If, upon seeing [them] on the opposite path, you do not announce it to anyone;
protecting your truth, go as you please, venerable sir.’”

Released by those thieves as he went on his way, he did not inform even his own relatives when he saw them. Then, when those [relatives] arrived, they seized the thieves and tormented them. As he was lamenting while beating his breast, the thieves said this to his mother:
"What are you intent upon? You are dwelling within our bellies;
Mother, being asked, tell us—how may we come to know that?"
“I am the mother of one who is intent on what is harmful, and this is the father who procreated him;
sisters and brothers as well—all these are his kinsmen here.
Seeing that he performs what ought not to be done, they do not restrain him.”
This indeed is the practice of the recluses, the noble ones who live by the Dhamma:
one who speaks the truth and is resolute, whom one should not turn away upon seeing.
For the bhikkhu who speaks the truth and is resolute, through his pure conduct—
“May all our kinsmen attain fearlessness; may they go in safety.
Thus released by the bandits, they went and said to Adhimutta:
“By virtue of your own well-performed deeds, O dear one, [we are saved] because of that monk who speaks the truth.”
“All have attained fearlessness; we have returned in safety.
Those five hundred thieves, having gained confidence, went forth in the presence of the novice Adhimutta.
Taking them with him, he went into the presence of his preceptor; first he himself was fully ordained, and afterwards those five hundred were ordained as well.
Having made them his own pupils, he ordained them. Abiding by the instruction of Thera Adhimutta, they all attained the supreme fruit of Arahantship.
Taking this matter into account, the deity said: "Knowing the True Dhamma, he shines in the midst of kinsmen.
She says that *sātataṃ* means "constantly," or "lasting for a long time" in terms of happiness. *Sabbāsaṃ vo* means "of all of you."
"By way of method" means by reason. "He is liberated from all suffering": it is not merely that he becomes superior, nor merely that he gains wisdom;

he does not grieve in the midst of sorrow, he shines in the midst of kinsmen, he is reborn in a happy destination, he dwells in happiness for a long time, and furthermore, he is liberated even from the entire suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). First.
2. Commentary on the Maccharisutta 32.

In the second [verse], "through stinginess and negligence": through stinginess, which has the characteristic of concealing one's own excellence, and through negligence, which has the characteristic of the loss of mindfulness.
For a certain person thinks: "If I give this to him, it will go to depletion."
"Or it will not belong to my household members"—thinking thus, one does not give a gift out of stinginess.
Another, being addicted to play and the like, does not even conceive the thought that "a gift ought to be given. Thus a gift is not given;
in this way, this so-called gift—which brings fame, which brings glory, which brings prosperity, and which brings happiness—is not given, and so forth.
He explained the reason. "By one desiring merit" means by one wishing for merit consisting of prior volition and so forth.
"The wise man knows what is to be given" means that one who knows there is a fruit of giving must certainly give; thus he speaks.
"That very same fool it touches" means that hunger and thirst touch that very same fool in both this world and the next world.
It follows after and does not abandon it. Therefore, because it touches that very [object], for that reason.

"Having removed stinginess" means having led away the stain of stinginess. "One should give a gift, overcoming the stain" means having become one who has overcome the stain, one should give a gift after having conquered that stain of stinginess.
"Among those who have died, they do not die"—this means that because of their lack of the habit of giving, they do not perish even when others have died.

For just as one who has died does not, despite being surrounded by an abundance of food, drink, and other requisites, rise up and share them out, saying, "Let this be for him, let that be for her," so too is one who lacks the habit of giving;
thus, the wealth of the dead and the wealth of one who lacks the habit of giving are said to be exactly the same.
Therefore, those who possess generosity and virtue do not perish even when such [others] have died; this is the meaning.

"As travelers together on a road, they give to those who have little": just as travelers journeying together along a desert path share and give their own provisions to other travelers who have little, even so...
But those who, traveling together through the trackless wilderness of saṃsāra, share even a small gift of merit with their fellow travelers and give it away, do not perish when others die.
"This is the eternal Dhamma" means this is the ancient Dhamma, or rather, this is the Dhamma of the ancient wise ones.
"Appasmeketi" means "some, when there is little to give. "Pavecchantīti" means they give.
"Bahuneke na dicchareti" means some, even though endowed with great wealth, do not give. "Sahassena samaṃ mitāti" means measured by a thousand; it is equal to a gift of a thousand.

“Hard to follow” (*duranvayo*) means difficult to pursue; “hard to fill” (*duppūro*) is the meaning. “One who lives according to the Dhamma” (*dhammaṃ care*) means one who practices the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
“Even one who sweeps the threshing floor” (*yo pi samuñjakaṃ care*) means even one who performs sweeping and the clearing away of straw from threshing circles and the like.

“While supporting a wife” (*dārañ ca posanto*) means while maintaining a wife. “Giving even when there is little” (*appakasmiṃ*) means even when there is only a small amount, such as a mere leaf-vegetable.

Having made a distribution, he practices the Dhamma as if he were giving it away. "A hundred thousand" (*sataṃ sahassānaṃ*) means a hundred of men calculated by thousands—that is, a hundred thousand. "Sacrificers of a thousand" (*sahassayāginaṃ*):
a sacrifice for a thousand monks, or a sacrifice produced with a thousand *kahāpaṇa* coins, is a "sacrifice of a thousand. Those who possess such [a sacrifice] are "sacrificers of a thousand."
Of those thousand sacrificers—by this, the alms-food given to ten koṭis of bhikkhus or ten koṭis of kahāpaṇas is shown.
He said that those who give such [amounts] do not equal even a fraction of one such as that.
This person, even while living as a gleaner, practices the Dhamma; even while supporting a wife, he practices the Dhamma; and even while giving only a small amount, he practices the Dhamma.
