These [sacrificers] do not equal even a fraction of such a person as he. Whatever was given by that poor man—even a single *paṭivīsaka* or merely a ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*)—the gift of all those [others] does not equal even a fraction of that gift.
A "fraction" (*kala*) means a sixteenth part, a hundredth part, or a thousandth part; here, a hundredth part is intended. Whatever was given by him...
He said this because the gift he had given was worth ten thousand koṭis when divided into a hundred parts; even one such portion could not equal the value of the other gifts.
As the Tathāgata was thus assigning a price to the gifts, a deity standing nearby thought:
"In this way the Blessed One, having pushed aside such a great gift as if with his foot, is casting it into hell as if it were a mere trifle, like a hundred pieces of jewelry."
Giving is like tossing [an offering] up toward the moon’s disk;
he addressed her with a verse in order to know how it could be that this [giving] yields such great fruit. Therein, *kena* means "for what reason. *Mahaggata* means "gone to greatness";
this is a synonym for "vast" (*vipula*). *Samena dinnassa* means "of a gift given by one who is impartial. Then to her...
The Blessed One, demonstrating the distribution of giving, said: "They give," "they cause to give," and so forth.
In that context, "established in the uneven" means being settled in uneven bodily, verbal, and mental actions. "Having cut" means having struck. "Having slain" means having killed.
"Having caused to grieve" means having made another fall into a state of sorrow. "Tear-faced" means mixed with tears. [This refers to] having caused another to weep.
For a gift given with tears on one’s face is called a "gift with tears. A sacrificial offering given after threatening or striking with a staff is called a "gift with a staff.

Thus, by virtue of my Perfect Enlightenment, I am not able to make a great gift bear little fruit, nor can I make a small gift bear great fruit. However, this great gift [is for the sake] of my own manifestation.

It is precisely because of its impurity that this [other gift] is called "of small fruit"; whereas the other, a limited gift, is called "of great fruit" precisely because of the purity of its own origin.
Demonstrating this point, he said, "In this way," and so forth. This is the second [section].
3. Commentary on the Sādhu Sutta.
33. "He uttered an *udāna* in the third [case]" means he uttered an expression.

For just as the oil that cannot be contained within a measure and flows over is called "residue" (*avasesaka*), and just as the water that cannot be contained within a pond and flows over it is called a "flood" (*ogha*), even so is this word of joy.
When one is unable to grasp it within the heart, and because it becomes excessive, it does not remain inside but issues forth;
that is called an *udāna*. The meaning is that he uttered such speech consisting of rapture (*pīti*).
Even through faith—that is, even by having faith in both the action and the fruit of action—the gift given is "good," meaning it is well-obtained and truly auspicious.
They speak of the offering (*āhuti*). But how is it that these two are said to be equal?
For one who fears for his life is unable to fight, and one who fears loss is unable to give. Indeed, one who says, "I shall both protect my life and fight," is not acting consistently.
However, having relinquished attachment to life, [one thinks], "Let there be either cutting off or death..."
Or, thinking, "We shall seize this sovereignty," one engages in battle with great enthusiasm. One who says, "I will protect my wealth and give gifts," does not actually give.
But having relinquished attachment to wealth, one gives with the very same enthusiasm as when thinking, "I will give a great gift.
Thus, giving and fighting are equal. And what is more? Even being few themselves, they [overcome] the many.

Regarding the phrase "they conquer": just as in battle even a few heroic men conquer many cowardly men, so too one endowed with faith and other virtues, by giving even a small gift, crushes great stinginess and attains a vast result of that generosity.
In this way, giving and battle are similar. Therefore it was said:
“If one gives even a little with faith,
by that alone one becomes happy in the other world.
To illustrate this meaning, the story of the Brahmin Wearing a Single Cloth and the story of the Sprout should be related in detail.
"Of what is acquired by the Dhamma" means: of wealth acquired by the Dhamma—that is, by righteous and equitable means—and of a person who has acquired the Dhamma.
Here, a "person who has acquired the Dhamma" refers to a noble person (ariya-puggala) who has attained the Dhamma. Thus, the meaning is:

that gift which is given from wealth acquired by the Dhamma to a noble person who has acquired the Dhamma is also excellent. "Of one who has acquired the Dhamma"—this refers to... [the rest of the sentence follows].
In this verse-line as well, the meaning is exactly the same. "Of wealth acquired through exertion and energy" means of wealth obtained by means of both initiative (*uṭṭhāna*) and vigor (*vīriya*).
"Vetaraṇī" is merely a figure of speech for the teaching;
the meaning is that one completely transcends not only the Vetaraṇī River, but also the Sañjīva, Kālasutta, and so forth, including all thirty-one great hells.

"Having discriminated in giving" means giving after having investigated. In this context, there are two kinds of investigation: the investigation of the offering (*dakkhiṇā*) and the investigation of the recipient (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
Among these, setting aside inferior and very inferior requisites, and having selected the most excellent and superior ones to give them, is called the "investigation of the offering.
Setting aside those of broken virtue, or those among the ninety-five types of external sectarians, and [giving] to those endowed with qualities such as virtue, is the investigation of the recipient.
Giving to those who have gone forth in the Dispensation is called "discerning the worthy recipients" (*dakkhiṇeyya-vicinanā*). Thus, giving is to be practiced by discerning in two ways.
"Praised by the Sugata" means it was commended by the Sugata. In that context, showing the discernment of the worthy recipients, he said, "Those who are worthy of offerings," and so forth.

By the phrase "just as seeds were mentioned," however, he spoke of the discernment of the gift itself (*dakkhiṇā-vicinanā*); for [the gift] is like a seed that has not perished once it has been discerned.
"Excellent gifts have been taken.
Regarding living beings as well, "restraint is good"; thus, the state of being restrained toward living beings is also auspicious.
This deity, having surpassed the benefits of giving mentioned by the others, began to speak of the benefits of virtue: "They wander without harming, not injuring [others]."
While wandering. "From the reproaches of others" means out of fear of being censured by another. "Fear" refers to the fear of reproach.
"But from giving, the footprint of the Dhamma is indeed better" means that compared to giving, the footprint of the Dhamma—namely, Nibbāna—is indeed superior.

"In former times and even earlier than those" means both in former times, such as during the era of the Buddha Kassapa, and even earlier than those, such as during the era of the Buddha Koṇāgamana; all [the Buddhas]...
"Or these, having existed in the past and even further back in the past, are called 'beings'. Third.
4. Commentary on the *Nasanti-sutta* (34).
In the fourth [sutta], "delightful things" refers to desirable objects such as forms and so forth. "Without returning"—a person who does not come back to the realm of death.

He is one who does not return to the realm of death, which is comprised of the round of existence in the three planes, but instead goes to Nibbāna, which is characterized by non-returning. For indeed, beings do not return again to Nibbāna;
therefore, it is called "non-returning. Bound to sense pleasures and heedless, he is said to be "one who does not return";
he is unable to reach that state, and thus he spoke these words. "Chandaja" means from the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*).
It has arisen. *Agha* refers to the suffering of the five aggregates. The second phrase is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Through the removal of desire comes the removal of *agha*" means that through the removal of craving (*taṇhā*), there is the removal of the five aggregates.

"Through the removal of *agha* comes the removal of suffering" means that through the removal of the five aggregates, the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is indeed removed. "Diverse" refers to the minds directed toward objects. "Lust of intention" is lust as it is intended.

Thus, having rejected sensual desire for objects (*vatthukāma*) here, sensual desire as defilement (*kilesakāma*) is what is called "sensual pleasure" (*kāma*). This meaning, however, should be clarified by the *Pasūra Sutta*.
For when the Elder said to the wanderer Pasūra, "A man’s sensual pleasure is lustful intention (*saṅkapparāga*"), Pasūra replied:
"Those variegated things in the world are not sensual pleasures; it is the longing for them that is sensual pleasure."
"You speak of sensual desire as the passion of intention;
yet by entertaining unwholesome thoughts,
even monks will become consumers of sensual pleasures."
He said: Then the Elder spoke to him:
"If those various sensual pleasures in the world are not what you call 'sensual pleasure'—namely, the passion of intention—"
Beholding delightful forms,
even the Teacher would become a consumer of sensual pleasures;
likewise by hearing sounds and smelling scents.
"Enjoying flavors and touching delightful tangibles, even the Teacher will become a partaker of sensual pleasures.
Now, regarding the phrase "here the wise": herein, the wise subdue desire and lust for these objects. It is a fetter.
"All" refers to the tenfold fetter (*saṃyojana*). "Nothingness" means being devoid of the defilement of lust (*rāgakiñcana*) and so forth.
"Sufferings do not pursue him" means that the sufferings of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) do not fall upon him.

Thus, the Venerable Mogharāja—having heard the verse beginning with "You have abandoned reckoning"—the Elder named Mogharāja, who was skilled in discerning the underlying connection within that assembly, [said] regarding this...
Thinking, "The meaning of this verse does not follow the logical sequence," and seeking to restore it to its proper order, he spoke as follows.
In that context, "here or hereafter" means either in this world or in the next world. Regarding the phrase "the supreme among men, who acts for the welfare of men":
although all those whose taints are exhausted are indeed supreme among men and act for the welfare of men, the Elder [specifically] [referred to] the One Possessing the Ten Powers.
He spoke thus with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). Regarding the phrase "those who honor him are worthy of praise":

if gods and humans honor one who is liberated in such a way, then as for those who honor that Blessed One—whether by body, speech, or by following his practice—are they worthy of praise or unworthy of praise?
With the word "monks" (*bhikkhū*), he addresses the Elder Mogharāja. "Having understood the Dhamma" (*aññāya dhammaṃ*)...

"Having understood the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, they too become 'transcenders of attachment'": this refers to those who honor that [Dhamma] through body, speech, or by following it in practice.
Having fully known the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths and abandoned doubt, they too become transcenders of attachment and worthy of praise. This is the fourth [discourse].
5. Commentary on the *Ujjhānasaññi Sutta*.
35. Regarding the fifth case, "those with a sense of reproach": there is no separate world-system called Devaloka (the World of the Gods).
Rather, these deities came having reproached [the Buddha] on account of the Tathāgata’s use of the four requisites. It is said that they thought thus:
"The ascetic Gotama [provides] for his monks robes made of cast-off rags, alms-food, lodging at the foot of a tree, and medicine consisting of fermented urine."
While he praises the setting of a limit on contentment alone, he himself wears fine robes such as those made of cotton, silk, and linen;
he eats the most excellent food fit for a king; he sleeps on a superior bed in a fragrant chamber like a celestial palace;
he partakes of medicinal treatments such as ghee and fresh butter; and during the day, he teaches the Dhamma to the great multitude.

They arrived grumbling, "His speech goes one way, but his action goes another. For that reason, the Elders who compiled the Dhamma gave them the name "Ujjhānasaññikā" (those characterized by grumbling).
*Aññathā santaṃ* means existing in another manner; *nikacca* means by guile or deception—the sense being "having deceived."
"Like a gambler": a gambler is called a fowler. For he, though not actually a thicket, displays the appearance of a thicket by concealing himself with branches, leaves, and so forth;
then, having killed the birds that approach—such as peacocks and partridges—he supports his family.
Thus, just as that gambler deceives others through this very deception and eats the flesh of birds, so too does the hypocrite.
"Of him who wanders about eating while deceiving the multitude through his skill in talk, having covered himself with refuse rags—
whatever he has consumed by theft, even the entire enjoyment of his four requisites is called 'enjoyed by theft,'" said the deities, referring to the Blessed One. "The wise understand this."
"The wise know whether this person is a doer or a non-doer. Thus those deities, thinking "We too are indeed wise like the Tathāgata," spoke in this way.
Then the Blessed One said, "They do not know," and so forth. In that context, "this practice which is firm" refers to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipadā).

"Strong and firm. By means of that practice, the wise and learned—those meditators who meditate through both the meditation on the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and the meditation on characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*)—are liberated from the bonds of Māra.
The meaning is that it is not possible to enter or undertake that practice merely by its being spoken or merely by hearing it. "The wise do not indeed perform [evil deeds]."

The wise and learned, having understood the worldly convention and knowing the arising and passing away of the world of conditioned formations, and having realized the Dhamma of the Four Truths, are extinguished by the extinction of defilements;
having crossed over attachment to the world, they do not act in this way—the meaning is that they do not say, "We have done such things.
Having established themselves upon the earth: [the sense is] "What we have done was improper; though we did nothing, we were spoken of as doers."

"Having descended from the sky and stood upon the ground"—this is the meaning. Feeling shame, they established reverence for the Blessed One as if he were Mahābrahmā; beholding the Blessed One as difficult to approach as a mass of fire, [they spoke].

"Transgression" (*accaya*) means an offense. "No, venerable sir, it was an overstepping" (*no... accāgama*) means that which proceeded by surpassing and overcoming us. "To be approached" (*āsādetabba*)—
"It should be struck. It is said that those deities struck the Blessed One with both body and speech.

Not bowing to the Tathāgata, they struck him with their bodies as they hovered in mid-air; and by uttering various kinds of improper words after citing the simile of the gambler, they struck him with their speech.
Therefore, they said, "We thought it should be approached [with hostility]. "May he accept it," [he said].
"May it be forgiven. "For the sake of restraint in the future" means for the purpose of exercising restraint in the time to come, so as not to commit such an offense or fault again.
"He displayed a smile" means he showed a joyful expression by revealing his upper teeth. Why? It is said that those deities...
They do not ask for forgiveness by way of their true nature; they treat the Tathāgata, the Supreme Person in the world with its gods, as if he were identical to the ordinary worldly masses.
Then the Blessed One, thinking, "When a discussion arises from others, I shall display the power of a Buddha and afterwards grant forgiveness," manifested a smile.
"To an even greater degree" means to an exceeding measure. He spoke this verse.
Thinking, "This one is angry with us," she spoke thus.
"Does not accept" means he does not forgive or endure it. "One whose anger is internal" refers to anger that has arisen within.
"Living while making hatred heavy" means dwelling while taking hatred as something weighty. "He binds on enmity" means such a person is like one binding on a knot.
It fastens that enmity upon oneself, establishes it there; the meaning is that one does not relinquish it.
"If no transgression were found" means if there were no urgent offense.
"If it were not manifest here" means if what is called an offense did not come into being. "Who here could be skilled? means if enmities did not subside, by what cause could one be skillful?
Regarding the verse beginning with *kassaccayā*: "Who has no transgression? Who has no offense? Who does not fall into delusion?
Who is always called 'wise'?"—it is said that the Blessed One manifested a smile for the purpose of having this verse recited.
Therefore, [the interlocutor] spoke the words "of the Tathāgata, the Buddha," and so forth, thinking: "Now, having demonstrated the power of the Buddha to the deities, I shall ask for forgiveness."
In this context, "of the Tathāgata" means of him who has thus come, and so forth, for such reasons.
"Of the Buddha" refers to one who has acquired this name by way of conventional designation (*paññatti*) based on reasons such as being awakened to the Four Truths.
Regarding the phrase "of those confessing their transgression," it refers to what was said by you: "Of those confessing their transgression... [omission] ...he binds enmity in return."
"That was well said; however, I do not rejoice in nor do I long for that enmity"—this is the meaning.
"I accept your word" means "I forgive your offense. The fifth [sutta].
6. Commentary on the Saddhā Sutta.
36. "Faith is a person’s second" means that for a person going to the world of the devas, the human world, and even to Nibbāna, faith is his second [companion];
it performs the function of a companion. "If lack of faith does not remain" means if lack of faith does not persist.
"Fame" refers to one's retinue; "renown" refers to the speaking of praise. "That indeed belongs to him" means...
Then it happens to him: "The attachments do not pursue him" means that the five attachments, such as the attachment of lust and so forth, do not pursue him.
"Those who indulge in negligence" refers to those who practice negligence and bring it about; they are said to "indulge" in it.

"He guards it like the finest wealth" means he guards it like the most excellent wealth, such as pearls, gems, and precious substances. "Contemplating" means by means of contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*).

And "contemplating" (jhāyanto). Therein, "contemplation of characteristics" (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna) refers to insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruit (phala). For insight is called "contemplation of characteristics" because it contemplates the three characteristics. The path is called "contemplation of characteristics" because it accomplishes the task brought forth by insight.
The fruit is called "contemplation of characteristics" because it contemplates the truth of cessation, which possesses such characteristics.

This is contemplation of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). However, the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) should be understood as "contemplation of the object" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*), because they contemplate the kasiṇa as their object.
By "supreme," the bliss of Arahatship is intended. This is the sixth [section].
7. Commentary on the *Samaya Sutta*.

37. "In the Sakka country" means: because of the exclamation, "Ah, these princes are indeed *Sakyas*," that single district which was the residence of the royal princes who had thus acquired the name *Sakka* is also called "Sakka" by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhisadda*).
In that Sakka country, in the Great Forest—that is, in a vast forest growing of its own accord, not planted, which was continuous with the Himalayas.
"By all who are Arahants"—this sutta was spoken on the very day they attained Arahantship.

Herein is the sequential account: it is said that the Sākiyas and Koliyas had the river named Rohiṇī, situated between the city of Kapilavatthu and the city of the Koliyas, dammed with a single embankment and cultivated for crops. Then...
In the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops were withering, the laborers from both cities gathered together.
Thereupon, the inhabitants of Koliya city said: "This water, being brought from both sides, will not suffice for either you or us;
however, our own crop will be produced by this water alone. This water..."
“Give us [some]! The inhabitants of Kapilavatthu said:
“While you stand with your granaries filled, we will not be able to go about at your house doors with baskets, sacks, and other containers in our hands, carrying red gold, blue gems, and black coins;
furthermore, our own crops will ripen from a single watering alone. This—
“Give us water! “We will not give it to you. “Neither will we give it to you.
Thus, as their talk escalated, one man stood up and struck another; he, in turn, struck yet another.
In this way, by striking one another and provoking the lineages of the royal families, they increased the conflict.
The Koliyan laborers said, “Seize those inhabitants of Kapilavatthu and roar against them!
As for those who lived with their own sisters like dogs, jackals, and the like—what will their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do for us?
The Sākiyan laborers replied, “Now you are like lepers with children...”
"Having seized them, roar out! As for those who are helpless, without protection, and like animals living in *kolarukka* trees—what will their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do for us?
They went and told this to the ministers appointed to that task, and the ministers told it to the royal families. Then the Sākiyas said: "By our sisters..."
“Let us display our strength and power to those with whom we have lived together,” they said, and set out prepared for battle.
The Koliyans also, saying, “Let us display our strength and power to those who dwell in the Kola trees,” set out prepared for battle.
At the very time of dawn, the Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion, surveyed the world and saw these [two groups].
Thus he saw them setting out, prepared for battle. Having seen them, he reflected: "When I have gone there, will this quarrel be appeased or not?
Investigating further, he thought: "If I go there, I shall relate three Jātakas for the sake of appeasing the quarrel;
then the quarrel will be appeased. Then, for the purpose of illustrating harmony, I shall relate two Jātakas."
“I shall teach the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Upon hearing this teaching, the inhabitants of both cities will each offer two hundred and fifty youths;
I shall ordain them, and then there will be a great assembly.
Having made this resolution, while these men were setting out prepared for battle, he did not inform anyone, but took his own bowl and robes and departed on his own.
Having gone into the space between the two armies, he sat down cross-legged, emitting rays of six colors.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, the inhabitants of Kapilavatthu thought, "Our preeminent kinsman, the Teacher, has arrived.
Has he perhaps seen our state of quarreling? Then they reflected, "It is not possible for [the Blessed One] to have come..."
“We must not let a weapon fall upon the body of another. Let the inhabitants of Koliyanagara kill us or bind us!
Having cast away their weapons and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down.
The inhabitants of Koliyanagara, having likewise reflected in this way, cast away their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down.
The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked, “For what reason have you come, Great Kings?
“Not for the sport of bathing, Blessed One, nor for mountain sports, nor for river sports, nor to see the mountains; rather, we have come having set up a battle at this place.
“On what account is your quarrel, Great Kings? “On account of water, venerable sir.”
“Great king, what is water worth? “It is of little value, venerable sir. “Great king, what is called earth is worth how much?
“It is priceless, venerable sir. “What are the khattiyas worth? “The khattiyas, venerable sir, are indeed priceless.
“Great king, why do you destroy priceless khattiyas for the sake of water, which has little value? In a quarrel, there is no such thing as a benefit.”
"Great King, by means of a quarrel, having created enmity in an improper place, a tree deity harbored a grudge against a black lion;
thus, for this entire eon, they have remained bound in hostility. Having said this, he related the Phandana Jātaka.
Then [he continued]: "Great King, one must not be dependent on others. For by being dependent on others, [a certain hare]..."
"In the story, when the Himalayas were three thousand yojanas wide, the herds of quadrupeds used to leap across to the great ocean.
Therefore, one should not be one who trusts in others. Having said this, he related the Pathavī-undriya Jātaka. Then [he continued]:
"Sometimes, O Great King, even a weak person sees a flaw or an opening in one of great strength; sometimes a person of great strength..."
“Even a weakling can prevail; for even a little bird, the *laṭukikā*, destroyed a mighty elephant,” he said, and related the *Laṭukika Jātaka*.
Having thus related three Jātakas for the purpose of settling disputes, he related two Jātakas to illustrate the value of harmony.
How so? “For, O Great King, no one is able to find a vulnerability in those who are harmonious.”
Having said this, he related the *Rukkhadhamma-jātaka*. Then, saying, "O Great King, no one was able to find a flaw in those who were in harmony;
but when they fell into mutual dispute, the son of the hunter took their lives and departed—thus there is no benefit whatsoever in quarreling," he related the *Vaṭṭaka-jātaka*. In this way, these...
Having related five Jātaka stories, at the conclusion he preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.
The kings were filled with faith and said: "If the Teacher had not come, we would have personally slaughtered one another until a river of blood flowed.
We would not have seen our sons and brothers at the doors of our homes, nor would we have received any news or counter-news from the Dispensation."
There would have been no one to bring us [food]; we would not have obtained our livelihood by depending on the Teacher.
However, had the Teacher lived as a householder, the sovereignty of the Four Great Islands, surrounded by two thousand islands, would have come into his hands;
moreover, he would have had more than a thousand sons, and thus he would have traveled about accompanied by a retinue of kshatriyas.
“However, having abandoned that very prosperity and gone forth, he attained supreme enlightenment; let him now move about surrounded by kshatriyas as well.
Thus, the inhabitants of both cities gave three hundred and fifty youths each.
The Blessed One, having ordained them, went to the Great Forest. They had gone forth out of profound reverence for him, not out of their own personal inclination.

Discontent arose in them. Their former wives also sent messages to them, saying, "Noble sons, may you be weary [of the life]; the household life does not endure," and so forth. They became even more weary.
The Blessed One, reflecting and knowing their state of discontent, thought: "These bhikkhus, together with a Buddha such as I..."
“Living together in one place, they become weary; well then, let me describe the beauty of Kuṇāla Lake to them, lead them there, and dispel their discontent.
Thus he described the beauty of Kuṇāla Lake. They became desirous of seeing it. “Bhikkhus, do you wish to see Kuṇāla Lake?
“Yes, Blessed One. “If that is so, come, let us go. [Then, for those] possessing psychic power—
“Blessed One, how shall we go to the place where you are going? “You must wish to go; I will take you and go by means of my own power.
“It would be well, venerable sir. The Blessed One took the five hundred bhikkhus, rose into the air, and alighted at Kuṇāla Lake.
He said to those bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, as for the fish in this Kuṇāla Lake—”
"You do not know my name; ask me. They asked him.
The Blessed One explained each question as it was asked. And he did not stop there;
having had the names of even the fish in that forest thicket asked, he likewise had the names of the trees at the foot of the mountain and the bipeds, quadrupeds, and birds asked.

He spoke. Then, seated upon a staff grasped with the beaks of two birds, King Kuṇāla approached, surrounded on the front, the back, and both sides by a multitude of birds. When the monks saw him, they thought:
"Venerable sir, this must be the king of these birds; these others are his retinue."
“It is so, monks; this too is my lineage, my tradition. “Venerable sir, we see these birds now.
But as for what the Blessed One said—‘This too is my lineage, my tradition’—we wish to hear that.
“Do you wish to hear it, monks? “Yes, Blessed One. “In that case, listen,” [the Blessed One said], and with three hundred verses:

Having adorned himself and recounted the Kuṇāla Jātaka, he dispelled their world-weariness. At the conclusion of the teaching, they all were established in the fruit of stream-entry, and through that very path, supernatural power (iddhi) also came to them.

The Blessed One, thinking, "Let this much suffice for these bhikkhus," rose into the air and returned to Mahāvana itself. Those bhikkhus, at the time of their departure, [reflected] upon the Ten-Powered One...
Having arrived by means of their own psychic power, they surrounded the Blessed One with their own psychic power upon returning and descended into the Great Forest.
The Blessed One, having sat down on the prepared seat, addressed those bhikkhus: "Come, bhikkhus, sit down.
I shall explain to you the meditation subject for the defilements to be abandoned by the three higher paths," and he taught the meditation subject.
The bhikkhus thought: “The Blessed One, having understood our state of dissatisfaction, led us to the Kuṇāla Lake and dispelled our discontent;
there he gave us the meditation subjects for three of the paths for those who had attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Yet it is not fitting for us to pass our time thinking, ‘We are stream-enterers. We must [strive] with every manly effort.”

"It is not fitting for them to be so. Having paid homage at the feet of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, they rose, shook out their sitting mats, and sat down separately at the foot of various mountain caves and trees.
The Blessed One thought: "These bhikkhus were already diligent in their meditation subjects by nature; moreover, now that they have found the means..."

There is no cause for a bhikkhu to become weary. As they go along, they will increase their insight and, having attained arahantship, they will come to me thinking, "We shall proclaim the qualities we have realized ourselves.
When they have arrived, the devas of ten thousand world-systems will assemble in a single world-system; it will be a great gathering.
"It will be fitting for me to sit in a secluded place. Thereupon, having prepared a Buddha-seat in a secluded spot, he sat down.
The elder who had first received the meditation subject attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Then another, and after him yet another—just like lotuses in a lotus pond—they all blossomed; five hundred [monks] did so, one after another. First of all...
The bhikkhu who had attained arahantship, thinking, "I shall inform the Blessed One," unfastened his cross-legged posture, shook out his sitting mat, rose up, and stood facing the One of Ten Powers.
In this manner, one after another, five hundred bhikkhus arrived in succession, as if entering the dining hall.
The first to arrive paid homage, prepared a sitting mat, and—
Having sat down to one side, desiring to announce the qualities he had realized, he thought, "Is there anyone else?
Finding there was none, he turned back and looked along the path by which he had come; he saw another, and yet another—indeed, he saw them all.
As they too came and sat down to one side, [he reflected: "This one did not speak because of envy toward him; this one [did not speak] because of envy toward him."
He did not speak. It is said that for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavā), two thoughts arise: "O, would that the world with its devas might quickly penetrate the qualities realized by me!
Yet, they do not wish to announce their realization to another, just like a man who has found a hidden treasure.
But as soon as that noble circle had thus entered, it was freed from those defilements— namely, clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu— from the eastern boundary of the Yugandhara mountains.
This was for the purpose of showing the loveliness of the world adorned by the appearance of a Buddha, like a great silver mirror-disk raised in the eastern direction upon its circular rim.
Having taken it up, he leaped over the full moon’s orb, which was as magnificent as a revolving wheel of silver, and set out upon the path of the wind.
Thus, at such a moment, at such a time, at such an hour, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Great Forest,
together with a great Saṅgha of monks— about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arahants.
In that regard, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of Mahāsammata, and those five hundred bhikkhus were also born into the family of Mahāsammata.
The Blessed One was born in a kṣatriya womb, and they too were born in kṣatriya wombs.
The Blessed One went forth as a king, and they too went forth as kings. The Blessed One renounced the white parasol and the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch held in his own hands.
Having renounced [their thrones], they went forth; they too, having abandoned the white parasols and relinquished the royal powers held in their hands, went forth.

Thus the Blessed One, in a pure place, during a pure part of the night—himself pure with a pure retinue, free from passion with a retinue free from passion, free from hatred with a retinue free from hatred, free from delusion...
He is free from delusion and has a retinue free from delusion; he is free from craving and has a retinue free from craving; he is free from defilement and has a retinue free from defilement;
he is peaceful and has a peaceful retinue; he is tamed and has a tamed retinue; he is liberated and has a liberated retinue; he shines exceedingly.
This is what is called the "ground for praise," where one may say as much as one is able. Thus, it was said with reference to these bhikkhus: "With about five hundred..."
“With all those hundreds of bhikkhus who were arahants.

*Yebhuyyena* means that for the most part they had assembled; those who were dull-witted did not assemble, nor did the non-percipient beings, the deities of the formless realm, and the deities who had entered meditative attainments.
Herein, this is the sequence of the assembly: it is said that the deities in the vicinity of the Great Forest were stirred.
“Come, sirs! Seeing the Buddha is of great benefit; hearing the Dhamma is of great benefit; seeing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is of great benefit.

Come, come! Making a great noise as they arrived, they paid homage to the Blessed One and to those who had at that very moment attained Arahantship with their taints destroyed, and stood to one side. By this same means, for each of them...

Having heard the sound, [he went] throughout the entirety of Jambudīpa—extending three thousand yojanas across the Himavat mountains by way of intervals of half a *gāvuta*, one *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, one *yojana*, and so forth; through the sixty-three thousand cities;
the ninety-nine million ports (*doṇamukha*); the ninety-six million harbors (*paṭṭana*); and the fifty-six mines of jewels.
In Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and in the two thousand minor islands—that is, throughout the entire Cakkavāḷa—and then in the second and third Cakkavāḷas;
thus it should be understood that the deities have assembled in ten thousand Cakkavāḷas.
For here, "ten thousand Cakkavāḷas" is intended as "ten world-systems. Therefore it was said: "By ten..."
"And deities from many world-systems have for the most part assembled.

When the deities have thus assembled, the entire interior of the world-system, up to the Brahma-world, becomes completely filled—like needles packed without any gaps inside a needle-case. In this regard, the height of the Brahma-world should be understood as follows:
It is said that a stone equal in size to a seven-storied iron palace, when dropped from the Brahma-world, reaches the earth in four months. In such a vast space,
there is no room for flowers or incense thrown from below to go upward, nor for mustard seeds thrown from above to descend downward.

Thus the deities became continuous. Just as the sitting place of a wheel-turning monarch is unconfined, so that high-ranking kshatriyas who arrive one after another find space there, while it becomes extremely crowded beyond that point;
even so, the Blessed One’s sitting place was unconfined, [accommodating] the high-ranking deities and brahmas who arrived one after another.
And they indeed found space; even in a place as narrow as the point of a hair, right near the Blessed One, ten or twenty deities stood having fashioned subtle bodies for themselves.
Beyond all of them, sixty or sixty deities stood.
"Of those belonging to the Pure Abodes" (*suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ*) means of those dwelling in the Pure Abodes.
The "Pure Abodes" (*suddhāvāsā*) are the five Brahma-worlds, which are the dwellings (*āvāsā*) of the pure ones—those non-returners whose taints are exhausted. Why did this thought occur?

It is said that those Brahmās, having emerged from their meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) according to its duration and looking upon the Brahma-abode, saw it as if it were a meal-house after a meal had been finished.
They saw the emptiness. Then, reflecting on where the Brahmās had gone and realizing that a great assembly was taking place, they thought:
"This assembly is vast; we have been left behind, and for those who are left behind, an opportunity is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, as we go, let us not go empty-handed, but having composed a verse each, let us proceed. And with that [verse], in the great assembly..."

"We shall make known our arrival and we shall speak in praise of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. Thus, because they had emerged from their meditative attainment and applied their attention, this thought occurred to them.
"They appeared before the Blessed One" means that in the text, they descended into the very place facing the Blessed One, in his presence.
These were spoken as if they were uttered by them, yet the meaning here should not be understood in that way.

Rather, while remaining in the Brahma-world, they composed these verses; then one descended upon the eastern rim of the world-system, one on the southern rim, one on the western rim, and one on the northern rim of the world-system. Then...
The Brahmā who had descended upon the eastern rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) entered the blue-kasiṇa attainment, emitted blue rays, and—
like one fastening a jeweled armor upon the deities of the ten thousand world-systems— made them aware of his arrival.
Since no one is able to traverse what is called the "Buddha-path" (*buddhavīthi*), he proceeded by way of that great Buddha-path itself.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing there, he recited a verse composed by himself.

Having entered the yellow kasiṇa attainment at the southern rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), the Brahmā who had descended emitted a golden radiance, as if draping a golden cloth over the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, thereby making known his arrival.

Having made himself known, he did exactly that. The Brahmā who had descended upon the western rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) entered the blood-kasiṇa (*lohitaka-kasiṇa*), emitted rays of red light, and—like surrounding the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a fine red woolen cloth—made his arrival known and did exactly that. [He did so] at the northern rim of the world-system.

The Brahmā Otiṇṇa, having entered the attainment of the white-kasiṇa and emitted white rays, made his presence known to the deities of the ten thousand world-systems as if he were draping them in a cloth of jasmine flowers; he did exactly so.
However, in the text, they appeared before the Blessed One. Then those deities, having paid homage to the Blessed One...
"Standing to one side" (*ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu*) thus describes both the appearance before [the Buddha] as if at a single moment and the state of standing to one side after having paid homage;
this occurred according to this sequence, yet it is presented here by combining them together.
However, in the *pāḷi* itself, the speaking of the verses is stated separately from that.
In this context, "great assembly" (*mahāsamaya*) means a great multitude. "Pavana" refers to a grove of trees. By both terms, the Blessed One said:
"But today, in this grove of trees, there is a great gathering of a multitude. Then, in order to show those to whom that gathering belongs, he said: "The hosts of devas have assembled.
In this regard, "hosts of devas" (*devakāya*) means a collection of devas. "We have come to this Dhamma-assembly" (*imaṃ dhammasamayaṃ*).
"Seeing that the host of devas had thus assembled, we too have come to this gathering of the Dhamma. For what reason?

'To see the unconquered Saṅgha'—the meaning is that we have come today to behold this unconquered Saṅgha, which has conquered the battle after crushing the three Māras this very day. Then, having spoken this verse, that Brahmā—
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood right at the eastern rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Then a second [monk] arrived in the same manner as described and spoke. In that context, "there, monks" (*tatra bhikkhave*) means the monks at that place of assembly.
"They concentrated" (*samādahaṃsu*) means they joined themselves with concentration (*samādhi*). "They made their own minds straight" means in their own minds...
Having removed all crookedness, curvature, and tortuousness, they made them straight.
"Like a charioteer holding the reins" means that just as when horses are moving evenly, a charioteer stands holding all the traces without urging or restraining them with the goad,
so too these five hundred [monks], endowed with the sixfold equanimity and guarding their sense doors, [stood]— all of them alike.
"The wise monks guard their sense faculties; it is to see them that we have come here, O Blessed One.
Having said this, he too went and stood in his very place.
Then the third one came and spoke in the same manner. In that context, "having cut the stake" refers to the stake of lust, hatred, and delusion.
"Having cut down": the "obstacle" (*paligha*) is indeed the obstacle of lust, hatred, and delusion;
the "city-gate bolt" (*indakhīla*) is indeed the city-gate bolt of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Having uprooted, they are unshakable":

these monks, being unshakable by the arrow of craving, having uprooted and completely eradicated the city-gate bolt, wander unhindered in the four directions. "Pure" means free from defilements. "Stainless" means spotless. This...
This is a synonym for that very term. "By the One with Eyes" means by the one possessing eyes through the five kinds of eyes.
"Well-tamed" means tamed in the eye, and likewise tamed in the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind. "Young elephants" means young *nāgas*. Herein, this is the etymological derivation:
they do not go (na gacchanti) under the influence of desire and so forth, thus they are *nāgas*; [they are so called] because the defilements have been abandoned by each respective path.
They do not come (*na āgacchanti*), thus they are *nāgas*; they do not perform various kinds of harm (*nānappakāraṃ āguṃ na karonti*), thus they are *nāgas*. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Mahāniddesa*.
Furthermore—
He does nothing whatsoever in the world,
having relinquished all fetters and bonds;
liberated, he clings to nothing anywhere.

“A nāga is called ‘such’ because of being such”—thus is the meaning to be understood here. “Susunāgas” means “excellent nāgas”; the meaning is that they have attained the perfection of being excellent nāgas.
“We have come to see the Blessed One, by whom such young nāgas as these have been tamed by an unsurpassed trainer of horses.”
He too went and stood in his very own place.

Then the fourth came and spoke in the same manner as before. "Those who have gone there" means those who have gone by way of taking refuge with full confidence. He too went and stood in his very own place.
This is the seventh [sutta]. 8. Commentary on the Sakalikasutta.
38. "In the Maddakucchi" means in a park of that name.
For when Ajātasattu was conceived in her womb, his mother thought, "This fetus in my womb will become an enemy to the king; what use have I for him?
and she had her womb massaged in order to cause an abortion. Therefore, it became known as "Maddakucchi. [Of the deer...]
However, because it was given for the purpose of providing a dwelling free from fear, it is called the Migadāya (Deer Park).
Now, at that time—the sequential account here is this:
Devadatta, having relied upon Ajātasattu and having employed both archers and Dhanapālaka, was unable to create an obstacle to the life of the Tathāgata.

Thinking, “I shall kill him with my own hands,” he climbed Vulture Peak Mountain, lifted up a rock the size of a large gabled house, and hurled it down, saying, “May the ascetic Gotama be reduced to powder!
It is said that he possessed great strength, equal to the power of five elephants. However, it is impossible for Buddhas to be harmed by the assault of another.
Thinking, "There might be a threat to my life," another rock rose up in the air and intercepted it as it was coming toward the Tathāgata’s body.
From the collision of the two rocks, a large splinter of stone flew up and struck the Blessed One from his back down to his feet; his foot felt as if it had been struck by a great axe.
With blood gushing forth, he appeared as if smeared with lac juice. The Blessed One looked upward and said this to Devadatta:
"Much demerit has been produced by you, O foolish man, you who, with a corrupted mind and a murderous intent, have caused the blood of the Tathāgata to flow.
From that time on, the Blessed One became unwell. The monks reflected:
“This monastery is desolate and uneven; it is unsuitable for many people, both kṣatriyas and others, as well as for those who have gone forth.
So they took the Tathāgata on a palanquin and carried him to Maddakucchi. Therefore it was said:
“At that time, the Blessed One’s foot had been wounded by a splinter.”
*Balavatiyo* means powerful. *Sudam* is a mere particle. *Dukkham* is the opposite of pleasure (*sukha*). *Tibbā* means intense. *Kharā* means harsh. *Kaṭukā* means sharp.
*Asātā* means not sweet. They are *amanāpā* because the mind does not incline toward them, nor do they cause the mind to incline or increase [in favor].
*Sato sampajāno* means being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding the endurance of feelings.
Having offered [the oblation]. "Without being afflicted" means not being oppressed, not falling under the sway of feelings that cause one to turn over and toss about.
Regarding the "lion’s posture": here there are four postures—the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures, the posture of the hungry ghosts, the lion’s posture, and the posture of the Tathāgata.
Among these, it is said: "Monks, for the most part, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side. This...
The posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures (*kāmabhogiseyyā*). For among them, there is generally no one who lies on their right side.
“Monks, for the most part, the departed spirits (*petā*) lie on their backs”—this is the posture of the departed spirits.

Because they have little flesh and blood, being merely a mass of interlaced bones, they are unable to lie on one side; they lie only on their backs. “Monks, for the most part, Sīha, the king of beasts... [the lion lies on his right side].
“Having tucked his tail between his thighs, he lies on his right side”— this is the lion’s posture (*sīhaseyyā*).
For the lion, the king of beasts, being preeminent in fiery energy (*tejussada*), places two of his forefeet in one place and his hind feet in another,
tucks his tail between his thighs, and [aligns] his forefeet, hind feet, and tail—
Having observed the place where [the other] stands, he lies down placing his head at the top of the two front feet;
even when waking after having slept for a whole day, he does not wake with alarm, but rather lifts his head and observes the place where the front feet and so forth stand.
If [any part] has moved from its position, [he thinks]: "This is not yours."
Thinking, "This is not worthy of my birth nor of my courageous nature," he becomes displeased and lies right there;

he does not go out for his range of activity. But when [the lion] remains without abandoning him, thinking, "This is worthy of both your birth and your courageous nature," he rises up joyful and elated, stretches with the stretch of a lion, shakes his mane, and three times...
Having uttered the lion’s roar, he sets out for his almsround. As for the fourth jhāna posture, it is called the “Tathāgata-posture.
Among these, the lion’s posture is the one mentioned here. For this is indeed called the supreme posture because its physical demeanor is full of fiery energy (*tejo*).

“Placing foot upon foot” means placing the left foot upon the right foot. “Overlapping” (*accādhāya*) means having placed it slightly beyond, that is, having set it down so as to slightly extend over [the other].
For when one ankle touches the other, or one knee the other, constant pain arises, the mind does not become one-pointed, and the bed becomes uncomfortable.
When they are placed so as not to touch each other, by being set apart, no pain arises, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the bed is comfortable. Therefore, he lay down in this manner.
“Mindful and clearly comprehending” means being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension that attend to the act of lying down.
The phrase “perception of rising” is not mentioned here because this was the Tathāgata’s bed of illness.
“Seven hundred”—in this sutta, all those deities came to the place where he lay on his sickbed. “He uttered an inspired utterance” (udānaṃ udānesi).
Those who have come to the sickbed might well be overcome with sorrow; however, seeing the Tathāgata’s endurance of these sensations, they thought:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of the Buddhas! Even while such sensations as these are occurring, there is not even the slightest change.
He lies with his body unmoving, like a golden statue placed upon a bed of honor and adorned for display."
“Now his facial complexion shines with even greater brilliance; endowed with radiance like the full moon, his face now glows like a blossomed lotus;
and the sphere of color on his body now becomes serene, like well-polished gold,” such was the inspired utterance that arose.
"Truly a nāga you are!"—here, "bhoto" is an address using the term *dhamma*. He is a *nāga* in the sense of being powerful. "Like a *nāga*" means by way of the state of a *nāga*.

In expressions such as "truly a lion," he is a lion in the sense of being fearless. In the sense of being well-trained through familiarity, or by knowing what is possible and what is impossible, he is a thoroughbred (*ājānīya*).
In the sense of being peerless, he is a leader (*nisabha*). For an ox (*usabha*) is the chief of a hundred cattle, while a bull (*nisabha*) is the chief of a thousand cattle.
A bull (*vasabha*) that is the leader of a hundred thousand cattle is called a *nisabha*. The Blessed One, however, claims the position of a leader (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) by virtue of being peerless;
it is for this very reason that he is here called a *nisabha*. He is a *dhorayha* in the sense of bearing the burden.
He is *danta* in the sense of being free from wickedness.
"Passā" means an unrestricted command. "Samādhi" refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship.

"Suvimutta" means well-liberated by the liberation of the fruit. However, a mind following after lust is called "inclined" (abhinata), while one following after hatred is called "depressed" (apanata).

By way of rejecting both of these, it is said to be "neither inclined nor depressed. "Neither constrained by volitional effort nor restrained" means not [constrained] by volitional effort (sasaṅkhārena).

The meaning is: those who have restrained and warded off the defilements by means of proper application; and because the defilements have been severed, they are composed through the concentration of fruition (*phalasamādhi*).
"To be transgressed" means to be harmed or disturbed. "Out of ignorance" means through lack of knowledge.
For it is said that Devadatta, being ignorant like a blind fool, would offend against such a Teacher—thus they speak while rebuking him.
"Pañcavedā" means those who uphold the five Vedas, with the Itihāsa as the fifth. "Sataṃ samaṃ" means for a hundred years.
"Tapassī" means having become dependent on asceticism. "Caranti" means wandering about.

"Na sammāvimuttaṃ" means that even if such Brahmins wander for a hundred years, their minds are not rightly liberated. "Hīnattarūpā na pāraṃ gamā" means they are of inferior nature and do not go to the further shore.
Thus, being of an inferior nature, they do not partake of Nibbāna.
There is also a reading, "hīnattharūpā," meaning those whose state is inferior, or those who have fallen away from their goal. "Overwhelmed by craving" (taṇhādhipannā) means overwhelmed by craving.

"Bound by vows and rules" (vatasīlabaddhā) means bound by such vows as the horse-vow and dog-vow, and by similar kinds of ascetic rules. They practice harsh austerities, such as the fivefold heat-exposure and lying on thorns.
*Tapaṃ*. Now, that deity, speaking of the liberating nature of the Teaching, said, "Not desiring honor," and so forth.
That has already been explained. [The Eighth. 9. Commentary on the First Sutta of Pajjunnadhītā.
39. "The daughter of Pajjunna": she is the daughter of the divine king Pajjunna, the rain-cloud deity belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings.
"I pay homage" means: "I worship your feet, Blessed One. "By the One with Vision": by the Tathāgata who possesses vision through the five kinds of eyes.
"The Dhamma has been awakened to": "This was previously heard by me only from others..."
"I was," he says. "I am now" means "I am at this present time. "I know as a witness" means I know it directly through the power of penetration (*paṭivedha*).
"Reproaching" means reproaching [it] by saying, "It has inferior syllables, words, and phrases," or "It is not conducive to liberation.
"Roruva" refers to two types of Roruva hells: Dhūmaroruva (Smoke-Roruva) and Jālaroruva (Net-Roruva). Among these, Dhūmaroruva is distinct.
Furthermore, *jālaroruva* is a name specifically for the Great Niraya of Avīci.
For there, while the fire is blazing and blazing, beings repeatedly utter cries; therefore, it is called "Roruva. *Ghora* means dreadful.

*Upetā khantiyā upasamena* means being endowed with the patience of having consented and asked for forgiveness, as well as with the patience of grasping [the Dharma] and the pacification (*upasama*) of lust and other defilements.
"And they have arrived. This is the ninth [verse].
10. Commentary on the Second Sutta of Pajjunna’s Daughter.
In the tenth [verse], by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the Dhamma and," the Saṅgha is also included; thus, it means that they have come here while paying homage to the Three Jewels.
She speaks. "Meaningful" means they possess meaning. "Even by way of many methods": whatever Dhamma she spoke, that Dhamma I would analyze even by way of many methods.
"Such a Dhamma": he shows that this Dhamma of the Blessed One is such—established in that, resembling that, and fit to be analyzed by many methods. "I shall expound": [he says this].

I shall speak. To the extent that it has been mastered by my mind—that which has been fully learned by me—I will explain its meaning in brief, without taking a day, just as one presses out a honeycomb in a single moment.
The remainder is self-evident. Thus ends the tenth [chapter].
The Fourth Chapter: The Section on the Satullapa Host.
5. The Chapter on the Blazing. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Blazing.
41. In the first discourse of the *Ādittavagga*, the phrase "by old age and by death" is merely a heading for the teaching;
however, the world is indeed ablaze with the eleven fires, beginning with passion (*rāga*). "By giving" means by the volition of giving.

"What is given is well-removed" means that through the volitions of the merit of giving, it belongs to the donor alone, just as goods removed [from a house] belong to the owner of the house; therefore, this was said. "Thieves carry it away" means...
Ill-gotten wealth is seized even by thieves and kings; fire consumes it; and even where it is kept, it perishes.
"By the end" means by death. "The body along with its possessions" refers both to the body itself and to the wealth that has not been lost due to thieves and the like.
"He goes to heaven" means he is reborn in the celestial realms, as was the case with the Great King Vessantara and others. First.
2. Commentary on the *Kiṃdada Sutta* 42.

Regarding the second [verse], "the giver of food": because even one who is very strong is unable to rise without having eaten two or three meals, whereas even one who is weak becomes endowed with strength after eating, it is therefore said, "the giver of food is the giver of strength. "The giver of clothing... [and so forth].
Because even one who is handsome becomes ugly, ill-clad, or naked, despised and unsightly; whereas one clothed in garments shines like a son of the gods, therefore it is said:
"He is a giver of clothing, a giver of beauty. "A giver of vehicles" means a donor of elephant-vehicles and so forth. Regarding those [vehicles], however:
"An elephant-vehicle is not suitable for a recluse..."
"One should not go by horse-carriage, nor by chariot;
this vehicle is appropriate for a recluse:
sandals that protect the aggregate of virtue."

Therefore, one who gives an umbrella, sandals, a staff, a bed, or a chair, as well as one who clears a path, constructs a ladder, builds a bridge, or prepares a boat—all these are indeed givers of vehicles.
It is called "a giver of happiness" because a vehicle brings about happiness.
It is called "an eye" because even for those possessing eyes, there is no seeing of forms in the darkness [without it].
He is called a "giver of lamps" and a "giver of eyes," and like the Elder Anuruddha, he also attains the perfection of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

He is a "giver of all" in the sense that he is a donor of everything, including strength and so forth. Even if one has wandered for alms through two or three villages and returned empty-handed, after bathing in a cool lotus pond and entering his dwelling, [he remains] for a moment...
For when one who has been lying on a couch rises and sits up, strength seems as if it were injected into his body.
And while wandering about outside, the visible-object base in his body is scorched by the wind and heat;
but for one who enters a sheltered place, closes the door, and lies down for a moment, the dissimilar continuity subsides and the similar continuity sets in.

It is as if the sphere of visible forms were brought in and placed inside. For one wandering outside, a thorn pierces the foot, a stump strikes him, and dangers such as reptiles as well as the fear of thieves arise;
but for one who has entered a shelter, closed the door, and lies down, none of those dangers exist. Likewise, for one reciting the Dhamma, there is the bliss of the joy of the Dhamma.
As he attends to the meditation subject, the bliss of tranquility arises. Likewise, as he wanders about outside, sweat breaks out and his eyes throb;
at the moment of entering his lodging, it is as if he has descended into a well, and the bed, chair, and other furnishings are no longer perceived.
But when he has sat down for a moment, the clarity of his vision returns as if a clear liquid had been poured in.
It appears as if it were real; the door-panels, windows, beds, chairs, and so forth, are all discernible. Therefore it is said:
"He is a giver of everything who gives a dwelling place.
And he is a giver of the Deathless, for he gives what is called the gift of immortality, as if filling a bowl with exquisite food.

“He who instructs in the Dhamma” means one who instructs in the Dhamma: he explains the commentary, recites the Canon, answers questions asked, points out meditation subjects, and organizes the hearing of the Dhamma; all such a person is said to “instruct in the Dhamma.
And it should be understood that among all gifts, this gift of the Dhamma alone is the foremost. For it has been said:
“The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts;
the flavor of the Dhamma surpasses all flavors;
the delight in the Dhamma surpasses all delights.”
“The destruction of craving conquers all suffering. Second. 3.
Commentary on the *Annasutta*. 43.
In the third [verse], “they rejoice” means they aspire. “He frequents” means he approaches, as in the case of the householder Citta, the Elder Sīvali, and others.
It follows after him like a shadow. Therefore—because it is only the giver of food who follows one both in this world and in the next—therefore.
The rest is self-evident. The third [sutta].
4. Commentary on the Ekamūla Sutta.
44. In the fourth [verse], "single-rooted" means that ignorance is the root of craving, and craving is the root of ignorance; however, here it is craving that is intended.
It is "twofold-turning" because it turns toward the two views of eternalism and annihilationism. And it is "three-stained" because of the three stains of lust and so forth.

Among these, delusion is its stain from the perspective of co-nascence, while lust and hatred are its stains from the perspective of decisive support (*upanissaya*). Furthermore, there are the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
Because she spreads out upon those five spreading-places, she is "five-spreading" (*pañcapattharā*).

And because she cannot be filled, she is the "ocean. Furthermore, because she turns toward and revolves within the twelve internal and external sense-bases (*dvādasāyatana*), she is "twelve-turning" (*dvādasāvaṭṭā*).
And because she has no firm footing, she is called the "abyss" (*pātāla*). [The verse says: "With a single root... the abyss; the seer crossed over, he went beyond."
The meaning is "he has transcended. This is the fourth [verse].
5. Commentary on the *Anoma-sutta* (Sutta 45):
Regarding the fifth, "of matchless name" (*anomanāma*), it means a name endowed with all virtues, a name that is complete; such is the meaning.
"Seeing subtle meanings": the Blessed One is a seer of subtle meanings because he perceives subtle matters such as the internal distinctions between the aggregates (*khandha*).
"Giver of wisdom": he is the bestower of wisdom by way of explaining the path for the attainment of analytical wisdom (*anvaya-paññā*). "Unattached to the mire of sensual pleasures":

he is unclinging to the mire of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). "Desiring": the Blessed One [desires] right there at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*mahābodhimaṇḍa*) by means of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

"He has gone; he does not go now," but this was said with reference to the past. "The Great Seer" (*mahesi*) means one who seeks or searches for the great aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth.
The fifth [discourse]. 6. Commentary on the *Accharā-sutta*.

46. Regarding the sixth [verse], "resounding with throngs of celestial nymphs": it is said that this son of the gods, having gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation and fulfilling his duties and observances, celebrated the *pavāraṇā* at the end of five years;
having mastered the two Matikas and learned what is proper and improper to do, he took up a meditation subject according to his own preference. Living a simple life, he entered the forest.
The Blessed One had prescribed the middle watch of the night as the portion for lying down.
When that time arrived, thinking, "I fear negligence," he lifted up his bed and, without food, devoted himself to his meditation subject day and night.
Then, internal winds like those of a surgeon arose within him and took his life. He remained right there at his post.

He passed away. For any bhikkhu who passes away while walking on the walking-path, or standing leaning against a support-pillar, or sitting with his robe placed on his head at the end of the walking-path, or lying down, or preaching the Dhamma from the decorated Dhamma-seat in the midst of the assembly—all such pass away while still in the midst of their duties (*dhura*). Thus, this [occurrence] on the walking-path...
Having passed away, because his supporting conditions were weak, he did not attain the destruction of the taints;
instead, he took rebirth like one awakening after sleeping at the gate of a great celestial mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
At that very moment, his personal existence manifested, three gavutas in height, like a golden archway.
In the celestial mansion, about a thousand nymphs, seeing him and thinking, "The lord of this mansion, a son of the gods, has arrived;
let us delight him," took up musical instruments and surrounded him. The son of the gods did not yet know that his time had come to pass away;
perceiving himself as one who had gone forth, he looked at the nymphs with shame, like a wearer of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika) upon seeing a woman who had come on a pilgrimage to a monastery. Above...
Adjusting his thick *dukūla* robe so that one shoulder was bared, he covered his shoulder-blade, lowered his sense-faculties, and stood with his head bowed.
By that very movement of his body, those deities recognized, “This is a son of the gods who has become a recluse,” and said:
“Noble sir, son of the gods, this is called the world of the gods; it is not a place for performing the duties of a recluse. [Enjoy] prosperity...”
“...the opportunity for experiencing [it]. He remained standing just as he was. The deities, thinking, “He does not yet perceive it,” played musical instruments.
Even then, he remained standing without looking around.
Then they placed a mirror before him that reflected his entire body. Seeing his reflection and realizing that he had passed away, he—
“I did not practice the ascetic life aspiring for this state;

I practiced it aspiring for the supreme goal, Arahantship,” he felt regret for his attainment, like a wrestler who has entered the arena thinking, “I will win a golden cloth,” but instead receives a handful of roots. He thought: “This is what is called the attainment of heaven.”
Thinking, “The appearance of Buddhas is rare,” he did not enter his celestial mansion;
instead, with unbroken virtue, surrounded by a host of nymphs, he approached the presence of the One Possessing Ten Powers, paid homage, stood to one side, and recited this verse.
Therein, “resounding with a host of nymphs” means it was filled with the sounds of singing and instrumental music by a multitude of nymphs. “Frequented by hosts of *pisācas*”:
He speaks of that very host of celestial nymphs (*accharāgaṇa*) as a "host of *pisācas*. He speaks with reference to the Nandana Grove (*nandanavana*).
For, due to his state of mind fixed on the path to liberation (*niyāma*) and the weight of his own dignity, he does not wish to call the assembly of gods a "host of gods";
instead, he calls it a "host of *pisācas*. And he does not call the Nandana Grove "Nandana," but rather "Mohana" (the Deluder). How so?

Thinking, "A journey will take place," he says, "Tell me, Blessed One, how the departure shall be, how the transcendence shall be, and explain to me the insight that serves as the proximate cause for my attainment of Arahatship.
Then the Blessed One, reflecting, "This son of the gods is indeed too much abraded; what now might this be? examines his own [mind].
Knowing that he had gone forth in the Dispensation, [the Teacher] thought: "Having passed away due to excessive energy, this man has been reborn in the world of the devas;
even today his physical form has appeared upon the walking-path, sustained by unbroken virtue.
And Buddhas, like a master painter who has not yet applied his intent to a beginner who has not yet prepared the wall, [do not immediately teach the highest Dhamma].
"Just as [the Teacher] first explains the preliminary practice, saying: 'First, purify your virtue; develop concentration;

straighten your wisdom regarding the ownership of kamma,' but then explains only the subtle and delicate insight into emptiness—which serves as the proximate cause for the path to Arahatship—to one who is already engaged and striving in practice;
and this son of the gods is such a practitioner of unbroken virtue."
Saying, "There shall be one path for the future," he spoke the words beginning with "It is called straight" while explaining insight into emptiness (*suññatā-vipassanā*).
Therein, "straight" refers to the Eightfold Path being called straight because of the absence of bodily crookedness and so forth.
"That direction is called fearless" is said with reference to Nibbāna; for in that there is no fear whatsoever, nor is there fear for one who has attained it.
"It does not exist" refers to what was said: "That direction is called fearless. "A chariot that makes no noise" intends the Noble Eightfold Path.
For just as an ordinary chariot creaks and rattles when its axle is unlubricated or when excessive people have mounted it, the Noble Path does not do so.
Indeed, even if eighty-four thousand living beings were to mount it all at once, it would not make a sound.

It does not creak and it does not shriek; therefore, it is called "not creaking" (*akūjana*). "Endowed with the wheels of Dhamma" means endowed with the wheels of Dhamma consisting of bodily and mental energy (*vīriya*).
Here, by the mention of "moral shame" (*hiri*), "moral dread" (*ottappa*) is also necessarily included. Its "protection" (*apālamba*) is like that of an external chariot.

Just as there is a wooden hand-rail for warriors standing on a chariot to prevent them from falling, so too for this chariot of the path, conscience and shame (*hirī-ottappa*) arising internally and externally serve as the hand-rail.

"The surrounding of mindfulness" means that just as a chariot is surrounded by a covering of lion-skin and so forth, so too for this chariot of the path, the associated mindfulness serves as the surrounding. "The Dhamma... [is as follows].
The supramundane path. "Preceded by right view" means that its preliminary movement (*pubbayāyikā*) is preceded by the right view of insight; thus it is "preceded by right view.
For just as a king sets out only after the road has been cleared beforehand by royal officers through the removal of the one-eyed, the lame, and so forth, even so is insight.

When the aggregates and so forth have been purified by means of right view through their impermanence and other characteristics, the right view of the path subsequently arises, fully understanding the state attained on that ground.
Therefore it was said: "I call Dhamma the charioteer, with right view as its forerunner.
Thus, having concluded his teaching, the Blessed One illuminated the Four Truths at the end. At the conclusion of the discourse...
The son of the gods was established in the fruit of stream-entry. For just as when a king is at his meal and a morsel the size of his own mouth has been lifted,
his son sitting on his lap makes a morsel of exactly that same size for himself, even so,
while the Blessed One was delivering a teaching culminating in Arahantship, beings [attained] the fruits of stream-entry and so forth according to their respective underlying predispositions.
They attain [the fruits]. This divine son, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), departed after worshipping the Blessed One with perfumes and other offerings.
The sixth [sutta]. 7.
Commentary on the *Vanaropa-sutta*.
47. Regarding the seventh verse, "Those established in Dhamma, endowed with virtue": he asks who are those established in Dhamma and who are those endowed with virtue.
The Blessed One, illustrating this question by means of the story of Thāvara, spoke the verse beginning with "The planter of groves.

Therein, "planters of groves" refers to those who plant flower-groves and fruit-groves. "Planters of woods" refers to those who, having demarcated a boundary around naturally occurring or planted forests, [establish] shrines (*cetiyas*), Bodhi-trees, walking-places (*caṅkamas*), pavilions, huts, caves, night-quarters, and day-quarters.
Those who plant trees that provide shade and give them away are indeed called "planters of groves.
"Bridge-builders" are those who construct bridges over uneven terrain or prepare boats for crossing water. "Well-diggers" refers to a hall for the distribution of drinking water.
"Wells" refers to any such thing as a lotus pond or a reservoir. "Shelters" refers to a dwelling house; the reading "upāsaya" also occurs.
“Merit always increases”: it does not increase for one who is thinking unwholesome thoughts or for one who is sleeping.
Rather, whenever one recollects [the Buddha], at that very moment his merit increases. It is with reference to this meaning that it is said, “Merit always increases.
“Established in the Dhamma, perfected in virtue”: because they are established in that Dhamma, by means of that very virtue...
"Established in the Dhamma and endowed with virtue. Alternatively, for those performing such meritorious deeds, the ten wholesome states (*dasa kusala-dhammā*) are fulfilled;
because they are established in these, they are "established in the Dhamma. And because they are endowed with that very same virtue, they are "endowed with virtue. This is the seventh [sutta]. 8.
Commentary on the *Jetavana-sutta*.

48. In the eighth [verse], "For this is that Jeta’s Grove," the divine son Anāthapiṇḍika spoke thus upon arriving for the purpose of praising both Jeta’s Grove and the Buddha and his followers. "Resorted to by the host of seers" means resorted to by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having thus described the praise of Jeta’s Grove in the first verse, he now speaks of the Noble Path, saying:
"Action, knowledge," and so forth. Therein, "action" (kamma) is the volition of the path; "knowledge" (vijjā) is the wisdom of the path; and "Dhamma" refers to the factors conducive to concentration.
*Dhammā*. "Virtue is the supreme life" shows that for one established in virtue, life is supreme.
Alternatively, *vijjā* refers to right view and intention; *dhamma* refers to effort, mindfulness, and concentration; *sīla* refers to speech, action, and livelihood. "The supreme life":
for one established in this virtue, what is called "life" is indeed supreme. By this, mortals are purified.
By this Eightfold Path, beings are purified.
"Therefore" means because they are purified by the path, and not by lineage or wealth; therefore.

"One should wisely investigate the Dhamma" means one should investigate the factors conducive to concentration by means of the proper method. "In this way, one is purified therein" means in this manner, within that Noble Path.
He is purified. Alternatively, "one should wisely investigate the Dhamma" means one should investigate the Dhamma of the five aggregates by means of skillful methods.
"Thus one is purified therein" means thus one is purified regarding those four Truths.
Now, speaking in praise of the Elder Sāriputta, he said: "Sāriputta... and so forth. Therein, "Sāriputta" means:
This is a statement of emphasis; he says that among these qualities such as wisdom, Sāriputta alone is superior. "By means of tranquility" means by the tranquility of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"Gone to the further shore" means gone to Nibbāna. He says that any bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna may be considered the very limit of excellence, for there is no one superior to the Elder. The rest is self-evident. The eighth [chapter].
9. Commentary on the *Maccharisutta* 49.

Ninth: “The stingy” (*maccharino*) means those possessed of stinginess (*macchera*). For a certain person, even when a bhikkhu extends his hand in the place where he himself dwells, does not pay homage;
yet, having gone elsewhere and entered a monastery, he pays homage with due respect.
He offers a sweet welcome, saying: "Venerable sir, please do not come to our dwelling place;
it is a well-provided area, and we are capable of attending to the noble ones with rice porridge, alms-food, and other necessities.
Thinking, "This lay follower is faithful," the bhikkhus favor him with rice porridge, alms-food, and so forth. Then, one elder went to that village for alms.
He goes about [for alms]. Upon seeing him, he either takes another path or enters a house.
Even if he comes face-to-face with him, he greets him by bowing with his hand and departs, saying: "Give alms to the venerable one; I am going on some business.
The elder, having wandered through the entire village, goes out with an empty bowl. This, first of all, is soft stinginess.
This is the name by which one who possesses it appears as a donor even though he is not a donor.
Here, however, what is intended is stubborn stinginess (*thaddhamacchariya*), by which one who possesses it— when monks have entered for alms and it is said,
"The elders are standing"— says things such as, "Do my feet ache?", and remains as stiff as a stone pillar or a stump.
"Having offered, he stands [there], nor does he perform the proper salutation. "Miserly" (*kadariya*) is a synonym for the term "stingy" (*maccharin*).
For even mild stinginess is called simply "stinginess," whereas that which is harsh is called "miserliness" (*kadariya*). "Abusive" (*paribhāsaka*):
having seen the monks standing at the door of the house, [he says], "Have you come after plowing? Have you come after sowing?"
"Having washed [us], why do you wash us again? We cannot even find ourselves, so how could we find you? Depart quickly!"—with such words they were revilers.
