"Causers of obstacles" means they create obstacles for the donor regarding heaven, for the recipients regarding gain, and for themselves regarding their own welfare;
thus, they are makers of these obstacles.
“Samparāya” means the world beyond (the next world). “Rati” means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. “Khiḍḍā” refers to the three kinds of play, beginning with physical play.
“Vipāko diṭṭhe dhamme” means that this is the result in the very life in which it has arisen.
“Samparāye ca duggati” means that in the future life there is an unhappy destination, as expressed by the phrase “they are reborn in the world of Yama.”
"Generous" (vadaññū): although the monks standing at the door of a house remain silent, in substance they are indeed saying, "Give alms.

In this regard, those who share out what is to be given—thinking, "We cook, but these [monks] do not cook; having approached those who cook, if they receive nothing there, where will they obtain it?"—they are called generous. They shine forth.
They shine with the radiance of celestial palaces (*vimāna*). "In those gathered by others" means in those assembled by others.

"And a happy destination in the future life" refers to a happy destination in the future life as it is said, "These are the heavens. Or alternatively, for both of these, after falling away from there, there is again only an unhappy or happy destination in the future life. The ninth [chapter].
10. Commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta 50.

In the tenth [verse], "reborn" (*upapannāse*) means having approached by way of rebirth. "Liberated" (*vimuttā*) means that immediately upon being reborn in the Aviha Brahma-world, they were liberated by the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship.
"The human body" (*mānusaṃ dehaṃ*) refers here specifically to the five lower fetters (*pañcorambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
[These words] have been spoken. "The celestial yoke" (*dibbayoga*) refers to the five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*). "They have transcended" (*upaccaguṃ*) means they have surpassed them.

*Upaka* and so forth are the names of those elders. Regarding the phrase "you speak what is wholesome for them": one who possesses this word "wholesome" (*kusala*) is called "one who speaks what is wholesome" (*kusalī*).
You speak—that is, you proclaim, praise, and extol—the wholesome and blameless [teachings] of those elders; you are wise.
"He says 'devaputta' (son of a god). "Having understood that Dhamma here" means those elders, having known that Dhamma here within your dispensation.

"Profound" means profound in meaning. "A celibate practitioner free from worldly attachment" refers to one who is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), meaning he became a non-returner. "Ahuvā" means "was. "Sagāmeyyo" means a resident of the same village. This is the concluding verse.
"Established by the compilers of the collection. Tenth.
The Fifth Chapter on Burning.
6. The Chapter on Aging.
1. Commentary on the Jarā-sutta 51.
In the first [sutta] of the Jarā-vagga, the response “it is good” is excellent. By the phrase “virtue until old age,” this is shown:
just as ornaments such as pearls, gems, and colored cloths shine only during youth, but not at the time when one is worn out by old age.
One who maintains those [unwholesome habits] incurs the reproach: “Even now this person seeks childishness;

he is surely mad. But such is not the case with virtue. For virtue shines at all times. Indeed, even when one guards virtue during childhood, there are no critics who say, “What is the use of his virtue?
This remains true during middle age and even in old age.
"Faith is good when firmly established": faith that has arrived by way of the Path, as in the case of Hatthāḷavaka, Cittagahapati, and others, is called "firmly established faith," and it is good.
Regarding the phrase "wisdom is the jewel of men," here "jewel" (ratana) should be understood in the sense of being honored and so forth. For this has been said:
"If a jewel is that which is honored, is not the Blessed One honored—the lion among men—and are not those who are honored in the world [also jewels]?"
The Blessed One is honored by them. If a "jewel" (ratana) is that which brings delight, is not the Blessed One the one who brings delight, the lion among men?
Those who act according to his word take delight in the bliss of the joy of meditative absorption (jhāna-rati-sukha).

If a "jewel" is that which is incomparable (atulya), is not the Blessed One the incomparable lion among men? For it is impossible to weigh him, having reached the perfection of qualities, by means of qualities. If a "jewel" is that which is difficult to obtain...
"A jewel! Is the Blessed One not indeed a rare lion among men?
If a 'jewel' is that which is for the enjoyment of extraordinary beings, is the Blessed One not extraordinary in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation?
However, here wisdom is called a "jewel" in the sense of its rare manifestation. "Merit" refers to meritorious volition; for because it is immaterial, it cannot be taken away. First.
2. Commentary on the *Ajarasā-sutta* (Sutta 52).
In the second [verse], "by non-decay" (*ajarasā*) means by not decaying; the meaning is "by non-failure. For virtue that has not failed is truly good.
One whose virtue has failed is not even supported by teachers, preceptors, and others; wherever he goes, he is simply cast out. This is the second [sutta].
3. Commentary on the *Mittasutta* 53.
In the third [verse], "a caravan" (*sattha*) refers to a traveling party, whether by foot or by cart.
A "friend" (*mitta*) is one who, when illness arises, carries one away by palanquin or some other vehicle and brings one to safety; thus he is a friend. "In his own home" means in his own house.
In the home. When such a disease arises, sons, wives, and others feel revulsion; yet the mother regards even the impure as if it were sandalwood.
Therefore, she is a friend in one's own house. Regarding "a companion in times of need":

he who carries out and brings to completion a task that has arisen is a companion (*sahāya*)—a friend—by virtue of traveling together (*saha-ayanabhāva*) through those duties. [This excludes] companions in drinking liquor and the like.
But they are not true friends. "For the sake of the future life" means for the benefit of the next world. Third. 4.

Commentary on the Vatthusutta (The Discourse on the Support) In the fourth [discourse], "Sons are the support": in their old age, sons are the support in the sense that they provide care. "The supreme friend": because she is a fit person to whom even secrets—which should not be told to others—may be spoken, the wife is called the supreme friend. Fourth.
5–7. Commentary on the First Janasutta, etc. 55.
In the fifth [sutta], "runs about" (*vidhāvati*) means that he runs hither and thither by way of traveling to other oceans and so forth. This is the fifth. 56.
In the sixth, "suffering" (*dukkhā*) refers to the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). This is the sixth.
57. In the seventh [verse], "the ultimate resort" (*parāyaṇa*) means accomplishment and support. This is the seventh [chapter]. 8.
Commentary on the *Uppatha-sutta* (The Wayward Path) 58.

In the eighth [verse], "lust is the wayward path" (*uppatho*) means it is not the path for one going toward a happy rebirth (*sugati*) and Nibbāna. "The wasting away of night and day" (*rattindivakkhayo*)...

It wastes away day and night, or during the days and nights. "Woman is impurity" (*mala*): the rest [of the verse] refers to external impurity, which can be cleansed by washing with ashes, lye, and so forth;
however, one who is defiled by the impurity of the female sex cannot be made pure—thus, woman is called "impurity.

"In this regard": in this matter, regarding woman, offspring cling. "Austerity" (*tapa*): [refers to] the restraint of the sense faculties, the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), virtues, energy, and the performance of difficult deeds.

This is the name [of the first sutta]. Here, however, with the exception of the practice of self-mortification (*dukkarakārikā*), every form of practice that scorches the defilements (*kilesa*) is permissible.
"The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means abstention from sexual intercourse. This is the eighth [section].
9. Commentary on the Second Sutta.
59. "In what does one take delight? means in what is he delighted? "The second" refers to the companion of one who goes to both a happy destination and Nibbāna.
"And wisdom governs him" means that wisdom instructs this person, saying, "Do this; do not do that. This is the ninth [verse]. 10.
Commentary on the *Kavi Sutta* (The Poet).
60. In the tenth [chapter], "metre is the source" means that metre, such as *gāyattī* and so forth, is the source of verses (*gāthā*).
For one beginning a verse with a prior introductory line begins by asking, "By which metre shall it be?

"Manifestation" (*viyañjana*) means generating. Indeed, a syllable generates a word; a word generates a verse; and a verse clarifies the meaning. "Dependent on names" means dependent on designations such as "ocean" and so forth.
For when one begins a verse, one begins by depending on some name, whether it be the ocean or the earth.
"Abode" (āsaya) means a foundation. For verses proceed when they have been composed; he is their foundation. This is the tenth [sutta].
The sixth chapter, the Jarāvagga, is concluded.
7. Addhavagga 1.
Nāmasuttavaṇṇanā 61.
In the first [sutta] of the Addhavagga, "nāmaṃ sabbaṃ addhabhavi" means that name overcomes and pervades everything.
Indeed, there is no being or formation that is liberated by means of a spontaneously born name or a conventional name.
For even in the case of a tree or a stone about which people do not know "this is its name," it has the name "nameless" itself. First.
2–3. Commentary on the Cittasutta and others.
62. In the second [verse], "all indeed follow its control": this is the exhaustive inclusion of those very things that fall under the control of the mind. This is the second. 63.
In the third as well, the method is exactly the same.
This is the third. 4–5. Commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta* and others.

64. In the fourth [verse], "What indeed is the fetter? means: what is his fetter, what is his bond? "Investigation" (*vicāraṇa*) refers to the feet; the singular is used for the plural. Investigation belongs to applied thought (*vitakka*); thus, applied thought is its feet. This is the fourth. 65.
In the fifth as well, the method is the same.
This is the fifth. 6. Commentary on the *Attahata-sutta*.

66. In the sixth [verse], *kenassubbhāhato* means "by what is he struck? (*abbhāhato*). The syllable *su-* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*). *Icchādhūpāyito* means "smoldering with desire" (*icchāya āditto*).
This is the sixth [verse]. 7–9. Commentary on the *Uḍḍita-sutta* and others: 67.
In the seventh [verse], *taṇhāya uḍḍito* means "overwhelmed by craving" (*taṇhāya ullaṅghito*). For the eye is indeed bound by the rope of craving.
The world is suspended from the ivory pegs of form; the ear and other [faculties] are suspended from sound and the other [objects]. Thus, the world is suspended by craving.

It is said that "the world is covered by death" because the karma performed in the immediately preceding existence is not distant—it lies within a single interval of consciousness—and yet, because beings are overwhelmed as if by a mountain by the powerful pain of the moment of death, they do not perceive it. This is the seventh [verse].
68. In the eighth [sutta], the question was asked by the deity in reverse order. This is the eighth. 69.
In the ninth, everything is quite clear. This is the ninth. 10.
Commentary on the Lokasutta.
70. “In what has the world arisen? means: he asks in what having arisen, the world is said to have arisen. “In the six” means:
when the six internal sense-bases (*āyatana*) have arisen, it is said to have arisen.

“He acts within the six” means: he forms intimacy with those very same six. “Depending on” means: it proceeds by depending on, approaching, and relying upon those very same [bases]. “Is vexed” means: [is afflicted].
In those very six [internal bases], one is distressed and oppressed. Thus, this question has come down by way of the internal sense-bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*);
however, it is appropriate to bring it forth by way of both the internal and external [bases]. For when these have arisen in the six internal sense-bases, they are said to be "arisen";
one forms intimacy with the six external [objects], and depending upon the six internal [bases], [one experiences] the six external [objects].
"He is tormented. Tenth. The seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Path (Addhavagga). 8.
The Chapter on Having Cut (Chetvāvagga).
1. Commentary on the Chetvā Sutta. 71.
In the first verse of the Chetvā-vagga, *chetvā* means having cut off or destroyed. *Sukhaṃ seti* means he sleeps happily because he is not scorched by the fever of anger (*kodhapariḷāha*).
*Na socati* means he does not grieve because his mental distress (*domanassa*) has been destroyed through the destruction of anger. *Visamūlassa*... [the root of the uneven]...
Of that which results in suffering. "Sweet at the end" (*madhuragga*):
when one returns anger for anger, reviles in return for being reviled, or strikes back for being struck, happiness arises; it is with reference to this that it is called "sweet at the end.
For in this context, the conclusion is what is meant by "the end" (*agga*). "The Noble Ones" (*ariyā*) refers to the Buddhas and others. First.
2. Commentary on the Rathasutta 72.
In the second [verse], it is called *paññāṇa* because one discerns by means of it. "The banner of the chariot":
for at the head of a great battle, having seen the banner from afar, the chariot becomes manifest [to others] as "this is the chariot of such-and-such a king. Therefore it was said:
“The banner is the sign of the chariot. Even fire is recognized from afar by its smoke. The kingdom of Coḷa is known as the kingdom of Paṇḍu;

thus even a kingdom is recognized by means of its king. Furthermore, even the daughter of a wheel-turning monarch is recognized only after she has obtained a husband, as “the wife of such-and-such a man.
Therefore, it was said: “Smoke is the sign of fire,” and so forth. Second.
3. Commentary on the Vittasutta 73.

Regarding the third [verse], "Faith is wealth here": because one who possesses faith obtains through faith even such riches as the supreme jewel and so forth, as well as the threefold excellence of family, the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure, and upon reaching the nine Brahma-worlds, finally even the vision of the deathless Great Nibbāna.
One obtains [this]; therefore, among riches such as gems and pearls, the wealth of faith alone is supreme. "Dhamma" refers to the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).

"Brings happiness" means it brings all forms of undefiled happiness, both with and without taints (*sāsavānāsava*). "Most excellent" means that in this world, among all flavors such as salt and sourness, truth alone is the sweetest.
For those established in truth, even a swift current— *Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be the beginning of a further illustration regarding the power of truth.*
It turns back even rivers, crushes even poison, wards off even fire, and makes even the gods rain;
therefore it is said that it is sweeter than all other tastes. They say that the life of one who lives by wisdom is the best;
for such a person living by wisdom, while remaining a householder, establishes themselves in the five precepts and provides offerings such as tickets for meals.

One lives by wisdom: either as a layperson, or as one gone forth who, having reflected on the purpose of the requisites acquired in accordance with the Dhamma—thinking, "This is for this purpose"—consumes them while taking up a meditation subject and establishing insight, thereby living by wisdom through the attainment of the noble fruits.
They say that such a person, a "wisdom-liver," lives the best kind of life. This is the third.
4. Commentary on the *Vuṭṭhisutta* 74.
In the fourth [verse], "seed" (*bīja*) refers to the seven kinds of grain-seeds that are best when they are sprouting;
for when those have risen, the country becomes secure and well-supplied with food. "Falling" (*nipatanta*) refers to the rain from clouds that is best; for when there is rain from clouds...
When there is [prosperity], various crops arise; the countryside becomes flourishing, secure, and well-supplied with food.
Among those who travel—those moving about on foot—the ox is the best. For by depending on them, beings dwell in happiness while consuming the five products of the cow.
Among those speaking in royal courts and similar assemblies, the son is the most excellent. For he [is the support] of his parents...
He does not speak what brings harm.
Having heard the previous question, "Knowledge is the best for those who soar," a certain deity standing nearby said out of her own inclination:
"O deity, why do you ask this question of the One of Ten Powers? I shall explain it to you."
He answered the question according to his own sectarian tenets. Then the other deity said to him: "O deity, you speak as one who is ruined;
you are so impudent and garrulous! I am the one asking the Blessed Buddha. Why did you answer me?
Having turned [the first deity] back, she asked that very same question of the One of Ten Powers. Then the Teacher, providing the answer to her, spoke the verse beginning with "Knowledge leaps up."

In this context, "knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of the four paths. For when it arises, it eradicates all unwholesome states; therefore, it is called "the best among those that fly upward.
"Ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to the great ignorance that is the root of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). For it is the worst among those who fall and sink downward.
Regarding the phrase "of those going forth," the Saṅgha is the peerless field of merit for those moving beings who travel on foot.
The Buddha is the most excellent. For when beings see him here and there with a clear mind, they attain safety. Regarding the term "Buddha":
whether he be one's own son or someone else, for anyone who speaks of him, the Buddha is the most excellent.
For by resorting to his teaching of the Dhamma, there is the release from bondage for many hundreds of thousands of living beings. This is the fourth [section].
5. Commentary on the Bhītā Sutta 75.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "What indeed is it that they fear here?"—what is it that they fear?

It is the Path (*magga*) that is spoken of through many causes by way of its thirty-eight objects (*ārammaṇa*), as it proceeds through various bases (*āyatana*). This being so, fearing what do these people cling to the sixty-two views (*diṭṭhi*)?
"He took [it]," he says. "Of vast wisdom" means of abundant wisdom, of overflowing wisdom. "He does not fear the next world":
when going from this world to the next world, he would have no fear. "Having set aside" means having put apart.
"Living in a house with abundant food and drink" means living in a house with much food and drink, like Anāthapiṇḍika and others. "Sharing" means even that which has been taken by a finger-tip.
He is one whose habit is to tear [food] with his fingernail and give it to another before eating himself. "Generous" (*vadaññū*) has the same meaning as already stated.
Now, having extracted the constituent parts of the verse, they should be shown: by the word "speech" (*vācā*), the four kinds of verbal good conduct are included;
by the term "mind" (*manasā*), the three kinds of mental good conduct; and by the term "body" (*kāyena*), the three kinds of bodily good conduct.
Thus, these ten courses of wholesome action are called the "factor of prior purification.
By the phrase "dwelling in a house with abundant food and drink," the requisites for sacrifice are included. "Faithful" is one factor; "gentle" is one; "generous" is one; and "charitable" is one.
Referring to these four factors, he said: "Established in these four qualities."

There is another method: the three factors beginning with "speech," the phrase "abounding in food and drink" includes the requisites for sacrifice, and "faithful, gentle, sharing, and generous" constitutes one factor. There is also what is called the "method of pairs": "speech and mind" is one factor;
"not committing evil deeds with the body while living at home with abundant food and drink" is the other.
One [verse] is: “Faithful and gentle”; one is: “Generous and kind-spoken. One who stands firm in these four qualities is said to be “established in the Dhamma.
When departing from this world for the next, he does not fear.
This is the fifth. 6. Commentary on the *Najīrati-sutta*.
76. Regarding the sixth [verse], "name and clan do not decay": the names and clans of past Buddhas are recited even unto this day;
therefore, it is said that they do not decay. However, the ancients say: "As time passes, they will no longer be known, yet there is simply no inherent nature of decay.
Regarding "laziness" (*ālasya*): it is slothfulness, by which one remains as if standing in a place where one has stood, or as if sitting in a place where one has sat.
He remains seated; even when rising from his seat, he does not maintain stability.
"Negligence" (pamāda) means negligence due to either sleep or the influence of the defilements (kilesa). "Non-exertion" (anuṭṭhāna) is the absence of energy in performing work at the time for work.

"Lack of restraint" (asaṃyama) is the absence of restraint in virtue (sīla), being one of loose conduct. "Sleep" (niddā) is an abundance of sleeping. Because of it, one sleeps even while walking, standing, or sitting.
"Even when lying down": *tandī* refers to adventitious fatigue caused by overeating and so forth. "Those six openings" refers to those six apertures or cavities.
"In every way" means in all manners. *Taṃ* is merely a particle. "One should avoid" means one should shun or abandon them. The sixth [chapter]. 7.
Commentary on the Sutta on Sovereignty (*Issariyasutta*).
77. "Sattame satthamalam" means a weapon seized by impurity. "Kiṃ su harantaṃ vārenti?"—what is it that they prevent while it is being carried away?

They prohibit its being taken away. "Vaso" refers to the exercise of command. "Itthī" (woman): because she is an article that must not be alienated, he said, "Woman is the supreme among articles, the most excellent of goods.
Alternatively, all Bodhisattas and Cakkavattis [are conceived] only within the mother's womb.
“They are being born,” he said, [referring to] “the woman is the best of treasures. Anger is the rust on the sword;

anger is like a sword seized by rust, or it is the rust upon the sword of wisdom, thus it is “rust on the sword. “Destruction” (*abbuda*) means a cause of ruin; the meaning is that thieves are the destroyers in the world.
“Carrying away” refers to one who goes taking *salāka*-food and so forth; for indeed, at the very time when the *salāka*-food and such are set out—
These things have been abandoned by people. A recluse who takes them away becomes dear to them;
those who do not take them away become remorseful on account of their loss of merit. This is the seventh [sutta].
8. Commentary on the Kāma-sutta.
78. Eighth: “He does not give himself away” means he should not give himself as a slave to another, with the exception of all bodhisattvas;
thus it is said. “He does not surrender [himself]” means he should not surrender himself to lions, tigers, and so forth, with the exception of all bodhisattvas;
thus it is said. “Wholesome” means gentle and soft. “Evil” means harsh speech. Eighth.
9. Commentary on the Pātheyya Sutta 79.
In the ninth [verse], "Faith binds the provisions for the journey": having generated faith, one gives gifts, guards moral discipline, and performs the Uposatha rites;
it is for this reason that it is so stated. "Fortune" (sirī) means sovereignty. "Abode" (āsaya) means a place of dwelling. Regarding sovereignty...
For indeed, when one has become intent upon this, enjoyments come to him from both land and water. Therefore this was said.
"He drags around" means he drags hither and thither.
The ninth [sutta]. 10. Commentary on the Pajjota Sutta.
80. “In the tenth [verse], ‘like a lamp’ (*pajjoto*) means like a light. ‘Awake’ (*jāgaro*) means like a wakeful brahmin. ‘Cattle are their companions in work, living together with their work’:
for those who live together with their work, cattle are indeed their companions in work; they are called ‘work-companions’ (*kamma-sahāyā*) and ‘work-duals’ (*kamma-dutiyakā*).
Agricultural work and so forth are accomplished together with herds of cattle. ‘The posture of cold’: cold for this sevenfold body...”
The mode of conduct is the means of livelihood. "Cold" refers to the plough. He says: "How indeed will he live, for whom not even a small portion of a field is tilled by ploughs?
This is the tenth. 11. Commentary on the Araṇa Sutta.

81. "Without conflict" (*araṇā*) means free from defilements (*nikkilesā*). "Lived" (*vusitaṃ*) means the dwelling has been lived. "Freedom" (*bhojisiyaṃ*) means the state of no longer being a slave. "Ascetics" (*samaṇā*) refers to ascetics whose taints are destroyed;
for they are, in an absolute sense, called "without conflict. "The lived does not perish" means that their dwelling in the Noble Path does not perish.
"They fully understand" means that, starting from the stage of the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), the trainees (*sekhā*) [understand] both the mundane and supramundane [realities].

"Having fully understood, they understand thoroughly. "Freedom" (*bhojissiya*) refers specifically to the constant state of being free from debt that belongs to those ascetics whose taints are destroyed.

"They pay homage" means they pay homage starting from the very day of their going forth. "Established" means established in virtue (*sīla*). "A female ascetic here" (*samaṇīdhā*) means an ascetic here.
"One of low birth" refers even to one who has gone forth from a family of outcasts (*caṇḍāla*). "Noble" (*khattiya*)—not only... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
"Even kṣatriyas, and even gods, pay homage to the ascetic who is endowed with virtue. Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].
This is the eighth chapter, the Chapter on Cutting.
Thus [ends] the *Sāratthappakāsinī*.
The commentary on the Devatāsaṃyutta of the Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā is finished. 2.
The Devaputtasaṃyutta.
1. First Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the First Kassapa Sutta. 82.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the *Devaputtasaṃyutta*: "A son of the gods" (*devaputta*) refers to those males who are born from the laps (*aṅka*) of the gods.

By name, these women are called *devadhītaro* (daughters of the gods). By way of name, one who is unknown is referred to as "a certain deity" (*aññatarā devatā*), while one who is well-known is referred to as "the son of a god named so-and-so" (*itthannāmo devaputto*).
Therefore, having said "a certain deity" below, it is said here "the son of a god.
They instruct; that is, they give instruction. It is said that this son of a god [was instructed] by the Blessed One in the seventh year after his enlightenment.
Having performed the Twin Miracle, he went to the city of the Thirty-three gods and, while teaching the Abhidhamma, spoke in the *Jhānavibhaṅga*:
“A ‘monk’ is a monk by convention; a ‘monk’ is a monk by profession. Thus he heard the exposition of the term “monk” being delivered:
“Think in this way; do not think in that way. Attend to the mind in this way; do not attend to it in that way.”
“Abandon this; enter upon and abide in this. Yet he did not hear such exhortation or instruction for bhikkhus from the Blessed One.
It was with reference to this that he said, “The Blessed One has proclaimed the bhikkhu, but has not instructed the bhikkhu.
Therefore—because you say that the instruction for the bhikkhu was not proclaimed by me—therefore... [taññevettha].
"May it occur to you" means: "May this instruction and exposition present itself to you.
For there are those who wish to speak on a question but are unable to do so by correlating it with the knowledge of omniscience;
or those who do not wish to speak but are able to do so; or those who neither wish to speak nor are able to do so.
The Blessed One did not make the burden of answering the question fall upon any of them. However, this son of the gods both desired to speak and was capable of speaking;
therefore, placing the burden upon him alone, the Blessed One spoke thus. He too answered the question.
In that context, "one should train in what is well-spoken" means one should train in that which is well-spoken—namely, that which is based on the Four Noble Truths and the ten bases of discourse.
One should train in the fourfold good verbal conduct based on the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
Regarding "the attendance upon ascetics" (*samaṇūpāsana*): that which is to be attended upon by ascetics is called "attendance upon ascetics";

it refers to the thirty-eight-fold meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and the meaning is that one should train in and cultivate that as well. Alternatively, attendance upon learned bhikkhus is also "attendance upon ascetics."
One should train for the sake of increasing wisdom by asking questions such as, “Venerable sir, what is wholesome? and so forth.

And for the sake of the tranquility of the mind, one should train in the tranquility of the mind by means of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Thus, three trainings have been explained by the son of the gods.
For by the first phrase, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) was explained; by the second phrase, the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*).
"By the calming of the mind, the training in higher consciousness"—thus, by this verse, the entire Dispensation (sāsana) is indeed revealed. First. 2.
Commentary on the Second Kassapa Sutta: 83.

In the second [verse], "one who meditates" means one who meditates with two jhānas. "One whose mind is liberated" means one whose mind is liberated through liberation from the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
"Reaching the heart's core" refers to Arahantship. "Of the world" refers to the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*).
"Independent" means independent of craving and views, or not dependent upon craving and views. "The benefit thereof" is the benefit of Arahantship. This is what is meant:
a bhikkhu who aspires to the benefit of Arahantship should be a meditator; he should be one whose mind is well-liberated.

Having understood the arising and passing away of the world, one should be independent. Furthermore, the "weaving-dharma" (*tantidhamma*) refers to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) in this teaching.
This is the second [sutta]. 3–4. Commentary on the *Māgha-sutta* and others:

In the third [sutta], *Māgha* is the name of a Sakka. Because he attained lordship over the gods by overcoming others through his conduct, he is called *Vatrabhū*. Alternatively, he is called *Vatrabhū* because he overcomes the asura named Vatra. This is the third [sutta].
85. The fourth [verse] has the same meaning as already stated. The fourth. 5.
Commentary on the Dāmalī Sutta 86.
In the fifth [verse], "he does not desire existence by that" means that for that reason he does not long for any kind of becoming (*bhava*). It is a sustained exertion.

This is not the case for a son of the gods; for one whose taints are exhausted, there is no completion of duties. Indeed, from the beginning, one whose taints are exhausted has exerted energy for the attainment of Arahantship.
Later on, thinking, "Let him not remain silent, but let him likewise make his energy firm and strive, thinking 'I have attained Arahantship,'" he spoke thus.
Then the Blessed One, thinking, "This son of the gods, instead of declaring the completion of duties for one whose taints are exhausted, speaks as if my teaching does not lead to liberation;
I shall declare the completion of his duties," said, "There is no duty," and so forth. It is said that this verse is not found interspersed among the three Piṭakas.
For elsewhere, the Blessed One has pointed out what is called a fault in energy.
It is not so. However, having set aside this son of the gods, he spoke thus for the purpose of showing the completion of duties for one whose taints are destroyed:

"In the past, while dwelling in the forest with his taints destroyed for the sake of destroying the taints, he applied energy by taking up a meditation subject; at a later time, if he so desires, let him do so, but if he does not desire it, let him dwell as he pleases."
Therein, they "plunge" means they find a firm footing. This is the fifth [verse]. 6.
Commentary on the *Kāmada Sutta*. 87.

Regarding the sixth [verse], "difficult to do": it is said that this son of the gods was formerly a practitioner of spiritual exercises (*pubbayogāvacara*), yet due to the abundance of his defilements, he required great effort.

Having suppressed the defilements and practiced the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he died before reaching the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*) due to the weakness of his prior spiritual support (*pubbūpanissaya*).
He was reborn in the world of the gods. Thinking, "I shall go into the presence of the Tathāgata and report the difficulty [of this practice]," he came and spoke thus.
In that context, "difficult" refers to that which is absolutely pure for ten years... up to sixty years.

The performance of the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) is indeed difficult. "Learners" (*sekha*) refers to the seven types of learners. "Endowed with virtue" (*sīlasamāhita*) means endowed and possessed of virtue.

"Firmly established" (*ṭhitatta*) means having a stable nature. Having thus answered the question asked, he now spoke the words beginning with "of one who has entered the homeless life" (*anagāriyupeta*) for the purpose of raising a further question. Therein, "of one who has entered the homeless life" (*anagāriyupeta*)...

For one who has entered the state of homelessness (*anagāriya*), even while dwelling in a seven-storied palace, a bhikkhu will simply take his bowl and robes and depart when an elder arrives and says, "This belongs to me. Therefore, he is called "one who has entered the homeless state.
"Contentment" (*tuṭṭhi*) means satisfaction with the four requisites. "By means of development" (*bhāvanāya*) means by means of the development of mental tranquility.
Having cut through the net of Death, those who delight day and night in the calming of the sense faculties steady their mind, which is otherwise difficult to steady.
Those whose minds are steadied, fulfilling contentment with the four requisites, do not weary.
Those who are content, fulfilling virtuous conduct (*sīla*), do not weary. Those seven types of trainees (*sekha*) who are established in virtue are noble ones (*ariya*).
They go having cut through the net of defilements, which is called the net of Death. "Difficult to traverse" means:

"It is true, Bhante, that those who delight in the calming of the faculties attain a concentration difficult to attain... [and so on] ...those established in virtue cut through the net of Death and go.
Why would they not go? But this, O Blessed One, is difficult to traverse and uneven.

He said, "A precipice. In this context, although the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is neither difficult to traverse nor uneven, there are nevertheless many perils on its preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapaṭipadā).
Therefore, it was spoken of in that way. They fall headlong—that is, with their heads downward by means of the head of knowledge (ñāṇasira).
And because they are unable to ascend the Noble Path, they fall instead into the path of the ignoble (anariyamagga).
They are so called. "The path equal to the Noble Ones": this very path is equal to the Noble Ones. "Even on the uneven":
even upon the uneven body of sentient beings, they remain even. The sixth [sutta]. 7. Commentary on the Pañcālacaṇḍa Sutta.

88. Regarding "in the seventh, in the crowded": there are two kinds of crowding—the crowding of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-sambādha*) and the crowding of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa-sambādha*).

Of these, it is the crowding of the hindrances that is intended here. "Opportunity" (*okāsa*) is a name for *jhāna*. "The bull who has withdrawn" (*paṭilīna-nisabha*) means the best among those who have withdrawn.
One who has "withdrawn" (*paṭilīna*) is said to be one who has abandoned conceit (*māna*). As it is said: "And how, monks, is a monk one who has withdrawn? [and so forth].
"It is so. Here, monks, a bhikkhu’s conceit ‘I am’ has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising.

"Paccalatthaṃsu" means they obtained. "Sammā te" refers to those who obtained mindfulness for the attainment of Nibbāna; they are also well-composed through supramundane concentration. Thus, mixed jhāna is spoken of. This is the seventh [section].
8. Commentary on the Tāyaṇa Sutta 89.
In the eighth [sutta], "purāṇatitthakaro" means a teacher who was formerly a *titthakara*. Here, "ford" (*tittha*) refers to the sixty-two views;
a "ford-maker" (*titthakara*) is a teacher who originates them. Namely: Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, ... [and so forth].
He was Saṅkicca. As for the "heretics," they are those such as Purāṇa and others. But how did this man, having generated such a view, come to be reborn in heaven?

It was due to his being a proponent of kamma. It is said that he gave offerings such as the Uposatha meals, established a system of care for the destitute, built rest-houses, had lotus ponds excavated, and performed many other meritorious deeds. By the result of that...
He was reborn in heaven, yet he understood the liberating nature of the Dispensation.

Thinking, "I shall go into the presence of the Tathāgata and speak verses connected with energy that are appropriate for the Dispensation," he approached and spoke the words beginning with "Cut the stream.
Therein, "cut" (*chinda*) is an unrestricted command. "Stream" (*sota*) refers to the stream of craving (*taṇhāsota*). "Exerting yourself" (*parakkamma*) means having exerted effort (*vīriya*).
"Having done. "Sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) refers both to the sensual pleasures of the defilements (*kilesakāma*) and to the sensual pleasures of the physical basis (*vatthukāma*).

"He dispels" means he removes them. "Oneness" (*ekatta*) refers to *jhāna*. This is what is meant: a sage does not attain, that is, does not obtain, *jhāna* without having abandoned sensual pleasures.
"If one should do it, let him do it"—if one should exert effort, one should indeed do so; one should not slacken that effort. "With firmness... [he should apply himself].
One should exert oneself and make it firm; for a wanderer who is lax is one whose renunciation is grasped with laxity.
"He scatters more dust" means he scatters even more defilement-dust on top. "It is better not to have done the misdeed" means it is indeed better that the misdeed was not committed at all.
"Whatever [else]" refers not only to having committed a misdeed, but to whatever else has been done that constitutes the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*).
Whatever is done laxly is of this very same nature. "Defiled" refers to the practice of self-mortification.
For in this teaching, the undertaking of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) for the sake of requisites is indeed defiled.
"Suspicious" means remembered with suspicion; it is that which is suspected and apprehended, thinking, "This too must have been done by him, and that too by him."
“Fundamental to the holy life” means being the beginning of the holy life of the Path, being its primary exertion. [This concludes] the eighth [sutta]. 9.
Commentary on the Moon Sutta (Candimasutta) 90.
Regarding the ninth: “The moon” refers to a son of the gods dwelling in the lunar mansion. “Everywhere” means in all [categories], such as the aggregates, bases, and so forth.
"Compassionate toward the world": for both you and him, it is exactly the same. "Hurrying": as if in haste. "You release":
this is a present tense verb used in the sense of the past. The ninth [verse]. 10.
Commentary on the Sūriya Sutta.

91. "The Sun" (*sūriyo*) refers to a son of the gods dwelling in the sun-deity’s celestial mansion (*vimāna*). "In darkness" (*andhakāre*) means in that which causes blindness by obstructing the arising of visual consciousness.
"He shines forth" (*virocati*) thus he is "Verocana. "Circular" (*maṇḍalī*) means having a circular shape.
"O Rāhu, do not swallow the one who moves in the sky"—this means he says, "O Rāhu, do not swallow the sun as it moves through the sky. But why does he say this to him?
Does he swallow? Yes, he swallows. For Rāhu’s body is vast:
in height it is four thousand eight hundred yojanas; its arm-span is twelve hundred yojanas; its thickness is six hundred yojanas; its head is nine hundred yojanas;
its forehead is three hundred yojanas; the space between its eyebrows is fifty yojanas; and its mouth—
The nostrils are two hundred yojanas [in length], the mouth-cavity is three hundred yojanas deep, and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet are two hundred yojanas in breadth.
The finger-joints are fifty yojanas [long]. Seeing the moon and sun shining, he became envious;
he descended onto their path of travel, opened his mouth, and stood there. [This was] the Moon Mansion.
The sun’s chariot is as if cast into the Great Hell measuring three hundred yojanas.
The deities dwelling in that chariot, terrified by the fear of death, cry out all at once.
Furthermore, that [tongue] sometimes covers the chariot with its hand, sometimes thrusts it beneath the jaw, sometimes rubs it against the tongue, and sometimes forms a cheek-puff.
As if eating, it places [the food] between its cheeks; yet, it is unable to restrain its speed.
If one were to stop it by forming a barrier, it would either break through that barrier and emerge, or it would pull back and lower itself.
Therefore, it moves together with the celestial chariot (*vimāna*). "My offspring"—thus say both the moon and the sun.
On the day the *Mahāsamaya Sutta* was preached, the sons of the gods attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Therefore, the Blessed One said, “My offspring”;
the meaning is, “He is my son. The tenth [chapter].
The first section.
2. The Chapter on Anāthapiṇḍika 1.
Commentary on the Candimasasutta 92.
In the first sutta of the second chapter, *kaccheva* means "like in a cleft. *Kacche* refers both to mountain clefts and river clefts.
“Ekodi nipakā” means those whose minds are one-pointed (ekagga) and who are endowed with the steadiness of wisdom (paññā-nepakka). “Satā” means mindful (satimant).

This is what is meant: those who, having attained the meditative absorptions (jhānas), dwell being one-pointed, wise, and mindful, will go safely like deer in a secluded mountain glen or a river valley. “Pāraṃ” means Nibbāna. “Ambujo” means a fish.

"Leaving behind strife" means leaving behind the defilements (*kilesa*). It is said that those who, having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), abandon the defilements through heedfulness, will go to Nibbāna like fish that have broken through a net. First.
2. Commentary on the Veṇḍu Sutta.
93. In the second [verse], *veṇḍu* is the name of that son of the gods. *Payirupāsiya* means having attended upon. *Anusikkhare* means they train.
*Siṭṭhipade* means in the words of instruction. *Kāle te appamajjantā* means those who practice heedfulness at the proper time.
This is the second [verse]. 3. Commentary on the Dīghalaṭṭhi Sutta.

94. In the third [sutta], "Dīghalaṭṭhi" means that in the world of the devas everyone is of equal measure, being exactly three *gāvutas* tall; however, because his physical form was long in the human world, he received this name.
Although he was reborn in the world of the devas after performing meritorious deeds, he appeared exactly as he did before. This is the third. 4.
Commentary on the Nandana Sutta.
95. In the fourth [verse], "Gotama," he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. "Unobstructed" (anāvaṭa):
for when the Tathāgata directs his omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), there is nothing—neither a tree nor a mountain—that is capable of obstructing it. Therefore he said, "unobstructed.
Having thus praised the Tathāgata, he spoke the words beginning with "Of what kind? while asking a question prepared in the world of the gods.
In this context, "he dwells having transcended suffering" means he lives having overcome suffering.

"Virtuous" refers to one who possesses mundane and supramundane virtue, an arahant whose taints are destroyed. Wisdom and the other qualities should also be understood as being mixed [both mundane and supramundane]. "They honor him" means they honor him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
This is the fourth [sutta]. 5–6. Commentary on the *Candana-sutta* and others.
96. "Without a foundation" (*appatiṭṭhe*) means without a basis below; "without a support" (*anālambane*) means without a prop above.

"Well-composed" (*susamāhito*) means well-concentrated both in access concentration (*upacāra*) and in absorption (*appanā*). "With mind sent forth" (*pahitatto*) means with a mind dispatched. "With delight and lust utterly destroyed" (*nandīrāga-parikkhīṇo*) means one whose delight and lust have been completely exhausted.

Delight and lust (*nandīrāgo*) refers to the three formative forces of karma (*kamma-abhisaṅkhārā*). Thus, by this verse, through the inclusion of the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*), [the meaning is established].
The five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are included; by the inclusion of the fetter of form (*rūpa-saṃyojana*), the five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are included;

and by means of delighting passion (*nandī-rāga*), the three formations of karma (*kamma-abhisaṅkhāra*) are included. Thus, he for whom these ten fetters and three formations of karma have been abandoned does not sink in the deep, great flood.
Or else, through the perception of sensual desire (*kāma-saññā*), there is existence in the sense-sphere (*kāmabhava*); through the fetter of form...

The existence of form (rūpabhava) is included; by its inclusion, the formless existence (arūpabhava) is likewise included. Through delight and lust (nandīrāga), the three types of karmic formations (kammābhisaṅkhāra) are included.
Thus, it is shown that he who has no such three formations within the three existences does not sink into the deep.
This is the fifth. 97. The sixth has the same meaning as already stated. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Subrahma Sutta 98.

Regarding the seventh [sutta]: It is said that the young deva named Subrahma, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, went to the Nandana grove for recreation and sat upon a seat prepared at the foot of a Pāricchattaka tree. Five hundred goddesses sat surrounding him.

Five hundred [women] climbed up the tree. One might ask: "Since even a tree a hundred yojanas tall bends down and comes within reach of the hand through the power of the deities' minds, why did they have to climb? It was because they were overcome by playfulness.
Having climbed up, they sang repeatedly with sweet voices and caused flowers to fall; taking them, the others [arranged them] in the form of single-stalked garlands and so forth.
They bind them together. Then, having climbed the tree, they die all at once by means of their life-cutting karma and are reborn in Avīci, where they experience great suffering.
Then, as time passes, a son of the gods [thinks]: "The sound of these women is no longer heard, nor do they drop flowers. Where [are they]?"
"Have they indeed gone? Reflecting thus, he saw that they had been reborn in hell;
overcome with grief for his beloved ones, he thought: "These have gone according to their karma, but how long is my own life-span?
He realized: "On the seventh day, I too shall pass away along with the remaining five hundred and be reborn in that very same place."

Having seen this, he was afflicted by an intense sorrow. Thinking, "In this world with its devas, there is no one capable of dispelling this sorrow of mine except for the Tathāgata," he went into the presence of the Teacher and recited the verse beginning with *niccam uttasantī*.
Therein, the word *idam* indicates his own mind; the second line is a synonym for the first; and *niccam* means...
And the meaning of the word *ca* (and) should not be understood as starting from the time he was reborn in the world of the gods;

rather, it should be known as "constant" starting from the time his sorrow arose. Regarding the phrase "when misfortunes have not yet arisen": this refers to those sufferings which will arise after seven days have passed from now.
And regarding the phrase "also when they have arisen": this refers to those [sufferings] of the five hundred nymphs in hell.
"Having seen these [sufferings] that have arisen and those yet to arise—thus, regarding these sufferings both present and future, my mind is constantly terrified;
I am as if burning within, O Blessed One"—in this way he shows it.

"There is no safety other than through the factors of enlightenment and the quality of asceticism (tapas)" means that apart from the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and the virtue of asceticism, there is no other way to find security.

The meaning is “I do not see. “From the relinquishing of all” means from Nibbāna. Although here the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) is mentioned first and the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) afterwards, in terms of actual meaning, the restraint of the sense faculties should be understood as coming first.
For when the restraint of the sense faculties is grasped, the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) is thereby grasped. Established in that, the bhikkhu...
One who is independent of support, having undertaken the ascetic quality known as the *dhutaṅga* practices, enters the forest and develops the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
While developing that, he simultaneously develops the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) together with insight (*vipassanā*).
The Noble Path that arises for him taking Nibbāna as its object—the Blessed One described this teaching by way of the Four Truths as "the relinquishing of all."
At the conclusion of the teaching, the young deva was established in the fruit of stream-entry. This concludes the seventh [sutta].
8–10. Commentary on the Kakudha-sutta and others:
Regarding the eighth, "the young deva Kakudha," it is said that he was the son of the attendant of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna in the city of Kola.
While still a child, living in the presence of the Elder, he developed jhāna and passed away, being reborn in the Brahma-world.
There too, they perceived him as none other than Kakudha Brahmā. "Nandasi" means you rejoice.
"What have you gained?"—for joy arises from obtaining something agreeable; therefore he spoke thus. "What has been won?"—for one who has [something]...
When a pleasing object, such as a robe, becomes worn out, one grieves; therefore, he spoke thus.
"Discontent does not overwhelm him" means that dejection does not overcome him. "Of one born to misery" means of one born to suffering, that is to say, one standing within the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
"Of one born to delight" means of one in whom craving has arisen. For such a person, misery—that is, the suffering of *saṃsāra*—has indeed arrived. "Suffering..."
For it is said: "One who has fallen into misery longs for pleasure. Thus, for one born into misery, there is delight;
and with the change of that pleasure, suffering surely arrives—thus, for one born into delight, there is misery.
The eighth [verse]. 100. The ninth is exactly as already explained. The ninth.
101. In the tenth [story], the word "a certain one" was spoken in order to demonstrate the power of the Elder Ānanda’s inferential wisdom (*anumāna-buddhi*). The tenth [story].
The second chapter.
3. The Chapter on Various Heretics (*Nānātitthiya-vagga*).
1–2. Commentary on the *Sivasutta* and others. 102.
The first [verse] of the third chapter has already had its meaning explained. First. 103.

In the second [verse], *paṭikacceva* means "just beforehand" or "first of all. *Akkhacchinno vajjhāyati* means "one whose axle is broken broods"; he ponders with intense anxiety. In the second verse, *akkhacchinnovā* means "as if one whose axle were broken. Second.
3–4. Commentary on the *Serīsutta*, etc. 104.

In the third [sutta], "giver" (*dāyaka*) means one whose nature is to give. "Master of giving" (*dānapati*) means that one gives as the master of whatever gift one bestows, not as a slave or a companion.
For he who enjoys sweet things himself while giving what is not sweet to others is [not a true master] of that which is called giving.
One who gives while being a slave to the gift to be given gives as a slave. One who gives only that which he himself consumes gives as a friend.
But one who maintains himself with whatever [food] and gives what is sweet to others gives as a husband, an elder, or a master. "I was such a person," he says.
Regarding the phrase "at the four gates": it is said that this king had two kingdoms, namely the Sindhava kingdom and the Sodhivākara kingdom, and his city was named Roruva.
At each of its gates, one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] arose daily, and within the city at the seat of justice, there were another hundred thousand.
Seeing such vast amounts of bullion and gold heaped up, he...
Having generated the knowledge that one is the owner of one’s own karma, he appointed his ministers, saying:
"Build alms-halls at the four gates and give gifts there from whatever income arises at each gate. Therefore it was said: "Gifts were given at the four gates.

Regarding the phrase "to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the needy, the destitute, and beggars": here, "ascetics" (samaṇā) refers to those who have entered the homeless life. "Brahmins" (brāhmaṇā) refers to...
To those who address others with the word "bho," and to those ascetics and brahmins whose evil has been stilled and whose evil has been cast out, he did not give anything.

"The wretched" refers to unfortunate, destitute people, such as those who are one-eyed, crippled, and so forth. "Travelers" refers to those journeying on the road. "Beggars" refers to those [who say]:
"What is given that is desirable, bestowed, lovely, pleasing, timely, and blameless—by giving, may the mind be gladdened; may you, sir, depart."
They wander about praising the virtue of giving by way of such passages as, "The Brahma-world... and so forth.
"Beggars" refers to those who wander about making requests, saying things such as, "Give even a handful," or "Give even a bowlful.
Because the first gate was obtained through the gift given to the women's quarters, there arose yet more wealth among the hundreds of thousands born therein.
Having dismissed the king’s ministers and appointed his own ministers, the queens gave a more magnificent gift than that which had been given by the king.
It was with reference to this that he said: "My gift has turned back," meaning that whatever gift of mine was being given there has now ceased.
The same principle applies to the other doors as well. "Koci" means in some place. "Dīgharattaṃ" means for a long time.
Eighty thousand years. It is said that for such a length of time, alms were given by that king. Third. 105.
The fourth [section] has its meaning already explained. Fourth. 5.
Commentary on the Jantu Sutta.
106. "Dwelling among the Kosalans in the fifth [chapter]" means that having received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the presence of the Blessed One, they went there and dwelt.

"Agitated" (*uddhata*) means being of an agitated temperament due to perceiving the unallowable as allowable, the allowable as unallowable, the blameless as blameworthy, and the blameworthy as blameless. "Arrogant" (*unnaḷa*)...
"High-proud" means those whose empty conceit has arisen; this is what is meant.
"Fickle" means possessed of fickleness through such things as the ornamenting of one's bowl and robes. "Garrulous" means harsh-mouthed; this is meant by "harsh-spoken.
"Loose-tongued" means having unrestrained speech, those who chatter away in vain words even throughout the day. "Forgetful" means those whose mindfulness is lost, devoid of mindfulness; here—
In this context, they forget what has been said. "Lacking clear comprehension" means devoid of wisdom (*paññā*).

"Unconcentrated" means lacking both access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*), like a boat tied up in a violent current. "With wandering minds" means with unsettled minds, like wild deer that have stepped onto a path.
"With unguarded faculties" means that, due to the absence of restraint, their faculties are wide open, just as they were during the time of being householders.
*Jantu*: a son of the gods with that name. *Tadahuposathe*: on that Uposatha day; the meaning is "on the Uposatha day. *Pannarase*: on the fifteenth [day];
this is a rejection of the fourteenth and other such days. *Upasaṅkami*: he approached for the purpose of exhortation. It is said that he thought:
"These monks have gone out after receiving a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the presence of the Teacher; now..."
“They are living negligently; moreover, when they are admonished while sitting in their separate places, how will they take it to heart?
I shall admonish them when they have assembled. Having thus resolved, he approached them on the Uposatha day once he knew they had gathered together.
“He addressed them with verses” means that, standing in the midst of them all, he spoke these verses.
In this context, because the faults of one devoid of virtue become manifest along with the discourse on virtue, he therefore spoke first of virtue, saying:
"In former times they lived happily," and so forth. Therein, "in former times they lived happily" means that previously the bhikkhus were easy to support and easy to maintain;
having wandered for alms in regular order through high and low families, they sustained themselves with whatever mixed alms-food they obtained.
He spoke thus with this underlying intention (*adhippāya*). "Without desire" means having become free from craving (*nittaṇhā*).
Having thus spoken in praise of the ancient bhikkhus, he now speaks of their dispraise, saying "they are difficult to support," and so forth.
In that context, "like village headmen in a village" means just as village overseers (*gāmakuṭā*) in a village oppress people in various ways [to obtain] milk, curd, rice, and so on.
"Having had [food] brought, they eat"—saying this, he intends: "In the same way, you too, established in improper search (*an-esanā*), should maintain your livelihood.
"They lie down" means that, being indifferent to recitation, questioning, and mental attention (*manasikāra*), they lie down with their hands and feet stretched out upon the bed.
"In other houses" means in the houses of others; the meaning is: among the families' daughters-in-law and so forth. "Infatuated" (*mucchitā*)...
"Intoxicated by the intoxication of defilements.
"Some" refers specifically to those for whom such a description is appropriate. "Cast away" means discarded. "Helpless" means without support.
"Pettas" (spirits) are deceased humans discarded in a charnel ground. For just as those discarded in a charnel ground are devoured by various birds and other creatures, [so too are they].
Even their kinsmen do not perform the duties of a protector for them; they do not guard them, nor do they protect them.

In this very way, such persons likewise do not receive instruction and admonition from their teachers, preceptors, and others; thus they are cast away and without a protector, being just like the departed spirits (petas). This is the fifth [simile].
6. Commentary on the Rohitassasutta 107.

In the sixth [verse], "where" (*yattha*) refers to the locative case denoting a single location within the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "Neither passing away nor being reborn" (*na cavati na upapajjati*) is understood here in terms of successive death and rebirth (*cuti-paṭisandhi*).
"By going" (*gamanena*) means by the movement of the feet. "I do not know that... [the rest of the verse follows].
"The end of the world," the Teacher said, referring to the end of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-loka*).
Regarding the terms "to be known" (*ñāteyya*) and so forth, the meaning is "that which is to be known, seen, and attained.

Thus, while the son of the gods asked about the end of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-loka*), the Teacher spoke of the world of conditioned phenomena. Perceiving that the Teacher’s answer accorded with his own question, he praised it, saying, "It is wonderful," and so on.
"Strong in his craft" (*daḷhadhammo*) means one who possesses a strong bow, endowed with a bow of the highest measure. "An archer" (*dhanuggaho*) means a teacher of archery.
"Well-trained" (*susikkhito*) means one who has practiced the art of archery for ten or twelve years.

"One who has mastered his hand" (*katahattho*) means one who has gained such manual skill as to be capable of piercing even a hair-tip at the distance of a bull's length. "One who has performed the preliminary practice" (*katūpāsano*) means one who has completed the preparatory exercises and demonstrated his skill.
"With a seat" means with his trunk. "He would overtake" means he would pass beyond.
By saying, "In the time it would take him to overtake the shadow of a palmyra tree, I would overtake a single world-system," he demonstrates the excellence of his own speed.
"From the eastern ocean to the western" means that just as the western ocean is distant from the eastern ocean, so too...

"He says, 'The one who traverses the path was far from me. It is said that standing on the eastern rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭi*), he extends his foot and steps upon the western rim of the world-system;
then, extending his second foot, he steps upon the rim of another world-system.
'Wish-attainment' (*icchāgata*) means simply wish. 'Elsewhere' indicates the state of non-proliferation (*nippapañca*). At the time of wandering for alms..."
This Kira, having chewed a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* and washed his mouth in Lake Anotatta, when the time arrives, goes for alms in Uttarakuru;
sitting on the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭi*), he performs his meal-duty, and after resting there for a moment, he speeds back again.
"Having a lifespan of a hundred years" means that at that time it is an era of long life, but this [Kira] lives for the remainder of a hundred years.
He began his journey toward the end of his life. "One who lives for a hundred years" means one who lives that hundred-year span without obstacles.
"Died in the interval" means he died in the interim before reaching the end of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
Even though he passed away there, having returned, he was reborn right here in this very world-system. "Without reaching" means without reaching the end of the conditioned world (*saṅkhāraloka*).
“Of suffering” means of the suffering of saṃsāra. “The making of an end” means the bringing about of a limit. “In this body” means in this personal existence (attabhāva).
“In one possessing perception and feeling” means in one who has perception and mind. “The world” means the truth of suffering. “The origin of the world” means the truth of the origin.
“The cessation of the world” means the truth of cessation. “The way leading [to it]” means the truth of the path. Thus: “I do not, friend... [the rest follows].
"I teach the Four Truths in relation to grass, wood, and so forth; however, I teach them in relation to this very body composed of the four great elements," he shows.
"Samitāvī" means one whose evil has been stilled. "Nāsīsati" means he does not long for. [This concludes] the sixth. 108–109.
The seventh and eighth have already had their meaning explained. [This concludes] the seventh and the eighth.
9. Commentary on the Susīma Sutta 110.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "Ānanda, even you do not approve of Sāriputta," the Teacher wished to speak in praise of the Elder.
Now, it is not proper to speak of someone's virtues in the presence of a person who is of a different disposition; for if such praise is spoken in his presence—
For it does not reach the very pinnacle. Indeed, when it is said, "A certain monk named so-and-so is virtuous," he might say, "What is his virtue?
His virtue is like that of an ox. Have you never seen anyone else who is more virtuous?
Or, when it is said, "He is wise," he might say, "What is his wisdom? Have you never seen anyone else who is wiser? By speaking such things, he creates an obstacle to the discourse on praise.
He does so. However, the Elder Ānanda was like the Elder Sāriputta;

having received excellent things, he would give them to the Elder, and having had his own attendant boys ordained, he would have them take formal admission (upajjhā) under the Elder and receive full ordination (upasampadā).
The Elder Sāriputta likewise did the same for the Elder Ānanda. For what reason? Because of their mutual virtues.
Having gained confidence. For the Elder Ānanda, having gained confidence in the virtues of the Elder [Sāriputta], thinking:

“My elder brother, having fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable age and a hundred thousand aeons, and having penetrated the sixteenfold wisdom, stands in the position of General of the Dhamma,” claimed the Elder as his own.
The Elder Sāriputta, too, [thinking]: “Of the Perfectly Enlightened One...”
"Ānanda performs for me all the duties that ought to be done by me, such as providing water for my mouth and so forth.

It is by depending on Ānanda that I am able to attain whatever meditative absorption (samāpatti) I desire. Thus, having gained confidence in the virtues of the Venerable Ānanda, he claimed him as his own.
Therefore, wishing to speak in praise of the Elder Sāriputta, the Blessed One began to speak in the presence of the Elder Ānanda.
In this context, the particle *pi* in the phrase *tuyhampīti* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). This is what is meant:
"Ānanda, Sāriputta’s conduct, range of activity, dwelling, advancing, retreating, looking forward and looking aside, and his drawing in and stretching out [of limbs] is pleasing to me;
it is pleasing to the eighty great elders; it is pleasing to the world with its devas. Is it pleasing to you as well?"
Then the Elder, finding an opening within his robe like a powerful wrestler, became joyful at heart and thought:
"The Teacher wishes to have the praises of my dear companion spoken. Today I shall obtain [the opportunity];
it is as if the moon were being brought forth from the midst of the clouds, or as if a great rose-apple tree—the banner of the island—were being shaken. Thus he spoke to the Elder Sāriputta.

Thinking, "I shall speak in praise," he first spoke the words beginning with "Of whom indeed, venerable sir, is it not a fool? (Kassa hi nāma, bhante, abālassa...), thereby clearing away the person through four phrases.

For a fool [speaks] out of foolishness, a wicked man out of hatred, a deluded man out of delusion, and one whose mind is perverted out of mental derangement; thus they speak of praise as "praise" or dispraise as "dispraise."
Or he does not know, "This one is a Buddha" or "This one is a disciple. However, those who are not fools and so forth do know; therefore, he says "not by the foolish," and so on.
"It would not please" means that it would not please only the foolish and so forth, but it would not fail to please anyone else.
Having thus refuted the person (puggala), he now speaks of the true praise in sixteen terms, beginning with "the wise one":
He said, beginning with "Venerable sir. Therein, "wise" means endowed with wisdom; this is the name for one who stands firm in the four kinds of skill.

For it has been said: "When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible—to that extent, Ānanda, he is 'wise'..."
"Bhikkhus" is sufficient as a term of address. Regarding the phrases "of great wisdom" and so forth, the meaning is "one who is endowed with great wisdom," etc.
Herein, this is the distinction between great wisdom and the others: What is great wisdom?

It is called great wisdom because it grasps the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the great aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha), the aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha).
She grasps them, thus she is one of great wisdom. She grasps the great points and non-points, the great dwellings and attainments, the great Noble Truths,
the great foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, the great faculties, powers,
factors of enlightenment, the great Noble Path, the great fruits of recluseship, and the great direct knowledges.
It is "great wisdom" (*mahāpaññā*) because it grasps the great ultimate truth, Nibbāna.

This [wisdom] became manifest for the Elder when he answered the questions on the "fivefold state of the worldling" (*puthujjana-pañcaka*) posed by the Teacher while standing at the gate of Saṅkassanagara after the Teacher had performed his descent from heaven (*devorohana*).

What is "wide wisdom" (*puthupaññā*)? It is wide wisdom because knowledge proceeds toward various aggregates (*khandha*). It is wide wisdom because [knowledge proceeds toward] various elements (*dhātu*).
In various and diverse bases; in various and diverse dependent originations; in various and diverse emptinesses and non-apprehensions;
in various and diverse meanings, teachings, definitions, and eloquences; in various and diverse aggregates of virtue;
in various and diverse aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; in various and diverse points and non-points; in various...
Puthupaññā (vast wisdom) is the knowledge that proceeds regarding the various dwellings and attainments, the various individual Noble Truths, the various individual foundations of mindfulness,
the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the various individual Noble Paths, the fruits of recluseship, the direct knowledges,
and having transcended the various phenomena common to ordinary people, it proceeds toward Nibbāna, the ultimate truth.
What is wisdom characterized by joy (*hāsapaññā*)? Here, someone who abounds in joy, abounds in rapture, abounds in contentment, and abounds in gladness fulfills his virtue;

he fulfills restraint of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. This is wisdom characterized by joy.
Wisdom of laughter (*hāsapaññā*). One who abounds in laughter and abounds in gladness penetrates what is possible and what is impossible;

thus it is wisdom of laughter. One who abounds in laughter fulfills the meditative attainments (*vihārasamāpatti*); thus it is wisdom of laughter. One who abounds in laughter penetrates the Noble Truths.

One who abounds in laughter develops the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Path; thus it is wisdom of laughter.
"Wisdom of laughter" (*hāsapaññā*) is so called because one who is full of laughter realizes the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) and penetrates the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
It is "wisdom of laughter" because one who is full of laughter—abounding in joy, satisfaction, and gladness—realizes the ultimate goal, Nibbāna.

Furthermore, the Elder, having been an ascetic named Sarada, made a resolution for the position of chief disciple at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassi. From that time forward, he practiced the fulfillment of virtue and other perfections while being full of laughter; thus, he was "one possessed of wisdom of laughter."

What is impulsive wisdom (*javanapaññā*)? Whatever form there is—past, future, or present... [as before] ...whether far or near—all form it impulsively cognizes as impermanent; thus it is impulsive wisdom. It impulsively cognizes it as suffering;
it impulsively cognizes it as non-self; thus it is impulsive wisdom. Whatever feeling there is...

[as before] ...whatever perception there is... whatever formations there are... whatever consciousness there is... [as before] ...all consciousness it impulsively cognizes as impermanent; thus it is impulsive wisdom. It impulsively cognizes it as suffering; it impulsively cognizes it as non-self; thus it is impulsive wisdom. This is impulsive wisdom.
Consciousness—past, future, and present... all consciousness is swiftly impelled as impermanent, suffering, and non-self:

this is impulsive wisdom (*javanapaññā*). The eye... up to... aging-and-death—past, future, and present—is swiftly impelled as impermanent, suffering, and non-self: this is impulsive wisdom. Form—past, future, and present—is impermanent... [and so on].

Having weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that form is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of being coreless, one swiftly courses toward the cessation of form, which is Nibbāna;
thus it is "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*). Feeling... perception... volitional formations...
consciousness... the eye... [and so on] ...aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, is impermanent in the sense of destruction... [and so on].

Having made [these things] manifest, one swiftly courses toward the cessation of aging and death, which is Nibbāna; thus it is "impetuous wisdom" (*javanapaññā*). Having weighed, scrutinized, and analyzed form—past, future, and present—and so on up to consciousness;

having weighed, scrutinized, and analyzed the eye—and so on up to aging and death—as impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation; having made them manifest...
Having made [the mind] swift toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death, it is called "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*).
What is "sharp wisdom" (*tikkhapaññā*)? It is called sharp wisdom because it swiftly cuts off the defilements (*kilesa*).

One does not tolerate a sensual thought that has arisen, nor a thought of ill will that has arisen, nor a thought of cruelty that has arisen; one does not tolerate whatever evil thoughts arise as they appear.
unwholesome states... arisen lust... hatred... delusion... anger... enmity...
contempt... domineering... envy... avarice... deceit... guile... obstinacy... aggression... conceit... arrogance... vanity...
negligence... all defilements... all misconduct... all volitional formations... all kamma that leads to existence.
She does not tolerate [defilements], but abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and reduces them to non-existence— thus she is one of sharp wisdom.
On a single seat, she has attained, realized, and touched with wisdom the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship,
the four analytical knowledges, and the six direct knowledges— thus she is one of sharp wisdom.
And while the Elder was teaching the *Vedanāpariggaha Sutta* to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, he stood right there and severed all defilements.
From the moment he realized the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*), he became known as one of sharp wisdom.
Therefore it was said: "Venerable sir, the venerable Sāriputta is of sharp wisdom."
What is penetrative wisdom? Herein, a certain person is full of agitation regarding all conditioned phenomena, full of terror, full of distaste, full of dissatisfaction, and full of lack of delight;
he does not find pleasure in any conditioned phenomena, but turns his face away from them.
He penetrates and shatters the mass of greed that has never before been penetrated or shattered—this is penetrative wisdom.

Penetrating wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññā*) is so called because it pierces and shatters the mass of hatred, the mass of delusion, anger, resentment, and so forth—things never before pierced or shattered—as well as all kamma that leads to existence.
One who has few desires (*appiccha*) is characterized by concealing one's own virtuous qualities and moderation in receiving the four requisites; this is the characteristic of having few desires.

Endowed with this characteristic: "Content" means being endowed with these three kinds of contentment—contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment with whatever one’s strength permits, and contentment with what is appropriate—regarding the four requisites.

"Secluded" refers to physical seclusion for those whose bodies are withdrawn from society and who delight in renunciation, and mental seclusion for those whose minds are purified and have attained supreme clarity.
And "seclusion from acquisitions" refers to persons who are without acquisitions and have reached the state beyond formations; he is a possessor of these three kinds of seclusion.

"Unassociated" means he is devoid of these five kinds of association: association by sight, association by hearing, association by conversation, association by enjoyment, and physical association. And this fivefold association [is avoided] by kings...
It arises together with eight types of persons: kings, high ministers, members of other sects, disciples of other sects, laymen, laywomen, monks, and nuns.
Since all of these do not exist for the Elder, he is "unassociated.
"Aroused in energy" means one who has exerted energy, perfected energy. In that regard, a monk who is aroused in energy, while walking...

It does not allow an arisen defilement to reach its proper place; it does not allow one who has arisen while standing to reach sitting, nor one who has arisen while sitting to reach lying down. Whatever arises in each respective posture, it suppresses right there.
With reference to this, the Elder did not stretch out his back on a bed for forty-four years; thus he is called "one who has aroused energy."
He said: "Vattā" means one who shakes off [faults]. Having seen the transgressions of the bhikkhus, he does not establish a schedule for his teaching by thinking, "I will speak today;
I will speak tomorrow," but rather he exhorts and instructs them right then and there—this is the meaning. "Vacanakkhamo" means he endures speech.
For while one person gives advice to another, he himself, when being advised by another, [endures it].
He becomes angry. Yet the Elder gives advice even to others, and when he himself is being advised, he receives it with his head bowed.
One day, it is said, a seven-year-old novice said to the Elder Sāriputta, "Venerable Sāriputta, the corner of your lower robe is hanging down.
