Without saying anything at all, the Elder went to one side and adjusted it so that it was perfectly circular.
Having put on [the robes] and returned, he stood with palms joined, saying, “Is this sufficient, Teacher?
“Though he had gone forth that very day, being only seven years of age, even he might instruct me; I accept it upon my head.”
He said:
"A proponent, whether the matter has been brought forward or not, having seen a transgression, says:
'Friend, a bhikkhu indeed should dress in this way, should robe himself in this way, should walk in this way, should stand in this way, should sit in this way.'"
He gives instruction according to the rule: "It should be chewed thus; it should be eaten thus.
He is one who censures evil: he would not look upon an evil person, nor would he listen to their words, nor would he dwell even within the same world-system as them.
"May I never be one of evil desire, lazy, or of inferior energy..."
“Of little learning, disrespectful, he was associated with something or other.
Thus he censures the evil person; and [he says], “One who is called a recluse must not be under the sway of lust, hatred, and delusion;
lust, hatred, and delusion that have arisen must be abandoned. In this way, he also censures evil qualities. For these two reasons, he is “one who censures evil.”
"Venerable sir, it is the Venerable Sāriputta," he says.
When the Venerable Ānanda had thus proclaimed the Elder’s true qualities with these sixteen phrases, [the Buddha asked]:
"Is it that Ānanda does not get to speak the praise of his own dear companion? Or rather, what has he said?"

"It is exactly so; is he not omniscient?"—thinking that no wicked person might find an opportunity to speak against him, the Teacher, making that praise of the Elder's qualities unshakable and spoken by an Omniscient One, and sealing it with the "Seal of the Victor," said, "It is even so," and so forth.
While the Tathāgata and the Elder Ānanda were thus speaking in praise of the Great Elder, those dwelling on the ground...
The deities arose and praised him with these very sixteen words.

Then the space-dwelling deities—the Sīta-valāhakas, the Uṇha-valāhakas, and the Cātumahārājika deities—arose, and so on up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world, and they praised him with these very sixteen words.
By this method, beginning with a single world-system, throughout the ten [directions]...
Deities from thousands of world-systems arose and spoke. Then Susīma, the son of a deity and the co-resident disciple of the Venerable Sāriputta, thought:
“These deities have abandoned their respective festival celebrations and gone here and there to speak only in praise of my preceptor; I shall go into the presence of the Tathāgata.”
"Having gone there, I shall deliver this very same eulogy spoken by the deity," he thought, and he did exactly that. To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "Then Susīma...
was spoken. Regarding the term *uccāvacā*:
in other contexts, what is excellent is called "high" (*ucca*) and what is inferior is called "low" (*avaca*). However, here, "high and low" (*uccāvacā*) means...

"Various kinds of color-appearance. It is said that in that assembly of deities, in the places where it was blue it was intensely blue, in the places where it was yellow it was intensely yellow, in the places where it was red it was intensely red, and in the places where it was white it was intensely white; thus, fourfold color-appearance became manifest.
For this very reason, the four similes beginning with "Just as if" have been introduced. In this context, *subha* means beautiful.
"Of noble birth" means endowed with a noble lineage. "Well-polished" means well-prepared through such processes as washing.
"Set upon a pale-red cloth" means placed upon a red blanket. "In the same way" means that, like a gem set upon a red blanket, they all began to shine forth simultaneously.
"Adornments" refers to the jewelry fashioned from more than five measures of gold.
For that [gold] is capable of withstanding rubbing and immersion. "Jambūnada" means gold produced in the river flowing from the branch of the Great Rose-apple Tree (*mahājambu*);
or, when the juice of the Great Rose-apple fruit enters the earth, golden sprouts arise—thus it refers to an ornament made from that gold.
"Well-smelted in the furnace-mouth of a skilled smith’s son" means by one who is very skillful...
It was heated and struck [into shape] by a smith’s son at the mouth of a forge. In the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*, an unworked object is taken as the example;
here, however, it is a worked object.
"In the distance" means when it has gone far away. "In the sky" means in the atmosphere. "Rising up into the sky" means leaping up into the atmosphere.
By this, his state as the "young sun" is shown. *Sorata* means endowed with gentleness (*soracca*). *Danta* means one who is tamed and free from worldly attachments.
*Satthuvaṇṇābhata* means one whose praise has been brought forth by the Teacher. For the Teacher, sitting in the midst of the eightfold assembly, brought forth the Elder’s praise in such a manner as:
"Bhikkhus, serve Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Thus, the Elder is "one whose praise has been brought forth."
It is called "waiting for the time. "Waiting for the time" means he aspires for the time of final Nibbāna. For one whose taints are destroyed neither delights in death nor aspires for life;
rather, like a man standing who has received his daily wage, he awaits the time.
The meaning is that he remains watching for it. Therefore it was said:
“I do not rejoice in death, nor do I rejoice in life;
I await my time like a servant awaiting his wages. (The Ninth) 10.
Commentary on the Discourse to the Disciples of Various Heretical Teachers (Nānātitthiyasāvakasutta-vaṇṇanā)

111. Regarding the phrase "disciples of various non-Buddhist sects" in the tenth [chapter]: it is said that they were proponents of kamma; therefore, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, they were reborn in heaven.

Believing, "We have been reborn here through our faith in our respective teachers," they thought, "Let us go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers and, standing there, speak in praise of our teachers."
Having arrived, they spoke in individual verses. In that context, *chinditamārite* means "in cutting and in killing.
*Hatajānīsū* means "in striking and in seizing wealth. *Puññaṃ vā pana* means he does not even perceive his own merit;
in short, he says there is no result of either merit or demerit. *Sa ve vissāsamācikkhī* means he—thus...
By saying, “There is no ripening of results for those who have committed evil nor for those who have performed merit,” he explains the confidence, the refuge, and the support for sentient beings;
therefore, he says that such a person is worthy of honor, veneration, and worship.
“Through austerity and self-reproach” means through bodily mortification and through loathing of evil. “Being well-restrained” means being endowed with such qualities.
"Or secluded. "Disgusted" means one who loathes evil through asceticism (*tapas*). "Clever" means wise.

"Well-restrained by the fourfold restraint" means well-restrained by the fourfold restraint. The "fourfold restraint" consists of these four components: being restrained from all water, devoted to all water, shaken off by all water, and suffused with all water.
In that context, "restrained from all water" means having all water [of defilement] restrained.
The meaning is: one who has rejected all cold water. It is said that he perceives living beings in cold water; therefore, he does not use it.
*Sabbavāriyutta* means endowed with the restraint of all evil. *Sabbavāridhuta* means one whose evil has been shaken off by the restraint of all evil.
*Sabbavāriphuṭa* means touched by the restraint of all evil. They declare what has been seen and heard.
When he declares what was seen as "I saw it" and what was heard as "I heard it," he does not conceal it.
"Indeed, he is no evildoer"—such a teacher is certainly not one who commits evil deeds.
"Various sectarians"—it is said that he was indeed an attendant to various sectarians; therefore, he speaks concerning them. [The name] Pakudhaka.
*Kātyāyana* refers to Pakudha Kaccāyana. *Nigaṇṭha* refers to Nātaputta. *Makkhali-Pūraṇa* refers to both Makkhali and Pūraṇa.
*Attained to asceticism* means having reached the pinnacle of the qualities of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
"Indeed, they are not far from true men" means he says that they themselves are the true men in the world. He replied: "This is a blow for these naked and shabby ones."
“Standing in the presence of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, he speaks in praise; therefore, I shall speak their dispraise”—thus he spoke with malice.
In that context, “by mere association” means simply by having walked together. “A wretch, a jackal” refers to a base black jackal. “Kotthuka” is a synonym for that same being.
“Of suspicious conduct” means one whose behavior is suspect. “Not like the virtuous” means not like the wise.
"He is not the equal of true men; why do you treat these heretics, who are like black jackals, as if they were lions?
"Having entered" means: thinking, "This man speaks in dispraise of such teachers;
therefore, I shall cause him to speak in their praise through this very mouth," he entered his body and took possession of it. Having thus entered, he was "appointed."
They are devotedly engaged in the loathing of defilements through asceticism. "Guarding seclusion" means guarding solitude.
It is said that thinking, "We shall guard seclusion regarding the hair," they pluck out their own hair; thinking, "We shall achieve seclusion regarding robes," they wander about naked;
and thinking, "We shall guard seclusion regarding almsfood," they eat either from the ground like dogs or directly from their hands.
Thinking, “We shall preserve our seclusion in dwellings,” they practice sleeping on thorns and so forth. “Attached to form” means established in form through craving and views.
“Delighting in the world of the gods” means having desires for the aspiration toward the world of the gods. “Mātīyā” means mortals;
he says that these very mortals truly provide right instruction for the sake of the world beyond.
"Having understood thus" means: having known by reflecting, "This one first spoke in dispraise of these [monks], but now he speaks in their praise;

who indeed could this be? "And those which have the color of light in the sky" means: those which have the color of the light of the moon, the sun, the twilight glow, Indra’s bow (the rainbow), the planets, and the stars in the firmament.
"All these are yours" means: all these are yours. "O Namuci" is an address to Māra. "Like bait for fish" means: as a lure for fish.
"Thrown for slaughter" means: just as one throws bait attached to a hook for the purpose of killing fish, so he says that these forms, by being praised by you, are thrown for the slaughter of beings.
"The young man of Gāmika" refers to this son of the gods, who was indeed an attendant of the Buddha. "Of the Rājagaha mountains" means of the mountains surrounding Rājagaha.
"Seto" means Kelāsa. "Aghagāminaṃ" means of those that go through the sky. "Udadhinan" means of the repositories of water. This is what is meant:

just as among the mountains of Rājagaha Vipula is the best, among the mountains of Himavanta Kelāsa, among those that travel through the sky the sun, among the repositories of water the ocean, and among the stars the moon—so too, among all things including the devas... [is this the best].
“The Buddha is the best in the world. Tenth.
The Third Chapter on Various Sectarians (*Nānātitthiyavagga*).
Thus [ends the third chapter] in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*.
The commentary on the Devaputtasaṃyutta of the Saṃyuttanikāya-ṭīkā is finished. 3.
The Kosala-saṃyutta.
1. First Chapter. 1. Commentary on the *Dahara-sutta*. 112.
In the first [sutta] of the *Kosalasaṃyutta*, "he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One" means that he inquired after his well-being and so forth.
The Blessed One [greeted] him; thus, he too shared in the same joy as the Blessed One.
Like cold water meeting hot water, they became harmonized and attained a state of unity. And with these words—“I hope, Master Gotama, that you are well, I hope you are comfortable;
I hope that Master Gotama and his disciples are free from affliction, free from illness, and are living in ease... —he spoke.
It is "conducive to greetings" (*sammodanīya*) because it generates a greeting consisting of joy and gladness, and because it is appropriate for greeting.

It is "worthy of being remembered" (*sāraṇīya*) because, due to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, it is fit to be sustained and continuously maintained over a long period, and because it is of a nature that ought to be remembered. It is [so called] because it is pleasant while being heard...
And it is "conducive to cordiality" because it brings happiness when remembered; it is "conducive to recollection" because of its purity of phrasing and its purity of meaning.

Having thus exchanged such "cordial" and "recollective" discourse in many ways—bringing it to its conclusion, completing it, and finishing it—he [proceeded] on account of the qualities and defects of the Tathāgata, since he had not seen him before.
Not knowing whether [the teaching] was profound or superficial, he sat down to one side; sitting there, he spoke the words beginning with "Is there existence?

in order to ask the Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One, about the question of the transcendence of the world and the entry into existence, having made the *ovaṭṭika* (the inner core) his starting point.
In this context, the particle *pi* in the phrase *bhavampi* is a grammatical particle used in the sense of inclusion; by it, he includes the six teachers.
The meaning is: "Does Bhava also, like Pūraṇa and the others, claim [to be] 'a Perfectly Enlightened One'?
However, the King asks this not out of his own personal conviction, but according to the claims accepted by the common people in the world.
Then the Blessed One, letting out the lion’s roar of a Buddha, spoke the words beginning with “For I, O Great King. Therein, “For I, O Great King” means:
“I have fully awakened to the supreme, most excellent, and all-knowing wisdom known as *sammāsambodhi*.

Regarding “recluses and brahmins”: they are recluses (*samaṇa*) by virtue of having gone forth into homelessness, and brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*) by virtue of their birth. As for the terms “those who possess a community” (*saṅghino*), and so forth:
They are "possessors of the Saṅgha" (saṅghino) because they have a Saṅgha, which is defined as a multitude of those who have gone forth.

They are "possessors of a group" (gaṇino) because they have such a group. They are "teachers of the group" (gaṇācariyā) because they are teachers of that group by way of instructing them in proper conduct.

They are "known," "renowned," and "famous. [The fame arose] thus: "They are of few desires and content; out of their state of having few desires, they do not even wear a cloth as a lower garment. This is how it arose.
“Possessing fame” (*yasassino*) means those for whom fame exists. “Founders of sects” (*titthakārā*) means makers of tenets.
“Respected as good” (*sādhusammatā*) means they are so regarded as “noble and true persons. “Of the many people” (*bahujanassa*) refers to the unlearned, blind, foolish worldling (*puthujjana*).
“Pūraṇa” and so forth are their names and clans; for “Pūraṇa” is simply his name, and likewise “Makkhali. Furthermore, because he was born in Gosālā, he is called “Gosāla.”
"Vutta" means spoken. "Nāṭaputta" means the son of Nāṭa. "Belaṭṭhaputta" means the son of Belaṭṭha.
"Kaccāyana" is the clan name of Pakudha. Because he wore a hair-blanket, Ajita was called Kesakambala.
"Tepi mayaṃ" refers to the three types of clamor: the clamor of the world-age, the clamor of a Buddha, and the clamor of a wheel-turning monarch.
In that regard, when there are one hundred thousand years remaining until the arising of the aeon, there is what is called the "Aeon-Commotion":

deities wander about proclaiming along the human pathways, "Friends, within one hundred thousand years from now the world will be destroyed; cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity. When there are one thousand years remaining...
Furthermore, there is what is called the "uproar regarding a Buddha" (*buddhakolāhala*): deities proclaim, "In a thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise;
surrounded by a Jewel of the Saṅgha who has entered upon the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, he will wander about teaching the Dhamma.
And: "In a hundred years from now, a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*) will arise."

There is what is called the "clamor concerning the wheel-turning monarch": "In one hundred years from now, a wheel-turning king endowed with the seven treasures, sovereign over the four continents, accompanied by a thousand sons, and capable of traveling through the air, will appear. Thus do the deities proclaim.
When these three clamors arise, these six teachers, having heard the clamor concerning a Buddha, attended upon their own teachers.

Having mastered the sciences of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel and others, they made the claim, "We are Buddhas," and traveling through the countryside surrounded by great crowds of followers, they eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. Their supporters approached the King and reported:
"Great King, Pūraṇa Kassapa... [and so on] ...Ajita Kesakambala is said to be a Buddha and is said to be omniscient."
The king said, “Invite them yourselves and bring them here. They went and were told by those [monks], “The king invites you;
receive alms at the king’s house. Though they were told again and again, they did not venture to go.
However, for the sake of protecting the feelings of their attendants, they consented and all went together. The king prepared seats.

“Sit down,” he said. Because those devoid of virtue possess what is called the "stain of sovereignty" within their own bodies, they were unable to sit upon the magnificent seats and instead sat upon wooden planks and the bare ground.
The king, saying, “By this much alone it is clear that there is no pure quality (sukkadhamma) within them,” did not give them food, but [instead gave] what had fallen from a palm tree.
Striking them as if with a pestle, he asked the question: "Are you Buddhas? Are you not Buddhas? They reflected:
"If we say, 'We are Buddhas,' the king will ask a question on the domain of a Buddha;
and when we are unable to answer, he might have our tongues cut out, saying, 'You wander about deceiving the great multitude, claiming, "We are Buddhas," yet you are not. Furthermore...
Thinking, "He might cause us harm," they said, "We are not Buddhas," in accordance with their own prior agreement. Then the king had them driven out from his house.

When they had departed from the royal residence, their supporters asked, "Did the teacher ask you a question and then bestow honor and respect upon you? They replied, "The king asked, 'Are you Buddhas? and then we..."

—“If this king, not understanding the question being discussed within the domain of the Buddha, should harbor ill-will toward us, he will produce much demerit. Out of compassion for the king, we said, “We are not Buddhas”;
yet we are indeed Buddhas, and our state of Buddhahood cannot be washed away even by water. Thus it was.
They said outside, “We are not Buddhas,” meaning they said in the presence of the king, “We are not Buddhas.
Taking this up, the king spoke thus. In that regard, when he says, “But Master Gotama is young in years and new in his renunciation,” he speaks by taking up their own admission.
In that context, “What? is a word of denial. These [others] are old in birth...
And those who have long since gone forth do not claim, "We are Buddhas. Master Gotama is young by birth and new to the going-forth; what can he possibly claim? The meaning is: "Do not claim it.

"They are not to be despised" means they are not to be looked down upon. "They are not to be held in contempt" means they are not to be treated with disdain. "Which four? refers to: [the four types of persons].
This is a question arising from a desire to speak. "Khattiya" means a prince. "Uraga" means a venomous snake. "Aggi" means fire itself.
"Bhikkhu"—in this term, however, out of skill in teaching, he includes himself among those who are virtuous renunciants.
And here, having seen a young prince, one does not step aside to let him pass, nor does one offer him a path, nor does one remove one's outer robe.

One who does not rise from his seat, who does not descend from the back of an elephant or similar vehicle, and who, by way of conceit, treats others with contempt while acting in other such ways of improper conduct, is said to "despise a khattiya. [Thinking: "This prince is indeed excellent;
he has large calves and a large belly—what indeed could he do anywhere to pacify any kind of danger from thieves?"
When one says things such as, "He will be able to rule the kingdom," one is indeed disparaging him.
When one fastens even a mere stick of ointment upon the ears and other parts of a young venomous snake, causing it to bite even a finger or a tongue, one is indeed treating the serpent with contempt.
"This venomous snake is truly excellent; like a water-frog, what can he possibly bite, and whom? [one might think].
One who says things such as, “He will be able to spread poison through his body,” is said to despise [fire].

One who takes even a fire the size of a firefly and plays with it in his hand, throws it into a mortar, or places it on his crest, the back of his bed, or in a cloth bag, is said to treat fire with contempt.
[One might say: “This fire is indeed excellent; which rice-gruel or meal shall we prepare with it?”
To speak such things as, "He will cook; what kind of fish or meat will he have? Whose cold will he dispel? is called disparaging.
Furthermore, to see even a young novice and then walk away without giving way is to commit the same impropriety described regarding princes;
thus, the bhikkhu is said to despise him. To say, "What a fine novice this is! What a large throat and large belly! Whatever... [is also disparagement].
One who says things such as, “He will be able to dwell having entered any forest whatsoever in order to master the word of the Buddha;
he will be pleasing when the time comes for the elders of the Saṅgha,” is said to be disparaging. Showing that all of this should not be done, [the Blessed One] said:
“He should not be despised, nor should he be disparaged.”
"Etadavoca" means he spoke this composition of verses. Now, these verses serve both to illuminate the general meaning and to illuminate specific meanings;
herein, they indeed illuminate both the general and the specific meanings. In that context, "khattiya" refers to one who is the lord (*adhipati*) of fields (*khettānaṃ*). For it has been said:
"O Vāseṭṭha, 'one who is the lord of fields'—this is precisely why a *khattiya* is called a *khattiya*. The second [occurrence]...
"the syllable was produced. "Endowed with birth" means endowed with birth through that very kṣatriya lineage.
"High-born" means born having transcended the three [lower] castes.
"For there is a reason" means there exists a cause. "Lord of men" means the chief among humans. "By royal punishment" means by the punishment levied by the king.
It is not indeed small; it is precisely ten thousand or twenty thousand [in number]. When that [wind] blows, it exerts a powerful assault upon that person.
"Guarding his life alone" means that, protecting his own life, he should avoid that noble warrior and not strike him.

"By various" (*uccāvacehi*) means by many kinds. "By colors" (*vaṇṇehi*) means by shapes. For by whichever shape he moves about so as to find his range—whether in the shape of a snake, or in the shape of a water-snake (*deḍḍubha*), or in the shape of a vein, or even as far down as the shape of a squirrel—he indeed moves about.
"Having encountered" (*āsajja*) means having reached. "The fool" (*bāla*): whatever fool he has struck, whether a man or a woman, him he would bite.
"Pahūtabhakka" means having much to eat; for there is indeed nothing that fire does not consume. "Jāli" means possessing a net (flames).
"Pāvaka" means fire; "pāvaga" is also a reading for this. "Kaṇhavattani": "vattani" means a path;
the path traversed by fire becomes black or dark, therefore it is called "kaṇhavattani."
"Having become great" means having become vast; for fire at times even reaches the extent of the Brahma-world.
"Sprouts grow there" means that in the forest burnt by the fire, sprouts grow. "Sprouts" refers to grasses, trees, and so forth;
for in a place burnt by fire, they grow and arise from the roots, even when only the root remains.
They grow; therefore they are called "shoots" (*pāroha*). Alternatively, they are "shoots" in the sense of growing again.
"With the passing of days and nights" means with the elapse of nights and days. They are born even in the heat of summer as soon as it rains.
Regarding the phrase "the bhikkhu burns with fire": here, one who reviles in return while being reviled, who scolds in return while being scolded, or who strikes back while being struck—
A monk who strikes back is unable to burn anything with the power of his spiritual heat (*tejas*).

However, he who does not revile one who reviles him, does not quarrel with one who quarrels, and does not strike back at one who strikes him—even if he has acted wrongly toward such a person—he is consumed by the power of that person’s virtue.
It is for this very reason that it was said: "He has neither sons nor offspring," meaning he has neither sons nor daughters.

Even their offspring—cows, buffaloes, chickens, pigs, and so forth—do not come into being; the meaning is that they perish. "Their heirs do not find wealth" means that even their heirs do not find any wealth.

"They become like the stumps of palmyra trees" means that those monks, consumed by [the power of] spiritual majesty (*tejas*), remain as mere sites, like a palmyra tree with its top cut off, in terms of having sons, daughters, and so on.
The meaning is "they do not grow.
Therefore—because they are burnt by the ascetic’s fiery power (*samaṇateja*) and thus become incapable of growth, like a palm tree with its crown cut off—for that reason.
"One should practice rightly" means one should practice correctly. But what is to be done by one who practices correctly?
The benefit to be obtained by relying on a khattiya consists of villages, towns, vehicles, mounts, and so forth;

the benefit to be obtained by relying on a snake consists of clothing, silver, gold, and so forth, through its being made to perform services; the benefit to be obtained by relying on fire consists of the cooking of gruel and rice, the dispelling of cold, and so forth, by means of its power;
and the benefit to be obtained by relying on a bhikkhu consists of [the teachings] through his influence.

Perceiving the benefits to be attained—such as hearing what has not been heard, purifying what has been heard, and reaching the path to heaven—one should not abandon these people entirely, thinking, "There is the aforementioned danger in relying on them; what is the use of them?
Rather, one who desires sovereignty should not treat them with contempt or disdain as previously described, but should instead act by rising before them and sitting down after them, and so forth.
The prince must be satisfied with skillful means; in this way, he will attain sovereignty from him.

Without placing trust in the snake by the snake-charmer, one should master the science of the nāga, seize it by the neck with a staff tipped with a goat’s foot, wash its fangs with a decoction of *visahara* root, place it in a basket, and go about playing with it. In this way, by depending on that [method],...

He will obtain fodder, shelter, and so forth. One who wishes to prepare rice gruel and the like should do so by kindling a fire with cow-dung powder and such, without placing it in a vessel or mortar out of misplaced trust, and without touching it with the hands;
in this way, by relying on that [fire], he will obtain the benefits. Even one who aspires to hear what has not been heard before [should act] toward a bhikkhu without excessive trust...
Without employing him in medical practice, agriculture, or similar tasks, he should be properly served with the four requisites.
In this way, by relying on him, one may attain the Buddha’s word never heard before, the resolution of questions never heard before, the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life,
the three types of success within a noble family, the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure, the nine Brahma-worlds, and even the vision of the great Nibbāna, which is the Deathless.
He said, "One should practice correctly with this very purpose in mind, thinking: 'I shall attain [this]'"; thus he spoke.
"He said this" means that, having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, being filled with confidence, he manifested that confidence by uttering these words beginning with "Excellent!
(*abhikkanta*). In this context, *abhikkanta* means "excellent," "very desirable," "very pleasing," or "most beautiful"—such is the meaning.
Here, with one instance of the word *abhikkanta*, he praises the teaching: "Excellent, Bhante, is this Dhamma-teaching of the Blessed One.
With the other, he expresses his own confidence: "Excellent, Bhante, is this [state] that has come to me through the Blessed One's Dhamma-teaching, namely, my confidence."
Beyond that, he praises the teaching itself by means of four similes. Therein, "upturned" (*nikkujjita*) means placed face-downward or having its opening turned downward.

"He would turn it up" (*ukkujjeyya*) means he would make it face upward. "Covered" (*paṭicchanna*) means concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth. "He would uncover it" (*vivareyya*) means he would remove [the covering].
"Of one who is lost" (*mūḷhassa*) means of one who is confused about the directions. "He would point out the path" (*maggaṃ ācikkheyya*) means [pointing it out] while taking [the person] by the hand.
“He would say: ‘This is the path. “In darkness” means in the fourfold darkness of the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the thick forest groves, and the mass of clouds.

This is what is meant: just as someone might set upright what had been overturned, so too, by raising me up from unrighteousness—me who was turned away from the true Dhamma and fallen into unrighteousness—and just as one might uncover what had been concealed, so...
From the time of the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation until now, you have revealed the teaching that had been shrouded by the thicket of wrong views;
just as one might point out the path to one who is lost, so have you disclosed to me—the one who has set out upon a bypath and a wrong path—the path to heaven and liberation;
and just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so have you [illuminated] the darkness of delusion.

"Since the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma in these various ways for me— who was submerged and unable to see the forms of the Jewels beginning with the Buddha— by bearing the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which conceals them, the Dhamma has been proclaimed by him in many modes.
Having thus praised the teaching, he manifested his state of serene confidence, his mind being clear toward the Triple Gem because of this teaching.

He said, “Esāhaṃ...,” and so forth. Therein, “esāhaṃ” means “this I. “Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca” means “I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus”; that is, I go for refuge to this Triple Gem.
“Upāsakaṃ maṃ, bhante, bhagavā dhāretu” means “May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*); thus [the Blessed One considers] “This one is a lay follower.”
"Let him hold [it]" means "let him know. "From this day forward" (*ajjatagge*) means beginning from today. Alternatively, the reading is *ajjadagge*;
the letter *da* is for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*), meaning "having made today the beginning. "As long as life lasts" (*pāṇupetaṃ*) means accompanied by life;
as long as my life continues, so long am I accompanied [by this], having gone for refuge with the three goings-for-refuge to a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has no other teacher.
"May the Blessed One accept me as a *kappiyakāraka* (one who prepares what is allowable)"—this is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, has been stated in its entirety in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* of the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*. First.
2. Commentary on the *Purisa Sutta*.
113. “In the second [verse], ‘having paid homage’ means that because he had gone for refuge in the previous sutta, he paid homage here.
‘Internal’ (ajjhatta) refers to one’s own internal state; the meaning is that they arise within one’s own continuum. Among greed and the others: greed has the characteristic of coveting;
hatred has the characteristic of hating; delusion has the characteristic of being deluded. ‘They harm’ means they afflict, destroy, and ruin.”
"Born of oneself" means born within oneself. "Like the bamboo or the reed that destroys its own fruit":
just as the bamboo or the reed harms and destroys its own fruit, so too do they harm and destroy; thus it is said. This is the second [verse]. 3.
Commentary on the Sutta on Aging and Death.
114. In the third [case], "apart from aging-and-death" means it is said that there exists one who is liberated from aging-and-death.
"Khattiya great landowners" refers to khattiyas who have attained great wealth.
For those khattiyas, at the very least, a hundred million [coins] are stored away as a hoard, and three jars of kahāpaṇas are kept in the middle of their houses for the purpose of daily expenditure.
Those who have established [their wealth] and set it aside are called wealthy kṣatriyas (*khattiya-mahāsāla*).

Those brahmins for whom eighty koṭis of wealth are deposited, and for whom one and a half jars of kahāpaṇas are set aside in the middle of their houses in a heap for the purpose of daily expenditure, are called wealthy brahmins (*brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla*). Those householders for whom forty koṭis of wealth are deposited...
They are called "great householders" because a jar of kahāpaṇa coins is placed in the middle of their house, piled up for the purpose of circulation.
They are "wealthy" (aḍḍha) because they are masters. They are "of great wealth" (mahaddhana) due to the vastness of their stored riches.

They are "of great possessions" (mahābhoga) due to the abundance of their articles of enjoyment, such as vessels of gold and silver. They are [so called] due to the profusion of their un-stored gold and silver.
They possess abundant gold and silver. Because they have an abundance of wealth and requisites that bring satisfaction, they are said to have "abundant wealth and requisites.
And because of the abundance of cattle, wealth, and the seven kinds of grain, they are said to have "abundant wealth and grain.
Even for those born as such lords, there is nothing other than aging and death; thus, even for those born and produced as such masters, there is nothing else [to escape].
Regarding aging and death: because of being born, there is no such thing as liberation from aging and death; it exists only within aging and death itself. Regarding terms such as "Arahant":
they are called *arahanto* because they are far (*ārakā*) from the defilements (*kilesa*). They are called *khīṇāsavā* because the four taints (*āsava*) have been exhausted (*khīṇa*) by them.
They are called *vusitavanto* because they have lived out and brought to completion the life of the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*). That which is to be accomplished by means of the four paths...

They are "those who have done what was to be done" because they have performed their task. They are "those who have laid down the burden" because these burdens—the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*), the burden of the defilements (*kilesa*), the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the burden of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*)—have been laid down by them.

They are "those who have attained their own goal" because their own welfare, known as *arahantship*, has been reached by them. They are "those whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed" because the tenfold fetter of existence has been completely exhausted by them.

"Released through right knowledge" means released by having known correctly. The meaning is that, having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths through path-wisdom, one is released by the release of the fruit.
"Subject to breaking" means having the nature of disintegration. "Subject to being laid down" means having the nature of being deposited.
For even for one whose taints are destroyed, there exists the state of not decaying, as it has been penetrated from the perspective of the object.
Nirvana, for it does not decay. However, here [the Buddha] spoke thus while demonstrating that this [world] is subject to decay.
It is said that the delivery of this sutta was prompted by a specific occasion; they say it was spoken while the Blessed One was seated at the cart-shed (sivika-sālā).
There, having seen various chariots and such, the Blessed One took what he had seen as a simile and uttered the verse: "The royal chariots indeed decay."
In this context, "they age" means they reach old age. "Royal chariots" refers to the chariots upon which a king mounts.
"Well-adorned" means beautifully decorated with gold, silver, and so forth. Furthermore, "even the body succumbs to aging":
when such external, non-clung-to chariots made of solid wood decay, what need is there to speak of this internal, clung-to body composed of flesh, blood, and the like?
The meaning is that even the body inevitably succumbs to decay. "The virtuous indeed proclaim it to the virtuous" means that the virtuous, together with the virtuous, proclaim:
"The Dhamma of the virtuous does not succumb to decay. The meaning is: "The Dhamma of the virtuous is Nibbāna;
it does not decay; it is unaging and deathless"—thus they speak. Or, because by resorting to Nibbāna, the nature of sinking...
Defilements are shattered; therefore, it is called "the good" (sabbhi). Thus, showing the reason for the first phrase, he said:
"The good indeed proclaim it to the good. For this is what is meant: the Dhamma of the good does not age;
therefore, the good proclaim it to the good. They declare that the undecaying Nibbāna is the Dhamma of the good.
This is the meaning. Or, "sabbhi" is a designation for those who are beautiful (*sundara*). The meaning is also:
that which is Nibbāna, being the Dhamma of the *sabba*, the virtuous ones (*santa*) proclaim and declare; that Dhamma of the virtuous does not undergo decay.
This is the third [verse]. 4. Commentary on the *Piyasutta*.
115. "In the fourth [verse], 'to one who has gone into seclusion' means to one who has gone to a private place.
'To one who is withdrawn' means to one who is secluded, being alone. "Thus it is, O Great King," the Blessed One said here, making this discourse his own utterance as the Omniscient One.
"'Of one seized by the Ender' means of one overwhelmed by death. This is the fourth.
5. Commentary on the Attarakkhita Sutta 116.
In the fifth [verse], "elephant corps" (*hatthikāya*) means a herd of elephants. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) means closing off or shutting.
By the phrase "restraint is good in all respects," he demonstrates the restraint of action that has not yet reached the point of breaking the path of action (*kammappatha*).
"Lajjī" means one who possesses a sense of shame (*hiri*). By the inclusion of "lajjī," "ottappa" (fear of wrongdoing) is also implicitly included here.

This is the fifth [verse]. 6. Commentary on the *Appakasutta* (The Shorter Discourse): In the sixth [verse], "exalted, exalted" means both sublime and abundant. "They revel" means they revel by means of the intoxication of pride (*māna*). "Excess" means transgression. "Snare" means a trap. "Afterwards" means after them. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Aḍḍakaraṇa Sutta 118.
In the seventh [sutta], "with sensual desire as cause" (*kāmahetu*) means rooted in sensual desire. "With sensual desire as source" (*kāmanidāna*) means by way of the condition of sensual desire.
"With sensual desire as basis" (*kāmādhikaraṇa*) means for the sake of sensual desire. All these terms are merely synonyms for one another. "Bhadramukha" means one with a handsome face. One day...
It is said that the king sat in the court of justice. There, the ministers who had arrived earlier and taken bribes treated those who were not owners as if they were owners.
When the king learned of this, he thought: "If they act in this way even in my presence, while I am the lord of the earth, what will they not do behind my back?
Now General Viṭaṭūba shall be known for his own sovereignty."
He thought, "What use have I for sitting in one place with such bribe-eaters and liars?
and so he spoke thus. "Spread quickly" means spread like a fish-net.

Just as fish do not know when they are entering a spread net, so too beings do not know when they are transgressing against objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma) through the defilement of craving (kilesakāma); this is the meaning. This is the seventh [chapter].
8. Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta 119.
Why does he ask in the eighth [verse], "Do you have any jasmine (*mallikā*)? It is said that this Mallikā was the daughter of a poor garland-maker;
one day, having taken some cakes from a shop, she was going along thinking, "I will go to the Mālārāma park and eat them."
Seeing the Blessed One entering for alms accompanied by the community of monks on the path back, she, with a mind full of faith, gave it to the Blessed One.
The Teacher signaled that he wished to sit down. The Elder Ānanda spread out a robe and offered it to him.
The Blessed One sat there, ate the cake, rinsed his mouth, and smiled.
She made it into a bowl. The Elder asked, "Venerable Sir, what will be the result for her?
[The Buddha replied: "Ānanda, today she gave the Tathāgata his first meal; this very day she shall become the chief queen of the King of Kosala.
And on that very same day, the king, having been defeated in battle by his nephew at Kāsīgāma, fled and was returning to the city when he reached Mālārāma.
Having entered, he waited for the arrival of the army. She performed her duties for him.
Pleased with her service, he had her brought into the inner apartments and established her in the position of chief queen.
Then one day he thought: "I have bestowed great sovereignty upon this daughter of a poor family."
"What if I were now to ask her, 'Who is dear to you? She will say, 'You, Great King, are dear to me,' and then she will ask me in return.
Then I shall say to her, 'You alone are dear to me as well. Thus he asked, engaging in pleasant conversation to generate mutual trust. But that queen was wise and a devotee of the Buddha.
She was an upholder of the Dhamma, an upholder of the Saṅgha, and possessed of great wisdom; therefore, she thought:
"This question must not be answered by looking at the king's face. She spoke with her own voice and questioned the king.
Because she had spoken with her own voice, the king, unable to turn back, also spoke with his own voice: "This has a specific reason regarding the Tathāgata..."
Thinking, “I shall report this to him,” he went and reported it to the Blessed One. *Nevajjhagā* means “he does not find.
“Just as one’s own self is dear, so too is the self of others dear to each individual being”—this is the meaning: just as the self of one person is dear, so too the self of all other beings is dear.
The eighth [sutta]. 9. Commentary on the *Yañña Sutta*.
120. "In the ninth [chapter], 'brought near to the pillar' means brought near to the pillar; they are bound to the pillar.
'They perform the preliminary rites'—by this much, the sacrifice undertaken by the king was announced to the Tathāgata by those bhikkhus.
But why was this sacrifice undertaken by the king? To ward off the effects of bad dreams. One day, it is said, the king, adorned with all his ornaments..."
While traveling through the city seated upon the back of a noble elephant, he saw a certain woman looking out from an open window;
his heart becoming bound to her, he turned back from that very spot, entered the inner palace,
and informed a man of the matter, saying, "Go and find out whether she has a husband or is without one."
He sent him. Having gone, he asked. She showed him, saying, "This is my husband, sitting in the shop.
The king's man reported the matter to the king. The king had that man summoned and said, "Attend upon me.
When he replied, "Your Majesty, I do not know how to attend," the king said, "One does not have to learn attendance from a teacher."
Having made him take up a shield and weapon by force, he appointed him as his attendant.
As soon as the attendant had gone home after serving him, the king summoned him back again and said: "An attendant must carry out the king's word;
go, for at a distance of one *yojana* from here we have a lotus pond for washing the head. From there, take some dawn-clay and a garland of red lotuses."
"Come! If you do not come this very day, we shall impose the king’s punishment," he said, and sent him off. Out of fear of the king, that man departed.
When he had gone, the king summoned the doorkeeper and said, "This very evening at dusk, close the gates;
do not open them even to those who claim to be 'the king's messenger' or 'the viceroy's messenger. That man [took] clay...
Having taken the lotuses, he arrived at the gate just as it was being closed; though he spoke much, failing to gain entrance, he went to Jetavana out of fear of danger.
The king, too, overcome by the fever of passion, sat at the wrong time, stood at the wrong time, and lay down at the wrong time;
finding no resolution, he fell into a monkey-like sleep while sitting wherever he happened to be.
And previously, in that very city, four sons of merchants, having committed the act of adultery,
were reborn in the iron cauldron named Nandopananda. Being cooked like a mass of froth,
they reach the bottom of the cauldron after descending for thirty thousand years, and they reach the top after ascending for thirty thousand years.

They reached [that state]. On that day, having looked toward the light, and desiring to recite one verse each out of fear of their own misdeeds, yet being unable to speak a full verse, they uttered only a single syllable each:
one said the letter *sa*, another the letter *so*, another the letter *na*, and another the letter *du*.
From the moment the king heard the voices of those hell-beings, he found no happiness.
He spent the remainder of that night [in this way].
When dawn had risen, the chaplain came and asked after his comfortable sleep. He replied, "Teacher, how could there be comfort for me?
and explained, "In my dream, I heard such sounds. The brahmin thought, "By this dream of this king's..."

“There is neither increase nor decrease; rather, whatever is in this house belongs to the ascetic Gotama and to the disciples of Gotama, while the brahmins receive nothing. We shall cause alms to be raised for the brahmins.
“This dream, Great King, is grave; among the three types of dreams, it is recognized as one [of the worst]. There will either be an obstacle to your kingdom,” or...
“Or there may be a danger to life, or perhaps the rain-god will not send rain,” he said. “How, O Teacher, can there be safety?
“It is possible to know by means of counsel, Great King. “Go, then, consult with the teachers and ensure our safety.
He assembled the brahmins in the carriage hall, announced the matter to them, and said, “Go each in turn and thus...”
“Speak! he said, and thus he formed three groups. The brahmins entered and inquired after the king’s well-being as he lay on his bed.
The king spoke according to the instructions already given to the family priest and asked, “How might there be safety?
The great brahmins replied, “Only by performing the sacrifice of all five hundred [officiants] can there be safety from this deed; thus it is, O Great King.”
"The teachers say so," they said. Having heard them, the king neither rejoiced nor rejected it, but remained silent.
Then the brahmins of the second group also came and spoke likewise; so too did the brahmins of the third group.
Thereupon the king commanded, "Let them perform the sacrifice. From that time on, the brahmins had oxen and other living beings brought for the purpose.
A great clamor arose in the city. Having learned of this occurrence, Mallikā sent the king to the presence of the Tathāgata.
He went, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One said to him:
“Well now, Great King, from where have you come so very early in the day? The king replied: “Today, Bhante, in a dream...”
“Four sounds were heard, and I asked the brahmins about them. The brahmins replied, ‘Great King, this dream is ominous;
having performed the sacrifice of all five hundred [animals], let us perform a counter-rite,’ and they began to do so.
“What were those sounds you heard, Great King? He reported them exactly as he had heard them. Then the Blessed One said to him: “In the past, Great King, in this very place...”
In that city, four sons of wealthy merchants, having been adulterers, were reborn in the Nandopananda iron cauldron;
they rose up at the end of sixty thousand years.
Therein, one—
“For sixty thousand years, in their entirety;
when will there be an end for those being cooked in hell?”—this verse he spoke out of a desire for a basis [for his question]. The second—
“Surely, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, being generous and endowed with virtue, I shall perform much wholesome merit.
Desiring this as his objective, he spoke this verse. Third.
“There is no end, whence could there be an end? No end is to be seen;
for then, O dear ones, the evil was committed by me and by you.
He spoke this verse out of a desire for a dwelling place. This is the fourth [story].
“We have lived a life ill-lived, we who, though possessing wealth, did not give while it was present, and failed to make an island for ourselves.
Being unable to recite this verse, they uttered each syllable one by one and sank right there. Thus it was.
“Great King, those beings in hell cried out according to their own karma. There is neither loss nor gain for you by reason of hearing that sound.
However, he spoke a discourse on the Dhamma, terrifying him with the fear of hell, saying, ‘The act of killing so many animals is indeed a heavy burden.
The king, gaining confidence in the One of Ten Powers, said, ‘I release them; I grant them their lives.’”
"Let them eat green grass, let them drink cool water, and let a cool breeze blow upon them," he said;
then, commanding his men, "Go and bring them here," they went, drove the brahmins away, released that multitude of living beings from their bonds,
and caused the drum of Dharma to be beaten throughout the city.
Then the king, sitting near the One of Ten Powers, said: "Venerable sir, a single night consists of three watches;
yet today, for me, two nights seemed as if joined together into one. That man, also sitting right there, said:
"Venerable sir, a league (*yojana*) consists of four *gāvutas*; yet today, for me, two leagues [seemed as if joined together into one]."
“...as if they had been made. Then the Blessed One, thinking: “The length of a night for one who is awake is evident;

the length of a league for one who is walking is evident; but for the foolish worldling caught in the cycle of existence, the beginningless round of saṃsāra is absolutely long indeed,” addressed this verse from the *Dhammapada* concerning the king, that man, and the beings in hell:
[The verse follows: “Long is the night for one who sleeps; long is the league for one who tires; long is the cycle of rebirth for the foolish worldling who does not know the Dhamma.”
“Long is the night for one who is awake; long is the league for one who is weary;
long is saṃsāra for fools who do not understand the True Dhamma.
At the conclusion of this verse, that man, the husband of the woman, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “Having understood this matter” means having known this reason.

Regarding the *Assamedha* and other sacrifices: it is said that in ancient times there were four bases of social integration known as *sassamedha*, *purisamedha*, *sammāpāsa*, and *vācāpeyya*, by which kings held the world together.

Among these, *sassamedha* refers to the taking of a tenth portion from the harvested grain; the meaning is that one is wise (*medhāvī*) in the production of crops. [The same applies to] great warriors...
The monthly provision of food and wages is called the *purisamedha*; the meaning is that one is wise (*medhāvī*) in winning over men.
Taking a written contract from the hands of poor people and providing them with wealth amounting to two thousand [pieces] for three years without interest is called the *sammāpāsa*.
For it causes people to look toward [the benefactor] rightly (*sammā*), and it establishes them as if bound by the heart; therefore—
“Right confidence” is what is meant. Speaking with gentle words in the manner beginning with “Dear father,” “Uncle,” and so forth, is called “speech that is pleasing”;

the meaning is that it is affectionate speech. Thus, a kingdom embraced by these four bases of sympathy becomes prosperous and flourishing, abundant in food and drink, secure, and free from affliction.
People rejoice with joy, clutching their children to their breasts.
They dwell with the doors of their houses left open. Because there were no bolts on the doors of these houses, this is called "boltless" (*niraggaḷa*).
This is the ancient tradition.
Later, however, during the time of King Okkāka, the brahmins [attained] these four bases of sympathy and this prosperity of the kingdom.
Having turned it over and made it root-upwards, they performed five kinds of sacrifices known as the *assamedha* (horse sacrifice), the *purisamedha* (human sacrifice), and so forth.
Among these, the *assamedha* is so called because horses (*assa*) are sacrificed (*medhanti*) or killed there.
It is terrifying due to the slaughter of ninety-seven hundred and five animals on that single middle day of the twenty-one-day sacrificial period required for the offering.

This is a designation for a sacrifice in which all forms of wealth are offered as a fee, with the exception of the earth and human beings. Here, they sacrifice a man, thus it is called a *purisamedha*.

This is a designation for a sacrifice in which the horse-sacrifice (*assamedha*)—including the earth and the aforementioned wealth as a fee—is to be performed by means of four types of sacrificial rites (*pariyañña*). Here, they cause [the victim] to look properly, thus...
*Sammāpāsa*: Having properly cast [the spear] day after day, one constructs an altar at the spot where it falls;

this is the designation for the *sattra-yāga* sacrifice that is to be performed by one traveling upstream from the place where the Sarassatī River disappears, using portable sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and other implements.
*Vājapeyya*: It is called *vājapeyya* because they drink the *vāja* (grain-offering) there. With a single *pariyañña*, [there are] seventeen...
This is a designation for a sacrifice to be performed with animals, consisting of a *beluva* tree altar and seventeen sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).

It is called *niraggaḷa* because there are no bolts (*aggaḷa*) here. This refers specifically to a variant of the horse sacrifice (*assamedha*), which is to be performed with nine circumambulations (*pariyañña*), together with the earth and men, and which has the name "All-Sacrifice" (*sabbamedha*) and the aforementioned wealth as its sacrificial gifts.
This is a synonym. "Great undertakers" means those with great duties and great tasks. "Those who have gone rightly" refers to the Buddhas and others who have practiced correctly.
"Without undertakings" means having no desires and no duties. "They sacrifice to their own kin" means they sacrifice among their relatives;

the meaning is that people give what was established by their ancestors—such as regular meals—and so forth, because it has been handed down from one to another without interruption. This is the ninth [chapter].
10. Commentary on the Bandhana Sutta 121.
Regarding the tenth [sutta], "Here, venerable sir, the king... these bhikkhus reported to the Venerable Ānanda the reason why those men had been treated so well.
It is said that the eightfold curved [bow] was given to King Kusarāja by Sakka.
The jewel had come down through a succession of generations. At the time of his adornment, the king said, "Bring that jewel.
The people reported, "We do not see it where it was kept. The king had those who move within the inner palace bound, commanding them, "Search for the jewel and bring it back.
When the Elder Ānanda saw them, he explained a means to recover the jewel. They reported this to the king. The king—

“The Elder is wise; do as the Elder says. The people of Paṭisāma placed a water-jar in the royal courtyard, had it surrounded by a curtain, and said to those men, “Put on a cloth, go there, and lower your hand [into the jar].
The jewel-thief thought, “To release or to use the king’s property...”
"It is not possible," he said. Having gone home, he placed the jewel under his arm, put on a cloak, and returned;
he threw it into a water-jar and departed. When the great crowd had withdrawn, the king’s men reached their hands into the jar, saw the jewel, took it out, and presented it to the king.
"It seems this jewel was shown [to us] by the Elder Ānanda according to the method he demonstrated."
“It has been seen! the great multitude raised a clamor. Those monks, reporting that matter to the Tathāgata, informed him of this occurrence.
The Teacher said: “It is not surprising, monks, that Ānanda should cause a jewel already in the hands of men to be brought forth;
for in former times, wise men, standing upon their own knowledge, [refuted] the theory of causeless rebirth.”
"Even for animals that have been born [there], they brought back goods placed upon their hands and gave them to the king," he said, and added:
"In Ukkaṭṭha, they desire a hero; among counselors, one who is not fickle;
one who is dear in matters of food and drink, and one who is wise when a matter arises."
He related the Mahāsārajātaka.
"Not that strong" means they do not say that bond is firm. "Made of iron" means made of metal.
"Deeply stained with passion" means thoroughly dyed red; or, stained by passion, they are "deeply stained with passion," due to the conceit that "this is essential."
"Night" is the meaning. "Longing" means attachment or craving. "They say" means they speak. "Carrying away" means that which drags one toward the four states of misery (*apāya*).
"Loose" means it does not stand by obstructing the postures (*iriyāpatha*) like a binding made of iron or rope;
for those bound by such a bond go even to foreign lands. "Hard to release" means [it cannot be released] except by supramundane knowledge (*lokuttara-ñāṇa*).
"Impossible to release. Tenth.
The First Chapter.
2. The Second Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Sattajaṭila Sutta 122.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the second chapter, "In the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother": this refers to the mansion of Migāra’s Mother within the monastery known as the Eastern Park.
Herein is the sequential account: in the past, at the height of one hundred thousand aeons ago, there was one...

Having invited the Blessed One Padumuttara and given a gift of one hundred thousand offerings to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, that female lay devotee prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and made this aspiration: “In the future, may I be the foremost attendant of a Buddha such as you.
After wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she [was reborn] under us...

In the time of the Blessed One, she took rebirth in the womb of Queen Sumanā in the city of Bhaddiya, in the house of the merchant Dhanañjaya, the son of Meṇḍaka. At the time of her birth, they gave her the name Visākhā.
When the Blessed One arrived at the city of Bhaddiya, she went out to meet him together with five hundred young women.
At her very first sight of him, she became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
Later, she went to the house of Puṇṇavaḍḍhana Kumāra, the son of the merchant Migāra in Sāvatthī. There, the merchant Migāra established her in the position of a mother;
therefore, she is called Migāramātā. [She resided] in the palace built by her.
"Outside the gate-tower" means outside the gate-tower of the palace, not the gate-tower of the monastery.
It is said that the palace was surrounded by a rampart provided with four gate-towers on all sides, like the Lohapāsāda.
Outside the eastern gate-tower among them, sitting upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the shadow of the palace, he sat gazing toward the eastern world-system.
"Parūḷhakacchanakhaloma" means those with long hair in the armpits, long nails, and long body hair;
the meaning is that they have long hair on the armpits and so forth, as well as long nails. "Khārivividhaṃ" means various kinds of khāris, that is, the requisites and belongings of one gone forth.
"Avidūre atikkamantī" means they enter the city by a nearby road. "Rājāhaṃ, bhante" means "I am the king, venerable sir."

"King Pasenadi of Kosala knows my name. But why does the king sit near the foremost person in the world and offer salutations with joined palms to such naked, emaciated, and wretched people? It is for the sake of winning them over.
For it occurred to him: "If I do not show even this much favor to them, they will say, 'Having abandoned our children and wives..."
"For this purpose we endure poor food, painful lodgings, and so forth; yet he does not even offer us a mere salutation with joined palms.
Thinking thus, they would have concealed what they had seen and heard and not spoken of it. But since it was done in this way, they would have spoken without concealment.
Therefore, he acted in this manner. Furthermore, he did so for the sake of knowing the Teacher's inclination.

“Kāsikacandana” means fine sandalwood. “Garlands, scents, and unguents” refers to one who wears garlands for the sake of beauty and fragrance, scents for the sake of fragrance, and unguents for the sake of beauty and fragrance.
“By living together” means by dwelling with them. “Virtue is to be known” means that by living together and associating with them, one should come to know whether this person is virtuous or immoral.
And furthermore, “not briefly, but over a long period of time”—that virtue must be known over a long duration.

It is to be understood at the proper time, not otherwise; for within two or three days, it is impossible to demonstrate the manner of one who is self-restrained or the manner of one whose faculties are guarded.
"By one who attends to it" means that by attending with the thought, "I shall grasp his virtue," and by reflecting upon it, it can be known, but not by anyone else.
"By one who possesses wisdom" means that even this can be known only by the wise person endowed with discernment; for a fool, even though he attends to it, is unable to know it.
"By trade" means by speech.
"For whoever among men lives by trade—
know this, Vāseṭṭha— he is a merchant, not a brahmin."
For here, "usage" (vohāra) means conventional expression (vohāra). In the passage, “There are four noble usages and four ignoble usages,” it refers to volition (cetanā).
In the passage, “Concept, designation, description, usage,” it refers to a conceptual description (paññatti).

In the passage, “He might use it as mere usage,” it refers to speech (kathā). Here too, this very same meaning is intended. For indeed, speech in the presence of someone is [contrasted with] speech in their absence.

One's speech does not accord with another; what is spoken in the absence of someone does not accord with what is spoken in their presence, and likewise, what was said previously does not accord with what is said later, nor does what was said later accord with what was said previously.
By the very way he speaks, it can be known: "This person is impure.
But for one of pure virtue, what was said previously accords with what is said later, and what was said later accords with what was said previously; and what is spoken in their presence...

He spoke thus to demonstrate that one’s purity can be known by what is spoken in the absence of others, and by what is spoken in the presence of others; therefore, one who speaks [truthfully] can be recognized as pure.
"Strength" (*thāma*) refers to the strength of knowledge (*ñāṇathāma*). For he who lacks the strength of knowledge will, when calamities arise, fail to grasp what ought to be grasped.

Not seeing what must be done, he wanders about like one who has entered a house without a door. Therefore he said: "In times of calamity, O Great King, strength is to be known. By "discourse" (sākacchā) is meant conversation. For the talk of one lacking wisdom flounders like a water-snake in water; but for one possessed of wisdom, eloquence follows immediately upon his speaking. It is by the very movement of the water— [The text continues: ...that one may know the difference between the two. Just as one might test the depth of a river by casting a stone into it, so too is the nature of a person known by their speech. Therefore, one should examine a person through their conversation. Thus it was said: "By discourse, O Great King, wisdom is to be known. This is the meaning. Furthermore, when a wise man speaks, his speech is well-constructed, coherent, and free from contradiction, like a well-woven garland of flowers. But the speech of one lacking wisdom is disjointed, inconsistent, and full of contradictions, like a tangled skein of thread. Therefore, one should discern the inner quality of a person by observing their speech. This is the method for testing others. Thus it was said: "By discourse, O Great King, wisdom is to be known. This is the meaning. Moreover, when a wise man speaks, his words are measured, appropriate to the occasion, and beneficial; they bring peace and lead to liberation. But the speech of one lacking wisdom is excessive, inappropriate, and harmful; it increases defilement and leads to bondage. Therefore, one should examine a person through their speech. This is the means for discerning the true character of beings. Thus it was said: "By discourse, O Great King, wisdom is to be known. This is the meaning. Furthermore, when a wise man speaks, his mind remains calm and composed even amidst opposition; he does not become agitated or lose his self-possession. But the mind of one lacking wisdom becomes disturbed and agitated at the mere sound of another's voice, like a shallow pond stirred by the wind. Therefore, one should observe the stability of a person’s mind through their speech. This is the way to understand the inner state of others. Thus it was said: "By discourse, O Great King, wisdom is to be known. This is the meaning. Finally, when a wise man speaks, his words are rooted in virtue, grounded in truth, and consistent with the Dhamma; they lead to the cessation of suffering. But the speech of one lacking wisdom is devoid of virtue, contrary to truth, and opposed to the Dhamma; it leads only to further suffering. Therefore, one should judge a person by the fruit of their speech. This is the ultimate test of character. Thus it was said: "By discourse, O Great King, wisdom is to be known. This is the meaning. Thus have I explained the method for discerning the qualities of others through their speech. May this be for your benefit and for the welfare of all beings. Thus it was said: "By discourse, O Great King, wisdom is to be known. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section on the examination of persons through their speech. May there be success. May there be well-being. May there be peace. May there be happiness. May all beings be free from suffering. May all beings be happy. May all beings be well. May all beings be peaceful. For a fish is known as either small or large. "Ocarakā" means those who move below; for even those moving along the mountain peaks are indeed "ocaraka" (those who move below).
"Ocaritvā" means having moved about, having investigated, or having understood various occurrences—that is the meaning.
"Rajojallaṃ" means both dust (*raja*) and dirt (*jalla*). "By color and form" means by color and shape. "Of limited vision" means...
By means of a light appearance. "With a semblance" means with a decorative trinket.
"A mere clay earring resembling [one]" means a clay earring that merely resembles a golden earring. "A half-penny of iron" means a half-penny made of iron. First. 2.
Commentary on the Discourse of the Five Kings.

123. In the second [verse], "forms" (*rūpā*) refers to the objective field of form (*rūpārammaṇa*) divided into blue, yellow, and so forth. "The peak of sensual pleasures" (*kāmānaṃ aggaṃ*): one who values forms says this is the highest and most excellent among sensual pleasures.
The same method applies to the others as well. "When" (*yataḥ*) means whenever. "The limit of the agreeable" (*manāpapariyantaṃ*):

that which has the production of the agreeable as its culmination, having the agreeable as its ultimate point. In this regard, there are two kinds of the agreeable: the agreeable pertaining to persons (*puggalamanāpa*) and the agreeable by convention (*sammutimanāpa*). The agreeable pertaining to persons...
That which is desirable and pleasing to one person is precisely what is undesirable and unpleasing to another.
For instance, even mole-crabs are desirable, pleasing, and agreeable to those living in border regions, yet they are extremely loathsome to those living in the Middle Country.
Furthermore, peacock flesh and the like are desirable to them, whereas for others, these are extremely loathsome. This is "agreeable to persons. The other is "agreeable by convention."
In the world, there is no such thing as a distinctively divided category of desirable and undesirable objects; rather, they must be shown by way of analysis.

And when analyzing, one should not do so by way of those who were excessively wealthy, such as Mahā Sammata, Mahāsudassana, or Dharmāśoka, for even today an object appears unpleasant to them. Nor should one analyze by way of those who are extremely destitute and lack food and drink.

It should not be analyzed even by way of those [gods]. For even the grains of rice from their *kaṇājaka* porridge have a flavor like that of rotten meat, yet it is exceedingly sweet, as if it were ambrosia (*amata*).

However, it should be analyzed by way of those of middle status—accountants, high officials, guild-leaders, householders, merchants, and so forth—who obtain what is desirable at times and what is undesirable at other times. And this object—
The javana is unable to delimit the desirable or the undesirable. For the javana feels lust for what is desirable and also for what is undesirable;
it feels aversion toward what is desirable and also toward what is undesirable. However, the resultant consciousness (vipākacitta) delimits the desirable and the undesirable with absolute certainty.
Indeed, even those with wrong view may close their eyes upon seeing sublime objects such as the Buddha, the Saṅgha, or great shrines.
They fall into mental distress; upon hearing the sound of the Dhamma, they plug their ears.

However, their eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness are exclusively wholesome resultant states. Even though dung-beetles and the like, having smelled the scent of dung, experience joy thinking, "We shall get to eat," their eye-consciousness at the sight of the dung is [wholesome resultant].
In the smelling of odors, the nose-consciousness, and in the tasting of flavors, the tongue-consciousness, are exclusively unwholesome resultant states.
However, the Blessed One spoke those words beginning with "And those forms, O Great King," with reference to things that are agreeable to a person.
"Candanaṅgalika" is the name of that lay follower. "It occurs to me, Blessed One" means: "It occurs to me, Blessed One."
One cause presents itself and becomes manifest: although those five kings,
adorned with loosened jeweled earrings, arrived with great royal majesty and supreme sovereign power while he was seated in his drinking hall,
from the very moment they stood in the presence of the One of Ten Powers, they became like lamps by day or like embers sprinkled with water.
Seeing that the sun, like a glow-worm at sunrise, had its radiance destroyed and its beauty lost, while the Tathāgata shone a hundredfold and a thousandfold more than them, the thought arose in him:
"Oh, how great indeed are those called Buddhas! Therefore he spoke thus.
*Kokanada* is a synonym for the lotus (*paduma*). *Pāto* means early in the morning. *Siyā* means it might be. *Avītagandha* means not devoid of fragrance.
"Unfading fragrance. "Aṅgīrasa" refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One. Indeed, rays of light issue forth from the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Blessed One;

therefore, he is called "Aṅgīrasa. Just as a lotus known as the *kokanada* may be in full bloom at dawn and possess unfading fragrance, even so, one should behold the Blessed One Aṅgīrasa, blazing like the sun shining in the sky.
This is the summary of the meaning here. "He covered the Blessed One" means he gave it to the Blessed One; such is the expression used here according to worldly convention.
It is said that the lay follower, having gained confidence in the virtues of the Tathāgata, thought:
"These people are giving me five upper robes out of faith in the Tathāgata’s qualities; I too shall give them to the Blessed One himself," and so he gave them. This is the second [section].
3. Commentary on the Doṇapākasutta 124.

Regarding the third [verse], "he eats a *doṇapāka* meal": the meaning is that he eats a *doṇapāka* curry (*kura*), which is cooked rice from a *doṇa* measure of grain, along with its corresponding soups and condiments.
"Having eaten" means having first dispelled the drowsiness following a meal for a short while.
Having rested, he went to attend upon the Buddha; however, on that day, while still eating, he remembered the One of Ten Powers, and having washed his hands, he departed.
As he walked, a powerful fever from the meal arose within him, so that he breathed with great gasps and sweat-drops fell from his limbs. On both sides of him—

"Standing at the mountain passes, they fan him with pairs of palm-leaf fans; yet, out of reverence for the Buddha, he does not venture to lie down"—it is with reference to this that it is said, "he was heavy-breathing.
"He spoke this verse": thinking, "The king suffers from immoderation in eating;
I shall provide him with a comfortable dwelling," the king spoke this. "Of the man" means of the sentient being.
"A hundred kahāpaṇas" means fifty for breakfast and fifty for dinner; thus it is a hundred kahāpaṇas.
"Having mastered [the verses]" means that after traveling a short distance with the king, he asked, "To whom shall I give this auspicious sword, Great King?
When told, "Give it to such-and-such a person," he gave the sword and, having approached the One of Ten Powers, stood before him and recited a verse.
"Speak, O Gotamas," having said this, the meaning is that he mastered what was spoken by the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "he indeed spoke during the distribution of food": how did he speak? According to the method instructed by the Blessed One.
For the Blessed One instructed him thus: "Young man, do not recite this verse like an actor at every single performance; [recite it] for the king..."
Standing where he is eating, you should say nothing during the first morsel and so forth, but speak when the final morsel has been taken;

upon hearing this, the king will surely discard the portion of rice. Then, once the king’s hands have been washed, remove the bowl, count the grains of rice, and having ascertained the amount of sauce required, bring that same quantity of rice on the following day for his breakfast.

"And having said this, you must not speak at the evening meal. Having assented with "Very well," because he had gone that day to eat the king's morning meal, he recited the verse according to the Blessed One’s instruction at the evening meal.
The King, remembering the words of the One of Ten Powers, discarded the bowl of food right there. When the king’s hands were washed, [the monk] removed the bowl.
Having counted the grains of rice and determined the amount of sauce required, they brought that same quantity of rice on the following day.
It was said that the young man would go to the presence of the Tathāgata day after day until he had reached the limit of a *nāḷika* of boiled rice;
he became a trusted confidant of the One Possessing Ten Powers. Then, one day, [the Buddha] asked him: "How much does the king [consume]?"
“...is eating? He replied, “A measure of boiled rice. [The king thought: “This will suffice for this much;
he is a man of substance. From now on, do not speak verses. Thus the king desisted right there. Regarding the phrase “both for the sake of the present life and for the sake of the future life”:
here, having one’s body well-nourished is what is meant by the purpose of the present life, while virtue (*sīla*) is the purpose of the future life. Regarding food:
"Knowing the proper measure is indeed what is called a factor of virtue.
This is the third [sutta]. 4. Commentary on the First Saṅgāma Sutta:
125. Regarding "Vedehiputta": *Vedehī* is a designation for the wise; thus, it means "the son of a wise woman."
The meaning is as follows. "Consisting of four divisions" means endowed with the four components known as elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
"Having arrayed themselves" means having caused them to put on their armor by fastening leather cuirasses and so forth. "In battle" means they fought.
For what reason? It is said that when King Mahākosala was giving his daughter to King Bimbisāra, [a conflict arose] between the two kingdoms.
The village named Kāsīgāma, which yielded a hundred thousand [measures of revenue], was given to his daughter.

When Ajātasattu had put his father to death, his mother also died shortly thereafter from the grief of separation from the king. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, thinking, "Ajātasattu has killed both his mother and father;
this village belonged to my father," brought a lawsuit for its sake. Ajātasattu also [thought], "It is mine..."
“Belonging to his mother”: for the sake of that village, even two maternal uncles and their nephews fought with one another.
One who has evil friends such as Devadatta and others is an “evil-friend. Those very people are his companions, thus he is an “evil-companion.
His mind inclines toward and leans upon those very people, thus he is “leaning toward evil. This is by way of [the examples of] Pasenadi, the Elder Sāriputta, and so forth.
