The state of having virtuous friends and so forth is to be understood. "He lies in suffering" means that he will lie in suffering while grieving over the elephants and other animals he has conquered.
The Blessed One spoke this again upon seeing the cause for his defeat.
"Victory engenders enmity" means that one who conquers engenders enmity; he acquires an enemy person. This is the fourth [verse].
5. Commentary on the Second Saṅgāmasutta 126.

In the fifth [verse], regarding the phrase "he went forth into battle": having incurred reproach for his defeat, he said, "Go to the monastery and listen to the conversation and discourse of the bhikkhus.
Then, during the night, by means of an elder who had gone forth under the name Buddhārakkhita, [he spoke] to the elder Dhammarakkhita.
“Should the king go after employing this stratagem, he will win again”—having heard this reason for victory thus stated, he set out on his expedition.
*Yāvassa upakappati* means as long as it is suitable or sufficient for him. *Yadā caññe* means when others.
*Vilumpanti* means they plunder the person who stands there having been plundered. *Vilumpati* means he is plundered. *Ṭhānaṃ hi maññati* means he considers it a standing place (or a firm position).
For he thinks, "It is the cause. "Yadā" means at whatever time. One who is victorious gains a victor;
a person who is winning later gains even one who is victorious over him. "Rosetāraṃ" means one who provokes or irritates. "Rosako" means an irritator or provoker.
"By the turning of karma" means by the transformation of karma, that is, by the giving of the result of that act of plundering. "He who was plundered is plundered" means he...
The plunderer is plundered. This is the fifth [verse]. 6.
Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta: 127.
Regarding the sixth [verse], "He approached": this refers to when Queen Mallikā was giving birth, [the Blessed One] had the lying-in chamber prepared.
Having granted protection, he approached her. He was displeased; that is, he thought: "Great power has been given to my daughter from a poor family.
Had she obtained a son, she would have received great honor; now she has fallen away from that," and thus he was displeased.
"A woman" refers to a certain woman as compared to the dull-witted Elamūga-putta.
*Seyyā*: "By those who are better" means by those who are superior. *Janādhipā*: he addresses the king, the lord of people, as "lord of people. *Sassudevā*:

"with the deities of one's mother and father" refers to the deities of one's mother and father-in-law. *Disampatī*: "lords of the quarters" refers to those who are the foremost in their respective directions. *Tādisā subhagiya*: "by such a fortunate wife.
The sixth [chapter]. 7. Commentary on the *Appamāda-sutta*.

128. *Samadhiggayha* means having fully grasped; the sense is "having taken up. *Appamāda* refers to the diligence of the one who causes [the state] to be produced. *Samodhāna* means conjunction or inclusion.
*Evameva kho*—for just as the elephant’s footprint is [the foremost], so too is the diligence of the one who causes [the state] to be produced;

and just as the remaining types of footprints are [the rest], so too are the remaining wholesome states belonging to the four planes. These are like the remaining footprints in relation to the elephant’s footprint.
They converge upon heedfulness; they revolve within heedfulness.
And just as the elephant’s footprint is the foremost and best among all other footprints, so too does he show that heedfulness is the foremost among all other qualities.
For even though it is mundane, insofar as it is the means for obtaining the sublime and supramundane states, it is indeed their very summit.
“They praise heedfulness” means that they praise heedfulness alone, thinking, “One who aspires to these things, such as long life, must practice heedfulness.
Or, because the wise praise heedfulness in the performance of meritorious deeds, the meaning is: therefore, one who aspires to long life and so forth must practice heedfulness.
“The attainment of the goal” means the acquisition of the goal. Seventh.
8. Commentary on the Kalyāṇamitta Sutta 129.
Regarding the eighth [sutta], "And that, moreover, for one with a good friend": this Dhamma is called "well-expounded" only for one who has a good friend, not for one who has a bad friend.
For although the Dhamma is indeed well-expounded for everyone, it is for one with a good friend...
But for one who desires to hear, who has faith, and who puts it into practice—just as medicine works for one who uses it—it fulfills its purpose, not for anyone else.
Therefore this was said. And here, "Dhamma" should be understood as the Dhamma of the teaching.
Regarding the phrase "this is only half," the Elder, it is said, reflected while in seclusion: "This so-called 'monk’s duty' (samaṇadhamma) refers to the instructor and the admonisher..."
“When a virtuous friend exists, for one who stands firm in personal exertion, success is achieved;
half comes from the virtuous friend and half from personal exertion. Then it occurred to him:
“I am standing on partial knowledge and am unable to contemplate the matter in its entirety; having questioned the Teacher, I shall become free from doubt. Therefore—
Having approached the Teacher, he spoke thus: "Of the holy life"—that is, of the Noble Path—"this, namely, good friendship":
the meaning is that this which is called good friendship constitutes one half; it comes from that half. Thus the Elder [said]:
"Right view and the other factors come from good friendship by one half each, while they come from individual manly effort by one half each."
It has been said. Although this was the elder’s wish, nevertheless,

just as when many stone pillars have been erected there is no differentiation such that "this much was erected by so-and-so" and "this much by so-and-so," and just as among sons born depending upon their mother and father there is no differentiation such that "this much was produced from the mother" and "this much from the father"—

There is no separation; likewise here too, this is of an inseparable nature, such that it is impossible to determine, "this much has arisen from spiritual friends as right view and so forth, and this much from one's own personal effort.
However, since half the virtue is obtained through spiritual friendship, it is called "half" according to the Elder’s intention, whereas [in reality] it is the entirety of the virtue.

"It is acquired" means that, according to the Blessed One’s intention, the entire [category] is called "acquired. As for "good friendship," this is taken as the section on acquisition in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).
In terms of meaning, it refers to the four aggregates acquired by relying on a good friend, by way of virtue, concentration, and insight;
some even say it includes the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) as well.
"Do not say so, Ānanda! Do not speak thus, Ānanda.
You are learned, you have attained the analytical knowledges of one in training, and you attend upon me having received eight boons; you are endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities.
It is not fitting for one such as you to speak in this way. For this entire holy life, Ānanda, is simply this: good friendship."

The Blessed One said this with reference to the fact that "the four paths, the four fruits, the three knowledges (vijjā), and the six direct knowledges (abhiññā)—all these have their root in a good friend alone.
Now, showing the reason by means of a verbal expression, he said: "Of one who has a good friend," and so forth.
In this context, *pāṭikaṅkha* means that which is to be expected, desired, or necessarily occurring.
"Here" means in this teaching. Regarding the phrases beginning with "develops right view," this is first of all a brief commentary on those eight initial terms:
right view has the characteristic of seeing rightly; right intention has the characteristic of directing [the mind] rightly;
right speech has the characteristic of encompassing rightly; right action has the characteristic of originating rightly.
Right livelihood has the characteristic of complete purification; right effort has the characteristic of right exertion;
right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing; right concentration has the characteristic of right composure.
Each of these has three functions. To wit: first, right view itself [purifies] by others as well as by itself...

Together with the opposing defilements, it abandons wrong view, takes cessation as its object, and perceives the associated states through non-delusion by way of dispelling the delusion that conceals them.
Right intention and the others likewise abandon wrong intention and so forth, and take cessation as their object. However, specifically in this case:
Right view correctly shows the co-nascent states; right intention directs them; right speech correctly grasps them;
right action correctly originates them; right livelihood correctly purifies them; right effort correctly exerts them;
right mindfulness correctly establishes them; and right concentration correctly sustains them.
In its preliminary stage, right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) occurs at various moments and has various objects; however, at the time of the Path, it occurs at a single moment and has a single object.
As for its function, right view receives four names, beginning with "knowledge regarding suffering" (dukkhe ñāṇa).

Right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) and the other factors likewise occur at various moments and have various objects in their preliminary stages, but at the time of the Path, they occur at a single moment and have a single object.
Among these, right intention receives three names according to its function: "intention of renunciation," and so forth.
Right speech and the other two [right action and right livelihood] are both abstinences and volitions; however, at the moment of the Path, they are only abstinences.
Right effort and right mindfulness—this pair also receives four names according to their functions by way of the "right strivings" and the "foundations of mindfulness. Right concentration...
However, both in the prior stage and at the moment of the path, it is precisely right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).

Thus, having first understood the commentary on the meaning of the eight initial terms stated by way of the method beginning with "right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*), it should now be understood in this way regarding the phrases "he develops [it] based on seclusion," and so forth. "He develops" means he increases; for himself...
It means that it produces [the mind] again and again within the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*), or brings it forth (*abhinibbatteti*).

"Dependent on seclusion" (*vivekanissitaṃ*) means dependent upon seclusion, or supported by seclusion; thus it is "dependent on seclusion. Seclusion (*viveka*) is the state of being secluded (*vivittatā*).

This state of being secluded is fivefold: seclusion by way of its constituent part (*tadaṅga-viveka*), seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*), seclusion by eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), seclusion by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-viveka*), and seclusion by escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*).

Thus, regarding these five kinds of seclusion, the meaning should be understood as follows: "He develops right view dependent on seclusion" means he develops right view dependent on seclusion by way of its factors (*tadaṅga-viveka*), dependent on seclusion by way of eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), and dependent on seclusion by way of escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*).

For indeed, when this yogi devoted to the development of the Noble Path is at the moment of insight (*vipassanā-khaṇa*), [right view] is dependent on seclusion by way of its function; by way of his inclination...
At the time of the path, one develops right view which, in terms of its function, is dependent on seclusion as abandonment, and in terms of its object, is dependent on seclusion as escape.
This same method applies to [right view] dependent on fading away and so forth; for fading away and the rest have seclusion as their meaning.
However, in this context, relinquishment (*vossagga*) is twofold: relinquishment as giving up and relinquishment as leaping forward. Therein:

"Relinquishment as giving up" (*pariccāga-vossagga*) refers to the abandoning of defilements through the factor of "partial eradication" (*tadaṅga*) at the moment of insight, and through "complete eradication" (*samuccheda*) at the moment of the Path.

"Relinquishment as plunging" (*pakkhandana-vossagga*) refers to the plunging into Nibbāna by way of being inclined toward it at the moment of insight, and by way of making it the object at the moment of the Path;
both of these [types of relinquishment] are included here in this mixture of mundane and supramundane states.
The method of explaining the meaning is appropriate here. For in the manner already described, this right view both abandons the defilements and leaps toward Nibbāna.
By the entire phrase "tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*), however, it is indicated that it both tends toward and has reached the state of relinquishment.

"Ripening and fully ripened"—this is what is meant. For this bhikkhu devoted to the cultivation of the Noble Path cultivates right view in such a way that it ripens for the purpose of relinquishing the defilements and for the purpose of launching out toward Nibbāna, and he cultivates it in such a way that it becomes fully ripened. This same method applies to the remaining path factors.
"Having approached" means having undertaken, having aimed at, or having depended upon. "Subject to birth" means having birth as its nature, having birth as its inherent character.
"Therefore" means because the entire Noble Path is obtained by relying on a spiritual friend; therefore. "Handa" is a particle used in the sense of encouragement.
"They praise heedfulness" means they extol heedfulness; therefore, heedfulness should be practiced. "For the realization of the goal."
The attainment of wealth. The eighth [chapter]. 9.
Commentary on the First *Aputtaka-sutta* (130).
In the ninth [sutta], "by day during the day" (*divā divassa*) means by day of the day; the meaning is at the time of midday. "Inheritance" (*sāpateyyaṃ*).

“Money. But what need is there to mention silver? This means: what kind of limiting statement could there be regarding the amount of “silver goods”—that is, wealth consisting of gold, silver, copper, iron, bronze, ploughshares, tortoise-shells, and so forth—whether in the form of solid bullion or as articles for use such as vessels and the like?
“Kaṇājaka” means rice mixed with broken grains. “With sour gruel as the second [item]” means...
"With sour gruel as the second. "Sāṇa" means made of hemp fibers. "A three-panel undergarment" refers to an undergarment made by sewing three pieces together at two places.
"An inferior person" means a base man.
Regarding the terms "upward-reaching" (*uddhaggikā*) and so forth: it is "upward" (*uddhaṃ*) because it yields fruit on successive levels, one above the other.
"Leading upwards" (*aggamā*) means directed upward. "Leading to heaven" (*sovaggikā*) means beneficial for heaven because it produces rebirth there.
"Having a pleasant result" (*sukhavipākā*) means its maturation is pleasant in the places where one is reborn.
"Conducive to heaven" (*saggasaṃvattanikā*) means because it brings about the production of excellent divine qualities such as celestial form and so forth. One does not establish such a gift of alms.
“Sātodakā” means having sweet water. “Settodakā” means having white water because of the whiteness of the water at the places where the waves break.
“Supatitthā” means having beautiful landing places. “Taṃ jano” means that people would not carry away that water by which it is sweet, even after filling their vessels with it.
“Na yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyya” means they would not perform whatever function of water is required by that water.

Whatever ought to be done, that he does not do. "Not drinking that" means not drinking that [liquor]. "And he performs his duties" means he performs the duties he himself must perform and the duties of skillful action;
the meaning is that he eats, engages in his work, and gives gifts. The ninth [sutta].
10. Commentary on the Second *Aputtaka Sutta* (Sutta 131).
"In the tenth [verse], 'he provided with almsfood' (*piṇḍapātena paṭipādesi*) means he joined it together with almsfood; the meaning is that he gave him almsfood.
'He departed' (*pakkāmi*) means he went away for some business such as attending upon the king. 'Later he became remorseful' (*pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosi*)"—so it is said.
It is said that on other days he would see that paccekabuddha, yet the thought to give did not arise in him.
But on that day, this third son of Queen Padumavatī, the paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī,
having spent the time on Mount Gandhamādana in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), emerged from it at the time of forenoon and went to Lake Anotatta.
Having washed his face, put on his lower garment on the surface of a slab of emerald, fastened his waistband, and taken up his bowl and robe,
he entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Rising into the air by means of psychic power (*iddhi*),
he descended at the city gate, donned his robes, took his bowl, and [stood] at the doors of the houses of the city-dwellers with a thousand-fold bundle.
As if setting them down, he gradually approached the gate of the merchant’s house with his graceful and excellent deportment.

On that day, the merchant had risen early, eaten a sumptuous meal, and was sitting at the porch of his house with a seat prepared, cleaning the spaces between his teeth. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, on that very day—
Having eaten in the morning and sat down, he gave rise to a mind of generosity; he summoned his wife and, saying, "Give alms-food to this ascetic," he departed.
The merchant’s wife thought: "In all this time, I have never before heard him say the word 'give'."

"Even though I am giving today, I am not giving to just anyone; I am giving to a Paccekabuddha who is free from lust, hatred, and delusion, who has vomited out the defilements, and who has laid down the burden.
Without giving this or that [ordinary food], I shall give excellent alms-food.
Having spoken thus, he went out from his house, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha with the fivefold prostration, took his bowl, and [entered] within the residence.

Having had him seated on a prepared seat, she prepared a meal with perfectly pure rice grains, and having carefully selected appropriate hard foods, curries, and soups, she filled his bowl, adorned it externally with perfumes, and placing it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, she paid homage to him.
The Paccekabuddha said: "To other Paccekabuddhas as well..."
Thinking, "I shall make a collection," he departed after offering words of appreciation without even consuming the food himself.
Then, as the merchant was returning from outside, he saw the Paccekabuddha and asked, "We said, 'Give almsfood to you,' and then departed;
have you received it? "Yes, merchant, I have received it. "Let me see," he said, and lifting his neck, he looked up.
Then the fragrance of his alms-food arose and struck his nostrils. Being unable to restrain his mind, he later became remorseful.
The passage beginning with "This would be better" is a demonstration of the manner in which remorse arises. And [he thought] regarding his brother’s only son and his inheritance...
"Because he deprived him of life": at that time, it is said, while his family was still undivided, his mother, father, and elder brother all passed away.
He then entered into a household life with his brother’s wife. His brother, however, had a son;
as the boy was playing in the street, people said: "This is a slave, this is a slave-girl, this is a carriage, this is..."
“The wealth belongs to you. Having taken their word, he said, “This slave belongs to me,” and so forth.
Then his younger father thought: “This boy speaks thus even now; when he grows old, he will cause a rift in the family.
I shall do what must be done for him right now. One day, taking an axe, he said: “Come, sir!”
"Son, let us go to the forest. Having led him to that forest, he killed him while he was crying out again and again, threw him into a pit, and covered it over with earth.
It is with reference to this that it was said. "Seven times" means seven occasions.

And here the meaning should be understood according to the distinction between prior and subsequent volition (*cetanā*). For in the giving of even a single alms-food offering, there is indeed a single volition.
He does not grant two types of rebirth-linking; however, by virtue of his prior and subsequent volitions, he was reborn seven times in heaven and seven times in the family of a wealthy merchant.
"Purāṇa" refers to the kamma consisting of the volition of giving alms-food to the Paccekabuddha.
"Pariggaha" refers to the property that has been acquired. "Anujīvino" refers to those who depend upon a single great family, numbering fifty or sixty [in total].
"Families live on"—this was said with reference to human beings. "One should not go taking anything at all"—this means one should not go having grasped any of this.
"Everything goes leaving behind"—the meaning is that everything has the nature of being left behind; its very nature is that it must be relinquished. The tenth [sutta].
The second chapter.
3. Third Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Persons (Puggalasutta). 132.

In the first [discourse] of the third chapter, one who is joined with darkness by means of such things as "reborn in a low family" is called *tamo* (darkness). This refers to bodily misconduct and so forth.

Furthermore, because he goes to the state of hell, he is "one whose final destination is darkness. Thus, by both [of these descriptions], only the darkness of the aggregates (*khandha-tama*) is spoken of.
Because he is endowed with the light [of birth] such as being "reborn in a high family," he is "bright" (*joti*); what is meant is that he has become luminous.

Furthermore, because he goes to the state of light through rebirth in heaven by means of good bodily conduct and so forth, he is "one whose final destination is light" (*joti-parāyana*). By this same method, the other two [categories] should also be understood.
"In a bamboo-worker family" means in a family of basket-makers. "In a hunter family" means in a family of deer-trappers and the like. "In a cartwright family" means in a family of leather-workers.
"In a scavenger family" means in a family of those who throw away flowers. "Of difficult livelihood" means of a painful livelihood. "Ugly" means having the color of a burnt stump, like a dust-demon.
"Unpleasant to look upon" means one whose appearance is disagreeable even to his own mother at birth. "A hunchback" means one with a crooked body.
"Blind" means one who is blind in one eye or blind in both eyes. "Lame" means one who is lame in one hand or lame in both hands.
"Cripple" means one who is crippled in one leg or crippled in both legs. "Palsy-stricken" means one whose limbs are paralyzed, such as a person who crawls on a bench.
"Of lighting materials" refers to the requisites for a lamp, such as oil, a bowl, and so forth. "In this way, O Great King"—here, one...
A person who, not seeing light externally, passes away right within the mother’s womb and is reborn in the states of misery (*apāya*), wanders for an entire *kappa*;
he too is one whose destination is from darkness to darkness. That person must be a deceitful individual (*kuhakapuggala*).
For it is said that such a rebirth occurs for a deceitful person.

And here, by the phrases "he is reborn in a low family, such as a family of Caṇḍālas," etc., both the failure of arrival (*āgamana-vipatti*) and the failure of previously arisen conditions (*pubbuppanna-paccaya-vipatti*) are shown.

By "poor," etc., the failure of currently existing conditions (*pavatta-paccaya-vipatti*) is shown. By "a life of hardship," etc., the failure of the means of livelihood (*ājīva-upāya-vipatti*) is shown. By "ugly," etc., the failure of the personal existence (*attabhāva-vipatti*) is shown.
By "afflicted with many illnesses," etc., the conjunction with causes of suffering is shown. By "not a recipient," etc., [the failure of requisites is shown].

There is both the failure of the causes of happiness and the failure of enjoyment. By such phrases as "misconduct of body," etc., there is the conjunction with the causes for having a future existence in darkness.

By such phrases as "with the breakup of the body," etc., there is the approach to that [darkness] in the next world. The bright side (the *śuklapakṣa*) is to be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
"He reviles" means he reviles by means of the ten grounds for reviling. "He insults" means: "Why do you stand here? What is the use of you? and so forth.
"Did we perform agricultural work and so forth?"—with such words of contempt he reviles him. "An irritator" means one who provokes.
"With an undistracted mind" means with a one-pointed mind. First.
2. Commentary on the Ayyikā Sutta.
133. In the second [verse], "worn out" (*jiṇṇa*) means worn out by old age. "Aged" (*vuḍḍha*) means aged in years. "Elderly" (*mahallikā*) means advanced in birth.

"Advanced in life" (*addhagatā*) means those who have passed through a long period of time. "Reached the final stage of life" (*vayoanuppattā*) means those who have arrived at the last stage of existence. Regarding "dear and pleasing":
it is said that when the King's mother had died, his grandmother stood in the place of a mother and cared for him; therefore, he felt a powerful affection for his grandmother.
It arose. Therefore he spoke thus. "By the elephant-treasure" means that an elephant worth a hundred thousand, adorned with ornaments worth a hundred thousand, is called the elephant-treasure.
The same method applies to the horse-treasure as well. A "choice village" is indeed a village yielding a revenue of a hundred thousand.
All of these are subject to breaking; for among them, some break even while being made, and some break once their construction is finished.
Just as some [fruit] has not yet been removed from the stalk, some is merely placed on the ground after being partially removed, and some is further removed than that;

even so, among sentient beings, some die after having taken rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), some while still in the womb before emerging from the mother’s belly, some immediately upon emerging, and some beyond that. Therefore he spoke thus. Second.
134. In the third [discourse], everything is quite clear. This is the third. 4.
Commentary on the *Issattasutta*. 135.
The introduction to the fourth [discourse] arises from a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppattika*). It is said that during the Blessed One’s first enlightenment, there was great gain and honor.
and it arose among the community of monks. The members of other sects, having lost their gains and honor, wandered among the families crying out thus:
“The ascetic Gotama says this: ‘Gifts should be given only to me, not to others;
gifts should be given only to my disciples, not to the disciples of others. Only to me...”

“Gifts given to me are of great fruit, but gifts given to others are not of great fruit; gifts given to my own disciples are of great fruit, but gifts given to the disciples of others are not of great fruit.
Is it indeed proper for him himself, while depending on alms-gathering, to create an obstacle to the four requisites for others who depend on alms-gathering? He does what is improper.
“It is unbecoming. As that report spread, it reached the royal palace. Having heard it, the king thought:
“It is impossible that the Tathāgata would create an obstacle to the gains of others. These people are striving for the Tathāgata’s lack of gain and disrepute.
If I were to remain right here and say, ‘Do not speak thus; the Teacher does not speak in such a way,’ [they would not listen].”
“If I were to speak now, this discourse would not lead to his conversion; I shall convert him at the very time when this great multitude has assembled.
Thinking thus, he remained silent while awaiting a festival day.
Later, when a great festival had arrived, he had a drum beaten throughout the city, thinking, “Now is the time for him.”
“Whether they be faithful or faithless, right-viewed or wrong-viewed, excluding the household-protecting children or women,
for all others who do not come to the monastery, the fine shall be fifty [pieces]. Having bathed early in the morning and partaken of his breakfast,
he himself, adorned with all his ornaments, went to the monastery together with a great military force.
As he was walking, he thought: "The Blessed One said to you, 'Gifts should be given to me alone...
[etc. ...what is given to other disciples does not bear great fruit. It is improper to ask him this; I shall ask a question instead.
And while answering my question, the Blessed One will refute the doctrine of the non-Buddhist sects at the conclusion. He then asked the question.
He asked: "Venerable sir, where indeed should a gift be given? [The Buddha replied:
"Wherever the mind has faith—that person, in that person it should be given; or rather, it should be given to him.
When this was said, the king looked toward those men by whom the words of the sectarians had been reported to him. By the king...
As soon as they were looked upon by him, they stood there crestfallen, with their faces cast down, scratching the ground with their big toes.
The King, making it known to the great multitude, spoke in a loud voice: "In a single stroke, venerable sirs, the heretics have been defeated!
Having spoken thus, he said: "The Blessed One has [conquered] Citta among the Nigaṇṭhas, the Acelakas, the Paribbājakas, and others—wherever he may be."
“He finds faith; but where, venerable sir, is a gift of great fruit? he asked. “This is another matter,” [the Blessed One replied].
“Great King, what you first asked was one thing, and what you asked later is another. Observe this: answering questions is my burden.
Having said this, he spoke the passage beginning with “But for one who is virtuous... In that context, *idha tyassa* means “here for you it would be. *Samupabyūḷho* means...

"Rāsibhūto" means one who has become a mere heap [of untrained parts]. "Asikkhito" means untrained in the art of archery. "Akatahattho" means one whose hand has not been perfected through practices such as binding the fist.
"Akatayoggo" means one who has not gained proficiency in [shooting at] heaps of grass, heaps of clay, and so forth.
"Akatūpāsano" means one who has not demonstrated his skill before kings or royal ministers. "Chambhī" means one whose body trembles.
Regarding the phrases "sensual desire has been abandoned" and so forth: sensual desire is abandoned by the path of Arahatship; ill will is abandoned by the path of Non-returning;
sloth and torpor, as well as restlessness, are abandoned by the path of Arahatship itself; remorse is abandoned by the third path (the path of Non-returning);

and doubt is abandoned by the first path. By the "aggregate of virtue of one beyond training" (*asekkha*) means that the aggregate of virtue belonging to one beyond training is itself beyond training.

This is called the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*). This same method applies everywhere. Here, by the first four terms, mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are explained.
The "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), which is exclusively mundane.

"Archery" (*issatta*) means the craft of archery. Regarding "strength and energy" (*balavīriya*): here, "strength" (*bala*) refers to the air element (*vāyodhātu*), while "energy" (*vīriya*) is simply physical and mental energy.
*Bhareti* means *bhareyya* (he should bear). Regarding “not for the sake of birth”: one should not bear a grudge because of birth, thinking, “This person is of noble birth.
*Khanti-soraccaṃ*: here, *khanti* is patience in the sense of endurance, and *soraccaṃ* is arahantship.
*Dhammā*: these two qualities. *Assame*: in a dwelling. *Vivane*: in a forest place; in a waterless forest, such things as four-cornered lotus ponds [should be built].
The meaning is "should have made. "Dugga" means in uneven places. "Crossings" (*saṅkamanāni*) means he should make crossings fifty or sixty cubits wide, with well-spread and pure sand.
Now, while explaining the conduct regarding alms-gathering for monks dwelling in these forest lodgings, [he says] "food" (*annaṃ*).
He said, "They drink," and so forth. Therein, "lodgings" refers to beds, chairs, and the like.
"With a serene mind" means that even when giving to one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), one should not give with a doubtful or defiled mind, but rather with a serene mind alone.
"Thundering" means roaring. "Satakkaku" means having a hundred peaks; the meaning is having many summits. "Abhisaṅkhacca" means having prepared.
"Having gathered together and made into a heap.
"Rejoicing" means having a mind that is satisfied. "Scatters" means he distributes it among the recipients of the gift; or, as if scattering it, he gives the gift.
"Streams of merit" refers to the streams of merit consisting of many volitions of giving. "It rains upon the giver" means just as in the sky...

Just as streams of water issuing from a risen cloud rain down, moistening, wetting, and saturating the earth, even so this stream of merit arising within the donor moistens, fills, and overflows that very giver.
Therefore it is said: "It rains upon the donor. This is the fourth [simile].
5. Commentary on the Pabbatūpama Sutta (The Simile of the Mountain) 136.

In the fifth [verse], "of those anointed on the head" (*muddhāvasittānaṃ*) means of those who have been anointed on the head by the consecration of a kṣatriya, having had the royal aspersion performed.

"Overwhelmed by greed for sensual pleasures" (*kāmagedhapariyuṭṭhitānaṃ*) means overwhelmed and overcome by greed for sensual pleasures. "Having attained stability in their own territories" (*janapadatthāvariyappattānaṃ*)...
"Of those who have attained stability in the countryside. "Royal duties" means royal affairs, tasks to be performed by kings.
"In these, indeed, I... means "in these, I [am engaged]. "Has entered upon exertion" means he has entered into activity.
It is said that this king goes to attend upon the Blessed One three times a day, and there are also many intermediate visits. His [schedule] was fixed...
The army of one who goes forth may be either large or small. Now one day, five hundred thieves thought:
"This king goes at an improper time with a small force to visit the ascetic Gotama;
we shall seize him on the way and take the kingdom. They hid themselves in the Andhavana forest. Kings, indeed, possess great merit.
Then, one man from among them himself emerged and informed the king.
The king, taking a great army, surrounded the Blind Forest and captured them all.
From the Blind Forest as far as the city gate, he stationed them on both sides of the road so close together that they could gaze at one another, eye to eye.
Having had stakes driven in, he caused him to be impaled upon them. It was with reference to this that he spoke thus.

Then the Teacher thought: "If I were to say, 'Great King, while a Perfectly Enlightened One such as I dwells as your resident priest, you have committed such a cruel deed; what you have done is improper,' then this king would be dejected."
"Having offered [the sacrifice], he would not be able to stand firm; rather, he will observe it as I speak the Dhamma by way of a sequence.
Beginning thus, he spoke the words "What do you think? etc., while commencing the teaching of the Dhamma.
In that context, *saddhāyiko* means "one who is to be trusted," the sense being: "one whose word you trust. *Paccayiko* is a synonym for the same, meaning "one whose word..."
The meaning is "you believe. *Abbhasamanti* means "equal to space.
*Nippothento āgacchati* means he comes crushing all beings from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā-world, grinding them down like fine grass-dust.
*Aññatra dhammacariyāyā* means that apart from the practice of Dhamma, there is nothing else to be done; [it refers to] what is comprised by the ten wholesome courses of action.
"Only the practice of Dhamma should be performed, venerable sir"—this is a synonym for "practice of equanimity" (*samacariyā*) and so forth.
"I announce" means I declare. "I make known" means I cause [you] to understand. "It overwhelms" means it overcomes.
"Elephant battles" refers to battles that must be fought after mounting elephants such as Nāḷāgiri, who are adorned with golden trappings. "Outcome" means the result.
"Sphere" (*visaya*) means either a place or a state of capability; for it is not possible for them to ward off aging and death.
"Wise ministers" (*mantino mahāmattā*) refers to great counselors endowed with wisdom, such as Mahosadha, Vidhura, Paṇḍita, and others.
"Buried in the ground" (*bhūmigata*) means having filled large iron cauldrons and placed them in the earth. "Set in the air" (*vehāsaṭṭha*) means having filled leather bags...
It was hung upon the scales, the rafters, and so forth, and placed filling the niches and other parts. "To cause to collide" means to break one against the other;
that is, to act so that two people do not travel by the same path.
"Striking the sky" means filling the atmosphere. Thus, in the phrase "old age and death," only these two mountains are taken here.
In the *Rājovāda*, however, it is said: "Old age comes, plundering all youth. Thus, these four—old age, death, disease, and misfortune—have indeed arrived.
Therefore, because it is not possible to conquer old age and death through elephant battles and the like, [the Buddha says]:
"One should establish faith" (*saddhaṃ nivesaye*); that is, one should establish and firmly settle faith. This is the fifth [chapter].
The Third Chapter.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Sāratthappakāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya*.
The commentary on the Connected Discourses on Kosala is finished.
4. The Connected Discourses on Māra.
1. The First Chapter.
1. Commentary on the *Tapokamma Sutta* 137.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the *Mārasaṃyutta*: "He was dwelling at Uruvelā" means that, having penetrated the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he was dwelling in dependence upon the village of Uruvelā.
"The first after his full enlightenment" means during the very first seven days immediately following his full enlightenment (*abhisambuddha*).
"By the practice of austerities" means by the practice of austerities performed for six years. "Māra the Evil One":
he is called Māra because he slays (māreti) those beings who have set out to transcend his domain; he is called Pāpimā because he incites others to evil or is himself engaged in evil.
He also has other names such as Kaṇha, Adhipati, Vasavattī, Antaka, Namuci, Pamattabandhu, and so forth.
There are many names [for this practice], but here only two are taken. "He approached":
having thought, "This ascetic Gotama thinks, 'I am liberated'; I shall declare his lack of liberation," he approached.
"Departing from the practice of austerity" means having departed from the practice of austerity. "You have missed it" means: "You are far from the path of purity."
He says: "Amaratapa" is the austere asceticism performed for the sake of immortality; it is the pursuit of self-mortification.
"It brings all harm" means that having realized, "No austerity whatsoever brings me any benefit," [he abandons it].
"Like a boat on dry land in the forest" means like a boat on dry ground in the wilderness. This is what is meant: just as a boat [is useless] on dry land in the forest...
Suppose a great multitude of people, having set aside their own goods and filled [the ship] with theirs, were to board and take hold of the rudder, pulling and hauling;
the exertion of that great multitude would be useless, failing to advance the ship even by a finger’s breadth or two fingers’ breadth, yet it would not be harmful.
In the same way, I consider all penance that does not lead to immortality to be harmful.
"Knowing that [the goal] exists, they released [him].
Now, in order to show the path by which the Buddha was born after abandoning that immortal asceticism, he spoke the passage beginning with "virtue" (sīla).
Therein, by the word "virtue," right speech, right action, and right livelihood are included; by "concentration" (samādhi), right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are included.
Through wisdom, they develop right view and right intention. They develop this very Noble Eightfold Path for the sake of enlightenment;
that is, while developing this Noble Eightfold Path for the purpose of awakening. And here, "for the sake of enlightenment" means for the sake of the path.

For just as people cook rice gruel specifically for the sake of rice gruel, and bake cakes specifically for the sake of cakes, and do nothing else, so too, for the sake of the path, they develop the path itself.
He develops it. Therefore he says, "Develop the path for awakening. "Supreme purity" refers to Arahantship.
"Subdued" means you have been subdued and defeated by me. First. 2.
Commentary on the Elephant King Discourse.
138. "In the second watch, during the pitch-black darkness of the night" means in the fourfold darkness that causes blindness at night.

"He sat in the open air" means that having gone out from the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), he sat at the end of the walking path upon a stone slab, placing his great outer robe on his head and undertaking a strenuous effort.

But surely, for the Tathāgata there is no path that has not been developed, no defilements that have not been abandoned, no unshakable state that has not been penetrated, and no cessation that has not been realized;
why then did he act in this way? It was for the sake of providing a goad for sons of good family in the future.
For in the future, sons of good family, having reflected upon the path traversed by me, might think: "One must dwell in an open-air residence."
Perceiving that they would perform the work of striving, the Teacher acted in this way. *Mahā* means great.
*Ariṭṭhaka* means black. *Maṇī* means a stone. "Thus his head becomes" means that his head becomes such as this: black in color, the size of a gabled chamber, and resembling a great rock.
"Subhāsubhaṃ" means that having undergone beautiful and ugly forms throughout a long period of wandering in saṃsāra, you have come here; thus he says.
Alternatively, "saṃsaranti saṃsaranto āgacchanto" means while wandering in saṃsāra, as you were coming.
"Dīghamaddhānaṃ" refers to the long path from the realm of Vasavatti down to Uruvelā, or else to the long duration of six years during the time of your ascetic practices prior to the Enlightenment.
"Having made a display of beauty and ugliness" means that having displayed various kinds of beauty and ugliness, you have come into my presence many times;
such is the meaning. It is said that there was no such display of beauty by which Māra had never before come into the Blessed One’s presence for the sake of causing terror.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus to him: "Enough for you with that. Here, "enough for you" (*alaṃ te*) means it is sufficient for you.
By this means, through the activity of displaying the terrifying forms of Māra. Second. 3. Commentary on the *Subha Sutta* 139.

In the third [verse]: "Well-restrained" means well-covered. "They do not follow Māra’s will": O Māra, they do not come under your control. "They are not bound to Māra": they are not your bound followers, students, or resident pupils. Third.
4. Commentary on the First Mārapāsasutta 140.

In the fourth [verse], "by way of wise attention" (*yoniso manasikāra*) means by way of skillful attention. "By way of wise right effort" (*yoniso sammappadhāna*) means by way of skillful energy, that is, causal energy.
"Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship. "He addressed" (*ajjhabhāsī*)—[referring to] this energy of his own...
Having attained Arahantship, he was not yet satisfied; thinking, "Now I shall encourage others as well, saying 'May you attain it too,' and I shall ward off [the enemy]," he spoke.

"By the snare of Māra" means by the snare of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Those divine and those human" refers to those divine and human qualities known as the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
There is indeed that which is called the snares of Māra, consisting of the strands of sensual pleasure; he says, "By all of these you are bound.

"Bound by the bonds of Māra" means bound by the bonds of Māra, or bound within the bonds of Māra. "O ascetic, you shall not escape from me" means, O ascetic, you shall not be released from my domain. This is the fourth [verse].
5. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Snare of Māra (Dutiyamārapāsasutta-vaṇṇanā) 141.

Regarding the fifth [discourse], "I am freed" (*muttāhaṃ*): I am liberated. The previous discourse was spoken during the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), whereas this one was spoken after the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) at the conclusion of the rains.
"Wandering" (*cārikaṃ*) refers to a gradual journey. (After the invitation ceremony,) he would travel no more than a *yojana* each day.
"Go, wander," he says. "Do not two by one way" means that two people should not go along a single path together;
for if they were to go thus, while one was teaching the Dhamma, the other would have to remain silent. Therefore, he spoke in this way.
"Beautiful in the beginning" means beautiful, lovely, and auspicious at the start. Likewise [beautiful] in the middle and at the end. And as for the beginning, middle, and end:
This [exposition] is twofold by way of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) and the Teaching (*desanā*). Therein, regarding the Dispensation: virtue (*sīla*) is the beginning;

serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the path (*magga*) are the middle; and the fruits (*phala*) and Nibbāna are the end. Alternatively, virtue and concentration (*samādhi*) are the beginning;

insight and the path are the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end. Or else, virtue, concentration, and insight are the beginning; the path is the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end.
The conclusion. Furthermore, regarding a four-line stanza in a teaching: the first line is the beginning, the second and third are the middle, and the fourth is the conclusion.
For stanzas of five or six lines, the first line is the beginning, the final line is the conclusion, and the remaining lines are the middle.
In a sutta with a single sequence of connection, the introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning, and the words "This was said" (*idamavoca*) are the conclusion.
The remainder is the middle. In a discourse with many connections, even though there are many connections in the middle, it is still the "middle";
the introduction is the beginning, and "this he said" is the conclusion.
"With meaning" means you should teach having made it meaningful. "With phrasing" means complete with both phonemes and words.
Having done so, teach it. "Entirely complete" means wholly perfect. "Pure" means free from defilement.
"The holy life" (brahmacariya) refers to the holy life of the Dispensation, which comprises the three trainings. "Proclaim" means reveal.
"Those of little dust in their eyes" means those whose nature is such that the dust of defilements is slight within the eye of wisdom; they are like fine linen cloth covered by a coarse hempen cloth.
The meaning is that there are those capable of attaining *arahantship* upon the conclusion of even a four-line verse.
"Assavanatā" means by way of not hearing [the Dhamma]. "Parihāyanti" means they fall away from the Dhamma through the loss of attainment.

"Senānigama" refers to a village established in the place where the army of the beings of the first eon settled, or it was the town named Senānī, the father of Sujātā. "Tenupasaṅkamissāmi" means "I shall go to that place."
"I will not dwell having dismissed you, having had monasteries and such built, and being attended by supporters;
rather, after displaying three thousand five hundred miracles to the three matted-hair ascetics, I shall approach them solely to teach the Dhamma.
Thus he approached them, [thinking]: "This ascetic Gotama is like one deliberating over a great battle..."
"‘Do not go two by one; teach the Dhamma,’ he said, and dismissed sixty men.
But even when this one man is teaching the Dhamma, there is no satisfaction for my mind; how could there be any when so many are teaching?
I shall prevent him. Having thought thus, he approached. (The fifth.)
6. Commentary on the Snake Sutta (Sappasutta) 142.
In the sixth [verse], "a weaver’s loom" (*soṇḍikākilañja*) refers to the loom used by liquor-makers for spreading out the dough.
"A bowl from Kosala" (*kosalikā kaṃsapātī*) refers to a serving bowl belonging to King Kosala, as large as a chariot wheel. "Gurgling" (*gaḷagaḷāyanta*) means roaring.
"By the smith’s bellows" means by the pipe used for blowing the smith’s forge. "While it was being blown" means while it was being filled with air from a bellows.
"Having understood thus"—thinking, "The ascetic Gotama is intent on striving but is sitting comfortably;
I shall disturb him"—he manifested a physical form of the kind described, moving here and there upon the ground of the fixed course (niyāmabhūmi) with the light of lightning flashes.
Having seen him, [he thought], "Who indeed is this being? Reflecting upon it, he understood, "This is Māra.

"Empty houses" means empty dwellings. "For the sake of lying down" means for the purpose of reclining. "I shall stand, walk, sit, and lie down"—the meaning is that he who frequents empty dwellings for the sake of these things is a sage (muni) self-restrained. He... [is] that sage.
The Buddha-Muni is one whose self-nature is restrained due to the absence of remorse regarding his hands and feet.

"He should wander there having relinquished" means that he should wander having relinquished—that is, having abandoned—attachment and craving for that self-nature. For such conduct is indeed appropriate for one such as him;
that is, for the Buddha-Muni who is established in such a state, it is fitting to wander after relinquishing craving for that self-nature.
This name is appropriate, fitting, and suitable.
"Wanderers" (*carakā*) refers to creatures that roam about, such as lions, tigers, and so forth. "Terrifying" (*bheravā*) refers to both animate and inanimate things that cause fear.
Among these, the animate are lions, tigers, and the like; the inanimate are such things as tree stumps and anthills during the night. These too—
For at that time, [fearful objects] appear like spirits (*yakkha*), and all things such as ropes and creepers appear like snakes. "Therein" means:
having gone to an empty dwelling amidst those terrors, the Sage who is the Buddha does not even experience a single quiver of his body hair.
Now, demonstrating the contemplation of the impossible, he said: "The sky might split," and so forth. In this context, "might split" refers to a crow's footprint.
It would bear fruit like a diamond or a piece of gold. "It would move" means it would move like a drop of water struck by the wind on a lotus leaf.

"Even if they were to drive a dart into the chest" means even if they were to thrust a sharp spear-dart into the breast. "Regarding the acquisitions" refers to the acquisitions consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*).
"They do not provide protection" means that when a sharp dart is being driven into the chest, [people seek] thickets, mountain caves, and so forth out of fear.
Those who enter [the forest] indeed seek refuge; however, the Buddhas, having utterly severed all fear, do not provide such a refuge. The sixth.
7. Commentary on the Supatiṭṭha Sutta.
143. "Having washed his feet at the seventh step" means having washed them for the purpose of taking on the seasonal temperature. However, dust and dirt do not adhere to the bodies of Buddhas;
even water, like a drop fallen upon a lotus leaf, rolls off and passes away.
Nevertheless, it is the duty (*vatta*) of those who have gone forth to wash their feet before entering a house where the feet have already been washed. In that regard, for the Buddhas—
There is no breaking of the observance; however, standing at the head of the observance, they wash.
For if the Tathāgata were neither to bathe nor wash his feet, they would say, "This one is not a human being. Therefore, without abandoning human conduct, he washes.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" means endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension that encompass sleep. "Approached" refers to the ascetic.

Thinking, "Gotama has been walking back and forth in the open air all night; having entered the fragrant chamber, he is sleeping—he must be resting very comfortably; I shall disturb him," she approached.
She said, "Why do you sleep? Why are you sleeping? What is this sleep of yours? [The Buddha asked: "Why indeed do you sleep? [She replied: "Why?"
“Are you sleeping now? “Like one unfortunate,” meaning like one who is dead or unconscious. “An empty house” means he says, “I have found my own home empty.
“When the sun has risen” means when the sun has come up.
For now other bhikkhus are sweeping, setting out drinking water, and preparing for their alms-round; why then do you just sleep?

*Jālinī* (the ensnarer): It is called *jālinī* because it stands having overspread the three realms of existence (*bhava*), like a net consisting of its own various constituent parts, such as the "eighteen modes of craving's wandering based on the internal [sense-spheres]" and so forth. *Visattikā* (the clinging one):

It is called *visattikā* because of its clinging here and there to form and the other aggregates, because it has poison as its root, and because it is the enjoyment of poison. *Kuhiñci netave*: "To lead anywhere" means to some place.

"To lead [me] away. "By the complete destruction of all acquisitions (*upadhi*)," means by the total exhaustion of all acquisitions, namely the aggregates (*khandha*), the defilements (*kilesa*), the formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "What is this to you here, Māra? means, "Māra, what business do you have here?
Why do you wander about, complaining from within like a tiny fly that cannot settle on hot ghee? This is the seventh [verse].
8. Commentary on the Nandati Sutta (144).
The eighth [sutta] has the same meaning as that explained in the Devatāsaṃyutta. The eighth.
9. Commentary on the First Āyu Sutta.
145. Regarding the ninth [verse], "little more": even if he lives longer, he is not able to live for another hundred years;
he lives for perhaps fifty or sixty years. "He addressed [him]" means that the ascetic Gotama says, "The lifespan of humans is short";
[the king] spoke thus, having overcome him through persistent opposition with the thought, "I shall speak of its long duration."
One should not despise that life; one should not despise it thinking, "This is short. "Like a child full of milk" means:

just as a young infant lying on its back, having drunk milk and resting on a soft cotton pillow, sleeps as if unconscious and does not consider whether anyone's life is short or long—so too is the person of integrity (*sappurisa*). "One should live with head aflame" refers to life.
"Knowing it to be limited, one should live as if with one's head on fire. This is the ninth.

**Commentary on the Second Sutta on Life (Dutiya-āyusutta), Verse 146:** In the tenth verse, "Like the rim of a wheel around the chariot hub": just as the rim of the wheel of a chariot traveling during the day revolves around the hub and does not leave it, so too does life revolve [around death]. This is the tenth.
The First Chapter. 2.
The Second Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Rock Sutta.
147. In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, "seated" means seated while undertaking his exertion in the manner previously described.
Knowing that he was sitting comfortably, Māra approached him with the thought, "I shall disturb him.
"He shattered" means that standing upon the mountain peak, he struck it; the rocks fell, striking one another without interval. "Entirely" means...
"Sakalaṃ" (the whole). "Sabbam" (all) is a synonym for that very same word. First. 2.
Commentary on the Kinnusīha Sutta. 148.
In the second [verse], "vicakkhukammāya" means with the desire to destroy the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*) of the assembly. Of the Buddhas...
He is not able to destroy his eye of wisdom; rather, he is able to make the assembly hear or see terrifying objects.
"Do you think you are victorious?"—do you think, "I am one who has won the victory"? Do not think so; there is no victory for you.
"In the assemblies" means in the eight assemblies. "Attained to power" means attained to the ten powers. Second.
3. Commentary on the Sakalikasutta 149.
In the third [verse], *mandiyā nū* means by way of dullness, that is, by way of a state of delusion (*momūhabhāva*). *Udāhu kāveyyamatto* means:
"Or perhaps intoxicated by poetry?"—just as a poet, while composing a poem, lies down intoxicated by that act of composition, so do you lie down. *Sampacurā* means many.
"Kimidaṃ soppase vā" means: why do you sleep when it is precisely time to sleep? "Atthaṃ samecca" means having encountered or reached a purpose.
For there is no such thing as my "non-inclusion," nor is there any purpose for me that has failed in inclusion. "Sallaṃ" refers to a sharp spear-head.
"Jaggaṃ na saṅketi" means that unlike someone who, while staying awake on paths frequented by lions and the like, would feel fear, so [I do not].
"Even when awake, I have no anxiety. Nor do I fear falling asleep; just as some people fear to sleep even on paths frequented by lions and the like, so too I do not fear sleeping.

'I do not regret it' means that just as when a teacher or a student has become unwell, the student—remaining occupied with recitation and questioning—lets the days and nights pass by [without attending to him]..."
"Things cause me remorse; thus, they do not cause me remorse. For there is no unfinished task whatsoever for me.
Therefore he said: 'I see no decline anywhere in the world. This is the third [verse]. 4.
Commentary on the *Patirūpa-sutta*.

150. In the fourth [verse], "in favor and against" (*anurodhavirodhesu*) means in passion (*rāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*). "Do not cling while practicing that"—while practicing this discourse on the Dhamma, do not become attached.
For when one is delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, some give applause, and passion arises toward them;
others listen disrespectfully, and aversion arises toward them. Thus, the preacher of the Dhamma [is subject] to favor and opposition.
"It clings" means: he says, "Do not cling in this way. "When he instructs another" means: that other person whom he instructs.

The Fully Awakened One is compassionate for their welfare; he sympathizes with them through their welfare. And because he is compassionate for their welfare, the Tathāgata is therefore completely free from attachment and aversion. This is the fourth [verse].
5. Commentary on the Mānasa Sutta 151.

In the fifth [verse], one who moves even in the sky while binding [others] is called "a wanderer in the atmosphere" (*antalikkhacaro*). "Snare" (*pāsa*) refers to the snare of lust (*rāga-pāsa*). "Mental" (*mānaso*) means associated with the mind (*manasampayutto*). This is the fifth. 6.
Commentary on the Patta Sutta.

152. In the sixth [section], "by depending on the five aggregates of clinging" (*pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ upādāya*) means having taken up the five aggregates of clinging, and showing them by analyzing them into their various aspects according to their specific characteristics (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*).

"He points out" (*sandasseti*) means he shows the specific characteristics and other attributes of the aggregates. "He encourages" (*samādapeti*) means he causes them to take it up. "He inspires" (*samuttejeti*) means [he arouses] enthusiasm for the undertaking.
He generates [joy]. "He gladdens" means he purifies and illuminates [the mind] by means of the qualities already penetrated. "Making it a bone" means making it essential;
having observed, "This is the goal we must attain," they become intent upon that teaching.
"Applying the mind" means fixing it in the heart. "With all one's heart" means with that entire consciousness which performs the action.
"Having paid attention. "With the ear applied" means with the ear fixed. "Placed in the open air" means placed for the purpose of heating.
"Form, feeling, perception"—these are the three aggregates beginning with form. "And whatever is conditioned"—by this, the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is included.
"Thus one becomes dispassionate toward that" means seeing: "I am not this; this is not mine."
Thus one becomes dispassionate toward those aggregates. "A secure self" (*khemattaṃ*) refers to a personal existence (*attabhāva*) that has become secure;

by this, he shows the moment of fruition (*phalakkhaṇa*). "Seeking" (*anvesantā*) means searching through all places comprised within the realms of existence, matrices, destinies, stations, and abodes of beings.
"Did not find" (*nājjhaga*) means did not see. The sixth [sutta].

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Six Bases of Contact (Chaphassāyatana-sutta) 153. Regarding the seventh [section], "of the six bases of contact" (*phassāyatanānaṃ*): this refers to the bases for contact that occurs at the six doors, in the sense of being born together and meeting [therein].
"A terrifying and fearful sound" (*bhayabheravaṃ saddaṃ*) means a sound that produces fear, similar to the sound of clouds, kettledrums, or a thunderclap. "The earth... [and so forth].
"I think it is sinking" means that this great earth seemed as if it were making a crashing sound.

"The world is infatuated here" means that the world is intensely attached to these six objects. "Māra’s realm" refers to the round of existence in the three planes, which serves as Māra’s domain. Seventh.
8. Commentary on the Piṇḍasutta 154.
Regarding the eighth [verse], "there are guests": on such an auspicious occasion, there are "guests" to be sent here and there, or gifts to be given to those who have arrived.
On the day of one's own departure, those of similar age, birth, and clan...
The young men gathered from here and there. The young women also, adorned according to their respective means, wandered about here and there.
There, the young women sent gifts to the young men of their choice;
and the young men, if there were no other [gift], surrounded the young women even with a cluster of flowers. Thus they became mutually infatuated.

They were possessed by him. It is said that on that very day, five hundred young maidens, while going out for a pleasure excursion to the park, would have seen the Teacher on the opposite path and offered him festival cakes.
The Teacher, for the sake of expressing appreciation for their gift, would have delivered an incidental discourse on the Dhamma;
at the conclusion of that discourse, all of them would have been established in the fruit of stream-entry. Māra [was concerned] regarding their attainment.
He entered [the village] thinking, "I shall create an obstacle. However, in the text (Pāḷi), it is stated only as far as: "May the ascetic Gotama not obtain alms-food.
But did the Teacher enter without knowing Māra’s possession? Yes, he entered without knowing. Why? Because of his lack of mental advertence (anāvajjanatā).
For it is not inappropriate for Buddhas to advert [thinking], "We shall receive food at such-and-such a place; we shall not receive it."
But having entered [the village], seeing that the boundary of human habitations had been breached, he reflected, "What is this?
Realizing it through his supernormal knowledge, he thought, "It is not fitting to break the Māra-encirclement for the sake of material gain," and so he departed without breaking it.
"He approached" means that, as if delighted by a victory over his enemies, yet having failed to receive even a single ladleful of food from the entire village, he went forth.
As the Blessed One was departing from the village, a village man approached him in disguise.
"I shall do so," he said, speaking this falsehood. It occurred to him: "When I have spoken thus, he will re-enter;
then the village boys, having searched the entire village and failed to obtain even a spoonful of alms, will come out from the village [and seize him]."
“Having said such things as ‘You have entered again,’ they will mock you.
But the Blessed One, thinking, “If he were to harass me in this way, his head would split into seven pieces,” did not enter out of compassion for him and spoke these two verses.
Therein, *pasavī* means he produced or brought forth. *Āsajja* means having approached or having struck. *Na me pāpaṃ vipaccatī* means “my evil does not ripen [into fruit].”
"My evil does not ripen; why do you think it is fruitless?"—this he says to show that one should not think thus, for there is indeed a fruit for the evil committed by you.
"Kiñcana" refers to the collection of defilements such as the "stain" (kiñcana) of lust, which are capable of crushing [the mind].
"Just like the Ābhassara deities" means that just as the Ābhassara deities subsist on joy, maintaining themselves through jhāna accompanied by rapture (pīti).
...they have such names, and "we shall become thus. Eighth. 9.
Commentary on the Kassakasutta.
155. Regarding the ninth: "connected with Nibbāna" means occurring by referring to Nibbāna. "With his hair shorn again and again..."
Having spread [the hair] repeatedly, with the front hair behind, the back hair in front, the left-side hair on the right, and the right-side hair on the left, his hair is disheveled.

"The sphere of visual-contact-consciousness belonging to me" means that both the visual contact associated with eye-consciousness and the sphere of consciousness itself belong to me alone. And here, by means of visual contact...

The phenomena associated with consciousness (*viññāṇa-sampayutta-dhammā*) are included; by means of the sense-base of consciousness (*viññāṇāyatana*), all consciousnesses that have arisen at the eye-door, such as adverting-consciousness (*āvajjana*) and so forth, are included.

The same method applies to the ear-door and the others. At the mind-door (*manodvāra*), however, "mind" (*mano*) refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) accompanied by adverting.

"Phenomena" (*dhammā*) refers to the objective phenomena (*ārammaṇa-dhammā*). "Mind-contact" (*manosamphassa*) is the contact associated with the life-continuum consciousness accompanied by adverting.
“Consciousness-sphere” (*viññāṇāyatana*) refers to impulsion-consciousness (*javana-citta*) as well as its object.

“O Evil One, let the eye be yours alone” means: whatever in the world is afflicted by cataracts, spectacles, and so forth—a locus of many diseases, a seat of corruption and decay—even down to a blind eye—let all that be yours alone. The same method applies to visible forms and the other sense objects.
“Whatever they call ‘mine’” refers to those goods which people say, “This is mine. And “those who say ‘me’” refers to those...
Persons say, "This is mine. If the mind is present here—meaning, if the consciousness exists in these instances—then [the Buddha says]:
"O ascetic, you shall not escape from my domain.
Regarding the phrase "that which they call," whatever belongings they speak of, that is not mine. Regarding the phrase "those who say," even those persons who speak thus [are not mine].
"Those are I. "You shall not see even my path"—you do not see the path by which I have gone through the various states of existence, wombs, destinies, and so forth.
This is the ninth [verse]. 10.

Commentary on the Sutta on Kingship (Rajjasutta) 156. In the tenth [verse]: "They cause one who does not kill to be killed" means by one who causes the non-killer to be killed. "They cause one who does not take a hide to be made to take it" refers to another's...
"By one who has not caused loss of wealth, nor caused it to be caused; by one who has not grieved, nor caused grief, nor is grieving, nor causing grief.
Thus the Blessed One, seeing people oppressed by fines and taxes under the rule of unrighteous kings within their realm and kingdom, thought thus out of compassion.
"He approached," [meaning] he thought: "Is it possible for the ascetic Gotama to exercise sovereignty?"
Thinking, "He will desire to exercise sovereignty, and sovereignty is indeed a ground for negligence; while he exercises sovereignty, it is possible to find an opening [to influence him].
I shall go and rouse his enthusiasm," he approached. "Foundations of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) means factors that bring about success.
"Developed" (*bhāvita*) means increased. "Cultivated" (*bahulīkata*) means practiced repeatedly. "Made a vehicle" (*yānīkata*) means made into a vehicle to which one is yoked.
"Made like": it is made like [a target]. "Established as a basis" means established in the sense of being a foundation. "Firmly set up" means not abandoned, constantly followed.
"Well-familiarized" means well-cultivated through constant practice, like an archer whose hand has mastered the art of hitting the mark without fail.
"Well-commenced" means properly undertaken, with the development brought to completion. "One should resolve" means one should contemplate.
"Of a mountain" means it would be a mountain. "Even two" means: let one mountain stand;
even twice as large a golden mountain is not enough for one person—it is not sufficient—this is the meaning. "Knowing thus, one should live equanimously":
knowing this, one should conduct oneself with equanimity (*sama*). "From whatever source": suffering indeed has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its source; that...

"From whatever source it arises"—thus is he who has seen [the truth]. "How would he bow?"—for what reason would that person bow toward those sensual pleasures which have become the source of suffering?
"Having understood the substrate (*upadhi*)"—having understood the substrate of the strands of sensual pleasure as "this is a fetter, this is a clinging.
"For the sake of its very removal, let him train"—let him train for the sake of the removal of that very substrate. The tenth [chapter].
The Second Chapter.
3. The Third Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse to the Many.
157. In the first [sutta] of the third chapter: *jaṭaṇḍuvena* means with a mass of matted hair.
*Ajinakkhipanivattho* means clothed in one [piece] and wrapped in another of deerskin, including the hooves.

*Udumbaradaṇḍaṃ* means having taken up a slightly curved staff of *udumbara* wood for the purpose of manifesting his state of fewness of desires. *Etadavoca* means that people in the world listen to the speech of a brahmin.
Among brahmins, he was an elder; among those who had gone forth, he was an elder.

Thus, having assumed the guise of a renunciant, while performing his duties on the meditation ground, he approached those bhikkhus, raised his hand, and spoke these words beginning with, "Sirs, you are young.
"Okampetvā" means shaking [the body] by striking the chest with the chin, causing it to lean downward.
Having done so. "Licking his tongue" means having extended his great, forked tongue and licked it up, down, and on both sides.
"Three-forked" (*tivisākha*) means having three branches. "Forehead-mark" (*nalāṭika*) means a frown; the meaning is the three folds of skin raised upon the forehead.
"He departed" means that, disregarding the words of those who knew him, he said, "You yourselves shall be roasted in oil."
Having taken one path, he went. First [is finished]. 2.
Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta: 158.
"It is indeed a gain for me! It is truly well-gained by me!"—[thinking thus] regarding such a Teacher and the Dhamma.
“It is my gain, it is my great good fortune that I have obtained fellow-celibates.

It is said that after that venerable one had later reflected upon his original meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), thinking, “I shall attain Arahantship,” he first took up a pleasing meditation subject;
then, having brought to mind the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, he generated pliancy of mind, gladdened and satisfied his heart, and sat down.
Then it occurred to him: "This bhikkhu Samiddhi appears as if he has taken a pleasing meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and is sitting down;
before he takes up his fundamental meditation subject and attains *arahantship*, I shall create an obstacle for him.
With this thought, he approached. "Go, then," said the Teacher, looking over the whole of Jambudīpa, [and saw that] in that very place...
He saw that the meditation subject would be suitable for him in that place, and therefore he spoke thus:
“I know mindfulness and wisdom. “Make forms” means: make many forms that are worthy of being seen.
“You will not pierce me” means: you will neither strike nor shake me. Second.
3. Commentary on the Godhika Sutta 159.
In the third [verse], "on the slope of Isigili" means on the side of the mountain named Isigili. "On the Black Rock" means on a rock of black color.
"Temporary liberation of mind" means that at each moment of absorption, one is liberated from opposing states.
"And he resolves upon the object" refers to the mundane attainment known as temporary liberation of mind (*sāmayikā cetovimutti*). "He touched" means he acquired it.
As for why he fell away—as far as the sixth time—why did he fall away? It was because of illness. It is said that the Elder had a chronic ailment consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm;
because of this, he was unable to fulfill the conditions conducive to and supportive of concentration.
"He falls away from the attainment he had attained.
'What if I were to take up a weapon?'—this, it is said, was what he thought.
For one who dies having fallen away from jhāna has an uncertain destination, whereas for one who has not fallen away from jhāna, the destination is certain: they are reborn in the Brahma-world."
Therefore, he desired to take up a blade. He approached [him] thinking: "This ascetic desires to take up a blade;
and such taking up of a blade is for one who is indifferent to both body and life.
Whoever is thus indifferent to both body and life is capable of attaining even Arahantship by comprehending the fundamental meditation subject."
"Even though I have tried to dissuade him, he will not desist; but once dissuaded by the Teacher, he will desist.
Thinking thus, as if out of concern for the Elder’s welfare, he approached the Blessed One.
"Jalāti" means "shining. "I pay homage at your feet, O Visionary One": I pay homage at your feet, O Visionary One endowed with the five eyes.

"Jutindharā" means those who possess majesty. "Appattamānaso" means one who has not attained *arahantship*. "Sekho" means one who is still in training, practicing the precepts and so forth, and who still has duties to perform.
"Jane sutā" means renowned among people. Regarding the phrase "the knife was brought": it is said that the Elder thought, "What is the use of this life for me?
and having lain down on his back, he cut his jugular vein with a knife; consequently, painful sensations arose.

The Elder, having suppressed that feeling, having grasped that very feeling, and having established mindfulness while contemplating his original meditation subject, attained Arahantship and, becoming one who has reached the goal simultaneously with his death (samasīsī), passed away into Parinibbāna. There are three kinds of those who reach the goal simultaneously:

one who reaches it simultaneously in terms of posture (iriyāpatha-samasīsī), one who reaches it simultaneously in terms of illness (roga-samasīsī), and one who reaches it simultaneously in terms of life (jīvita-samasīsī).

In this context, when one establishes insight while resolving upon one of the postures among the standing and so forth, thinking, "I will reach Arahantship without breaking this posture," then his attainment of Arahantship and the breaking of the posture occur simultaneously.
This is called "the simultaneous peak of the posture" (*iriyāpatha-samasīsī*). However, when [one falls away] due to any one of the eye-diseases and so forth...
One who possesses mindfulness thinks, "Without even rising from this posture, I shall attain Arahantship," and applies insight;
then his attainment of Arahantship and his recovery from the illness occur simultaneously. This is called "one for whom the head [of the illness] and the head [of the goal] are level.
However, some define "level-headedness" here as occurring through final Nibbāna in that very posture and with respect to that very illness. But for one who—
The destruction of the taints and the destruction of life occur simultaneously. This is called "one who has a head-to-foot [attainment].

And it has been said: "That person for whom the exhaustion of the taints and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after one another—this person is called 'one with a head-to-foot [attainment].'"

In this context, there are two "heads": the head of occurrence (*pavatti-sīsa*) and the head of defilement (*kilesa-sīsa*). Here, the head of occurrence is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and the head of defilement is ignorance (*avijjā*).
Among these, the life-faculty exhausts the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), while ignorance [exhausts] the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*).

There is no simultaneous arising of these two consciousnesses. However, immediately after the path comes the fruition (*phala*), and immediately after the fruition comes the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Emerging from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), there arises reviewing knowledge; that may be complete or incomplete.
For even if one’s head were being cut off by a sharp sword, one or two instances of reviewing knowledge would necessarily arise.
However, due to the rapid succession of consciousnesses, the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya) and the exhaustion of the life-span appear as if they occurred at the same moment.

"Having uprooted craving together with its root" means having eradicated craving along with its root of ignorance by means of the path of Arahatship. "Parinibbuto" means completely extinguished through the Nibbāna without residue.
"Vivattakkhandha" means with his shoulders turned over. "Semānaṃ" means lying down on his back;
however, although the Elder was lying on his back, because he was accustomed to sleeping on his right side, his head—
It stood having turned around from the right side. "The state of smoking" (*dhūmāyitatta*) means the condition of being smoky;
for at that moment, [clouds] like smoke-clouds and like darkness-clouds arose. "Consciousness seeks" means it searches for the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
"By not being established" means by the non-establishment of the rebirth-linking consciousness; [it refers to] the causes for non-establishment.
