The meaning is as follows: *Beluvapaṇḍuvīṇaṃ* means a great golden lute that is pale yellow in color like a ripe *beluva* fruit.
*Ādāya* means having placed it under his arm. *Upasaṅkamī* means he approached, having assumed the appearance of a young boy, thinking: "I do not know the place where the Elder Godhika was reborn;
I shall ask the ascetic Gotama and become free from doubt. *Nādhigacchāmi* means... [he did not find].
"I do not see [anyone]. "Overcome by sorrow" means touched by grief. "She fell" means she fell upon the back of his feet. Third. 4.
Commentary on the *Sattavassānubandha-sutta* (160).
In the fourth [sutta], "for seven years" refers to six years prior to the Awakening and one year after the Awakening.
“Seeking an opening” means looking for a flaw, thinking: “If I see even the slightest impropriety in the Blessed One’s bodily doors and so forth, I shall reproach him.
“Failing to find one” means not seeing even a speck of dust’s worth of a lapse. Thus he said:
“For seven years I followed the Blessed One, step by step;”
“I shall find no opening against the Perfectly Enlightened One, who possesses mindfulness.
“He approached” means he approached with the thought, “Today I will overpower the ascetic Gotama and depart.
“You are meditating” means he says, “You are sitting there meditating, absorbed in meditation. “Has your wealth been lost? means “Have a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold] been lost?”
"Or have you been defeated? Have you come to this village? [He asks:

"What evil deed, exceeding all bounds, did you commit within the village, that you wander in the forest unable even to look another person in the face? "They will be able" means they will maintain friendship.
"Having dug up" means having excavated. "The craving consisting of greed for existence" refers to the thirst known as *bhava-lobha*. "I meditate, free from taints" means...
"Having become free from craving, I meditate with two jhānas. He addresses Māra as "the kinsman of the heedless," for Māra is indeed the kinsman of whoever in the world is heedless.
"If you have awakened to the Path"—that is, if the Path has been realized by you—"then depart!"—that is, go away—from the domain of death.

Nirvana is that which has become a place free from the domain of death. "Those who go to the further shore" includes those who have already gone to the further shore, as well as those who will go to the further shore, and those who desire to go to the further shore—all these are "those who go to the further shore.
"Deceptive appearances" refers to the deceptions of Māra. "Practiced by the perverse" means practiced by those who are hostile; [as it is said]: "The lifespan of humans is short..."
When it is said, “Days and nights pass away,” the statements such as, “The lifespan of humans is long; days and nights do not pass away,” are the reasons for the opposite view.
“Thrillings” refers to the visions of the form of a king elephant, a snake, and so forth, occurring at various times. “Causing disillusionment” means causing weariness [with the world].
In the passages beginning with “he went around,” although the past tense is used, the meaning should nevertheless be understood through the use of alternative verbal forms (vikappa).
This is what is meant: Just as a crow, seeing a stone the color of fat, might go around it thinking, "Perhaps I might find something soft here;

perhaps there might be some flavor," and then that crow, finding no flavor there at all, would depart from that place and the stone would remain, even so we too, like that crow, having assailed Gotama as he was like that stone—
"Finding neither gratification nor intimacy, O Gotamas, we shall become disenchanted and depart. This is the fourth [sutta]. 5.
Commentary on the Māradhītusutta (The Discourse on the Daughters of Māra) 161.

Regarding the phrase "without speaking" (*abhāsitvā*): here, the syllable *a-* is merely a particle; the meaning is "having spoken" (*bhāsitvā*). It may also be read as "having caused to speak" (*abhāsayitvā*).

[This is] the reading. "They approached" means: [Seeing that he] was sitting there extremely dejected, having drawn lines on the ground with a stick like a young cowherd boy, [the monks thought], "What could be the reason? and they approached, thinking, "We shall ask and find out.
"You are grieving," he thought. "Like an elephant in the forest": just as female elephants sent from the forest [by hunters] [behave toward] a wild forest elephant...
"Having enticed the elephant by showing him the graceful movements of women, they bind him and bring him back; in this way we shall bring him.

"The realm of Māra" refers to the cycle of existence within the three planes. "They approached" means that, having reassured their father by saying, "Please wait a short while, we shall bring him," they approached him.
"High and low" means of various kinds. "A hundred and one each" means making them into groups of one hundred and one respectively.
"By the phrase *kumārivaṇṇasataṃ*, [he means] one hundred existences (*attabhāva*) as a maiden.
By both phrases, *atthassa pattiṃ* and *hadayassa santiṃ*, he spoke specifically of *arahatta* (Arhatship).
*Senaṃ* refers to the army of defilements (*kilesa*), for that is indeed called the "army of the agreeable and pleasant. *Ekāhaṃ jhāyaṃ* means "I, being alone, meditating. *Sukhamanubodhin*" means...

I realized the bliss of arahantship. This is what is meant: having conquered the army of lovely and pleasant forms, I, meditating alone, realized the bliss of arahantship, which is reckoned as "the attainment of the goal" and "peace of heart.
Therefore, I do not cultivate intimacy with people, and for that very reason, I do not enter into companionship with anyone.
"How does one dwell much? means: by dwelling frequently with which state? "Not having obtained" (*aladdhā*) means: not having acquired. "Yaṃ" (*yo*) is merely a particle.
This is what is meant: when that person meditates frequently with whichever jhāna, sensual perceptions (*kāmasaññā*) remain excluded from him, not having been acquired at all.
"One whose body is tranquil" means one whose body of inhalation and exhalation is tranquil due to the fourth jhāna.

"One whose mind is well-liberated" means one whose mind is thoroughly liberated by the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. "One who does not form volitional formations" means one who does not perform the three types of karmic volitional formations.
"One who is homeless" means one who is without attachment. "Having known the Dhamma" means having understood the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "One who meditates without applied thought."

"Meditating with the fourth jhāna, which is without applied thought (*avitakka*). Regarding the phrases "does not become agitated" and so forth: he does not become agitated by hatred (*dosa*), he does not become forgetful through lust (*rāga*), and he does not become sluggish through delusion (*moha*).
When these three root defilements are grasped, one thousand five hundred defilements are indeed included.
Alternatively, by the first term, the hindrance of ill-will (*byāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) is grasped; by the second, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).

By the third [term], beginning with sloth (*thina*), the remaining hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are indicated. Thus, by this abandonment of the hindrances, he shows one whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted.

"Crossed the five floods" means he has crossed the flood of defilements pertaining to the five sense-doors. "The sixth": he has also crossed the sixth flood of defilements pertaining to the mind-door.
Alternatively, by the mention of the five floods, the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are intended; by the mention of the sixth, [the higher fetters].
The five higher fetters are to be understood. "One who moves among groups and assemblies" means one who moves among both groups and assemblies;
thus, the Teacher is called "one who moves among groups and assemblies. "They will surely move along" means that other people of faith will also certainly follow.
"He" refers to this Teacher. "A home" means a place of attachment. "Homeless" means without attachment.

"Acchejja nessatī" means "having cut off, he will lead away"; it is said that having snatched [them] from the hand of the King of Death, he will lead them to the further shore of Nibbāna. "Nayamānānaṃ" means "among those being led.
"Selaṃ va sirasūhacca, pātāle gādhamesatha" is like placing a great rock the size of a gabled house upon one's head and seeking a foothold in the abyss.
"Khāṇuṃ va urasāsajja" is like striking a stump with one's chest.
“Apetha” means depart. Having concluded the teaching with the words “Thus he spoke,” the compilers of the collection (saṅgītikārā), shining brilliantly, uttered this verse.
In that context, “daddallamānā” means shining exceedingly, gleaming. “Āgañchuṃ” means they came. “Panudi” means he cast out.
“Tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃ va māluto” means just as cotton from a *simbali* tree fallen from its fruit [is driven away] by the wind.
Or as the wind blows away and carries off cotton from a seed-pod, so it "blows away. Fifth.
The Third Chapter.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*.
The commentary on the Māra-saṃyutta of the Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
5. Bhikkhunī-saṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the Āḷavikā Sutta 162.
Regarding the first sutta of the *Bhikkhunīsaṃyutta*, "Āḷavikā": she was born in Āḷavī and went forth into homelessness after departing from the city of Āḷavī itself.
"The Blind Wood" (*andhavana*): [she had previously] collected wealth for the purpose of renovating the stupa of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa.
Because five hundred thieves who had already blinded their eyes lived right there after gouging out the eyes of a noble person (ariyapuggala) named Yasodhara, a Dhamma-preacher,
that forest came to be known from then on as "Andhavana" (The Blind Forest). It is said that it was located about one *gāvuta* to the south of Sāvatthī and was protected by the king.
Gutta. There, monks and nuns who desire seclusion go. Therefore, she too, desiring physical seclusion, approached that forest.
"Escape" (*nissaraṇa*) means *nibbāna*. "By wisdom" (*paññāya*) means by the knowledge of reflective observation.
"You do not know that state" means you do not know either this state of *nibbāna* or the state of the path leading to *nibbāna*.
You know. "Like spears and spikes" means they are similar to spears and spikes in the sense of piercing.
"The hammering of the aggregates" means the aggregates are the hammering-tools for them. First.
2. Commentary on the Somā Sutta.
163. "The second state" refers to arahantship. "Difficult to attain" means difficult to endure.
"With two-finger wisdom" means with limited wisdom; or, because women spin thread by grasping a cotton spindle with two fingers, a woman is called "one of two-finger wisdom.
"While knowledge is occurring" means while the knowledge of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) is proceeding.

"Contemplating the Dhamma" means for one who is contemplating the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, or specifically the pentad of aggregates which serves as the object for insight in its preliminary stage.
"Or anything else" refers to whatever might exist through the modes of craving, conceit, or views, such as "I am.
This is the second [section].
3. Commentary on the Kisāgotamī Sutta 164.
Regarding the third [sutta], "Kisāgotamī": she was called *kisā* because of her lack of flesh and blood; *Gotamī*, however, was her personal name.

It is said that formerly, in a certain family in Sāvatthī, a fortune of eight hundred million pieces of gold turned entirely into charcoal. When the householder saw that the wealth had become charcoal...
Without taking it away, thinking, "Surely there will be someone meritorious;
by his merit it will become as it was before," he filled jars with gold and bullion, placed them in the marketplace, and sat down nearby.
Then, a daughter of a poor family, who had gone to the street thinking, "I will bring firewood and vegetables for half a māsaka," saw that householder.
He said, "There is this much wealth in the shop; how much will there be in the house? "What did you see, mother, that you speak thus?
"This gold and silver. Thinking, "She must be possessed of merit," he asked where she lived, returned his goods to the shop, approached her parents, and spoke thus: "To us..."
“There is a boy in our house who has reached marriageable age; give this girl to him. “Master, why do you play with those who are poor?
“Friendship indeed exists even with the poor; give her to him. She will become the mistress of the household.
Having taken her, he brought her home. Following their cohabitation, she gave birth to a son. The son, on foot...

While wandering about, she passed away. Having been reborn into a destitute family, even after marrying into a great clan, she was overcome by intense grief, crying out, "I have met with the loss of my son!
She prevented the performance of her son's funeral rites and, taking his corpse, wandered through the city wailing aloud.
One day, having gone into the presence of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers along the great Buddha-road, she said:
"Blessed One, give medicine for the sake of my son's health. [The Blessed One replied: "Go and wander through Sāvatthī;
fetch mustard seed from a house where no one has ever died. That shall be the medicine for your son. She [went] to the city...
Having entered and proceeded from the house at the head of the street according to the method described by the Blessed One, she went from house to house begging for white mustard seeds.
When told, "Where will you find such a house?", she wandered through several houses and thought, "It seems this is the nature of all people, not only of my son.
Then, having discarded the corpse in the open space, she departed.
She requested the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). The Teacher sent her to the nuns’ quarters, saying, “Let her go forth.
At the very touch of the razor, she attained *arahantship*. It was with reference to this elder nun that it was said, “Then Kisāgotamī...
She was alone (*ekamāsī*); *rudammukhī* means as if with a weeping face. Regarding the phrase “I am one whose son is utterly dead”: [End of fragment]
*Antaṃ atītaṃ accantaṃ*: this is a neuter noun. This is what is meant:
just as the death of a son has passed away, so too am I one whose sons have died; now there is no further "death of a son" for me.
*Purisā etadantikā*: even my men are limited by this very end. That which was the limit of the death of my sons is also the limit for my men.
"This indeed is the end; I am now incapable of seeking out a husband.

"Delight has been destroyed everywhere" means that my craving-delight regarding all aggregates, bases, elements, realms of existence, wombs, destinies, stations, and abodes has been destroyed. "The mass of darkness" refers to the mass of ignorance (*avijjā*).
"Shattered" means split asunder by knowledge. This is the third [chapter].
4. Commentary on the Vijayā Sutta 165.

Regarding the fourth [verse], "with the fivefold [drum]" means with that which is endowed with five qualities: namely, stretched (*ātata*), stretched across (*vitata*), stretched and stretched across (*ātatavitata*), solid (*ghana*), and hollow (*susira*).
"I offer it to you alone" means I give everything to you. "I have no need for it" means I have no requirement for it.
"By the putrid body": even a body of golden hue is indeed a putrid body in the sense that it is constantly oozing and trickling;
therefore he spoke thus. "By its breaking up": by its nature of disintegration. "By its perishability":
by its quality of falling into dust and powder. "I am distressed": I am afflicted and oppressed. "I am ashamed": I feel shame. "Tranquil attainments": the eightfold mundane attainments.
It is called "peace" (*santā*) because of the continuity of its object and the continuity of its factors. "In all places" means in all form and formless existences;

since those two types of existence are included, it is said that "in the sense-sphere existence already mentioned and in the eight attainments"—in all these locations, he declares, "my darkness of ignorance has been dispelled. This is the fourth [chapter].
5. Commentary on the Uppalavaṇṇā Sutta 166.
In the fifth [verse], "supupphitagga" means a *sāla* tree that has blossomed beautifully from its very top.
"Na atthi te dutiyā vaṇṇadhātū" means there is no second element of beauty (*vaṇṇadhātu*) for you; there is no second element of beauty equal to yours, one that resembles you.
She says, "There is no other bhikkhunī. [The other replies: "Those who come here might be just like you;
just as you, having come here, find no intimacy or affection, so too would they be exactly like you.
"In the space between the eyebrows" means: even though I am standing right there in the middle of the two eyes, at the bridge of the nose, you do not see me.
"Vasībhūtamhi" means "I am one who has attained mastery. This is the fifth [verse]. 6.
Commentary on the Cālā Sutta (167).
In the sixth verse, "Ko nu tam idam ādapayi? means "Who indeed was that dull-witted fool who made you grasp this [wrong view]? "Pariklesam" means...
And other various kinds of calamities as well. Now, in order to crush that which Māra said—“Who indeed incited you to this?”—and to show:
“It was not some blind fool who incited me; rather, the Teacher, the supreme person in the world, taught the Dhamma,” she spoke the verse beginning with “The Buddha.
Therein, “he established me in truth” means he established me in Nibbāna, the ultimate truth.
"Those who do not understand cessation" means those who do not know the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*). This is the sixth [verse].
7. Commentary on the *Upacālā-sutta* 168.

Regarding the seventh [verse], "they go again into the power of Māra": it means they repeatedly fall under the sway of the Māra of death, the Māra of defilements (*kilesa-māra*), and the Māra of the son of a deva (*devaputta-māra*).
They come under his control. "Incensed" means tormented. "Where Māra has no access" means where Māra has no access for you.
"Therein" means in that Nibbāna. Seventh. 8.
Commentary on the Sīsupacālā Sutta.
169. "In the eighth [verse], 'samaṇī viya dissasi' means you appear like an ascetic woman (*samaṇī*).

'Kimiva carasi momūhā' means for what reason do you wander about like one who is utterly deluded (*momūha*)? 'Ito bahiddhā' means outside of this teaching (*sāsana*). 'Pāsaṃ ḍentī' refers to *pāsaṇḍā*;
the meaning is that they cast the snare of views (*diṭṭhipāsa*) into the minds of beings. However, the teaching releases one from the snare; therefore, it is called *pāsaṇḍa*."
It is not so called; rather, those outside of this [teaching] are indeed heretics (*pāsaṇḍa*). "They have faith" means they sink down, they become attached.
Now, while discussing the question, "For whom have you shaved your head?", he said, "He was born in the Sakya clan," and so forth.

In that context, "the Conqueror of All" (*sabbābhibhū*) refers to one who stands having overcome all aggregates, bases, elements, states of existence, wombs, destinations, and so on. [He has conquered] Death, Māra, and the rest.

He is the "Dispeller of Death" because he drives away death. He is the "Unconquered in All Respects" because he is undefeated in all things, whether regarding passion and the like, or in the battle against Mara.
He is the "Liberated in All Respects" because he is liberated from all things, such as the aggregates and so forth. He is the "Unattached" because he does not rely on craving or views.

He has "Attained the Destruction of All Kamma," meaning he has attained the state of Arahantship, which is defined as the destruction of all kamma. Regarding the phrase "in the destruction of the substrata":
It is liberated from the object, namely Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhisaṅkhaya*).
This is the eighth [verse]. 9. Commentary on the *Selasutta* 170.
In the ninth [verse], "By whom was this fashioned? means by whom was this made? He speaks of the "image" (*bimba*) with reference to the personal existence (*attabhāva*).

Because it is the basis for suffering, "Agha" refers specifically to the personal existence (attabhāva). "The destruction of causes" means through the cessation of causes by way of the deficiency of conditions. Ninth.
10. Commentary on the Vajira Sutta:
In the tenth [verse], "No being is found here," [it means that] in this mere heap of formations, no being exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha).
The name is not apprehended. "While the aggregates exist" means while the five aggregates are present and established in their respective modes.
"Convention" means that there is merely the designation "being. "Suffering" refers to the suffering of the five aggregates.
"Nothing other than suffering" means that apart from suffering, nothing else arises or ceases. The Tenth.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhikkhunī-saṃyutta in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the commentary on the Saṃyutta-nikāya.
6. Connected Discourses on Brahmā 1.
First Chapter 1.
Commentary on the Sutta of Brahmā’s Entreaty
172. Regarding the first discourse of the *Brahma-saṃyutta*, this reflection arose in the mind as a practice common to all Buddhas.

When did it arise? It arose on the eighth day after he had become a Buddha, at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, after he had eaten the tooth-stick and medicinal myrobalan brought by Sakka, King of the Devas, and had rinsed his mouth.

Having partaken of the alms-food of Tapussa and Bhallika from exquisite stone bowls brought by the Four World-Protectors, and having returned once more, as soon as he was seated under the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, [the Buddha] attained it.
"Attained" means realized. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Profound" is a term used as the opposite of "shallow."

"Difficult to see" (*duddasa*) means that because of its profundity it is difficult to see; it cannot be seen with ease. Because it is difficult to see, it is "difficult to awaken to" (*duranubodha*);
it must be understood with difficulty; it cannot be understood with ease. "Peaceful" (*santa*) means extinguished (*nibbuta*). "Sublime" (*paṇīta*) means unsurpassable.
These two [terms] are spoken specifically with reference to the supramundane (*lokuttara*). "Beyond the sphere of reasoning" (*atakkāvacara*) means by means of logic...
It is not to be traversed or plunged into [by the physical senses]; it is to be traversed by wisdom alone. "Subtle" means delicate.
"To be known by the wise" means it is to be understood by the wise who have entered upon the right practice. "Delighting in attachment": beings cling to the five strands of sensual pleasure;
therefore, they are called "attachments. Or else, the eight hundred modes of craving's movement cling [therein]; for that reason as well—

They are called "abodes" (*ālaya*). Because they delight in those abodes, they are "delighting in abodes" (*ālayarāmā*). Because they take pleasure in abodes, they are "pleased with abodes" (*ālayaratā*).
Because they are thoroughly gladdened by abodes, they are "thoroughly delighted by abodes" (*ālayasammuditā*).

For just as a king who has entered a well-prepared park, endowed with trees laden with flowers and fruit, delights in each of those excellences, being thoroughly gladdened, joyful, and overjoyed; so too [is it for them].

They do not feel weary of it, nor do they wish to depart even at evening; thus, through these two—attachment to sensual pleasures (*kāmālaya*) and attachment to craving (*taṇhālaya*)—beings find delight.

Delighting in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāravaṭṭa*), they dwell without weariness. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing them these two kinds of attachment as if they were a pleasure garden, said: "Delighting in attachment," and so forth.

In this context, *yadidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning should be understood as "that which is here" when referring to a location, and as "this which" when referring to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Regarding the term *idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppāda*: the conditions for these [factors] are "conditions-appropriate-to-this" (*idappaccayā*);

the state of being such conditions is "conditionality-appropriate-to-this" (*idappaccayatā*); and that conditionality is itself dependent origination—thus it is "dependent origination as conditionality-appropriate-to-this."
This is a designation for the conditions such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

"The stilling of all volitional formations," and so forth—all this refers to Nibbāna itself. For it is by coming to that [Nibbāna] that all the stirrings of volitional formations are stilled and completely pacified;

therefore, it is called "the stilling of all volitional formations. And because by coming to that, all acquisitions (*upadhi*) are relinquished and all craving (*taṇhā*) is exhausted, [it is so called].
All lusts of the defilements fade away; all suffering ceases. Therefore, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation is called *vāna*.

Furthermore, because this craving binds (*vināti*) existence to existence, or because it binds (*saṃsibbati*) action together with its fruit, it is called *vāna*; and that which has emerged from that is "without bonds" (*vānato*).
“Nirvana. “That would be weariness for me” means that teaching those who do not understand would be weariness for me;
it would be an affliction for me—this is the meaning. What is stated is that there would be both physical weariness and physical affliction.
However, in the case of the Buddhas, neither of these two exists in their minds. The particle *api ssu* is a fixed expression used in the sense of emphasis (*anubrūhana*). It [is said]: “Not...”
He explains: "This mere reflection arose, and these verses also occurred to me.

*Anacchariyā* means not marvelous (*anu-acchariyā*). *Paṭibhaṃsuṃ* means they became the object of knowledge known as intuition (*paṭibhāna*), and thus they reached the state of being fit for reflection.
*Kicchenā* means with difficulty, not by a painful practice; for to the Buddhas, all four paths are indeed practices that are easy.

...they exist. However, at the time of fulfilling the perfections (pāramī), while still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, he would cut off the heads of arriving supplicants—even when they were beautifully adorned and prepared—draw out their blood from their throats, pluck out their well-anointed eyes, and give away his son, the lamp of his family lineage, his beloved wife, and so forth; and in other such instances similar to those of Khantivādi...
This was said with reference to the path leading to [the goal] for one who undergoes cutting, breaking, and so forth, throughout various bodily existences (*attabhāva*).
Here, the syllable *ha* in *halanti* is merely an expletive; the meaning is *alaṃ*. "To proclaim" means to teach.

Thus, it is sufficient to teach, it is enough to teach, that which has been attained with such difficulty. The sense is: "What is the purpose of teaching? It is said: "By those who have transcended lust and hatred."

"By those touched by lust and hatred, or followed by lust and hatred"—the "逆流" (*paṭisotagāmi*) refers to that which goes against the current of permanence and so forth; it is the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, understood as "impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.
"Stained by passion" means stained by the passion of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), the passion for existence (*bhavarāga*), and the passion for views (*diṭṭhirāga*). "They shall not see" means:
They will not see [the world] through its true nature as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul; and since they do not see it thus, who would be able to cause them to grasp it so?
"Enveloped by a mass of darkness" means overwhelmed by a heap of ignorance. "By way of indifference" means by way of a state of lack of concern; the meaning is: by way of a lack of desire to teach.
But why did his mind incline in this way? Is it not the case that he thought: "I am liberated, I shall liberate others; I have crossed over, I shall help others cross"?
“What need have I for the guise of an unknown man? Having realized the Dhamma here, and having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world together with its devas.
Having thus made this aspiration and fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he attained omniscience. Is this true? It is true; it was by the power of such reflection that he did so.

His mind inclined in this way. For as he reflected upon the density of the defilements of beings and the profundity of the Dhamma after attaining omniscience, the density of the defilements of beings and the profundity of the Dhamma became manifest to him in every respect.
Then it occurred to him: "These beings are like gourds filled with sour gruel, like buckets filled with buttermilk."
“Like a rag soaked in fat and oil, or like a hand smeared with collyrium, they are filled with defilements, utterly corrupted, dyed by lust, fouled by hatred, and bewildered by delusion;
what indeed will they penetrate? As he reflected thus, his mind inclined toward this through the power of contemplating the thicket of defilements.
“And this Dhamma is as deep as the mass of water that supports the earth; it is as if hidden behind a mountain.”
It is as difficult to see as a mustard seed placed [on a hair-tip], and as difficult to comprehend as joining the tip to the tip of a hair split a hundredfold.
Indeed, while I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift that I had not given, no virtue that I had not guarded, and no perfections that I had not fulfilled. Yet—
Even as I was dispersing the host of Māra as if it were powerless, the earth did not tremble; even as I was recollecting my past lives during the first watch, it did not tremble;
even as I was purifying the divine eye during the middle watch, it did not tremble;
but only as I was penetrating dependent origination during the last watch did the ten-thousandfold world system tremble.
"Thus, even by one such as I, with sharp wisdom, this Dhamma was penetrated only with great difficulty. How then will the common people of the world penetrate it?
It should be understood that his mind inclined in this way through the power of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, his mind inclined thus because he desired to teach at the request of Brahmā; for the Blessed One knew: "My..."
“While my mind is inclined toward indifference, Mahābrahmā will request a teaching of the Dhamma from me.
These beings, moreover, hold Brahmā in high esteem. Thinking, ‘The Teacher indeed was unwilling to teach the Dhamma;
then Mahābrahmā requested him and he taught it,’ they will listen with eager anticipation, reflecting: ‘Truly, the Dhamma is peaceful! Truly, the Dhamma is sublime!’”
It should be understood that for this reason also, his mind inclined toward inaction rather than teaching the Dhamma.

Regarding Sahampati: it is said that during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was an elder named Sahaka who, having attained the first jhāna, was reborn as a Brahmā with a lifespan of an eon in the plane of the first jhāna. There he was known as "Sahampati Brahmā."
They perceive it. It is with reference to this that he said, "of Brahmā Sahampati.
"Alas, sir, he is perishing!"—it is said that he uttered this sound in such a way that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system, having heard it, all assembled together.
"Yatra hi nāma" means "in which world indeed. "Appeared before them" means [before] those ten thousand Brahmās.

He appeared together with them. "Of little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhajātiko*): those whose nature is such that there is little or limited dust of greed, hatred, and delusion in the eye of wisdom are "of little dust in their eyes.
"By reason of not having heard" (*assavanatāya*): by way of not having heard [the Dhamma]. "They will become":
those who, through ten meritorious deeds performed under previous Buddhas, have fulfilled their obligations and reached maturity—like lotuses at the touch of the sun's rays.

It shows that desiring only the teaching of the Dhamma, at the conclusion of even a four-line verse, there will not be just one or two, but many hundreds of thousands who have realized the Dhamma and are worthy of entering the plane of the Noble Ones.
"Appeared" (*pāturahosi*) means he became manifest. "Contemplated by those with stains" (*samalehi cintito*) means contemplated by the six teachers who were stained. They...

For previously, having arisen, they taught the defiled doctrine of wrong view as if scattering thorns throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, or as if sprinkling poison. "Open this"—this means open this aperture.
"The door to the Deathless"—the Noble Path which serves as the door to the Deathless, Nibbāna. "Let them hear the Dhamma awakened by the Stainless One."
"May these beings hear the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which has been fully awakened to by the Blessed One, the Stainless One, due to the absence of the stains of passion and the like"—
thus he entreats the Blessed One.
"As one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain" means as one standing right there upon the peak of a solid rock mountain.
For one who stands [on top], there is no need for such actions as turning the neck or stretching out the arms in order to see.
"Like that" means like its counterpart, the simile of the rocky mountain. This, however, is the summarized meaning here:
just as a man with eyes, standing right on the summit of a rocky mountain, would see the people all around him, so too, O Sumedha of beautiful wisdom, you [should look].

Having ascended the palace made of Dhamma with his all-encompassing eye of omniscience, O Blessed One, you who are yourself free from sorrow, look upon the people who have fallen into sorrow and are overwhelmed by birth and aging; hold them in your care and examine them.
This, however, is the intended meaning here: just as if one were to clear a vast field on the foot of a mountain and establish boundaries for the furrows therein...
Suppose they were to build huts and kindle fires at night, and there were a darkness endowed with four factors;

then, for a man with keen vision standing on the summit of that mountain and surveying the ground, neither the fields, nor the field boundaries, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping therein would be discernible. In the huts, however, only the glow of the fire-flames would be visible.

If it were so perceived, then for the Tathāgata who has ascended the palace of the Dhamma and surveys the multitude of beings, those beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of the Buddha-eye even when sitting on the right knee in a solitary dwelling;
they are like arrows shot in the night. But those individuals who are vessels for training and have performed wholesome deeds, even if they are far away, [come within his range].
Those who are established [in virtue] come within the range of perception like a fire or like the Himavanta mountain. And this has been said:
“The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himavanta mountain;
The wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.”

“Entreaty” means a request. “With the Buddha-eye” refers to both the knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*).

For these two kinds of knowledge have the name “Buddha-eye”; the knowledge of omniscience has the name “Universal Eye” (*samantacakkhu*); and the three knowledges of the paths have the name “Dhamma-eye.
Regarding the terms “with little dust in their eyes” and so forth, for those who—according to the method already stated—possess the eye of wisdom...
Those for whom the dust of passion and so forth is slight are "those with little dust" (apparajakkhā). Those for whom it is great are "those with much dust" (mahārajakkhā).
Those whose faculties, such as faith, are sharp are "those with sharp faculties" (tikkhindriyā). Those whose [faculties] are dull are "those with dull faculties" (mudindriyā).
Those whose very modes, such as faith, are beautiful are "those of good disposition" (svākārā). Those who perceive the reason when it is explained can easily [attain the goal].

They are capable of being made to understand; they are easy to instruct. Those who see both the next world and wrongdoing as fearsome are called "those who see the next world and wrongdoing with fear.
Here, however, is the canonical text: "A person endowed with faith has little dust in their eyes; a person lacking faith has much dust in their eyes."
A person who is energetic and one who is lazy; one with established mindfulness and one with muddled mindfulness; one who is concentrated and one who is unconcentrated;
a wise person and an unwise person—one who is greatly defiled. Likewise, a faithful person with keen faculties...
[and so on] ...a wise person who sees fear in the blame of the world beyond, and an unwise person who does not see fear in the blame of the world beyond. This is called "the world."

The world of aggregates, the world of sense-bases, the world of elements, the world of fortunate existence, the world of the origin of fortunate existence, the world of unfortunate existence, and the world of the origin of unfortunate existence.
One world: all beings subsist by nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds:
the three feelings. Four worlds: the four nutriments. Five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging.
Six worlds: the six internal sense bases. Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness.
Eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: the ten sense bases. Twelve worlds: the twelve sense bases.
Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements. All defilements are called "vajjā" (blameworthy). All...
Misconduct is blameworthy; all volitional formations are blameworthy; all kamma leading to existence is blameworthy.
Thus, regarding this world and this blame, a keen perception of danger is established, just as toward an executioner with a raised sword.
In these fifty ways, he knows, sees, understands, and penetrates these five faculties.
“This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of others.
*Uppaliniyaṃ* means in a lotus grove; the same method applies to the other [terms] as well. *Antonimuggaposīnī* refers to those that are nourished while submerged within [the water].
*Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni* means standing having emerged above the water. Among these, those which have emerged...
Those that remain standing, awaiting contact with the rays of the sun, are those that bloom today.
However, those that stand submerged in the water will bloom tomorrow. Those that do not emerge from the water but grow submerged within it will bloom on the third day.
Furthermore, there are others, such as the "diseased" lotuses (*sarogoppalādi*), which do not even emerge from the water.
There are those flowers that will not bloom at all and will become food for fish and turtles; these have not been included in the text.
However, having been brought forward, they are explained [here]. For just as there are those four kinds of flowers, even so there are four types of persons:

one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), one who gains knowledge through an elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), one who is led to understanding (*neyyo*), and one for whom the words are the limit (*padaparamo*).
In this regard: "The person for whom there is a breakthrough to the Dhamma at the very moment it is uttered is called a person who gains knowledge by a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

The person for whom there is a breakthrough to the Dhamma when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is analyzed in detail is called a person who gains knowledge by an expanded explanation (*vipañcitaññū*). The person for whom [there is a breakthrough] from a mere recitation..."
For one who inquires thoroughly, attends wisely, and serves, frequents, and honors spiritual friends, there comes about the gradual realization of the Dhamma;
such a person is called "one to be guided" (*neyya*).
As for that person who, despite hearing much, speaking much, retaining much, and reciting much, does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma in this very life—

...he is called a person for whom the word is the limit. In this regard, the Blessed One, surveying the ten-thousandfold world system which is like a grove of lotuses, [distinguishes them as follows]:

"Those that bloom today are like those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*); those that bloom tomorrow are like those who understand through an expanded explanation (*vipañcitaññū*);

those that bloom on the third day are like those who are led to understanding (*neyyo*); and those flowers that are food for fish and turtles are like those for whom the word is the limit (*padaparamo*)."

He saw them. And seeing them, he saw them in every respect: "So many have little dust in their eyes; so many have much dust in their eyes; and among those, so many are those who understand through a condensed teaching.
In this regard, for three types of persons, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma achieves its purpose within this very lifetime.
For those who take the words as the ultimate, there is a latent predisposition for future benefit.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the teaching of the Dhamma that brings welfare to these four types of persons, and having generated the desire to teach it, further divided all beings within the three realms of existence into two classes according to their capacity and incapacity. With reference to whom it was said: "Which beings are incapable?"
Those beings who are possessed of an obstruction of karma, possessed of an obstruction of defilements, and possessed of an obstruction of fruition;
who lack faith, lack desire [for the good], and lack wisdom; who are incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness regarding wholesome states—these beings are incapable.
Which beings are capable? Those beings who are not possessed of an obstruction of karma... [and so on]... these are they.
“Beings are capable. Therein, having set aside all incapable persons and having discerned only the capable persons through his knowledge, he divided them into six classes, saying:

“So many are of lustful temperament (rāga-carita), so many are of hateful or deluded temperament (dosa-moha-carita), and so many are of speculative, faithful, or intellectual temperament (vitakka-saddhā-buddhi-carita).
Having done this, he thought, “I shall teach the Dhamma.”
*Paccabhāsīti* means he replied. *Apārutā* means opened. *Amatassa dvārā* means the door to the Deathless;
for that is the door to Nibbāna, which is designated as the "Deathless," and he shows that it has been opened and set forth by me.
*Pamuñcantu saddhan* means let everyone release and relinquish their own faith. Regarding the meaning of the latter two lines: for I [have done this] of my own...
"Although this sublime and supreme Dhamma is proficient and well-expounded, I did not speak it because I perceived weariness in body and speech.
But now, let all people bring forth vessels of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations.
"He vanished" means that after honoring the Teacher with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, he disappeared and returned to his own place.
The meaning is as follows. After he had departed, the Blessed One thought, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?

Knowing that Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away and that the group of five monks had been of great assistance, and desiring to teach them the Dhamma, he went to Isipatana in Bārāṇasī and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. This is the first [chapter].
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Reverence (Gāravasutta) 173.
“The second [thought] arose”: this thought arose during the fifth week. “Without reverence” means devoid of reverence toward others;
the meaning is that he did not establish anyone in a position of respect. “Without deference” means devoid of deference; the meaning is that he did not establish anyone in a position of seniority.
In the phrases beginning with "sadevake," the term "sadevake" means together with the devas. Although both Māra and Brahmā are included here by the mention of "devas"—
for Māra, known as Vasavatti, exercises power over all, while Brahmā, possessed of great majesty,
radiates light throughout a thousand world-systems with a single finger— [the same applies] with two fingers for two [thousand], and so on, up to ten fingers for ten [thousand].

He radiates light throughout thousands of world-systems; lest it be said that he is more endowed with virtue than these, the terms "together with Māras" and "together with Brahmās" are stated separately.
Likewise, those called *samaṇas* are learned, virtuous, and wise by way of belonging to a single school (*nikāya*) and so forth;
the *brāhmaṇas* also are learned and wise by way of the science of sites (*vatthuvijjā*) and so forth—lest it be said that he is more endowed with virtue than these.
It is said: "May they not be allowed to speak among this generation together with recluses and brahmins.
As for the phrase "together with devas and humans," this was stated by including everything that has been grasped without exception.

Furthermore, here the first three phrases are spoken in terms of the world (*loka*), while the latter two are spoken in terms of the generation (*pajā*). "More perfected in virtue" (*sīlasampannataro*)—by virtue...
"More perfect" means "more excellent. The same method applies to the remaining [qualities] as well.

And here, the four qualities beginning with virtue (sīla) are described as both mundane and supramundane, whereas the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) is exclusively mundane; for this is the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa).
Regarding the phrase "appeared": [the Buddha thought], "This Teacher, seeing no one superior to himself in virtue and so forth from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence..."

Thinking, “I shall dwell having honored, revered, and relied upon only the nine supramundane states realized by me,” the Blessed One considered the cause, considered the purpose— the specific increase— and thinking,
“I will go and inspire him,” he became manifest before him; the meaning is that he stood facing him.

Regarding the phrase "and they dwell," if someone were to say, "Because of the word 'they dwell,' there must be many Buddhas even in the present," he should be refuted by this statement: "The Blessed One, venerable sir, is now an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Furthermore, [the Buddha said]:
"I have no teacher; my equal is not found.
In the world with its devas, there is no one who is my peer."
The non-existence of other Buddhas should be demonstrated by means of such suttas as these.
Therefore—because all Buddhas are reverent toward the true Dhamma—for that reason. "By one desiring greatness" means by one aspiring to a state of greatness.
"Remembering the teaching of the Buddhas" means by one who keeps the teaching of the Buddhas in mind. Second.
3. Commentary on the Brahmadeva Sutta 174.
In the third [verse], "alone" means being solitary in postures such as standing and so forth; it means dwelling alone.
"Withdrawn" means withdrawn from and detached by way of the body. "Diligent" means established in non-forgetfulness through mindfulness. "Ardent" means endowed with the ardor of energy.

"Pahitatta" means one whose self is sent forth. "Kulaputtā" refers to sons of good family by virtue of their conduct. "Sammadeva" means not out of debt, not out of fear, and not being driven by the need for a livelihood;

rather, even those who have gone forth in whatever manner, provided they fulfill the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, are said to have "gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the right way.
"Brahmacariyapariyosāna" refers to the culmination of the holy life of the Path.
The noble fruit is the culmination. "In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence.
"Having realized for oneself through direct knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*) means having known it personally and made it manifest to one's own experience.

"Having attained" (*upasampajja*) means having acquired and fulfilled [the path], he dwelt [in that state]. And while dwelling thus, "birth is exhausted... [etc.]... he directly knew" (*abbhaññāsi*). By this, his stage of reviewing is shown.
But what birth of his has been exhausted, and how did he directly know it? It is said: first of all, his past birth is not exhausted, because it was already exhausted previously;
nor is his future birth, because there is no effort directed toward that; nor is his present birth, because it still exists.
However, due to the non-cultivation of the Path, that [birth] which would arise in one, four, or five-aggregate existences—distinguished by one, four, or five aggregates—[is what is meant].
Birth: That [birth] has been exhausted by the attainment of the state of non-arising through the cultivation of the Path.
Having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the cultivation of the Path, he knows—knowing that "in the absence of defilements, even though karma exists, it will not lead to rebirth in the future."
“Lived” (*vusitaṃ*) means dwelt, fully dwelt; the meaning is that it has been performed, practiced, and brought to completion. “The holy life” (*brahmacariyaṃ*) refers to the holy life of the Path.

“Done what was to be done” (*kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ*) means that the sixteenfold task—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing with respect to the four truths through the four paths—has been brought to its conclusion.
“There is nothing further beyond this state” (*nāparaṃ itthattāyā*) means that there is now no more of this present condition.

Thus, there is no cultivation of the path for the sake of performing the sixteen functions or for the destruction of the defilements. Alternatively, "to this state" (*itthattāya*) means from this state of being;
he directly knew: "From this very kind of present continuity of aggregates, there is no further continuity of aggregates;
these five aggregates, however, remain with their roots cut, like a tree whose root has been severed, once they have been fully understood."
"A certain one" means one person. "An arahant" means he was among the arahants, the disciples of the Blessed One who were arahants.
"In regular succession" means walking in *sapadāna* (successive) order, proceeding by visiting each house in turn. "Approached" means while approaching.
But his mother, upon seeing her son, went out from the house, took his bowl, and [entered] the interior of the dwelling.
Having led him inside, he had him sit on a seat that had been prepared.

"He regularly offers an oblation" means that at all times he presents a portion of food as an offering; however, on that particular day, there was a ritual of *bhūta*-balikamma being performed in that house.
The entire house was smeared with green cow dung, strewn with parched grain, and encircled by garlands of forest flowers.
Having placed it in various pavilions where flags and banners were hoisted, and having lit staff-lamps, it was adorned with fragrant powders, garlands, and the like;
a smoke-vessel was suspended all around it. That brahmin woman, too, rising early in the morning, bathed with sixteen jars of scented water and adorned her person with every kind of ornament.
At that time, having seated the one whose taints were utterly destroyed, and without giving him even a single bowlful of rice-gruel, she thought, "I shall feed the Great Brahmā.

She filled a golden platter with milk-rice, mixed it with ghee, honey, sugar, and other ingredients, and took it toward the back of her residence, where there was a raised platform adorned with green plaster and other decorations. Taking that platter, she—
Having gone there, he placed a ball of milk-rice in each of the four corners and in the center;
then, taking one ball in his hand, he set his knee upon the ground until it was covered by a stream of ghee flowing as far as the world-cycle (kappa), saying:
"May the venerable Great Brahmā eat, may the venerable Great Brahmā taste, may the venerable Great Brahmā be satisfied."
“While speaking thus, he fed the Brahmā.

This thought occurred to him as he smelled the fragrance of the virtue of that great one whose taints were exhausted—a fragrance that had overspread the world of the devas and reached even the Brahmā-world.
“He would cause me to be stirred” means he would urge me on, he would join me to right practice. “This...”
Indeed, having seated such a supreme recipient of offerings— one whose taints are utterly exhausted— and yet failing to give even a single bowlful of rice-gruel,

she wanders about performing sacrifices to spirits, abandoning the scale as if weighing with her hand, abandoning the drum as if beating her belly, and abandoning the fire as if blowing on a glowworm.

"I shall go there," it is said, meaning: "I shall shatter his wrong view, lift him out from the path to the states of woe, and act in such a way that he ascends the path to heaven after scattering eighty million pieces of wealth throughout the Buddha’s Dispensation.
"Far from here" means the Brahma-world is far from this place; for even a stone the size of a gabled chamber, when dropped from there by a single person—
Traveling forty-eight thousand *yojanas* day and night, it would take four months to reach the earth;
even the lowest Brahma-world is that far away. "The sacrificial offering for whom" means that the Brahma-world of whichever Brahmā one offers the sacrifice to is far off.
"The path to Brahmā": here, the "path to Brahmā" refers to the four wholesome *jhānas*.
"But their life-path consists of the fruition-jhānas. Not knowing that path to the Brahma-world, what are you muttering and prattling?
For the Brahmas subsist by means of jhāna accompanied by rapture;
they do not consume cow's milk boiled with grass seeds. Do not exhaust yourself for no reason."
Having spoken thus, that Great Brahmā again raised his hands in *añjali*, bowed down, and pointing out the Elder, said:

"O Brahmin lady, this is the Brahmā-deva," and so forth. In this context, "free from acquisitions" (*nirūpadhika*) means devoid of the acquisitions of defilements, volitional formations, and sensual qualities.
"Attained to the state of a super-god" (*atidevapatta*) means having attained the status of a god beyond gods, the status of a Brahmā beyond Brahmās. "Not supported by others" (*anaññaposī*)...
"Except for this present existence, he does not support any other existence, nor sons or wife; thus he is 'one who supports no others' (anaññaposī).

'Worthy of offerings' (āhuneyyo) means he is fit to receive the alms-offering (āhunapiṇḍa). 'A knower of the Vedas' (vedagū) means one who has reached the end of suffering by means of the knowledges (veda) consisting of the four paths.
'One of developed self' (bhāvitatto) means one who stands having developed and increased the self. 'Unstained' (anūpalitto) means unstained by the taints such as craving."
He is tormented. "He moves about seeking food" means he wanders in search of nutriment.
"There is nothing for him behind or before": here "behind" refers to the past and "before" refers to the future;
he says that for one who is free from desire and lust regarding the aggregates of the past and the future, there is neither what is behind nor what is before.

In the passage beginning with "peaceful" (*santa*), he is "peaceful" because of the pacification of lust and other defilements. He is "smokeless" (*vidhūma*) due to the departure of the smoke of anger; he is "unafflicted" (*anīgha*) due to the absence of suffering;

and he is "one who has laid aside the rod" (*nikkhittadaṇḍa*) because, even when wandering about carrying a sword, staff, or other weapons, he lacks the intention to kill. Regarding the phrase "among the timid and the steadfast" (*tasathāvaresu*):
here, ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) are called "timid," while those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are called "steadfast. However, the seven types of trainees (*sekha*) are "timid."
It is impossible to say; they are not stationary, yet when they associate, they associate only with that which is stable.
"So tyāhuṭim" means "he [offers] that oblation to you.
"Visenibhūto" means one who has become free from the army of the defilements. "Aneho" means free from craving. "Susīlo" means by virtue of the morality of one whose taints are destroyed.
"Virtuous. "Well-liberated in mind" means his mind is thoroughly liberated by the liberation of fruition (*phala-vimutti*). "One who has crossed the floods" means he has crossed over the four floods.
By this sequence of discourse, Brahmā, while praising the Elder, directed the Brahmin toward the [right] sphere.
However, the final verse was placed there by the compilers of the Council (*saṅgītikāra*). "He established the offering" refers to the offering of the four requisites.
He established [it]. "Sukhamāyatikaṃ" means having happiness as its future result; the meaning is that it brings about happiness in the future.
This is the third [sutta]. 4. Commentary on the *Bakabrahmasutta* 175.
In the fourth [sutta], "a pernicious view" (*pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ*) refers to the base eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). "This is permanent" (*idaṃ niccaṃ*)—this [is] together with...
One says that the state of Brahmā, which is actually impermanent, is "permanent. "Stable" (*dhuva*) and so forth are synonyms for that very same thing.

In this context, "stable" means firm. "Eternal" (*sassata*) means existing at all times. "Absolute" (*kevala*) means unbroken and complete. "Of an indestructible nature" (*acavanadhamma*) means having a nature that does not decay.
For in such passages as "this is not born," there is no one here who is born or who lives.
"Or one who is dying, or one who is passing away, or one who is being reborn—none of these exist; it is with reference to this that he speaks.
And as for the phrase "and there is nothing else beyond this," it means that there is no other escape higher than this state of Brahmā and his company.
In this way, a deeply rooted view of eternalism has arisen in him. And being one who speaks thus, [he does not know] the three higher stages of meditation or the four...
It rejects everything from the path and the four fruits down to Nibbāna. When did this view arise in him?
At the time of his rebirth on the plane of the first jhāna; some say it was on the plane of the second jhāna. Here is the account of the sequence:
it is said that this Brahmā, having been reborn in the lower realms, had gone forth as a seer (*isi*) during a time when no Buddha had appeared.
Having gone forth, performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, and attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he passed away without falling away from his jhāna.
He was reborn in the Vehapphala Brahma-world, which belongs to the plane of the fourth jhāna, where he took up a lifespan of five hundred aeons.
Having remained there for the full duration of that life, he underwent a downward rebirth; having developed the sublime third jhāna, he [was reborn] in the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world.
Having taken up a lifespan of sixty-four eons, he was reborn there. Having developed the second jhāna there, he took up a lifespan of eight eons and was reborn among the Ābhassara devas.
Having developed the first jhāna there, he was reborn on the plane of the first jhāna with a lifespan lasting for an eon.
At that initial time, he knew both the kamma he had performed and the place where he had been reborn.
As time passed by, however, having forgotten both [the past and the future], he gave rise to the eternalist view (*sassatadṛṣṭi*).

"Enveloped in ignorance" (*avijjāgata*) means one who has gone into, or is possessed of, ignorance—one who is ignorant and blinded. "Yatra hi nāma" means "one who indeed. "Vakkhati" means "he speaks. By the connection with the particle "yatra," however, it is used as a statement regarding the future.
When this was said, that Brahmā—just as a highway robber, while enduring two or three blows, does not inform his companions even though he knows—[acted].
Just as one being struck repeatedly might point out, "So-and-so and so-and-so are my companions," even so, being rebuked by the Blessed One, he regained his mindfulness;

thinking, "The Blessed One is looking at every step I take, desiring to crush me," he became afraid and, pointing out his own companions, spoke the words beginning with "seventy-two. This is the meaning.
"O Gotama, we seventy-two people were reborn here by virtue of meritorious deeds.
Having mastery over ourselves, not being subject to others, we cause others to be subject to us;

having transcended both birth and aging, O Blessed One, because we have reached the end of our knowledge, we are designated as 'Vedagus' (those who have attained the goal of knowledge). This is our final rebirth in the Brahma-world. Thus they addressed him.

"Many people, indeed many people, long for us, thinking: 'This venerable one is Brahmā, Mahābrahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the Wielder of Power, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Ordainer, the Almighty, the Father of all that has been and is to be.
Thus they aspire and yearn."
Then the Blessed One said to him, beginning with the words, "For this is but little. Therein, "this" refers to that life-span of yours which you here consider "long";
this is but little, it is trifling. "Of a hundred thousand nirabbudas" means of a hundred thousand nirabbudas according to the calculation of nirabbudas.
"I know the life-span" means: "I [know] that so much life remains for you now."
“I know it. Blessed One, you say, ‘I am Anantadassī,’ and you say, ‘I am Anantadassī, one who has transcended birth and the rest.
‘What is my past?’—if you are Anantadassī, then being so, tell me this:
what is my past? ‘Virtue and conduct’—this refers simply to moral discipline (*sīla*). ‘And that which I should know’—”
"Tell me that which I might know as spoken by you," he says.
Now, explaining this to him, the Blessed One said, "That which you have sent away," and so forth. Herein, this is the intended meaning:
it is said that in the past, after being born in a noble family and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he thought, "I shall bring an end to birth, aging, and death."
Having gone forth into the ascetic life and attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), he became a master of the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Having constructed a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges, he spent his time delighting in the joy of meditation.
At that time, caravans of five hundred wagons would periodically set out across the desert wilderness (*marukantāra*). However, during the day in the desert...
"It is not possible to go; it is night-time for traveling.
Then, as the oxen yoked to the lead cart of the first caravan were going along, they turned back and faced the path by which they had come.
All the carts likewise turned back, and when the dawn rose, they realized they were on the return path. And that was the day they were to cross the wilderness.
All the wood and water were completely exhausted; therefore, thinking, "Now there is no more life for us," the men tied their oxen to the wheels and lay down within the shadow of the carts.
The ascetic, too, having emerged from his leaf-hut early in the morning, sat at the door of the hut watching the Ganges.
He saw the Ganges being filled by a great flood of water, coming along like a rolling mass of jewels;
seeing it, he thought: "Are there perhaps beings in this world who are suffering from the lack of such sweet water?
While reflecting thus, he saw that caravan in the desert of Maru and thought, "May these beings not perish!"
“May this great mass of water, having been cut off from here and there, flow toward the caravan in the desert wilderness,” he resolved with a mind of supernormal power (*abhiññā*).
With the mere arising of that thought, the water went there as if it had been poured into a channel.

The people, awakened by the sound of the water, saw the water and were filled with joy and satisfaction; they bathed, drank, and gave water to their oxen, and then reached their desired destination in safety.
They arrived. The Teacher, wishing to show that former deed of the Brahmā, spoke the first verse. Therein, *apāyesi* means "he caused to drink";
the syllable *a-* is merely a particle. *Gimmanī* means "in the summer. *Samparete* means "when [the world] was struck and overcome by the heat of the summer sun.
At another time as well, the ascetic, having constructed a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges, lived there depending upon a forest village.
At that time, robbers had raided that village, seized its wealth, and were departing with cattle and young calves.
The cows, the dogs, and the people were all crying out with a great clamor.
Hearing that sound, the ascetic thought, "What is this? As he reflected, he knew, "Fear has arisen among the people," and [thought], "In me..."

Thinking, "May these beings not perish," he entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and upon emerging, he created an army of four divisions on the highway before the thieves with his mind of direct knowledge.

Seeing him, the thieves who were returning from their plundered spoils thought, "It seems the king has arrived," and they abandoned their loot and fled. The ascetic [declared]: "Whatever belongs to anyone, let that remain theirs."
He made the resolve, “Let it be so,” and it became exactly thus. The great multitude attained safety.
The Teacher, showing this past deed of his as well, spoke the second verse. Therein, “at the bank of the Eṇī” means on the shore of the Gaṅgā.
“Being led away as a captive” means being taken away after having been seized; the meaning is also “being led away as one condemned to death.”
Again, on another occasion, a certain family living upstream on the Ganges established a friendship with a family living downstream.
Having tied together a fleet of boats and loaded them with much solid food, soft food, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they came down the current of the Ganges.
As the people ate, feasted, and danced, they went along.
Singing as they went along in the celestial chariot of the gods, they were filled with intense joy.
Seeing them, the Naga of the Ganges became enraged and thought, "These men pay me no heed at all; now I shall cast them into the very ocean!
Having manifested a massive body, he split the waters in two, rose up, spread his hood, and let out a great roar.

He stood there. When the great crowd saw him, they were terrified and raised a cry. The ascetic, sitting in his leaf-hut, heard them and thought, "These people are coming along singing and dancing, filled with joy; but now they have raised a cry of fear—what could it be?
As he directed his attention, he saw the Naga king and thought, "May no beings perish while I am looking on," and he entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for supernormal power (*abhiññā*).
Having entered [the meditative state] and cast off his human form, he manifested the appearance of a garuḍa and showed it to the nāga king.
Terrified, the nāga king withdrew his hood and entered the water; the great multitude attained safety.
The Teacher, showing this past deed of his as well, spoke the third verse. In that context, *luddena* means "by the cruel one. *Manussakamyā* means...
The meaning is: "out of desire for human pleasures" and "with the desire to harass humans.
At another time, having gone forth into the ascetic life, this person became an ascetic named Kesava.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, as a young brahmin named Kappa, was Kesava’s attendant and pupil, serving his teacher.
He was one who responded with "What shall I do?", who was pleasant in his conduct, endowed with wisdom, and devoted to his master's welfare.
Kesava was unable to live without him and maintained his livelihood entirely dependent upon him. The Teacher, showing this as well as his previous karma, spoke the fourth verse.
In that context, "one who dwells bound" (*baddhacaro*) refers to a pupil; he was, moreover, the senior pupil.
"He thought me one possessed of perfect wisdom" means: thinking, "This one is truly wise and endowed with vows," Kappa was your pupil at that time—I was he.
"Do you know others as well? means not only my life-span, but also others.
"You surely know others as well. For you are indeed a Buddha; the meaning is that because you are a Buddha, therefore you know.
'For this radiance of yours shines forth' means that because you are a Buddha, this blazing majesty of yours stands illuminating the entire Brahma-world. This is the fourth [verse].
5. Commentary on the Aññatarabrahma Sutta 176.

Regarding the fifth [sutta]: "Having attained the fire element" means that, having performed the preparatory work for the fire-kasiṇa, he emerged from the foundational jhāna and resolved, "Let flames issue forth from my body. By the power of that resolving consciousness, from his entire body—
Just as flames go out, so too one who has attained the fire-element is said to have "entered that attainment. Having thus entered it, [the Elder asked:

"In which Brahma-world? Why did the Elder go there? It is said that when the Elder had entered the fire-element and saw the Tathāgata sitting above that Brahmā, he thought: "This person is one who pierces with the arrow of knowledge; I too must go there."
Because he had been there, he went [there]. The same method applies to the departure of the others as well.
For that Brahmā, having failed to perceive the majesty of the Tathāgata and the disciples of the Tathāgata, would have been incapable of entering the Vinaya; therefore, that assembly took place.
Therein, the mass of flames rising from the body of the Tathāgata passed beyond the entire Brahma-world into the cloudless sky.
They leaped forth, and they were six-colored; however, the radiance of the Tathāgata’s disciples remained their natural color.

"Do you see it transcending?"—by this he asks: "Do you see the brilliant radiance of the Blessed Buddha as it surpasses the light of the bodies, celestial mansions, ornaments, and so forth of other Brahmās in this Brahma-world? "I do not, dear sir."
"That view" refers to that former view of mine: "There is no other ascetic or brahmin capable of coming here.
That [view] is no longer mine. Why would I speak? For what reason should I say it?

Regarding the statements "I am eternal" and "I am permanent," it is said that this Brahmā has two views: the view of acquisition (*laddhi-diṭṭhi*) and the view of eternalism (*sassata-diṭṭhi*). In that regard, toward the Tathāgata...
As he beheld the disciples of the Tathāgata, his wrong view was abandoned. The Blessed One, however, gave a great discourse on the Dhamma here.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Brahmā was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, through the Path, his eternalist view was abandoned;
therefore, he spoke as follows.

"Brahmapārisajja" means "attendant of Brahmā. Just as there are young novices who carry the belongings for the elders, those who are the attendants of the Brahmās are likewise called "Brahmās. As for the phrase "he approached him": why did he send [the messenger] specifically to the elder?
It is said that his confidence in the elder arose through just such a brief exchange of conversation; therefore, he sent him to that very person.
"He sent others as well" means: "Are there others like you four people, or are you four alone possessed of such great psychic power (*mahiddhika*)?

"Those possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijja*) means endowed with the three knowledges consisting of the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*). "Attained to psychic powers" (*iddhipatta*) means having attained the knowledge of the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*). "Skilled in reading the minds of others" (*cetopariyāyakovida*) [means skilled in knowing the mental states of others].

They were skilled in the movements of the mind. Thus, here the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) have been described in their essential form; the divine ear (*dibbasota*), however, is already included by virtue of them.

"Many" means that such disciples of the Buddha possessing the six higher knowledges are many, exceeding the path of calculation, wandering about and making the whole of Jambudīpa radiant with the yellow robes (*kāsāva*). This is the fifth [chapter].
6. Commentary on the Brahmaloka Sutta (177).
In the sixth [verse], "each by a door-post": each [deity] stood leaning against a single door-post like a gatekeeper.

"Prosperous" (*iddha*) means enriched by the bliss of *jhāna*. "Flourishing" (*phīta*) means well-flowered with the flowers of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). "Not enduring" (*anadhivāsenta*) means...
"Unable to endure this," he said; that is, sitting in the midst of those created Brahmās, he spoke these words beginning with "Do you see me?
Regarding the verse "Three *supaṇṇas*," the number five hundred should be construed either by way of form (*rūpa*) or by way of individual (*panti*).
By way of form first: "three *supaṇṇas*" refers to three hundred forms of *supaṇṇas*; and "four swans" refers to four hundred forms of swans.
"Five hundred tigress-leaders" means that certain deer resembling tigers are called "tigress-leaders"; there were five hundred of those who had the appearance of tigress-leaders.
"Three rows of golden-winged birds" means three hundred rows of *supaṇṇas*. "Four [rows] of swans" means four hundred rows of swans.
"Five hundred tigress-leaders" means five hundred rows of tigress-leaders. "Meditators" means...
"This is my splendor while meditating in my celestial mansion," he shows. "Illuminating" means shining forth.
"In the northern direction"—it is said that this golden celestial mansion (kanakavimāna) is situated in the northern direction from the place where those Great Brahmas reside;
therefore, he spoke thus. His intention, however, was: "While dwelling in such a golden celestial mansion, for whom am I..."
"I shall go to attend upon another. "Having seen the peril in form" means having seen the fault in form consisting of birth, aging, and destruction.
"Always trembling" means having seen form as always trembling, shaking, and agitated by cold and other such conditions.
Therefore, the wise one does not delight in form, because he sees the peril in form and [sees it] as always trembling.
He sees form; therefore, that teacher of beautiful wisdom, being wise, does not delight in form. The sixth [sutta]. 7.
Commentary on the Kokālika Sutta: 178.
In the seventh, "measuring the immeasurable" means measuring the person whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), thinking, "His virtue is this much..."
"Such is his concentration, such is his wisdom"—measuring in this way.
"Who here, being wise, would speculate?"—this explains that only one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), while measuring another whose taints are destroyed, might so speculate.
But as for the worldling (puthujjana) who attempts to measure him, "I consider him hindered, one whose wisdom is overturned. The seventh [chapter].
8. Commentary on the Katamodakatissa Sutta 179.
In the eighth [verse], "akissava": *kissava* is said to mean wisdom (*paññā*); thus, "one without wisdom" is the meaning. The eighth [is concluded]. 9.
Commentary on the Turū Brahmā Sutta.

180. In the ninth [verse], "afflicted" (*ābādhika*) means one who is afflicted by the disease mentioned in the immediately preceding sutta in the manner of "boils the size of mustard seeds," and so forth.
"Severely ill" (*bāḷhagilāna*) means extremely sick. "Turū" refers to the elder named Turū, the preceptor of Kokālika;
having attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), he was reborn in the Brahma-world. Beginning with the earth-dwelling deities, he said, "It is improper..."
Having heard through tradition that Kokālika’s evil karma had reached the Brahma-world because he had falsely accused the two chief disciples with his final words, [the Buddha thought]:
“Lest this poor wretch perish even as I am watching, I shall advise him so that he may gain confidence in the hearts of the Elders.
Having come there, he stood before him. It was with reference to him that it was said:
“Turū the Independent Brahmā. *Pesalā* means those of lovely virtue. “Who are you, friend?”—saying this, even while still lying down, he opened his eyes wide like a leopard’s and spoke thus.
“See how much you have transgressed!”—he said this to show that not seeing the great swelling on his own forehead, Turū thought he ought to be reproved for a pimple no larger than a mustard seed.

Then, knowing that "this poor fellow has not attained right view; like one who has swallowed poison, he will not act upon anyone's words," [the Blessed One] spoke the verse beginning with "For a man...
and so forth. In this context, *kuṭhārī* means harsh speech, which is like an axe.

*Chindati* means it cuts right at the roots, which are reckoned as the roots of wholesome merit (*kusalamūla*). *Nindiyaṃ* refers to a person of bad character who is worthy of censure. *Pasaṃsati* means...
Having honored one who has attained the highest goal, he says, "He is one whose taints are destroyed. Or, he censures one who is worthy of praise;
that is, he accuses with the final charge one who is indeed praiseworthy and whose taints are destroyed, saying, "This man is immoral.
He sifts for misfortune with his mouth; he is said to sift for that transgression with his mouth. By means of that misfortune, there is no happiness.
One does not find [anything greater]. For the result of praising those who deserve blame and blaming those who deserve praise is indeed equal.
That which is called the loss of wealth at dice—even with all one's possessions and even with oneself—is a minor offense.
But that which [is done] toward the Sugatas—that is, toward persons who have gone rightly—[the mind...]
One might become corrupt; this very corruption of the mind is a far greater misfortune than that.
Now, in order to demonstrate its greater magnitude, he said: "A hundred thousand," and so forth.
Therein, "a hundred thousand" refers to one hundred thousand *nirabbudas* by way of the *nirabbuda* calculation. "Thirty-six" refers to another thirty-six *nirabbudas*. Five...

Thus, by the reckoning of *abbuda*, there are five *abbudas*. "Whoever reviles the Noble Ones" refers to the measure of the lifespan in that hell where one who reviles the Noble Ones is reborn. This is the ninth [sutta].
10. Commentary on the Kokālika Sutta.
181. Regarding the passage, "In the tenth [chapter], the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One": who was this Kokālika, and why did he approach?
It is said that he was the son of the merchant Kokālika in the city of Kokālika in the district of Kokālika;
