having gone forth, he resided in a monastery built by his father under the name Cūḷakokālika, and he was not a disciple of Devadatta. He...

For there was a son of a brahmin named Mahā-Kokālika. While the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, the two chief disciples, traveling on a tour of the countryside together with about five hundred bhikkhus, found that the time for entering the rains retreat was approaching;
desiring to dwell in seclusion, they dismissed those bhikkhus and, taking their own bowls and robes, [proceeded] to that country.
Having reached that city, they went to that monastery. There, Kokālika showed them the proper duties (*vatta*).
After exchanging greetings with him, they took his promise, saying, "Friend, we shall dwell here for the three months of the rains; do not tell anyone," and they stayed.
Having stayed there and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony on the day of the invitation, they said, "Friend, we are going."
They asked Kokālika for leave to depart. Kokālika said, "Friends, stay for this one day and you shall go tomorrow.
On the second day, having entered the city, he addressed the people: "Friends, even though the two Chief Disciples have come here and are staying, you do not know of it;
no one has invited them even with basic requisites. The city-dwellers asked, "Where—?"
“Venerable sirs, Elders, why did you not tell us? “What is the use of telling us, friends? Do you not see two monks sitting on the Elder’s seats?
These are the Chief Disciples. They quickly assembled and gathered together ghee, molasses, and other offerings, as well as robes and cloths.
Kokālika thought: “The Chief Disciples, being supremely few in desires, will not accept the gain that has arisen through the use of incited speech;
not accepting it, they will say, ‘Give this to the resident monk. Having caused that various gain to be taken, he went into the presence of the Elders.
Upon seeing him, the Elders refused it, saying, “These requisites belong neither to us nor to Kokālika.”
They departed. Kokālika thought, "How can they depart without accepting for themselves and without having me give anything?

and he conceived a grudge. Those monks also went into the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and then, taking their own retinue, while wandering on tour through the countryside, eventually returned to that very city in that kingdom.
The city-dwellers recognized the elders, prepared an offering together with requisites, erected a pavilion in the center of the city, and gave the gift;
they also presented requisites to the elders. The elders handed these over to the Saṅgha of monks.
Seeing this, Kokālika thought: "In the past these were of few desires, but now they have become possessed of evil desires. Even in the past..."

Thinking, "I believe they are like those who are of few desires, contented, and secluded," he approached the elders and said, "Friends, you were like those of few desires in the past, but now you have become wicked monks. Saying,
"I shall destroy their standing right where it is rooted," he departed in great haste, went to Sāvatthī, and approached the Blessed One.
It should be understood that this Kokālika approached for this very reason.
As soon as the Blessed One saw him approaching in great haste, he reflected and knew: "He has come wishing to revile the Chief Disciples.
And as he reflected, "Is it possible to stop him?", he realized: "It is not possible to stop him."

Having seen that one who dies without having offended against them will certainly be reborn in the Paduma hell, [the Buddha] three times forbade him, saying, "Do not say so," for the purpose of silencing the dispute—thinking, "He does not even stop one who reviles Sāriputta and Moggallāna"—and to demonstrate the great gravity of reviling the Noble Ones.
In this context, *mā hevaṃ* means "do not speak thus. *Saddhāyiko* means...
A mine of faith, inspiring confidence, or one whose words are to be trusted. "Trustworthy" means one whose words are to be believed.
"He departed" means he departed, being impelled by the power of his karma; for karma that has found its opportunity cannot be warded off, and it did not allow him to remain there.
"Not long after he had departed" means that not much time passed once he had departed.

"His entire body was covered" means that even after directing his attention to a space the size of a hair-tip, his whole body became completely overspread with pustules that had emerged by breaking through the bones.
However, because of the power of the Buddhas, such karma does not yield its result while the Buddhas are present;
rather, it yields its result as soon as one has departed from their range of vision. Therefore...
Not long after he had departed, pustules broke out on him. "The size of *kalāya* beans" means the size of chickpeas (*caṇaka*).
"The size of young *veluva* fruits" means the size of tender *veluva* fruits. (*"The size of *billā* fruits"* means the size of large *veluva* fruits.
"They burst open" means they broke. When they had broken, his entire body became like a ripe jackfruit. With his limbs thus festering, [he stood] at the gateway of the Jeta Grove.
Like a fish that has swallowed poison, he lay upon kadalī leaves. Then, the people who had come one after another to hear the Dhamma said:
"Shame on Kokālika! Shame on Kokālika! He has done what was improper; relying on his own mouth, he has met with ruin and disaster.
Hearing them, the guardian deities uttered cries of "shame! After the guardian deities, the deities of the sky [did the same].
By this means, he acquired a single kamma-formative force reaching as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Then his preceptor, having come and realized that he was not receiving instruction, rebuked him and departed.

"He passed away" means that after the preceptor had departed, he died. Regarding "the Paduma hell": there is no separate hell named Paduma; rather, he was reborn in a certain location within the great Avīci hell itself, where one must be cooked according to the number of lotuses.
Twenty *khāris*—measured by the Magadhan *pattha*—make four *patthas* in the kingdom of Kosala, which constitutes one *pattha* there.
By that *pattha*, four *patthas* make an *āḷhaka*; four *āḷhakas* make a *doṇa*; four *doṇas* make a *mānikā*; four *mānikās* make a *khārī*;
and twenty *khāris* make a *vīsatikhārika*. A "cartload of sesame" (*tilavāha*) refers to a cartload of fine sesame seeds from Magadha.
Regarding "the Abbuda hell": there is no separate hell named Abbuda. Rather, this is the name for a place within Avīci itself where one must be cooked according to the count of *abbudas*.
The same principle applies to the Nirabbuda and other hells as well.
Furthermore, the calculation of the years here should be understood in this way: just as one hundred times one hundred thousand makes a *koṭi*, [so too should the higher numbers be reckoned].
In this way, one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭis* is called a *pakoṭi*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is called a *koṭipakoṭi*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭipakoṭis* is a *nahuta*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *nahutas* is a *ninnahuta*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *ninnahutas* is one *abbuda*; twenty times that is a *nirabbuda*. This same method applies [to the subsequent numbers].
"In all cases. Tenth.
The First Chapter.
2. The Second Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Sanaṅkumāra Sutta 182.
In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, "on the bank of the Sappinī," means on the bank of the river named Sappinī. Regarding "Sanaṅkumāra":

it is said that while he was still a young boy with five locks of hair (*pañcasikha*), he developed meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and was reborn in the Brahma-world, remaining in the very form of a youth.
He wanders about. Because of this, they perceive him as a "Kumāra" (Prince); however, because of his ancient nature, he is called "Sanaṅkumāra.
"Janetasmim" means among those born; that is the sense. "Among those who follow lineage"—among those in the world who rely on lineage, the Kṣatriya is the best.
"Endowed with true knowledge and conduct" is according to the exposition in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*.

Or by the three beginning with knowledge of past lives; or by these eight true knowledges (vijjā) according to the method of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta—namely, insight-knowledge, mind-made psychic power, and the six direct knowledges (abhiññā);

or likewise by the seven true states (saddhamma)—consisting of perfect observance of the precepts, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, and the four fine-material-sphere jhānas. Thus...

Endowed with conduct consisting of the fifteenfold division of qualities, he is the best among gods and humans—this brāhmaṇa whose taints are exhausted is the most excellent among both gods and humans. First.
2. Commentary on the Devadatta Sutta.
183. In the second [section], "not long after he had departed": having split the Saṅgha, he went from Veḷuvana to Gayāsīsa before long. "Assatari" means one born to a mare by a donkey.
This is the second. 3. Commentary on the Andhakavinda Sutta: 184.
In the third [section], "Andhakavinda" refers to a village of that name. "He approached": [thinking] "Even now the Teacher is exerting effort..."
“He exerts himself and applies himself; I shall go to his presence, stand there, and speak a verse connected with energy that is appropriate to the teaching. Thus he approached.
“Remote” means situated beyond the reach of people, outside the vicinity of human habitation. “Liberation from the fetters” means—
While utilizing those lodgings, he should not use them for the sake of robes and such requisites; rather, he should dwell there for the sake of liberation from the ten fetters.

If he finds no delight in those lodgings while living in the Saṅgha, he should dwell in the midst of the Saṅgha—like dust springing up on the back of a donkey—not wandering in the forest for the sake of protecting the minds of his supporters and others. Thus, he is one who has guarded himself.

Dwelling there with mindfulness, like a bull that is fierce toward its own calf yet does not gore or butt its fellow cattle, he should live with his self guarded, intent upon the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), without harming or disturbing his fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*).
Now, explaining the conduct for a monk wandering for alms while living in the Saṅgha, [the Blessed One] said: "From family to family," and so forth.
In this context, "wandering for alms" means wandering for the sake of food.

"One should resort to remote lodgings" means that even when one has entered the midst of the Saṅgha to dwell there, one should not live in the vicinity of the main hall planting palm or coconut trees and so forth while mingling with attendants and others;
rather, having produced mental pliancy and gladdened and satisfied the mind, one should again resort to remote lodgings.
"He would dwell" means he speaks in praise of the forest itself. "From fear" means from the fear of *saṃsāra*. "In fearlessness" means in *nibbāna*.
"Being liberated" means he would dwell having become intent upon it.
"Where there are terrors" means in that place where there are terrifying beings with consciousness, such as lions and tigers, and those without consciousness...
In that part of the night, there were many things such as stumps and creepers; "reptiles" refers to snakes of the *dīghajātika* species and the like.
"The bhikkhu sat there" means the bhikkhu was seated in such a place. By this, he illustrates the following:
just as you now, having disregarded the terrifying objects present there, as well as the reptiles, the flashing of lightning, and so forth—
"Sitting down, even so do the bhikkhus, devoted to striving, sit down.
"I have seen this" means it was seen by me with certainty.
"This is not 'thus it has been said'" means that I do not say this on the basis of mere conjecture, nor on the basis of logic, nor by the authority of the scriptures. "In one holy life..."
By means of a single teaching of the Dhamma. For here, "teaching of the Dhamma" (dhammadesanā) is intended in the sense of the holy life (brahmacariya).
"Those who have abandoned death" (maccuhāyino) refers to those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), having relinquished death.
Regarding the phrase "ten and tenfold ten": here, "ten" (dasā) means simply ten; "tenfold ten" (dasadhā dasa) means one hundred; and "others" refers to ten more than that.
"I see hundreds of those in training," he says. "Those who have entered the stream" means those who have entered the stream of the Path.
"Not going to the states of the lower animals" is merely a way of teaching; the meaning is that they are not subject to rebirth in the states of misery.

"I am not even able to count them" means that out of fear of telling a lie, he says this with reference to the vast teaching on the qualities of a Brahmin, implying that he cannot count how many beings possess such a share of merit. This is the third [section].
4. Commentary on the Aruṇavatīsutta 185.
In the fourth [verse], "Abhibhū and Sambhava" refers to Abhibhū and Sambhava. Among them, the Elder Abhibhū was foremost in wisdom, like the Elder Sāriputta;
the Elder Sambhava was foremost in concentration, like Mahāmoggallāna. "They grumbled" means...
They disparage [it], or they think of it as something base. They criticize means: "What is this? What is this?"—they speak to one another.
They revile means: they speak at length again and again. "With the lower half of the body" means with the part of the body starting from the navel downwards.
Only this much is recorded in the text (*pāḷi*). However, the Elder [said]: "The natural form..."

He displayed his manifold supernormal transformations (*iddhi-vikubbana*) as they have been described in such passages as: "Having abandoned the form of an elephant, he takes on and displays the form of a garuḍa, or having taken on the form of a garuḍa, he displays it," and so forth. Then the Elder thought:
"How might this teaching of the Dhamma, when taught, be dear and pleasing to all? Thereupon, reflecting [on the matter], he spoke these verses.
“‘All religious sects and all gods and humans praise human effort according to their own respective doctrines;
there is no one who speaks in dispraise of energy. I shall teach by making it connected with energy;
thus this teaching of the Dhamma will be dear and pleasing to everyone,’—having understood this and having searched through the three Piṭakas, he spoke these verses.”
In this context: "Exert yourselves" means practice the energy of exertion (*ārambha-vīriya*). "Strive forth" means practice the energy of striving forth (*nikkama-vīriya*).
"Apply yourselves" means apply effort; "exert yourselves. "The army of Death" refers to the army of defilements (*kilesa-senā*); shake it off.
"The cycle of birth and wandering" refers to both birth and the wandering in saṃsāra, or the saṃsāra characterized by birth. "The end of suffering."
"He will make" means he will bring about the end of the suffering of saṃsāra. But what did the Elder do to make himself known throughout a thousandfold world-system?
First, having attained the blue kasiṇa, he pervaded all places of light with darkness;
then, having attained the white kasiṇa, he pervaded the places of darkness with radiance. Then, when beings asked, "What is this darkness? [he replied: "It is..."
When their attention was aroused, he showed them light. When they were in the place of light, there was no need for further illumination;
as they investigated, "What is this light?", he showed himself to them. Then, while they were saying, "It is the Elder!", he recited these verses.
They heard his voice as if he were sitting in the midst of the entire assembled company and teaching the Dhamma. The meaning is also...
This became clear to them. Fourth. 5.
Commentary on the Parinibbāna Sutta. 186.
Regarding the fifth [section], "at Upavattana, in the Mallas' Sal Grove": for just as from the bank of the Kadamba River, by way of the gate of the Royal Mother’s monastery...
One must go to the Thūpārāma. Thus, on the opposite bank of the river named Hiraññavatī, there was a Sāl forest park.
Just as the Thūpārāma is situated relative to Anurādhapura, so it was with respect to Kusinārā.
Just as the road from the Thūpārāma entering the city by the southern gate proceeds facing east and then turns northward, so too [is the layout] here.
From the garden, the row of *sāla* trees went facing east and then turned north; therefore, it is called "Upavattana.

In that Upavattana, in the *sāla* grove of the Mallas, "between the twin *sāla* trees" means within the space between those *sāla* trees standing with their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves interwoven with one another.
"Accomplish [this] through diligence" means by not being separated from mindfulness.

"Accomplish the duties that ought to be done. Thus the Blessed One, just as a wealthy householder lying on his deathbed might explain the essence of his wealth to his sons, likewise, lying on the bed of final Nibbāna, he spoke, condensing all the exhortations given over forty-five years into this single phrase on heedfulness. This is the Tathāgata’s...
"The final words" refers to the speech of the compilers of the collection.
Following this, in order to show the preparations for the Parinibbāna that the Blessed One made before he attained Parinibbāna, it is said:
"Then the Blessed One entered the first jhāna," and so forth. In that context, while the Blessed One had attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha*):
Seeing the cessation of inhalation and exhalation, gods and humans cried out all at once with the perception that "The Teacher has attained final Nibbāna.
The Elder Ānanda also asked the Elder Anuruddha, "Venerable sir, has the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna?
The Elder replied, "Friend Ānanda, the Tathāgata has not yet attained final Nibbāna; rather, he has entered the cessation of perception and feeling."

“He has attained [the attainment of cessation],” he said. But how did he know this? It is said that the Elder, entering those various attainments together with the Teacher, proceeded as far as the emergence from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and then he knew:
“Now the Blessed One has entered cessation; and within cessation, there is no such thing as passing away.”
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...

[and so on] ...having emerged from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna. In this context, however, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna in twenty-four places, and the second jhāna in thirteen places.
Likewise, he attained the third jhāna... and the fourth jhāna in fifteen places.

How so? First, he attained the first jhāna in these twenty-four places: the ten foul objects (asubha), the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra), the eight kasinas, loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and the delimited space (paricchedākāsa). However, excluding the thirty-two aspects—
He attained the second jhāna upon the ten foul objects (*asubha*) and the remaining thirteen [meditation subjects]; upon those same [thirteen], he attained the third jhāna.

However, upon the eight kasinas, the [four] divine abidings of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), the delimited space, and the four formless attainments—upon these fifteen bases—he attained the fourth jhāna. And this too is merely a summary account.
But as the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, was entering the city of Nibbāna,

he entered all the meditative attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand million; having experienced the bliss of all those attainments, he entered [Nibbāna] as if bidding farewell to his kinsmen by embracing them.

Regarding the statement, "Immediately after emerging from the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One attained final nibbāna," there are two kinds of "immediacy": immediacy following the jhāna and immediacy following the reviewing consciousness.

Emerging from the fourth jhāna and attaining final nibbāna at that very moment while the mind has descended into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is called "immediacy following the jhāna. Having emerged from the fourth jhāna...
Furthermore, after reviewing the factors of jhāna, for one who has descended into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), there is parinibbāna right there;

this is called "immediately following the review. These two [moments] are indeed immediate. However, the Blessed One, having attained jhāna and emerged from it, reviewed the factors of jhāna and then attained parinibbāna through the neutral life-continuum consciousness associated with the truth of suffering. Those...

For indeed, whether they be Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or noble disciples—even down to a mere ant—all pass away by means of the resultant consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), which is indeterminate (*abyākata*) and belongs to the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*).
"Beings" (*bhūta*) refers to sentient beings (*satta*). "Peerless" (*appaṭipuggala*) means devoid of any rival or counterpart. "Attained to power" (*balappatta*) refers to the tenfold [powers].
He attained the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). "Subject to arising and passing away" means having the nature of arising and passing away.
"Their subsiding" means the subsiding of those conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*). "Bliss" means that the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) Nibbāna itself is bliss; this is the meaning.

"Then there was" refers to the earthquake mentioned in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, stating, "With the final passing away (*parinibbāna*), there was a great earthquake"; for that [earthquake] causes the hair to stand on end (*lomahaṃsanaka*).
And he was terrifying. "Endowed with the excellence of all aspects" means endowed with the qualities of the excellence of all aspects.
"I had no inhalation or exhalation" means that inhalation and exhalation did not arise. "Unshaken" means unshaken due to the absence of *ejā* (agitation), which is defined as craving.
"Aiming for peace" means aiming at, depending upon, or referring to *nibbāna* without remainder (*anupādisesa*). "Possessing the eye" means possessing the eye by way of the five kinds of eyes.
“Parinibbūta” means he has attained final nibbāna through the nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*).
“With a mind that is not clinging” means with a mind that is not attached, not contracted, but rather fully blossomed. “He endured the feeling” means he patiently accepted the feeling;
he did not, being driven by the feeling, roll hither and thither. “Liberation” means liberation from all obstructions by way of any phenomenon whatsoever.
The attainment of the state of non-designation has become like the Nibbāna of an extinguished lamp. This is the fifth [chapter].
The second section.
Thus, in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*...
The commentary on the Brahmā-saṃyutta of the Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā is finished. 7.
The Brāhmaṇa-saṃyutta.
1. The Chapter on Arahants.
1. Commentary on the Dhanañjānī Sutta. 187.
In the first sutta of the Saṃyutta on Brahmins, "Dhanañjānī" refers to one of the Dhanañjānī clan; it is said that she belonged to the Ukkaṭṭha clan.
It is said that other brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā; their doctrine is that those of the Dhanañjāni clan emerged by breaking through the crown of his head.
Why did he utter this inspired utterance (*udāna*)? It is said that this brahmin was a holder of wrong view;
when told "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha," he would cover his ears, being as stubborn as a khadira log. But the brahmin lady...

The noble female disciple was a stream-enterer (sotāpannā). On the day the brahmin gave alms, he provided rice porridge with little water to five hundred brahmins, while the brahmin lady provided various flavored foods for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
On the day of the brahmin’s giving, because she was under his authority and had abandoned stinginess, the brahmin lady served him with her own hands. [Thus it was] for the brahmin lady...
However, on the day of the almsgiving, the brahmin would leave his house early in the morning and flee.

Then one day, without consulting his wife, the brahmin invited five hundred brahmins and said to his wife, "Tomorrow, madam, five hundred brahmins will be eating at our house. "What should I do, brahmin? she asked.
"There is nothing else for you to do; others will handle all the cooking and serving.

However, as for the fact that you—whether standing, sitting, sneezing, or coughing—utter the salutation 'Homage to the Buddha' to that shaven-headed ascetic, do not do it even for a single day tomorrow. For when the brahmins hear it,"
"They are displeased, saying, 'Do not cause a rift between me and the brahmins.
Whether you are separated from the brahmins or from the devas, as for me, having recollected the Teacher, I am unable to remain without paying homage.
"Lady Kulasatikā, in that village they even strive to close the very gate; yet you [refuse to close] the mouth that ought to be closed by only two finger-breadths!"

"You cannot even wait until it is time for the brahmins to eat. Although he spoke thus again and again, being unable to dissuade him, [the husband] took the sword with a jeweled hilt that was placed at the head of the bed and said:
"Lady, if tomorrow, when the brahmins are seated, you pay homage to that shaveling ascetic, I shall cut you from the soles of your feet..."
"Starting from the soles of my feet up to the crown of my head, I shall mince you like a shoot of bamboo and heap you into a pile," he said, and uttered this verse:
"With this circular blade, from foot to head,
I shall cut you like a bamboo shoot, If you do not act falsely."
“If you say ‘Buddha,’ if you speak of ‘Dhamma,’ and if you praise the ‘Saṅgha,’ then you live in my home.
But the noble female disciple was as difficult to shake as the earth and as impossible to overturn as Mount Sineru. She spoke to him thus:
“Even if you were to cut off my limbs one by one at your will, O brahmin, I would never cease from the teaching of the Supreme Buddha.
I am not a mere woman of the Okkāka clan who can be restrained; I cannot be held back by the Conqueror.”
“I am the daughter of the Best of Buddhas; either release me or kill me!
Thus, roaring with what is known as the "Roar of Dhanañjānī," she spoke five hundred verses.
Unable to touch or strike the brahmin woman, the brahmin said, “Madam, do whatever you please.”

He threw his sword onto the bed. On the following day, having had the house smeared with green cow dung and decorated here and there with jars full of parched grain, garlands, perfumes, and other ornaments, he had five hundred brahmins prepared with rice porridge mixed with fresh ghee, sugar, and honey, and very little water;
then he announced that it was time for the meal.
The Brahmin’s wife also, having bathed herself early in the morning with scented water, put on a new garment worth a thousand pieces,
draped over one shoulder a cloth worth five hundred pieces, and adorned herself with all her ornaments; then, taking a golden spoon,
she was serving the food to the Brahmins in the dining hall when she approached that Brahmin who was seated in the same row as them.
While she was bringing the food, the wooden vessel was poorly placed and it slipped. From the slipping and clashing, a painful sensation arose.
At that moment, the One of Ten Powers remembered. Because of his perfection of mindfulness, however, he did not let the bowl of milk-rice fall;
instead, setting it down slowly on the ground, he stood with palms joined in reverence before five hundred brahmins.
Setting [his bowl] aside, he extended his joined palms toward the Bamboo Grove and uttered this inspired exclamation.
At that time, among those brahmins, some had finished eating, some were in the act of eating, some had merely placed their hands into the food, and for some the meal was merely set before them.
Upon hearing that sound, as if struck by a club as large as Mount Sineru...
Feeling pain and mental distress as if their heads had been struck or their ears pierced by a thorn, they thought,
"We have been brought into this house by this man of heterodox views," and became angry. Casting away the morsels of food in their hands and spitting out what was held in their mouths,
and seeing the bow, they reviled the brahmin like crows and departed in all directions.
Seeing the Brahmin departing after he had split apart in this way, the Brahmin looked at the Brahminī from her head down and,
reproaching her in various ways, saying, "It was precisely because we foresaw this very danger that we did not obtain you when we entreated you,
lady, starting from yesterday," he spoke these words beginning with, "But it has turned out exactly thus."
"He approaches" means: "The ascetic Gotama is honored by villages, towns, and kingdoms; it will not be possible to go there and frighten him by saying just anything.
I shall ask him only this one question. While going, he composed the verse beginning with "What must be cut off?
[thinking]: "If he says, 'I approve of the killing of such-and-one,' then..."
‘Those whom you do not like, you wish to kill; you have arisen for the destruction of the world. What use is the state of a recluse to you?’—thus I shall refute him.
If he says, ‘I do not approve of the killing of anyone,’ then I shall refute him by saying, ‘Then you do not even desire the killing of passion and the other defilements.
Why then do you wander about as a recluse? Thus, this is a dilemma with two horns.
Thinking, "The ascetic Gotama will be unable either to swallow this question or to spit it out," he approached him.
"He exchanged greetings" means that, not showing his state of anger due to his own pride in being learned, he exchanged greetings while speaking sweet words.
The question was told in the *Devatā-saṃyutta*. The rest has already been explained in detail below. First.
2. Commentary on the *Akkosasutta* 188.

Regarding the second [discourse], "Akkosaka Bhāradvāja": he was indeed a Bhāradvāja, but because he arrived reviling the Tathāgata with approximately five hundred stanzas, the compilers of the collection adopted the name "Akkosaka Bhāradvāja" for him.

“Offended and displeased” means that he became angry with wrath and displeased with dejection, thinking: “By this ascetic Gotama, who has caused my eldest brother to go forth, a loss has been inflicted upon me and my faction has been split. “He reviles” means: “You are a thief!
You are a fool! You are deluded! You are a rogue! You are a camel! You are a ram! You are an ox! You are a donkey! You are an animal! and so forth.
“You are a denizen of hell!”—thus he reviles with these ten grounds for abuse.

“He reviles” means that he reviles by saying such things as: “Be off, you shaveling ascetic! You act as if you were beyond punishment; now I shall go to the royal court and have punishment inflicted upon you.
“He shares in common” means he eats together. “He reciprocates” means he returns a favor for what has been done. [Regarding] the Blessed One...
Why did he say, "O Gotama"? It was because he had heard it said: "This is yours alone, brahmin; this is yours alone, brahmin.
Thinking on the basis of hearsay, "The seers, when angered, utter curses like Kisavaccha and others," the fear arose in him:
"I think the ascetic Gotama is cursing me. Therefore, he spoke thus.
“Of one with teeth” means of one who is free from malice. “Such a one” means one who has attained the characteristic of suchness (tādilakkhaṇa).
“By that, evil falls upon him alone” means that by that anger, evil accrues to that very person. “The mindful one attains peace” means that being endowed with mindfulness, he endures it.
“Of both who are healing” means of both who are healing; or rather, this is the reading: *ubhinnaṃ tikicchantānaṃ*.
The person who, being mindful, attains tranquility, acts for the benefit of both [self and others], heals, and accomplishes [the goal]—people consider such a person to be a fool.

What kind of people? Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma. "In the Dhamma" means either in the Dhamma of the five aggregates or in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Unskilled" means those ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are blind fools, lacking proficiency in that Dhamma. This is the second [verse].
3. Commentary on the *Asurindakasutta* 189.
In the third [sutta], "Asurindakabhāradvāja" refers to the younger brother of Akkosakabhāradvāja.
"Enraged" means angry for that very reason. "And that victory belongs to him" means that victory belongs to him alone; the sense is that he is the one who wins.
Of what [is it said]? It is of that forbearance—the forbearance and endurance of one who understands, who perceives the virtue in enduring—which belongs to that very one who understands;
it is his victory. But the fool, speaking harshly, merely imagines victory, thinking, "It is my victory. This is the third [verse]. 4.
Commentary on the *Bilaṅgīka Sutta* (The Discourse on the Bilangika)
190. Regarding the fourth [reciter], "Bilaṅgika Bhāradvāja": he was indeed a Bhāradvāja;
however, because he had various kinds of pure and prepared sour gruel made and sold, thereby accumulating great wealth, the compilers of the collection gave him the name "Bilaṅgika Bhāradvāja.
He remained silent [thinking]: "My three elder brothers have been ordained by this man."
Being exceedingly angry and unable to say anything, he stood there in silence. The verses, however, have already been explained in the Devatāsaṃyutta.
This is the fourth [sutta].
5. Commentary on the Ahiṃsaka Sutta.

191. Regarding "Ahiṃsakabhāradvāja": this one is indeed Bhāradvāja; however, because he asked a question concerning non-harming (*ahiṃsaka*), the compilers of the collection adopted this name for him. Alternatively, he was Ahiṃsaka by name and Bhāradvāja by clan.
He said, "I am Ahiṃsaka; let the venerable Gotama know me as such. And "tathā cassa" means "if it were so, you would be [thus]."
The meaning: "He does not harm" means he does not vex or cause suffering.
This is the fifth [sutta]. 6. Commentary on the Jaṭā-sutta (192):

Regarding the sixth, "Jaṭā Bhāradvāja," this one is indeed a Bhāradvāja; however, because he asked a question concerning matted hair (*jaṭā*), the compilers of the collection spoke of him thus. The rest has already been explained in the *Devatāsaṃyutta*. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Suddhika Sutta (193).

Regarding the seventh [sutta], "Suddhika Bhāradvāja": this person was also a Bhāradvāja; however, because he asked questions concerning purity (*suddhika*), the compilers of the collection spoke of him in this way.
"Though virtuous, one who practices austerity" means: even while being endowed with virtue, one who performs the practice of austerity (*tapokamma*).
"Endowed with true knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*): here, "true knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the three Vedas; "conduct" (*caraṇa*) refers to the conduct of one's lineage.

He says that this [brahmin] is purified, but other people are not; thus, this brahmin possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijjo brāhmaṇo*) is purified, whereas these other people called by the name "others" are not purified.
Even while prattling much, even while prattling much, he says: "Only the brahmin..."
The meaning is: even if one were to speak a thousand such words as "it is purified. *Antokasambu* means internally putrid due to the nature of internal defilements (*kilesa*).
*Saṃkiliṭṭho* means endowed with defiled bodily actions and so forth. This is the seventh [sutta]. 8.
Commentary on the *Aggika-sutta*.

194. Regarding the eighth [discourse], "Aggikabhāradvāja": this man was also a Bhāradvāja; however, the compilers of the collection gave him this name because of his practice of tending the sacrificial fire (*aggi-paricaraṇa*). "Was present" means he was joined [to the assembly].
"He stood there"—why did he stand there? It is said that at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world, saw this brahmin and thought:
“This brahmin, having taken such supreme milk-rice and thinking, ‘I shall feed the Great Brahmā,’ is wasting it by burning it in the fire;
he is entering upon a path to the states of misery. If he does not relinquish this conviction, he will surely fill the realms of misery.
I shall go to him to teach the Dhamma, shatter his wrong view, ordain him, and [establish him] in the four paths.”
And I give the four fruits. Therefore, having entered Rājagaha in the morning, he stood there.
“With the three knowledges” means with the three Vedas. “One of pure birth” means one endowed with a lineage that is pure back through seven generations of ancestors.
“Learned in many things” means learned in many various kinds of texts. “He might enjoy the Soma”—that is, the one possessed of the three knowledges.
He says that this brahmin is fit to eat this milk-rice, whereas for you it is unfit.

"He knew" means he understood and penetrated it through the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*). "He saw heaven and the states of woe" means he saw both heaven and the states of woe with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*).
"The destruction of birth" refers to Arahantship. "One who has reached the culmination through direct knowledge" means one who, having known [this], has attained final consummation (*vosita-vosāna*).

"From the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence (bhavagga), there is no brahmin equal to you, O Gotama; there is no brahmin endowed with noble birth who has exhausted the taints (khīṇāsava) like you. You alone are a brahmin.
Having spoken thus, he filled a golden bowl and offered the milk-rice to the One Possessed of Ten Powers (Dasabala). The Teacher [related] his past life...
Having illuminated this, while declining the food, he spoke the verse beginning with "gāthābhigītaṃ me. In that context, "gāthābhigītaṃ" means sung to by verses.
"Abhojaneyyaṃ" means not fit to be eaten. This is what is meant:
"O Brahmin, for all this time while I have been established in the practice of wandering for alms, you were unable to give me even as much as a ladleful."
"Now, however, by spreading out all the qualities of a Buddha for you as if scattering sesame seeds upon a palm-leaf fan, I have made them manifest;
thus, this food is like something obtained by a singer through singing. Therefore, 'this song of verses sung by me is unfit to be eaten.
For those who see clearly, O Brahmin, this is not the Dhamma—O Brahmin, it is neither the goal nor the Dhamma."
For those who clearly see, there is no such rule as "this kind of food must be eaten.
Even when it comes to a meal of pure rice porridge, the Buddhas reject it if it is accompanied by songs; having received food through songs, the Buddhas simply set it aside.
"When there is Dhamma, O Brahmin, there is livelihood"—that is to say, O Brahmin, when there is Dhamma, by looking to the Dhamma and being established in the Dhamma.
"For those who maintain their lives, this is the proper conduct and this is the livelihood: having brought forth such [food], one should eat only what has been acquired in accordance with the Dhamma.
Then the brahmin thought: "Previously, I did not know whether the ascetic Gotama possessed virtues or faults.
But now, having recognized his virtues, I wish to distribute about eighty million pieces of wealth from my own house into the Sasana."
He was born [with such views], and he says, "These requisites given by me are unallowable. "I am not to be accepted as an alms-receiver by the ascetic Gotama.
Then the Blessed One, dispatching his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and examining the course of that man's mind, perceived:
"This man considers all the requisites given by himself to be 'unallowable. Indeed, regarding whatever food this discussion has arisen..."
"This alone is not permissible; the rest are faultless," he said, beginning with the words "and by other [means]," while demonstrating to the brahmin the way of giving the four requisites.
Therein, "with anxiety stilled" means having anxiety stilled by means of [restraining] the hands and so forth.
"With food and drink" is merely a formal designation for the teaching. But this is the meaning: by others [than these], you [should think], "I shall relinquish."
Serve with requisites such as robes that have been properly inspected. For this is the teaching of the Tathāgata: "It is a field for one who seeks merit.
This means that for you, who seek merit and desire merit, it has been prepared like a fertile field that yields abundant harvests even from a small seed. Eighth.
9. Commentary on the Sundarikasutta 195.
Regarding the ninth [sutta]: "Sundarikabhāradvāja" is one who received this name because he offered oblations to the sacrificial fire on the bank of the river Sundarikā.
"By the Sundarikā" means by the river of that name. "Offers the fire" (aggiṃ juhati) means he kindles it by casting offerings into it. "Agnihutta" (the fire-sacrifice).
"He attends upon" means he serves the fire-sanctuary by sweeping, smearing with cow dung, making offerings, and so forth.
"Who indeed might eat this remains of the oblation?"—it is said that when the brahmin saw the milk-rice remaining after the offering in the fire, he thought:
"The milk-rice placed in the fire has been eaten by Mahābrahmā; however, there is this remainder."
“If I were to give this to a brahmin born from the mouth of Brahmā, then my father would be satisfied along with his son,
and the path leading to the Brahma-world would be well-cleansed for him. Then, rising from his seat to see the brahmin,
he looked toward the four quarters, thinking, “Who indeed might eat this remains of the sacrificial offering?”
"At the foot of a tree" means at the foot of the oldest tree in that grove.
"Seated with his head covered" means seated with his body and head covered. But why did the Blessed One sit there?
It is said that at dawn, while surveying the world, the Blessed One saw this brahmin and thought: "This brahmin is of such a nature..."
Having taken the finest milk-rice and thinking, "I shall feed the Great Brahmā," he wasted it by burning it in a fire...
[and so on] ...saying, "I give the four paths and the four fruits.
Therefore, rising early, having attended to his physical needs, and taking his bowl and robes, he went and sat at the foot of that tree in the manner described. Then, why?
“Why did he cover his head? [The answer is: To ward off the falling snow and the cold wind; the Tathāgata was indeed capable of enduring it.
However, had he sat down without covering himself, the brahmin would have recognized him from afar and turned back;
this being the case, the conversation would not have taken place. Thus the Blessed One thought: “When the brahmin arrives, I shall uncover my head.”
"Then, having seen me, he will initiate a conversation; following the course of that conversation, I shall teach him the Dhamma.
It was for the purpose of initiating such a conversation that he acted in this way.
"He approached," [referring to] the brahmin: "This man, having covered his head, has been devoted to striving throughout the entire night. To him..."
Thinking, "Having given the water of hospitality, I will give him this remnant of the sacrificial offering," he approached him, perceiving him to be a brahmin.
As soon as the head was uncovered, seeing the short hair at the nape of the neck, he said, "This worthy one is shaven" (*muṇḍo*).
Then, looking more closely and not seeing even a single remaining lock of hair, he spoke with contempt, "This one is bald" (*muṇḍako*).
He said: "From there" means from that very place where he stood when he saw [them]. "Even though shaven-headed" means they have their heads shaved for some reason or other.
"Do not ask about birth": if you desire the great fruit of giving, do not ask about birth; for birth is no cause for being worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*).
"But ask about conduct" means, moreover, ask about conduct consisting of the various virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth.
Ask. For this is the cause of being worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇeyya*). Now, explaining that matter, he said:
"From wood, indeed, fire is born," and so forth. Herein, this is the intended meaning: here, fire is born from wood;

yet it does not perform the function of fire merely because it was born from *sāla* wood and the like, nor does it fail to perform it because it was born from wood such as a wooden trough for drinking water; rather, it performs its own...
However, one born from any source whatsoever, provided they possess the excellence of qualities such as integrity (*accaya*), indeed acts [righteously].
Thus, it is not only one born into a brahmin family or similar high castes who is worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*); one born into a caṇḍāla family or similar low castes is not excluded.

Rather, whether of low birth or high birth, a sage whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava-muni*), being steadfast and restrained by moral shame (*hirī*), becomes a thoroughbred (*ājānīya*). By virtue of this excellence of qualities, headed by steadfastness and moral shame—
One who possesses birth is the most worthy of offerings. For he sustains virtues through steadfastness (*dhiti*) and restrains faults through moral shame (*hiri*).

Furthermore, in this context, "the sage" (*muni*) is one endowed with the quality of sagacity (*mona*); "possessing steadfastness" means being energetic; "a thoroughbred" means one who knows what is cause and what is not;
and "restraining through shame" means standing firm after having restrained evil deeds by means of moral shame.
"Tamed by truth" means tamed by the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*). "Endowed with self-mastery" means endowed with the mastery of the sense faculties (*indriya-damana*).
"One who has reached the end of the Vedas" means one who has reached the end of the four Vedas of the paths, or one who has gone to the end of the defilements by means of the four Vedas of the paths.

"One who has lived the holy life" means one who has dwelt in the dwelling of the holy life of the paths. "To whom the sacrifice has been brought" means one to whom the sacrifice has been offered and for whom the sacrifice has been prepared. "One should invite him" means...
He by whom the sacrifice has been prepared should invite that ultimate Brahmin.
However, this invitation—“We invite Indra, we invite Soma, we invite Varuṇa, we invite Īsāna, we invite Yāma”—is useless.
As for the phrase “at the proper time,” while inviting him, one should say, “Venerable sir, it is time; the meal is ready,” specifically at the time of midday itself.

One should invite him. "He offers to one worthy of offerings" means that whoever, having thus addressed one whose taints are exhausted at the proper time, establishes there an offering of the four requisites, he is said to offer to one worthy of offerings;
it does not mean one who is merely casting [offerings] into an insentient fire.
Thus, hearing the Blessed One’s words, the brahmin gained confidence, and now, manifesting his own faith, he said: "Certainly..."
He spoke the verse beginning with *suyiṭṭhaṃ*. Its meaning is as follows: "Surely this which I have now offered will be well-offered and well-poured;
however, what was previously burned in the fire was useless. "Another person" refers to the blind, foolish worldling who says, "I am a brahmin, I am a brahmin.
*Habyasesaṃ* means the remains of the offering. "May your honor eat," and so forth.
This should be understood in the same manner as stated in the previous sutta.
"Na khvāhaṃ" means "Indeed, I do not. But why did he speak thus?
It is said that as soon as that food was brought, the deities from the four great continents and two thousand minor islands, perceiving that "the Teacher will eat," [arrived].

Just as those who take flowers, fruits, and so forth, along with ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses, and having pressed the honeycomb, extract the honey, they likewise took only the nutritive essence produced through divine power and placed it [into the vessel].
Because of that, it became subtle; and since the objects of human beings are coarse, it was due to the coarseness of their own material objects.
It does not undergo proper digestion. However, when sesame seeds are added to cow’s milk, it becomes coarse and mixed;
and since the food of the gods consists of subtle matter, [the milk] does not undergo proper digestion due to its subtle nature.

It is not digested even in the womb of an arahant who is a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*). As for an arahant who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), [his food is digested]...

However, [the Blessed One] would transform it by the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). But for the Blessed One, he would transform it by the natural heat of his own karma-born radiance (*kammaja-teja*).
"Appaharite" means in what is not cultivated (*aharite*). For if he were to throw it onto cultivated grass, the grass would become rotten due to the oily gruel.
And Buddhas do not transgress the training rule regarding the destruction of living plants (*bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada*); therefore, he spoke thus.
However, it is permissible to throw them in a place where there are large grasses reaching up to the neck.
Regarding "in water without living beings": for if one throws [the food] into a small amount of water containing living beings, those creatures die; therefore he spoke thus.
But in the case of deep, vast water which does not become turbid even when a hundred or a thousand bowls have been thrown in—such as that...
It was permissible in the water. "He caused it to sink" means he caused it to submerge right along with the golden bowl.
"It makes the sound *cicciṭāyati*, *ciṭiciṭāyati*" means it produces such a sound. Now, is this the power of the milk-rice, or is it that of the Tathāgata? It is that of the Tathāgata.
For after this brahmin had caused that milk-rice to sink, he ascended the path and, without even coming into the presence of the Teacher, [departed].
The Blessed One thought, "Having seen such a marvel, she will come into my presence;
then, by breaking her grip on wrong view through a teaching on the Dhamma, I shall lead her into the Dispensation and give her the drink of the Deathless.
By the power of his resolve, he acted accordingly.
"He kindles wood" means while burning wood. "For this is external" means that this so-called burning of wood is external to the Noble Dhamma.
If purity were to come about by this, then those who burn forest fires and the like, who burn much wood, would be purified first.
"Wholesome" means wholesome among the aggregates and so forth. "I kindle the light within myself" means...
"In my own heart," means "I kindle the flame of knowledge within my own continuum.

"Ever-burning" means that the fire is constantly blazing through the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) which is bound to adverting (āvajjana). "Ever-collected in mind" means one whose consciousness is always correctly established.
"I lead the holy life" (brahmacariyaṃ carāmi): having taken up the holy life practiced at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he speaks thus.

For conceit, brahmin, is like a load of a *khāri* measure. Just as a load of a *khāri* being carried on the shoulder touches the earth wherever it is stepped upon even while standing above, even so conceit, raised up by relying on grounds for conceit such as birth,
clan, and family, causes one to sink into the four states of misery while generating envy here and there.
Therefore he said: "Pride, O Brahmin, is indeed a burden of a khāri for you. Anger is smoke:
in the sense of being an impurity to the fire of your knowledge, anger is smoke. For by that, the fire of your knowledge, being defiled, does not shine. Falsehood is ashes:
in the sense of being devoid of nutritional essence (ojā), false speech is called ashes. For just as a fire covered by ashes does not blaze, so too [your fire] because of false speech...
He shows that knowledge is concealed. "The tongue is the sacrificial ladle" means:

just as you have a sacrificial ladle made of one of gold, silver, bronze, wood, or clay for the purpose of performing a sacrifice, so too do I have an abundant tongue as a sacrificial ladle for the purpose of performing the sacrifice of the Dhamma—thus he says.
"The heart is the place of the fire" means: just as you have a place for the fire on the riverbank, so too do I...
The heart of sentient beings is the place of light by virtue of being the site for performing the sacrifice of the Dhamma. "Self" refers to the mind.

"The Dhamma is the lake": just as you, having tended the fire, bathe in the Sundarikā River with your body defiled by smoke, embers, and soot, I have no need for an external lake such as the Sundarikā.
But the Dhamma of the Eightfold Path is my lake; there I bathe even a hundred beings, a thousand beings, or eighty-four thousand beings all at once.
"The bathing place of virtue" shows that the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) is the bathing place for that Dhamma-lake of mine.
"Untroubled" means that, unlike your river Sundarikā, which becomes turbid when four or five people bathe together...

The sand at the bottom and top becomes stirred up; but my lake is not like that—even when hundreds of thousands of living beings descend into it to bathe, it remains undisturbed and perfectly clear. "Praised by the good" means commended by the wise among the wise.
Or, in the ultimate sense, he is called "the good" (sabbhī) because he is praised by the wise. "Of the good" (sataṃ) [refers to those] who are virtuous.
"Praised. They "cross over" means they go to the further shore, which is Nibbāna.
Now, having extracted the factors of one who has grasped the Noble Path, [the Buddha] spoke the passage beginning with "Truth is the Dhamma," etc.
Therein, "truth" (*sacca*) refers to truth in speech. By the word "Dhamma," he indicates right view, intention, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. "Restraint" (*saṃyama*)...
By this, right action and right livelihood are included. Or, by the word "truth" (*sacca*), the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is included;

in terms of its meaning, this is right view. For it has been said: "Right view is both the path and the cause. When right view is included, right intention is also included because it belongs to that same category.
By the word "dhamma," right effort, mindfulness, and concentration are included. By the word "restraint" (*saṃyama*),...

Speech, action, and livelihood. In this way, too, the Eightfold Path is shown. Alternatively, "Truth" (sacca) refers to the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca), which in its essential meaning is Nibbāna.
By the term "Dhamma," the five factors—right view, intention, effort, mindfulness, and concentration—are included.
"Restraint" (saṃyama) comprises the three: speech, action, and livelihood. In this way, too, the Eightfold Path is shown.
"Brahmacariya" means this very thing called the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "Abiding in the middle" means abiding in the middle, having avoided both eternalism and annihilationism.
"Attainment of Brahmā" means the supreme attainment. Regarding the phrase "you should pay homage to those who have become straight," here the letter *ta* is used for metrical conjunction;
the meaning is: "You should pay homage to those who have become straight, those whose taints are exhausted. "I call that person one who has the Dhamma as his essence."
"Whoever practices in this way, I declare that person to be 'one who is guided by the Dhamma, concealed by the Dhamma,' and one who stands having driven out unwholesome states with wholesome states.
Thus [ends] the ninth. 10. Commentary on the *Bahudhītarasutta* (The Discourse to Bahudhītara)
196. At dawn, while surveying the world in a certain forest grove during the tenth watch, he perceived the underlying potential for that brahmin’s attainment of arahantship.
Thinking, "I shall go and provide him with support," he went there and dwelt in that forest grove.
"They have been lost" means that after plowing, they had abandoned their work and were wandering toward the wilderness to eat [the crops] belonging to the brahmins.
Having gone, they become fugitives. "In the cross-legged posture" (pallaṅka) means a seat where the thighs are bound together on all sides. "Having folded" (ābhujitvā) means having bound them.
"Having set the body erect" (ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya) means having placed the upper part of the body straight, aligning the eighteen vertebrae tip-to-tip.
"Having established mindfulness facing the object" (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā) means having established mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
The meaning is: "having placed it near the mouth. For this very reason, it is said in the Vibhaṅga:

"This mindfulness is established, well-established, either on the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth; therefore it is said: 'having established mindfulness directed toward the mouth' (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā).
Alternatively: "'Parī' has the sense of embracing (pariggaha). 'Mukha' has the sense of outlet (niyyāna). 'Sati' has the sense of establishing (upaṭṭhāna). Therefore it is said..."
"Having established mindfulness directed toward the face"—the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*.
In brief, this means: "having established mindfulness that has discerned the way out.
And as he sat down in this manner, he sat having emitted the six-colored, solid rays of a Buddha. He approached while wandering about, overcome by dejection.
Thinking, “Ah, this ascetic is sitting quite comfortably,” he approached him.
“Not seen for six days” means they have not been seen since the beginning of the sixth day. “Wicked” means inferior sesame seeds.
It is said that when those sesame seeds were sown in a sesame field, it rained on that very same day, causing the sesame seeds to sink into the soil.
They were unable to gather either flowers or fruit. Even those that had grown were attacked by insects which fell upon them and ate the leaves;
only single leaves or pairs of leaves remained on the stumps.
When the brahmin went to inspect the field and saw this, he became dejected, thinking, "My sesame seeds have been taken away by growth, and now even they are lost. Thus he was filled with grief.
Having taken hold of this, he spoke this verse:
"With great effort" (*ussoḷhikāya*) means that by exerting themselves, they move about with their ears, toes, and so forth raised, and thus they leap up.
It is said that as his wealth gradually became exhausted, his storehouses became empty because there was nothing left to be put into them. Of him...
Mice coming from here and there through seven houses entered those empty storehouses and danced as if they were playing a garden game;
having caught them, he spoke thus:
"Covered with *uppāṭaka* creatures" means covered with *uppāṭaka* insects. It is said that for the sake of that brahmin’s bed...
There was no one to tend his bed of grass and leaves from time to time.
Having worked in the forest during the day, he would return in the evening and lie down upon it. Then, insects that bore through the skin would consume his body, making it a single mass of holes;
taking hold of him, [the deity] spoke thus.
They became widows whose husbands had died. For as long as that brahmin possessed wealth in his house, those women, though they were widows, were permitted to live in their husbands' families.
But when he became destitute, they were driven out by their fathers-in-law, mothers-in-law, and others with the words, "Go to your father's house. Thereupon, they returned to his very house.
While the brahmin was at his mealtime, the women living there sent their sons, saying, "Go and eat with your uncle.
When those boys poured [the food] from the bowl into their hands, the brahmin could find no space for his own hand.
Taking that situation into account, he spoke this verse.
"Piṅgalā" means tawny-black. "Tilakāhatā" means one whose limbs are covered with spots of various colors such as black and white.
"Awakens by kicking with the foot" means that he rouses [the sleeper] by striking him with his foot while he has fallen asleep.
It is said that this brahmin, being harassed by the sound of mice and being eaten by leeches, could not obtain sleep all night long and thus sleeps at dawn.
Then, while his eyes were barely closed, [the creditor] kicked him to wake him up, saying: "What are you doing, brahmin?
The interest on the debt you incurred both before and after has reached its peak; seven daughters must be supported.
Now the creditors will come and surround the house; go and work!"
Having taken that [debt], he spoke this verse:

"Creditors" refers to those from whose hands he had received loans. It is said that he indeed took loans from many people—from one person a single kahāpaṇa, from another two, from another ten... and so on, up to a hundred from yet another.
Not seeing the brahmin during the day, they thought, "We shall seize him as soon as he has departed from his house," and so they went at the early dawn and reproached him.
Having seized him, he spoke this verse.
When that brahmin had spoken these seven verses concerning suffering, the Blessed One said: "Whatever, O brahmin..."
She spoke of her suffering, and showing that "all this is not mine," she expanded her teaching of the Dhamma to the brahmin with verses in reply.
Having heard those verses, the brahmin gained faith in the Blessed One, established himself in the refuges, went forth, and attained arahantship.
To demonstrate this, it was said: "When this was said, [the Blessed One replied], 'Bhāradvāja by clan... and so forth.
In that context, *alattha* means he obtained.

Furthermore, after the Blessed One had caused that brahmin to go forth and taken him with him to Jetavana, on the following day he went to the gate of the King of Kosala’s palace with that elder as his attendant monk.
Hearing that "the Teacher has arrived," the king [descended] from the palace...
Having descended and paid homage, he took the bowl from the Tathāgata’s hand, led him up to the upper palace, and had him sit upon a noble seat.
He washed the Teacher’s feet with scented water, anointed them with oil of a hundredfold potency, and had rice-gruel brought.
Taking a silver-handled golden spoon, he offered it to the Teacher. The Teacher covered his bowl. The king—
Falling at the feet of the Tathāgata, he said, "Venerable Sir, if there is any offense on my part, please forgive me.
"There is none, Great King," [the Buddha replied]. "Then why do you not accept the rice-gruel? "There is an obstacle, Great King.
"But, Venerable Sir, is this obstacle something that can only be obtained by those who do not accept the rice-gruel? I am capable of providing the obstacle."
"Take it, venerable sir," he said. The Teacher took it. The elder monk, having been hungry for a long time, drank as much rice-gruel as he desired.
After the king had given him hard and soft foods, at the conclusion of the meal, he paid homage to the Blessed One and said:
"Blessed One, you were born into the Okkāka clan that has come down through tradition; having renounced the glory of a universal monarch (cakkavatti),..."
“Having gone forth, you have attained the highest state in the world; what, venerable sir, is your impediment? “Great King, this elder’s impediment is similar to our own.
The king, having paid homage to the elder, asked: “Venerable sir, what is your impediment? “A debt, Great King,” he replied.
“How much is it, venerable sir? “Count them, Great King. As the king counted, “One, two, a hundred, a thousand,” his fingers were not enough.
Then, having summoned a man, he said: “Go, my good man, and have the drum beaten in the city, saying:
‘Let all those who owe debts to the Brahmin Bahudhītika assemble in the royal courtyard. When the people heard the drum, they gathered.
They assembled. The king had the letters brought from their hands and gave each of them a full amount of wealth;
among that, the gold alone was worth a hundred thousand [pieces]. Again the king asked:
"Is there any other obstacle, venerable sir? "Debt, O Great King, can be cleared by paying it back, but these seven girls—"
“I have great impediments,” he said. The king sent out vehicles and had his daughters brought for him;
having made them his own daughters and sent them to their respective family homes, he asked, “Venerable sir, is there any other impediment? “The brahmin woman, Great King,” he replied.
The king sent out a vehicle and had his brahmin woman brought; having established her in the position of a mother-in-law—

He asked again: “Venerable sir, is there any other impediment? When it was replied, “There is none, Great King,” the king had robes and cloths provided and said, “Venerable sir, please consider whatever belongs to me as yours for the sake of your monkhood.
“Yes, Great King,” he replied. Then the king said to him, “Venerable sir, all the requisites, such as robes, almsfood, and so forth—”
“They shall belong to us. You, having taken the Tathāgata’s counsel, should practice the duty of a recluse.
The Elder, practicing the duty of a recluse with such diligence, before long attained the destruction of the taints. The tenth [story].
The first section.
2. The Chapter on Lay Followers (Upāsakavagga) 1.
The Commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta (197) "In Magadha" refers to the country of that name. "In Dakkhiṇāgiri" refers to Rājagaha.
On the southern side of the mountain where [the Buddha] stood surrounded, there was a country;
in that country, the monastery there had the same name. Regarding "Ekanāḷā, a brahmin village": *Ekanāḷā* is the name of that village.
However, many brahmins resided there, or else it was a brahmin domain; therefore, it is called a "brahmin village."

Now at that time: at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa in the Magadha country, at the Dakkhiṇagiri Mahāvihāra, awaiting the ripening of the faculties of a certain brahmin—at that time.
Of Kasibhāradvāja: that brahmin lived by means of agriculture; he was a Bhāradvāja.
This was his clan. "About five" means five measures; the meaning is that there were exactly five hundred ploughs, neither fewer nor more.
"Yoked" means harnessed; the sense is that they were placed upon the necks of the oxen and fastened to the yokes with thongs.
"At the time of sowing" means at the time of sowing, the moment for casting the seed. In that regard, there are two kinds of sowing: sowing in mud and sowing in soil.
What is intended here is the sowing of soil; moreover, it is the auspicious sowing on the first day.
Regarding this, there was a perfection of requisites: three thousand oxen were stationed there, all of them with horns adorned with gold and hooves made of silver;
they were all decorated with white garlands and five-fingered scents, and were complete in their five limbs.
Endowed with every auspicious mark, some were black, the color of collyrium; some were white, the color of crystal;
some were red, the color of coral; and some were dark-brown, the color of emerald.

Thus, these five hundred farmers—all dressed in garments of dark blue, adorned with perfumes and garlands, with flower-wreaths fastened upon the right shoulders of their upper arms, and their limbs radiant with yellow orpiment, realgar, and collyrium—[proceeded].
Ten ploughs proceeded as single groups. The heads, yokes, and goads of the ploughs were inlaid with gold.
On the first plough, eight oxen were yoked; on the remaining ones, four each.
The rest were brought for the purpose of relieving those that grew weary. In each group, one person ploughed with a single seed-cart, and one person sowed.
But the brahmin, having had his facial hair trimmed early in the morning, bathed, anointed himself with fragrant perfumes, put on a garment worth five hundred pieces of gold,
draped over one shoulder a cloth worth a thousand pieces of gold, placed twenty finger-rings— two on each finger— on his fingers,
fastened lion-ear earrings on his ears, and bound a Brahma-diadem upon his head, [wore] a golden garland.
Placing it around his neck and surrounded by a host of brahmins, he supervised the work.

Then his brahmin wife, having had milk-rice cooked in many hundreds of vessels and loaded onto large carts, bathed in scented water, adorned with every ornament, and surrounded by a host of brahmin women, went to the worksite.
His house, too, was smeared with green cow-dung and strewn with parched grain.
The field was adorned with full water-jars, plantain trees, and banners and flags, and offerings of perfumes, flowers, and the like were well-prepared;
in various places, flags and banners were raised high. Together with the attendants and laborers, the assembled crowd numbered two thousand five hundred;
all wore new garments, and for everyone, milk-rice alone had been prepared as food.
Then the brahmin had a golden bowl washed, filled it with milk-rice, and prepared it by mixing it with ghee, honey, and molasses;
he then had the ritual offering for the ploughing performed. The brahmin’s wife had five hundred farmers provided with vessels made of gold, silver, bronze, copper, and iron;
taking a golden spoon, she went about serving them the milk-rice. The brahmin—
Furthermore, having had an offering performed, he put on sandals with red straps, took a red-gold staff, and wandered about calling out, "Give rice-porridge here! Give ghee here! Give sugar here!
This, first of all, was the procedure regarding the work.
Furthermore, in whatever monastery the Buddhas dwell, there they have five daily duties,
namely: the duty before the meal, the duty after the meal, the duty during the first watch of the night, the duty during the middle watch of the night,
and the duty during the last watch of the night.

In this regard, this is the duty before the meal: having risen early in the morning, the Blessed One—having performed his preparatory duties such as washing his face for the sake of favoring his attendants and for the sake of bodily comfort—spends the time until the hour for the alms-round seated in a secluded place.
Then, at the hour for the alms-round, he puts on his lower robe, fastens his waistband, dons his upper robe, and takes his bowl.
Sometimes he enters a village or a town for alms alone, and sometimes surrounded by the community of monks;
sometimes in his ordinary manner, and sometimes while many miracles are taking place.
For instance, as the Lord of the World enters for alms, gentle winds go before him and clear the earth, and the clouds release droplets of water.
Dust-raising winds blow along the road, settling it so that they stand above as a canopy; other winds gather flowers and scatter them over the path.
Elevated portions of the ground sink down, and depressed portions rise up.
At the moment of setting foot upon them, the ground becomes level, or lotus flowers with pleasant touch receive his feet. [At the] threshold...
As soon as his right foot was placed inside, rays of six-colored light issued forth from his body;
streaming like golden liquid and appearing as if draped in variegated cloths, they circled hither and thither, transforming the palace, the gabled chambers, and other structures.
Even elephants, horses, birds, and the like, remaining in their respective places, let out sweet sounds.
Likewise, there were musical instruments such as drums and lutes, and ornaments for the bodies of people. By that sign, people knew:

"Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms. Well-dressed and well-robed, they took perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, departed from their houses, entered the street, and paid respectful homage to the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having honored and paid homage [to him], they requested, "Venerable sir, give us ten bhikkhus, twenty for us, a hundred bhikkhus for us.
Then, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and preparing a seat, they respectfully served him with almsfood.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he surveyed their mental continuities and taught the Dhamma in such a way that some—
Some establish themselves in going for refuge; some in the five precepts; some in one of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning;
and some, having gone forth, in the supreme fruit of arahantship. Having thus assisted the great multitude, he rises from his seat and goes to the monastery.
There, in the fragrant pavilion, he sits upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him, [surrounded] by the bhikkhus.
He waits for the conclusion of the monks' meal. Then, when the monks have finished their meal, the attendant informs the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One enters the fragrant chamber. This, first of all, is the duty before the meal.
Then, having thus performed his duties before the meal, the Blessed One sits in the attendance hall of the fragrant chamber and washes his feet.
Standing upon the footstool, he exhorted the community of monks: "Monks, strive with diligence! Rare is the arising of a Buddha in the world;
rare is the attainment of human birth; rare is the perfection of faith;
rare is the going forth into homelessness; rare is the hearing of the true Dhamma. Thereupon, some asked the Blessed One for a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The Blessed One gives them a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suited to their own character.
Then, having all paid homage to the Blessed One, they go each to his own night-quarters or day-quarters:
some to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to one or another of the mountains and so forth, some to the abode of the Four Great Kings... and some to the abode of the Vasavattīs.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the fragrant chamber, if he so desires, lies down for a moment in the lion’s posture on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Then, his body refreshed, he rises and surveys the world during the second watch.
During the third watch, the great multitude in whatever village or town he dwells near, before the meal—
Having given a gift, after the meal, well-robed and well-clad, he takes perfumes, flowers, and other offerings and assembles at the monastery.

Then the Blessed One, having approached with a miracle appropriate for the assembled company, sits upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma Hall and teaches the Dhamma, suited to the time and suited to the occasion. Then, perceiving that it is time, he dismisses the assembly.
The people, having paid homage to the Blessed One, depart. This concludes the post-meal duties.

Having thus completed his post-meal duties, if he wishes to bathe his limbs, he rises from the Buddha’s seat, enters the bathing pavilion, and has his limbs warmed by the water prepared by his attendant. The attendant, too—
Having brought the Buddha’s seat and shaken it out, he prepared it in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber.
The Blessed One, having put on his lower robe of fine red color, fastened his waistband, and arranged his upper robe, arrived there and sat down.
He remained alone for a moment in seclusion. Then, monks came from here and there to attend upon the Blessed One.
There, some asked questions, some requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and some entreated for a hearing of the Dhamma.
The Blessed One spent the first watch of the night fulfilling their intentions. This was his duty during the first watch.
At the conclusion of his duties in the first watch, when the monks had paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world system [assembled].
Finding an opportunity, they approach the Blessed One and ask questions, even as little as four syllables, according to their preparation.
The Blessed One spends the middle watch of the night answering the questions of those various deities.
This is his duty during the middle watch.

Furthermore, having divided the final watch of the night into three parts, he spends one part walking back and forth to relieve the bodily fatigue of his body, which has been oppressed by sitting since before the meal.
In the second part, having entered the fragrant chamber, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, mindful and clearly comprehending. In the third part, he rises.

Having sat down, he surveys the world with his Buddha-eye for the purpose of seeing those individuals who have performed meritorious deeds through giving, virtue, and so forth, in the presence of previous Buddhas. This is the duty of the final watch of the night.
Surveying thus at that time as well, he saw that the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja was endowed with the necessary potential (upanissaya) for Arahatship.

“Once I have gone there, a conversation will take place; at the conclusion of that conversation, having heard the teaching on the Dhamma, this brahmin, together with his wife and children, will establish himself in the three refuges.

He will distribute eighty koṭis of wealth throughout my dispensation, and later, having gone forth from the household life, he will attain arahantship. Knowing this, he went there and initiated the conversation.
He taught the Dhamma. To demonstrate this matter, the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One" was spoken.

Therein, "at the time of the morning" (*pubbaṇhasamayaṃ*) is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is "during the morning. "Having dressed" (*nivāsetvā*) means having put on [the lower robe].
This is said by way of changing the robes worn in the monastery. "Taking bowl and robe" (*pattacīvaram ādāya*) refers to the bowl...
"With hands" means having taken the robe with the body, having received it, and having held it.
It is said that when the Blessed One was about to enter for alms, a stone bowl the color of an indranīla gem came between his two hands, like a bee into the center of a pair of blooming lotuses.
Having received that bowl thus come between his hands with both hands, and [the robe]...
"Having put it on so as to be even all around the body"—this is what is meant.
"He approached him by that way" means he approached alone by the very path by which the workmen were to go. But why did the monks not follow him?
For whenever the Blessed One wished to go somewhere alone, until the time for the alms-round arrived, he would close the gate.
He sat within the inner fragrant chamber. By that sign, the monks knew: "Today the Blessed One wishes to go alone for alms;

surely he has seen someone who must be disciplined. Taking their own bowls and robes, they circumambulated the fragrant chamber, paid homage, and went out on their almsround. And at that time, the Blessed One acted in this manner.
"Therefore the monks did not follow after him.
"The meal distribution was in progress" means that while those five hundred farmers were sitting with their gold vessels and other utensils, their meal distribution had been interrupted.
"He stood to one side" means he stood in such a place where the brahmin could see him.
He stood on a high place within range of sight, where it was convenient to hear the conversation.
