Having stood there, he emitted from all sides a radiance from his body that surpassed the brilliance of the moon and sun, and which was tinged with the luster of silver and gold;
because the Brāhmaṇa was enveloped by this light, the walls, trees, clods of earth, and other objects in his workshop appeared as if they were made of gold.
Then, while eating and plowing, the people set aside all their tasks and beheld his body,
adorned with the eighty minor marks and embellished by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; it was graced by a halo of fathom-wide radiance, like a lotus pond moving about,
or like the vault of heaven illuminated by a mass of rays from a cluster of stars, or as if entwined with streaks of lightning.

And having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One standing to one side, shining with glory like a golden peak, they washed their hands and feet, raised their joined palms in reverence, and stood surrounding him.
Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja saw the Blessed One standing for alms, surrounded by them; having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“I indeed, ascetic, plow and sow,” he said.

But why did he speak thus? Was it because of a lack of faith in the Tathāgata—who is serene on all sides, inspiring confidence, and has attained the supreme self-mastery and tranquility—or was it because, despite having prepared porridge for two thousand five hundred people, he had not received even a single spoonful of alms?

"Out of stinginess?"—in neither sense. However, seeing people who were unsatisfied with the sight of the Blessed One and had abandoned their work, he thought, "He has come to bring about the ruin of my business," and thus he spoke out of displeasure.
Furthermore, having seen the perfection of the Blessed One’s physical marks, he thought: "If this man had not been employed in his business, all the people in Jambudīpa..."
“If he were like a crest-jewel upon his head, what purpose of his would not be accomplished?
Yet, in this very way, by not engaging in work due to laziness, he wanders for alms even on auspicious days such as those for sowing. Thus, dissatisfaction arose in him.
Therefore he said: “I, ascetic, both plough and sow; having ploughed and sown, I eat.”
This was his intention: "Even my own business affairs do not fail; moreover, I am not endowed with such marks as you are.
You too should plow, sow, and eat. What need have you for anything that would not succeed for one endowed with such marks?
Furthermore, he heard: "A prince has indeed been born in the Sakyan royal family."
“Having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattirājja), he went forth into homelessness.

Therefore, now, recognizing him as such and leveling an objection by saying, “Having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, you are weary,” he speaks thus. Furthermore, this brahmin possesses sharp wisdom;
he does not speak out of malice toward the Blessed One, but rather, having seen the Blessed One’s perfection of form and his perfection of merit...

Honoring him, he spoke thus even for the sake of initiating the conversation. Then the Blessed One, demonstrating to the world with its devas his own status as the foremost ploughman and sower, said, "I too, brahmin," and so forth, according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Then the brahmin thought: "This ascetic says, 'I too plough and sow,' yet he does not..."
“I see his large ploughing implements, such as the yoke and the plough; why then would he speak a falsehood?

Thus reflecting, and looking at the Blessed One from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair, he—having mastered the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*)—perceived that he was endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks of a Great Man.
He then concluded, “It is impossible for one such as this to speak a falsehood.”
Having conceived great respect for the Blessed One, he abandoned his talk of being a mere ascetic and addressed the Blessed One by his clan name;
yet, saying "Indeed, we do not see [the power] of Master Gotama," and so forth, he spoke.

But because it is the majesty of Buddhas to speak by way of the commonality of previous qualities (*pubbadhammasabhāgatā*), the Blessed One, illuminating that majesty of a Buddha, said: "Faith is the seed," and so forth.

But what here is the similarity of the preceding state (*pubbadhammasabhāgatā*)? Is it not the case that when the Blessed One was asked by the brahmin about the equipment for plowing and so forth—the implements of agriculture—he spoke of "faith as the seed" (*saddhā bījaṃ*) by way of its similarity to the seed that had not been asked about? And if this were so, would the discourse not be incoherent?
For there is no such thing as an incoherent discourse of the Buddhas; nor [is there a lack of coherence] regarding the preceding state...
They speak out of a lack of common ground. However, the connection here should be understood as follows:
the Blessed One was questioned by the brahmin regarding plowing in terms of the equipment for plowing, such as the yoke and the plow.

Out of compassion for him, and not omitting the fact that "this was not asked," [the Blessed One] began from the very root in order to explain plowing together with its root, its purpose, its equipment, and its fruit.
Showing this, he said: “Faith is the seed,” and so forth. In this context, the seed is the root of plowing, because when it exists, the work must be done, and when it is absent, it need not be done;
and because the work is to be performed in proportion to the seed. For when the seed exists, they plow, but not when it is absent.
And skillful farmers plow the field according to the measure of the seed, not less, thinking, “Lest our crop should fail.”

It is not excessive [to say this], lest "our effort be in vain. And because the seed itself is the root, the Blessed One, demonstrating the equipment for plowing starting from the root, spoke thus—"Faith is the seed"—showing the preliminary factor of his own plowing by way of its commonality with the seed, which is the preliminary factor of that brahmin’s plowing.
In this way, the commonality of the preliminary factors here should also be understood.
If it is asked: "Why was that which was not asked stated afterwards, after having already stated what was asked?
It is because of its beneficial nature and its capacity to connect with the Dhamma. For this brahmin is wise, yet because he was born into a family of wrong views, he is devoid of faith;
and being wise but devoid of faith, by means of the faith of others, he does not proceed in a manner contrary to his own [spiritual] domain.

He does not attain distinction; even though his faith is accompanied by the turbidity of defilements, it is weak and cannot quickly achieve its purpose when confronted by powerful wisdom, like an ox yoked to the same pole as an elephant.
Therefore, one who establishes that brahmin in faith should later say to him: "Your faith is an aid."
This meaning was previously stated by way of skill in teaching. Furthermore, rain that is beneficial to a seed is effective only when mentioned immediately after [the seed];
thus, because it is effective in relation to the phenomenon (*dhamma*), this meaning may be stated later as well.
It should be understood that other such things, like the plow-pole and the yoke, were also mentioned previously.
In this context, faith has the characteristic of serene confidence, or it has the characteristic of conviction. "Seeds" refers to the five kinds of seeds:
root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, crown-seed, and seed-seed as the fifth.
All of these are reckoned simply as "seeds" in the sense of that which grows.
In this context, just as the seed, which is the root of a brahmin’s farming, performs two functions—
establishing itself below with its root and causing a sprout to emerge above— so too does faith, which is the root of the Blessed One’s farming,
establish itself below by means of the root of virtue and cause the sprouts of serenity and insight to emerge above. And just as that [seed], by means of its root...
Just as that [plant] grows by taking up the essence of the earth and the essence of water through its stalk for the purpose of gathering the ripening of the grain,

so too does this [tree of Dhamma] grow by taking up the essence of serenity and insight through the root of virtue and the stalk of the Noble Path for the purpose of gathering the ripening of the grain of the Noble Fruit. And just as it,
having been established on good ground, attains growth through the emergence of roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and joints...
Having reached growth, increase, and abundance, and having produced milk, it brings forth a rice-ear filled with many grains of rice; even so, this [faith],
having become established in the continuum of consciousness, reaches growth, increase, and abundance through the six purifications,

produces the milk of purification of knowledge and vision, and brings forth the fruit of arahantship, which is filled with the various analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and direct higher knowledges (abhiññā).
It brings about [the result]. Therefore it is said: "Faith is the seed.
But why, when fifty or more wholesome states arise together, is faith alone called the "seed"? Because it performs the function of a seed.
For just as among those [states], consciousness alone performs the function of cognizing, [so too does faith perform the function of a seed].
Thus, faith performs the function of a seed. And it is the root of all wholesome states. As it is said: "One who has conceived faith approaches;
approaching, he pays homage... pe ...and with wisdom he penetrates and sees it.

It is called *tapa* because it burns away unwholesome states and the body. [It is the basis] for the restraint of the sense faculties, energy, the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and those who perform difficult deeds.
This is a synonym; however, in this context, it is the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) that is intended.
"Rainfall" is of many kinds, such as rain showers, wind-showers, and so forth; here, rain shower is intended.
For just as a seed seized by a rain shower for a brahmin, along with the crop rooted in that seed, sprouts, does not wither, and reaches fruition, even so for the Blessed One—
Faith, when supported by restraint of the sense faculties, and the qualities such as virtue rooted in faith, grow;
they do not wither but reach fulfillment. Therefore he said: "Austerity is the rain.
Regarding the phrase "wisdom is mine," the word "mine" (me) mentioned here should also be applied to the preceding terms: "Faith is my seed; austerity is mine..."
“‘Rainfall’—what does this illustrate? Just as, brahmin, when you have sown a field, it is well if there is rainfall;

but if there is not, water must still be supplied—even so, when I have joined the plough-pole of wisdom to the two oxen of moral shame, bound them together with the yoke-rope of the mind, yoked the bullocks of energy, and prodded them with the goad of mindfulness, my own...”
When the seed of faith has been sown in the field of the mental continuum, there is no such thing as a lack of rain;
for me, however, this constant austerity of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is the rain.
"Wisdom" (*paññā*) is of many kinds, distinguished by the realms of sense-desire and so forth; here, however, it is intended as the wisdom of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
"Yuganaṅgala" means both the yoke and the plough; thus it is "yuganaṅgala.
Just as a brahmin has a yoke and a plough, so too does the Blessed One have two kinds of insight and wisdom.
In this context, just as the yoke serves as a support for the pole, is bound to the pole at the front, serves as a support for the ropes, and causes the oxen to move together as one—
It sustains [them]; thus, wisdom is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for those qualities that have moral shame (*hiri*) as their foremost. As it is said:
"All wholesome states have wisdom as their superior," and "They say that wisdom is the best among wholesome things, like the king of stars among the constellations.
In the sense of being the precursor to wholesome states, it also stands at the forefront. As it is said: "Virtue and glory..."
"The Dhamma of the virtuous follows after the wise. However, because it does not arise apart from moral shame (*hiri*), it is "yoked to the shaft.

Because it serves as the supporting condition for the yoke-rope of concentration—which is reckoned as the mind—it is the support for the ropes. Because it prevents both excessive exertion and excessive laxity, it maintains the unified movement of the oxen of energy;
and just as a plough is joined to the ploughshare at the time of tilling, [so too is this].

It splits the solid mass of earth and tears up the root-continuities; likewise, wisdom joined with mindfulness at the time of insight splits the density of the continuity, collection, function, and object of phenomena, and tears up all the root-continuities of the defilements.
And that is indeed supramundane; however, the other may also be mundane. Therefore he said: "Wisdom is my yoke and plough."
*Hirī* is so called because one feels shame regarding evil states. By the inclusion of that term, *ottappa* (fear of wrongdoing), which is inseparable from it, is also included.

An *īsā* is a wooden pole used to support a yoke and plough. For just as a brahmin’s *īsā* supports the yoke and plough, so too does the Blessed One’s *hirī* support the yoke and plough known as mundane and supramundane wisdom (*paññā*).
Because in the absence of moral shame (*hiri*), wisdom (*paññā*) is absent.

And just as a yoke and ploughshare connected to a pole perform their function—remaining steady and not slackening—so too, wisdom connected to moral shame performs its function, being steady, not slackening, and uninterrupted by moral shamelessness (*ahirika*).

Therefore he said: "Moral shame is the pole. It is called *mano* because it knows (*munāti*); this is a name for consciousness (*citta*). But here, by the term "mind" (*manas*), that which is associated with it [is meant].
"Concentration" is intended here. "Yoke-rope" means a rope-fastening. That is threefold: the fastening of the yoke together with the pole;
the fastening of the oxen together with the yoke; and the single fastening of the oxen together with the charioteer.
In this regard, just as the brahmin’s yoke-rope, having bound the pole, the yoke, and the oxen into one, directs them toward their respective tasks, so too...

The Blessed One’s concentration binds all those qualities of moral shame (*hiri*), wisdom (*paññā*), and energy (*vīriya*) together upon a single object through its nature of non-distraction, and establishes them in their respective functions. Therefore, it is said: “Mind is the yoke.

It is called *sati* because it remembers things done long ago and so forth. It is called *phāla* because it cleaves [the field]. It is called *pājana* because they drive [the plough] by means of it. That [is what is meant] here.
“Pācana” (the harrow) is what is said; this is a name for a goad. A plough and a harrow together are “phālapācana.
Just as a brahmin’s plough and harrow [are used], so too is the mindfulness associated with insight and associated with the path for the Blessed One.
In that regard, just as the harrow protects the plough and goes before it, so too does mindfulness [protect] wholesome and unwholesome states.
Investigating the courses of phenomena or establishing them as objects, wisdom guards the ploughshare of insight.
For this reason, it is called "guarding," as in such passages as "he dwells with a mind guarded by mindfulness.

Furthermore, it stands at the forefront by way of non-forgetfulness; for wisdom understands phenomena that have been cultivated through mindfulness, not those that have been forgotten. And just as a winnowing fan...
Just as a goad shows oxen the fear of being pierced so that they do not sink down, and restrains them from going onto a wrong path;

even so, mindfulness shows the oxen of energy the fear of the states of misery (apāya) so that they do not sink into indolence, and by restraining their wandering in the improper range known as the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa), it enjoins them to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and thus restrains them from going onto a wrong path. Therefore he said: "Mindfulness is my ploughshare."
"Guarded in body" means protected by the threefold good conduct of the body. "Guarded in speech" means protected by the fourfold good conduct of speech.
Up to this point, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha has been explained. Regarding the phrase "restrained in food within the belly":
since all requisites are included here by way of food, the meaning is that one is restrained, self-controlled, and free from defilement with respect to all four kinds of requisites.
By this, the virtue of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhisīla*) is stated. "Restrained in the belly" means restrained and self-controlled in the belly, which is to say, moderate in eating;
by this, the virtue of using the requisites with moderation (*paccayapaṭisevanasīla*) is stated through the medium of moderation in food.
What does this illustrate? Just as you, O Brahmin, having sown seed, [erect] a thorny fence for the sake of protecting the crop...
Just as when one constructs a tree-lined fence or a wall enclosure, the herds of cattle, buffalo, and deer, finding no way inside, do not ravage the crops;

even so, having sown the seed of faith, I construct this threefold enclosure consisting of the restraint of body, speech, and livelihood, for the sake of protecting the various kinds of wholesome crops.
By means of this, the herds of cattle, buffalo, and deer of unwholesome states such as lust and the rest—
"Not plundering the various kinds of wholesome grain because they do not obtain entry.
Regarding the phrase "I make truth the sickle" (*saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ*): here, truth (*sacca*) is non-deception in two ways. "Sickle" (*niddāna*) means cutting, reaping, or uprooting.
This accusative case (*upayogavacana*) should be understood as having the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇatthe*). This is the meaning here: [truth is the instrument by which one cuts].

“I perform the weeding by means of truth. What is meant? Just as you, having prepared an external field, perform the weeding of the weeds that damage the crops—either by hand or with a sickle—so too, I, having prepared the internal field, perform the weeding of the weeds of deception that damage the crop of wholesome states by means of truth.
This is knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*).
Or rather, "truth" (sacca) should be understood here as such. By this, he shows: "I shall perform the weeding (*niddāna*) of the three [defilements], beginning with the perception of self.
Alternatively, "weeding" (*niddāna*) means that which cuts, mows, or uproots.
Just as you perform the weeding of a slave or a laborer—meaning you employ one who cuts, mows, or uproots the grasses by saying, "Mow the grasses"—[so too should one act toward the defilements].
Thus he shows: "I make this true. Alternatively, *sacca* means the truth of right view (*diṭṭhisacca*).
"I make that my eradication; I make it to be cut, to be reaped, and to be uprooted. Thus, in these two alternatives, the meaning is appropriate through the application of the method (*upayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "gentleness is my liberation": here, that which was described as "virtue" (*sīla*)—namely, non-transgression of body and non-transgression of speech—is not what is intended by the term "gentleness" (*soracca*).
For that has already been stated by the passage beginning with "one who guards the body. What is intended, however, is the fruit of arahantship (*arahatta-phala*).
For that is called "gentleness" because of its delighting in the beautiful state of Nibbāna. As for "liberation" (*pamocana*): [it refers to being liberated from the defilements].

The resolution concerning yoga. This is what is meant: Just as your release would not be a true release because it must be joined again either this evening, on the second day, or in a future year, so it is not for me. For there is no such thing as an intermediate release for me.
Indeed, from the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara onwards, I have been [yoked] to the plow of wisdom...
Having yoked the oxen of energy, I did not release them even while plowing the great furrow for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons,
until I fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment. And when that entire period had been exhausted,
as I sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree upon the invincible throne, the fruit of Arhatship— surrounded by all virtues— was attained.
When that arose, I released it by completely laying down all exertion, thinking, "It shall not be yoked again now.
It was with reference to this meaning that he said, "Gentleness is my release.
Regarding the phrase "Vigour is my yoke and burden," here "vigour" refers to the undertaking of physical and mental energy. "Yoke and burden" means—
“Dhurāyaṃ dhorayhaṃ” means they bear the burden.

For just as a plough drawn by a bull’s burden breaks through the density of the earth and tears up the root-creepers, so too the plough of wisdom drawn by the Blessed One’s energy breaks through the aforementioned density and tears up the creepers of the defilements. Therefore he said:
“Viriya is my yoke and draught-ox. Alternatively, it is called *dhura* because it carries the initial burden, and *dhorayha* because it carries the fundamental burden;
thus, *dhuradhorayha* means both the yoke and the draught-ox.
Just as for a brahmin, when each plough possesses its respective yoke and draught-ox pulling it, there arises both the destruction of the grass and roots and the excellence of the crop.

He accomplishes; thus, by carrying the yoke of the Blessed One’s energy—which is distinguished as the four right strivings—he accomplishes both the destruction of whatever unwholesome states have arisen and the attainment of wholesome states. Therefore he said: "Energy is my yoke-bearing beast.

Regarding the phrase "the bearer of security from bondage" (*yogakkhemādhivāhana*): here, because it is secure from the bonds (*yoga*), Nibbāna is called "security from bondage" (*yogakkhema*); with reference to that—
It is called *adhivāhana* because it is drawn along, or because it is drawn forward. "The drawing toward security from bondage" (*yogakkhemādhivāhana*) means the drawing toward security from bondage.
This is what is meant: "Just as your draft-ox is drawn toward one of the directions, such as the east, so too is my draft-ox drawn toward Nibbāna. While being drawn in this manner...

It goes on without turning back. Just as your oxen pulling the plough return to the edge of the field after reaching it, this [stream of consciousness] does not turn back but simply continues from the time of Dīpaṅkara onwards.
Or rather, because the defilements abandoned by each respective path need not be abandoned again—just as, for example, what has been cut by your plough [need not be cut again].
Furthermore, at another time, the grasses must be cut;

likewise, by means of the first path, one goes on abandoning the defilements associated with views, by the second, the gross ones, by the third, those remaining as subtle residues, and by the fourth, all defilements—going without turning back.
Alternatively, "goes without turning back" means being devoid of returning.
The meaning is: "having sacrificed, it goes. "That" refers to that draft-ox. Thus the meaning here should be understood.

And as for your draft-ox going in this manner, it does not go to that place where, having gone, the farmer—being free from sorrow, stainless, and without grief—does not grieve. But rather, it goes to that place where, having gone, he does not grieve.

"Where, by means of the cultivation of mindfulness, one who has gone forth—being urged on by this draft-ox of energy—becomes like me, a farmer, free from sorrow and free from dust, and does not grieve;
that unconditioned state called Nibbāna, which is the uprooting of all the arrows of sorrow, he goes to.
Now, concluding with the summary, he spoke the verse beginning, "In this way is this farming. Its brief meaning is as follows: for whom...
Brahmin, this ploughing has faith as its seed, is assisted by the rain of austerity, and employs wisdom as the yoke and pole,
with conscience as the shaft bound together by the rope of the mind. Having struck the ploughshare of mindfulness with the plough of wisdom,
having taken up the goad of mindfulness, and having guarded it by the protection of body, speech, and food, one makes truth the furrow and gentle speech the unyoking, with energy as the draft-oxen.
By plowing with the plow that is directed toward ultimate security (*yogakkhema*) and does not turn back, one brings to completion the fourfold fruit of recluseship;
that plowing has the deathless as its fruit. This very plowing has the deathless as its fruit. "The deathless" is said to be *nibbāna*;
the meaning is that it has *nibbāna* as its benefit. Furthermore, this plowing does not have the deathless as its fruit for me alone.
"No one is a brahmin by birth; rather, whoever—whether a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, a sudra, a householder, or a renunciant—plows this plowing, having plowed it, is liberated from all suffering.
Thus the Blessed One concluded his teaching for the brahmin, bringing it to its conclusion with the attainment of arahantship as the ultimate goal, which is Nibbāna.
Then the brahmin, having heard this teaching of profound meaning, realized: "While I eat the fruits of my plowing, I become hungry again on that very same day;
but for him, the fruit of his plowing is the fruit of the Deathless, and by eating its fruit, one is liberated from all suffering.
Understanding this, he became filled with faith and, manifesting his confidence, said, "May the venerable Gotama eat," and so forth. All of that [is related] from there.
And furthermore, it is exactly as stated. First.
2. Commentary on the Udaya Sutta. 198.
In the second [sutta], "he filled with rice" means having filled [the bowl] with rice prepared for his own sake along with curry and condiments.
He gave it. It is said that the Blessed One, while surveying the world at the time of dawn, saw that brahmin;
having performed his bodily care early in the morning, he entered the fragrant chamber, closed the door, and sat down.
Seeing the food being brought for him, he alone hung his bowl upon the tip of his shoulder, emerged from the fragrant chamber, and [stood] with the bowl at the city gate.
Having led him out and entered the city, he proceeded in order and stood at the gate-porch of the brahmin’s house.
Seeing the Blessed One, the brahmin gave him the food he had prepared for himself; it was with reference to this that it was said.
"On the second day as well" means on the second day too. "On the third day as well" means on the third day too. It is said that these were three days.
As the Blessed One was going continuously to the door of the brahmin’s house, there was no one else at all who could arise and take the bowl from between them;
the great multitude stood watching. “He said this”:
although the brahmin had filled and given the bowl for three days, he did not give it out of faith, thinking, “At the door of my house...”
Fearing reproach, thinking, "He has come and stood there as one gone forth, yet they give him not even so much as alms while they eat," he gave [the food].
Having given it for two days, he returned without saying anything. The Blessed One also departed without saying anything.
But on the third day, being unable to endure it any longer, he spoke these words: "This man is a glutton," and so forth.
The Blessed One also repeated these words up to the third time for the sake of making him speak. In that context, *pakaṭṭhako* means one who is greedy for flavors.

Having heard the brahmin’s words, “Again and again they sow the seed,” the Teacher said, “Brahmin, you have withdrawn after giving alms-food for three days; in this world, there are indeed sixteen things that must be done again and again.”
Having said, "The phenomena (dhammā)," he began this teaching in order to demonstrate those phenomena.
In that context, "they sow again and again" means that they do not stop thinking, "It is enough for now," after one crop cycle, but rather they continue to sow in subsequent crop cycles as well.
"It rains again and again" means that it does not stop after raining on a single day, but continues to rain on successive days as well.
It rains again and again throughout the years, and thus the countryside becomes prosperous. By this method, the principle should be understood everywhere.
Regarding the word "supplicants" (*yācaka*), the Teacher, through his skill in teaching, includes even himself in this term to demonstrate it.
"Milkers" (*khīranika*) refers to those who produce milk, the cowherds. For they do not merely seek the udder once; seeking it again and again, they [milk] the cow.
The meaning is "they suck. "He is exhausted and quivers" means that this being, by means of that posture, is both exhausted and quivering.
"Womb" refers to the belly of animals such as dogs, jackals, and so forth.
"Cemetery" means a charnel ground; the meaning is that they repeatedly carry dead beings there again and again. And "having found the path for the sake of no further becoming..."
The "path to non-renewal of existence" (apuna-bbhavāya maggo) is Nibbāna; the meaning is, "having attained that.
"Thus spoken" means thus spoken by the Blessed One while standing in the middle of the street, teaching the sixteen repetitive teachings (punappuna-dhamma).
"He said this" refers to what was said at the conclusion of the teaching by one who had gained faith, together with his wife, children, friends, and kinsmen, toward the Blessed One.
Having prostrated at his feet, he spoke these words beginning with, "Excellent, O Lord! This is the second [sutta]. 3.
Commentary on the Devahita Sutta, Verse 199:
Regarding the third verse, "by winds": this refers to abdominal winds. It is said that while the Blessed One was performing austerities for six years, [winds arose].
When he was consuming food such as boiled lentil soup, his abdominal wind was provoked by both poor food and the hardship of his bed.
Later, even while eating choice food after attaining enlightenment, that affliction would manifest from time to time;
it was with reference to this that it was said. "He was an attendant" refers to the period during the First Enlightenment when there was no fixed attendant.
He was an attendant. Indeed, at that time, there was no one among the eighty great elders of the Teacher who had not previously been an attendant.
Those mentioned in the Canon as attendants were Nāgasamāla, Upavāna, Sunakkhatta, Cunda the novice, Sāgata, Bodhi, and Meghiya.
However, at this particular time, the elder Upavāna would rise early in the morning and sweep the courtyard.
He performed all services for the Blessed One: offering tooth-sticks, providing bathing water, taking up his bowl and robes, and following him.

Regarding the phrase "he approached": it is said that during the first period of enlightenment, for twenty years, the forest was smokeless, and even the heating of water was not permitted by the Blessed One for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. And that brahmin [prepared] a cooking hearth...
Having had large tubs bound together, he placed them on a hearth, caused hot water to be prepared, and made his living by selling that [water] along with bathing powders and other such items.
Those desiring to bathe would go there, pay the fee, bathe, anoint themselves with perfumes, put on garlands, and depart. Therefore, the Elder approached that place.
"Desiring what? means longing for what. "Seeking what? means searching for what.

"Honored, he should honor those worthy of honor"—this the Elder began to say as praise for the One Possessing the Ten Powers. It is indeed the custom that one who has gone for the sake of medicine for the sick should speak in praise of the sick person.
For having heard such praise, people will respectfully provide the necessary medicine.

They think thus. Having obtained suitable medicine, the sick person recovers quickly. Furthermore, when speaking, it is not permissible to speak concerning the meditative absorptions (jhāna), liberations (vimokkha), attainments (samāpatti), paths (magga), or fruits (phala).

However, it is permissible to speak only of the practice leading to arrival, such as: "He is virtuous, modest, conscientious, learned, a bearer of the tradition, and a protector of the lineage. "Worthy of honor" refers to the eighty great elders (mahātheras).
"Worthy of worship" (pūjaneyya) means they are to be worshipped by the world together with its devas. "Worthy of honor" (sakkareyya) means they are to be honored.

"Worthy of veneration" (apaceyya) means veneration is to be performed for them. The Elder spoke thus, proclaiming this quality of the Blessed One, who was worshipped, honored, and venerated by them. "To be taken away" (hātave) means to carry away.
A "large lump of molasses" (*puṭaṃ mahantaṃ guḷapiṇḍaṃ*) refers to a large ball of raw sugar. It is said that he asked, "What is causing discomfort for the ascetic Gotama?
and having heard, "It is wind in the stomach," he replied, "In that case, we know the medicine for this;
mix this molasses with a little water from here and give it to him to drink at the conclusion of his bath. Thus, [he prescribed] warm water.
“There will be a plastering on the outside; by this, the inside will be finished,” thinking thus, he said, “It will be comfortable for the ascetic Gotama.
Having spoken, he put [the medicine] into the elder’s bowl and gave it to him.
“He approached” means that when that illness had subsided, [thinking], “The Tathāgata has been given medicine by Devahita...”
“The gift was given, and by that very act the disease was pacified! Oh, what a gift, what a supreme gift this is for the brahmin!
Thus the story spread in detail. Hearing this, the fame-seeking brahmin thought, “Even with just this much, my reputation has spread far and wide.
Filled with joy and desiring to make it known that he himself had performed the deed, he gained confidence in the One of Ten Powers with just that much and approached him.
*Dajjāti* means one should give. *Kathaṃ hi yajamānassā* means for what reason (*kena kāraṇena*) does it succeed for one who is sacrificing?
*Ijjhatī* means it succeeds; it becomes of great fruit. *Yovedī* means he who has known, he who has understood; he has made it known and manifest.
There is also the reading *yovetī*, meaning he who understands, he who knows. *Passatī* means he sees with the divine eye. *Jātikkhayaṃ* refers to Arahantship.

"Having completed the higher knowledges" (*abhiññāvusita*) means: having known [them], he has "completed" them; that is, he has reached the state of one who has finished his task (*vosānaṃ katakiccataṃ*).
"Thus for the sacrificer" (*evaṃ hi yajamānassa*) refers to one who sacrifices in the manner of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). Third. 4.
Commentary on the Mahāsāla Sutta.
200. In the fourth case, "coarse and with coarse coverings" means worn-out and with worn-out coverings. Why did he approach?

It is said that in his house there were eight hundred thousand pieces of wealth. After he had performed the marriages for his four sons, he gave them four hundred thousand [pieces]. Then, when his Brahmin wife passed away, his sons divided the property among themselves.
“If he brings another brahmin woman, the family will be ruined because of the child conceived in her womb.
Come now, let us look after her. So the four of them looked after her, providing her with excellent food, clothing, and other necessities, and massaging her hands and feet;
and one day, when she had woken from her daytime sleep, they—
Massaging his hands and feet, they spoke of the specific dangers of the household life and requested:
“We shall serve you for as long as we live in this manner; please give us the remainder of our wealth as well.

The brahmin again gave one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] to each of them, and setting aside only what was necessary for his own clothing and wrap, he gave away all his other possessions and enjoyments.
Having divided [the inheritance] into four portions, he distributed them. His eldest son attended upon him for several days.
Then one day, as he was returning after bathing and had stopped at the gatehouse, his daughter-in-law said to him:
"Did you give your eldest son a hundred or a thousand, or even more? Is it not true that [each of] all [the sons] received two?"
“Two hundred thousand [coins] have been given; do you not know the way to the houses of my other sons?
Enraged, he cried, “Begone, outcaste! and went to another’s house. After a few days there as well, having been driven away by this very same means, he went to yet another.
Thus, failing to gain entrance even into a single house, he went forth into the wandering life of the Paṇḍaraṅgas.
While wandering for alms, having become worn out by old age with the passing of time, his body withered by poor food and painful sleep, he returned from his almsround and lay down on a bench.
Having fallen asleep and then waking up, he sat up and looked at himself;
seeing no support among his sons, he thought: "The ascetic Gotama, they say, has a clear complexion and an open face."
"He is pleasant to converse with and skilled in hospitality; it would be possible to approach the ascetic Gotama and receive his hospitality.
Having thus arranged his lower garment and upper cloak and taken his alms-bowl, he approached the Blessed One.

"They are having me driven out of the house after taking leave of my wife"—meaning that they have seized everything belonging to me, and knowing my state of poverty, they have consulted with their own wives and are having me expelled from the house.
"I rejoiced; having become joyful, I was satisfied and delighted. I desired existence; I longed for growth.

"They ward off that very pig"—the meaning is: just as dogs, forming packs and barking repeatedly, ward off a pig by making a great clamor again and again, so too my wives, speaking much to me, drove me away while crying out.

“Unworthy” means base persons. “Vile” means low. “They speak” means they say. “In the form of a son” means by way of being a son. “One who has reached the age of decline” means one who has passed through the three stages of life and stands in the final stage.
“They abandon” means they forsake. “Without enjoyment” means without use. “The fodder is taken away”:
for as long as a horse is young and endowed with speed, they give it various kinds of fodder; when it is old and without enjoyment, they remove that from it in its final stage of life.
He receives no fodder; he wanders through the forest with the cows, eating dry grass.
Just like that horse, I too—having lost all my wealth in old age and being destitute—wander as a senior elder among the houses of others, begging for alms like a child’s father.

*Yaṃ ce* is a particle. This is what is meant: "Those sons of mine who are disobedient, disrespectful, and not subject to my will—for them, it is said, a staff is indeed better, more excellent. Now, in order to show its excellence, the words "even a fierce ox," and so forth, were spoken.
*Pure hoti* means it goes at the front; the meaning is that it is easy to go by placing it in front. *Gādhamedhati* means that when descending into water, it finds a firm footing in deep water.
*Pariyāpuṇitvā* means having learned by heart or having mastered through recitation. *Sannisinnesu* refers to such [brahmins] seated together.
On the day of the assembly, when his sons had entered that hall adorned with all their ornaments and were seated upon costly seats in the midst of the brahmins, he spoke:
"This is my time," he said, entering the middle of the assembly, raising his hand, and declaring, "Sirs, I wish to recite verses for you; listen when they are spoken."
“Bhāsa, brahmin, we shall listen,” he said, and even while standing, he spoke:
“At that time, there was a custom among men that whoever ate what belonged to his parents but did not support his parents should be put to death.
Therefore, those sons of the brahmin fell at their father’s feet and entreated him, saying, “Father, give us our lives! He—
Because he was tender toward his father’s sons, he said, “Sirs, do not let my children perish; they will support me.
Then the people said to his sons, “If, sir, from this day forward you do not properly care for your father, we shall have you executed.
Terrified, they led him home and cared for him. To demonstrate this, the text says: “Then, indeed, that wealthy brahmin... and so forth.
It was said. Therein, "having led him" means they had him seated on a chair and carried him away after lifting him up themselves.
"Having bathed him" means they anointed his body with oil, rubbed it, and bathed him with fragrant powders and the like.
They also summoned the brahmin woman and said, "From today onwards, attend properly to our father. If you fall into negligence, [we shall expel you] from the house."
Having said, "We shall drive you out," they fed him choice food.
Due to that excellent meal and a comfortable sleep, after a few days had passed, the brahmin’s strength was restored and his faculties were refreshed.
Looking at his own body, he thought, "This prosperity of mine has been obtained by means of the ascetic Gotama," and [prepared] a gift.
Having taken it, he went into the presence of the Blessed One. To show this, the passage beginning with "Then indeed he... was spoken.

Therein, "he said this" means that having placed the pair of cloths at the feet [of the Buddha], he spoke these words. Furthermore, at the conclusion of his going for refuge, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, four meals per day were given by my sons; from those, I have given two to you."
“I will give [one], and we two shall eat [the other] ourselves. “Brāhmaṇa, do not offer a separate meal;
let us go to the very place that pleases us. “Very well, sir,” the brāhmaṇa replied, and having paid homage to the Blessed One, he went home and addressed his sons:
“Sons, the ascetic Gotama is my friend; he has two meals set aside for him...”
“They have been given; when they arrive, do not neglect them. “Very well, dear father,” he replied.
On the following day, in the morning, the Blessed One took his bowl and robe and went to the door of his eldest son’s residence.
As soon as the son saw the Teacher, he took the bowl from his hand, led him into the house, seated him upon a magnificent couch, and served him with exquisite food.
On the following day the Teacher went to the house of the other, and on the next day to the house of another; in this manner he visited the houses of them all in succession.
They all likewise paid him the same honor.
Then one day, a festival had been prepared at the house of the eldest son, and he said to his father: "Father,..."
“For whom shall we bestow blessings? “We know no one else; is not the ascetic Gotama my friend?
“In that case, invite the ascetic Gotama together with five hundred bhikkhus for tomorrow’s meal.
The brahmin did so. The Blessed One accepted, and on the following day, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, [went] to him.

He went to the door of his house. Having led the Teacher into the house, which was smeared with green cow dung and adorned with every kind of ornament, he had the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha sit on prepared seats and gave them rice porridge with little water and various kinds of solid foods.
Even while the meal was still in progress, the Brahmin’s four sons sat down in the presence of the Teacher.
They said, "Master Gotama, we have looked after our father and did not neglect him; behold his physical form!
The Teacher said, "You have done well; supporting one's mother and father is indeed the established custom of the ancient wise ones.
Having spoken thus, he related the Mahānāga Jātaka, and having illuminated the Four Truths, he taught the Dhamma.

He taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the brahmin, together with his four sons and four daughters-in-law, directed his knowledge according to the discourse and was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
From that time forth, the Teacher did not go to their house at all times.
This is the fourth [story].
5. Commentary on the Mānatthaddha Sutta (201) In the fifth [sutta], "conceited" (*mānatthaddha*) means stiff with conceit like a leather bag filled with air. Regarding "the teacher":
when one is learning a craft, the teacher does not impart the craft to one who does not pay homage; yet at other times, he does not even acknowledge his presence.

"He does not know. It occurred to him: "Since this ascetic does not offer even a mere greeting when a brahmin such as myself—one endowed with noble birth—has arrived, therefore he knows nothing at all.
"Filled with wonder" means possessed of a satisfaction such as had never occurred before. And "in whom? means in which [beings] could it exist?
"Kyassā" means "of which person. "Apacitā assu" means they would be worthy of showing honor.
By this verse, because of his skill in teaching (*desanākusalatā*), he includes himself among those who should be honored; thus he demonstrates that he is worthy of worship.
The fifth [chapter]. 6. Commentary on the *Paccanīka-sutta*.
202. In the sixth [verse], when it is said, "everything is white," one who creates an opposition by way of the method beginning with "everything is black" experiences pleasure and happiness;

thus, he is "one who finds satisfaction in opposition. And as for "having removed contentiousness": the meaning is that he listens after having removed contentiousness, which is characterized by the desire for superiority in argumentation. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Navakammikasutta (Sutta 203). Regarding "Navakammika Bhāradvāja":
it is said that he would have trees cut down in the forest, construct palaces, gabled houses, and other structures right there, then transport them to the city and sell them;
thus, he made his living by means of building work (*navakamma*).
"Navakammika-Bhāradvāja" means Bhāradvāja by clan who was a builder.
"Having seen him, this occurred to him" means that having seen the Blessed One sitting there emitting six-colored rays, this thought occurred to him. "In the forest" means in this woodland thicket.
"The forest has been uprooted by me" means the forest of my defilements (*kilesa*) has been uprooted. "One who is without a forest" means one who is free from the forest of defilements.
"Alone I delight; alone I rejoice. Having abandoned discontent (*arati*) means having discarded weariness with regard to remote lodgings and with regard to meditation.
This is the seventh [verse].
8. Commentary on the *Kaṭṭhahāra-sutta*.

204. In the eighth [verse], "pupils" (*antevāsika*) refers to those who acquire a craft by performing services; these are "dharma-pupils. "Seated" means seated while emitting six-colored rays of light. "Of profound nature" (*gambhīrarūpa*) means having a profound intrinsic character.

"Abounding in terrors" (*bahubherava*) means abounding in terrors consisting of both sentient and insentient beings situated therein. "Pervaded" (*vigāhiya*) means having entered into. "With body unmoving," etc., are qualifications of the body;
the meaning is "with a body of such a kind. "Truly of most beautiful form" (*sucārurūpaṃ vata*).
"Truly, you meditate on a most beautiful meditation," he says.

"The sage dwelling in the forest" means the Buddha-sage who has taken refuge in the forest. "This" refers to this very reason for your sitting in the forest; it appears to me as something wonderful. "With a joyful mind" means with a contented heart.
"He dwelt in the forest" means he lived in the forest. "I think" means I myself think. "Companionship with the Lord of the World" means association with Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the World.
"Desiring" (*ākaṅkhamāno*) means wishing. "The unsurpassed triple heaven" (*tidivam anuttaram*) is said with reference specifically to the Brahma-world.
"Why has your reverence resorted to this lonely forest?"—I thought, "It is because I am desiring the Brahma-world.
If that is not so, then tell me, why has your reverence [come]? He asks this. "For the attainment of Brahmā" (*brahmapattiyā*) means for the attainment of the supreme state.
"Here, why do you perform this austerity?"—thus he asks in another manner.

"Doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) is craving (*taṇhā*). "Delight" (*abhinandanā*) refers specifically to craving by way of its aspect of delighting. "In manifold elements" (*anekadhātūsu*) means in objects that possess various intrinsic natures.
"Diverse" (*puthū*) refers to craving in its many modes or the remaining defilements. "Always settled" (*sadāsita*) means constantly dependent upon them.
"Arising from the root of ignorance" means they have come into being with ignorance as their root.
"Longed for" means that craving itself is called "longed for" in the sense of causing one to long for things, thinking, "May this be mine, may that be mine.

"All have been brought to an end by me" means all craving has been made to reach its limit and become endless by me through the supreme path. "Together with its root" means together with the root of ignorance.
"Without approach" means not approaching. "Pure vision regarding all phenomena" indicates omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"The unsurpassed enlightenment" is said with reference to *arahantship*. "Auspicious" means supreme.
"I meditate" means I meditate by means of two jhānas. "Confident" means free from timidity. This is the eighth [verse].
9. Commentary on the Mātuposaka Sutta 205.
In the ninth [verse], *pecca* means having gone from here [to the next world]. The ninth [sutta is concluded].
10. Commentary on the Bhikkhaka Sutta.
206. "In this world" (*idha*) means in this state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*). "The foul-smelling nature" (*vissaṃ dhammaṃ*) refers to the foul-smelling unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*).

"Having banished" (*bāhitvā*) means having abandoned them by means of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). "By reckoning" (*saṅkhāya*) means by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "He indeed is called a monk" (*sa ve bhikkhūti vuccatī*):
he is indeed called a monk because his defilements have been shattered (*bhinnakilesatta*). The tenth [chapter].
11. Commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta 207.
In the eleventh [verse], *pacceti* means he desires or longs for. "Excellent, venerable sir," he said while entreating him.
It is said that this man was a lay friend of the Elder; therefore, the Elder [thought], "This poor fellow, even though he has obtained me as a friend, still holds wrong view..."

“Having taken it, do not become one who fills the states of misery,” he entreats. Furthermore, he entreats thinking: “He has a large retinue; when he has gained confidence, five hundred families will follow him.
“For the sake of benefit” means for the sake of advantage, for the sake of merit, for the sake of a purpose. “Evil” means unwholesome deeds such as the destruction of life.
“I wash away” means that having entered water up to my neck, I wash it away and cleanse it.
“Dhamma” is a verse whose meaning has already been explained.
The eleventh [chapter] is finished. 12. Commentary on the Khomadussa Sutta (Sutta 12).
Regarding “Khomadussa by name”: it received this name because of the abundance of *khoma* cloth there. “In the assembly” (*sabhāyaṃ*).
In the hall. "It touches" means it releases drops; it rains. It is said that the Teacher, desiring to approach that assembly hall, made a resolution:
"If I approach in this very manner, there will be discomfort for those of a sensitive constitution; therefore, I shall approach for one specific reason.
By the power of his resolve, he caused rain to fall. "The custom of the assembly hall" refers to [the practice of] not disturbing those sitting comfortably, but rather [passing by] on one side.
Entering [the assembly] in such a manner is what is called the "custom of the assembly" (sabhādhamma); it is not entering directly after causing the great crowd to move aside.
The Blessed One, however, came directly; therefore, they became angry and, reviling the Blessed One, said: "Who are these shaven-headed ascetics? Who will know the custom of the assembly?
"Santas" refers to wise, virtuous persons. "Having abandoned" means these...
Having abandoned lust and the rest, they preach the Dhamma for the sake of the subduing of lust and the rest; therefore, they are called "saints" (santo). The twelfth [chapter].
The second section on lay followers (Upāsakavagga) is concluded.
Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī...
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta of the Saṃyuttanikāya-ṭīkā is completed.
8. Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the Nikkhanta Sutta (209).
Regarding "at the Aggāḷava Cetiya" in the first discourse of the Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta: this refers to the foremost shrine at Āḷavī.

Before the Buddha had appeared, there were dwellings and shrines belonging to yakkhas, nāgas, and others, such as Aggāḷava, Gotamaka, and so forth. After the Buddha had appeared, [these became Buddhist sites].
Having removed them, people built monasteries; they were given those very same names.
"By Nigrodhakappa" means by the elder Kappa who dwelt at the foot of a banyan tree. "Ohiyyaka" means one who has been left behind. "Vihārapāla" (monastery-keeper):
it is said that he was then inexperienced and unskilled in taking up the bowl and robes. Then the elder monks said to him: "Friend, these..."
"Sit down, looking at the sandals, walking-stick, and other such items," they said, and having appointed him as the guardian of the monastery, they entered for alms.
Therefore it is said, "the monastery guard. "Having adorned himself" means having adorned himself with ornaments according to his own means.
"He ruins the mind" means he destroys and ruins wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*). "How can that be found here? refers to this:
When passion has arisen, from where can that cause be obtained?
That "other" by whom—whether another person or a teaching—I might dispel my lack of delight and immediately produce delight;
even my teachers and preceptors have left me behind in the monastery and departed.
"From home" means having gone forth from the household life. "To homelessness" means having entered the state of renunciation; this is the meaning.

"From the dark side" means they rush forth from the dark faction, the faction of Māra. "Sons of the exalted" means sons of those who are exalted, men of great influence who have become members of the royal nobility.
"Possessing strong bows" means possessing strong bows, those who wield the supreme measure of the teacher’s bow. A thousand.
“Those who do not flee” refers to those who might surround one on all sides with arrows;
showing the number of such non-fleeing warriors, he said, “a thousand. “More than this” means more than that thousand.
“They will not pierce me” means they will not be able to move me. “Firmly established in the Dhamma” means having dispelled discontent (anabhirati) and [established] delight (abhirati).
It is established in its own dispensation-dhamma, which is capable of producing [results]. This is what is meant:

Suppose a trained archer, while thousands of arrows are being discharged from all sides, takes up his bow and strikes every arrow in mid-air before it reaches the body, causing them to fall at his feet.
In that case, not even a single archer could hit two arrows simultaneously.
“They do not shoot; rather, these women shoot five arrows each at once, by way of the object of form and so forth.
Even if they shoot in this manner in numbers exceeding a thousand, they will not be able to move me.
“For I have heard this as a witness” means that I have heard this directly from [the Buddha’s] presence. “The path leading to Nibbāna” refers to insight (vipassanā).
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For that is the preliminary path to Nibbāna; however, he said "the path" (*magga*) by means of a change in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
In that context, "my mind is delighted" (*me mano nirato*) means that my mind is delighted in that path leading to Nibbāna, which consists of my own nascent insight (*vipassanā*).
"O Evil One" (*pāpima*)—he addresses the defilements (*kilesa*) with this. "O Death" (*maccu*)—he likewise addresses those very same things. "You shall not see even my path"—just as...
"You do not even see the path I have traveled through the womb and other states of existence; I shall act accordingly. First. 2.
Commentary on the Aratī Sutta (Discourse on Discontent) 210.
In the second [verse], "he goes out" means he goes out from the monastery. "On the following day" or "at the time" means on the second day, at the time for going on alms-round.
It is said that this elder was deeply devoted to the monastery. "Dislike and like" refers to dislike for the Teaching and like for the strands of sensual pleasure.
"And all thoughts pertaining to the household life" means having completely abandoned evil thoughts based on the house, which is the abode of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"The forest" refers to the great forest of defilements. "Anywhere" means upon any object whatsoever. "One who has emerged from the forest" is one who is free from the forest of defilements.
"Free from delight" (arato) means devoid of the delight of craving (taṇhā-rati).
"The earth and what is above it" (pathaviñca vehāsaṃ): this refers to the beauty of women, men, clothing, ornaments, and so forth, which reside on the earth;

and that which resides in the air, such as the radiance of the moon, the sun, and so forth. "Whatever has become form" (rūpagataṃ) means simply form itself. "Sunk in the world" (jagatogadhaṃ) means sunk within the world, [including] that which is within the earth.
The meaning is "gone to the abode of the Nāgas. *Parijīyati* means it decays (*parijīrati*). *Sabbamaniccaṃ* means all that is impermanent.
They say this is the Elder’s great insight (*mahāvipassanā*). *Evaṃ samacca* means having thus come together.
*Caranti mutattā* means they dwell having understood their own state of being.
"Underlying tendencies" (*upadhī*) refers to the underlying tendencies of defilements and volitional formations. "Attached" (*gadhitā*) means greedy.

"In what is seen and heard" refers to forms seen with the eye and sounds heard with the ear. "And in what is touched and sensed": here, by the term "resistant" (*paṭigha*), odors and tastes are included;

by the term "sensed" (*muta*), the object of tangible contact is meant. "He who is not smeared herein" means he who is not smeared by the stains of craving and views regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure.

"Then the sixty thoughts based on the unwholesome, which are accompanied by applied thought, are settled upon the multitude of people"—the meaning is: "then the many unwholesome thoughts based on the six objects of perception are settled upon the multitude of people.
"And one does not go anywhere into a faction because of them"—by means of those [thoughts], one should not fall into any faction of defilements.
"Nor should one be a speaker of what is indecorous"—that is, one should not be a speaker of indecorous words.
It would not be so. "That monk" means such a monk as this is called a monk.
"Dabba" means one of a *dabba* nature, a wise man. "Long-composed" means one whose mind has been concentrated for a long time.
"Circumspect" means endowed with circumspection, one of mature wisdom. "Free from longing" means devoid of craving. "The state of peace" means *nibbāna*.
"The Sage has arrived" means he has attained [the goal]. "Depending on it, he is fully extinguished;
he awaits the time"—depending on Nibbāna, he is fully extinguished by the full extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*), and thus he awaits the time of final Nibbāna. Second.
3. Commentary on the Pesala Sutta.
211. "In the third [verse], 'he despises' means: 'What are these old men? They have neither the Canon (pāḷi), nor the Commentary (aṭṭhakathā), nor sweetness of phrasing and syllables;
but for us, both the Canon and the Commentary appear through hundreds and thousands of methods. Thus, having passed them by, he thinks [this].
'Gotama'—he addresses himself as such because he is a disciple of the Buddha Gotama. 'The path of conceit' means both the object of conceit and..."
And mental concomitants. "Vippaṭisārī ahuvā" means he was remorseful; the meaning is "he became.
"Magga-jino" means one who has conquered the defilements by means of the Path. "Kittiñca sukhañca" means both renown and physical and mental happiness.
"Akhilodha padhānavā" means here one who is unblemished and diligent, endowed with energy. "Visuddho" means he would become purified. "Asesaṃ" means without remainder.
The remainder is ninefold. "One who brings an end through clear knowledge" (*vijjāyantakaro*) means one who brings an end to the defilements by means of clear knowledge.

"One who has become tranquil" (*samitāvī*) means one who has become tranquil because of the tranquility of passion and the other defilements. This is the third [verse]. 4. Commentary on the *Ānanda-sutta*.
212. Regarding the fourth [case], "lust": the Venerable Ānanda was highly esteemed and possessed of great merit;

thus, kings, royal ministers, and others would invite him and have him sit within their own residences. Even women adorned with every ornament would approach the Elder, pay homage to him, and fan him with palm-leaf fans;
they would sit down near him, ask questions, and listen to the Dhamma. In that regard—
The Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having recently gone forth, was unable to grasp a suitable meditation object, and his mind was agitated by lust for the form of a woman.

Being a clansman of upright nature who had gone forth out of faith, he thought, "If this lust of mine increases, it will destroy my welfare both in this present life and in the life to come. Having reflected thus, while still sitting right there—
Revealing himself to the elder, he said, "By sensual lust," and so forth.
Therein, "extinguishing" (*nibbāpana*) means the cause for the extinguishing of lust. "By way of inversion" (*vipariyāsa*) means by way of perversion.

"Beautiful, accompanied by lust" refers to a desirable object that serves as a basis for lust. "Look upon it as other" means look upon it as impermanent. "And not as self" means do not regard it as a self.
"Do not see. "Let it be directed toward the body" means: let it be directed toward the body for you. "And develop the signless" means:
because the signs of permanence and so forth have been removed, insight is called "signless"; he says, "develop that. "The full comprehension of conceit" means:

both the full comprehension through seeing and the full comprehension through abandoning of conceit. "Peaceful" means: peaceful due to the subsiding of lust and the other defilements. This is the fourth [section].
5. Commentary on the Subhāsita Sutta 213.
In the fifth [verse], "by means of five factors" (*aṅgehi*) means by means of causes (*kāraṇehi*) or by means of constituent parts (*avayavehi*).

For the four [qualities] beginning with abstaining from false speech are the causes for well-spoken speech, while the four beginning with truthful speech are the constituent parts. And since the word *aṅga* here has the sense of a cause, the term "by four" (*catūhi*) is used in the ablative case.
[The word] *hoti* [is used here]; the instrumental case is employed in the sense of a constituent part (*avayavatthe*). *Samannāgatā* means accompanied by, occurring together with, and endowed with.
*Vācā* refers to the speech of utterance, which is described as "speech, voice, and expression," and as "gentle and pleasant to the ear.

Furthermore, it includes the intimation (*viññatti*) expressed by the phrase, "Whatever action is performed by means of speech," as well as the abstention from the four types of verbal misconduct, and so forth.

“This is called right speech”—thus, abstinence [is mentioned]; and “Harsh speech, bhikkhus, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently repeated, leads to rebirth in hell”—thus, volition is also mentioned as speech. But that [volition] is not intended here. Why?
Because it is not something to be spoken. “Well-spoken” means well-said. By this, he indicates that it brings about benefit. Not...
“Not ill-spoken” means it is not poorly spoken; by this, he shows that it does not bring about harm and is fit to be abandoned [by its opposite].
“Blameless” means free from the thorns of lust and so forth; by this, he shows its purity of cause and the absence of the four faults. “Beyond reproach” means liberated from censure;
by this, he shows its perfection in every respect. “By the wise” means by the learned; by this, he shows that fools are no authority in matters of blame or praise.
"He speaks only what is well-spoken" refers to one of the four factors of speech within the teaching that is framed by way of the individual;
it is a statement regarding the absence of fault in that particular factor of speech. "Not ill-spoken" is the prevention of speech that is the opposite of that very factor of speech.

By the phrase "not ill-spoken," he demonstrates the abandoning of wrong speech (*micchāvācā*). By the phrase "well-spoken," he indicates the characteristic of the speech that ought to be spoken by one who has abandoned wrong speech.
However, here, for the purpose of illustrating the constituent parts (*aṅga*), he states only what ought to be said, without repeating what was already stated previously.

This same method applies to the phrases "only the Dhamma," and so forth. And herein, by the first [phrase], speech that brings about concord and is free from the fault of malicious talk (*pisuṇavācā*) is described;
by the second, counsel that does not deviate from the Dhamma and is free from the fault of idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*); by the others...

By the phrase "devoid of the two types of harsh speech," he refers to pleasant and truthful words. With the words "By these, indeed... and so forth, he concludes that speech by directly demonstrating those constituent parts (*aṅga*).

He thereby refutes that which others consider to be well-spoken—even if it is speech such as falsehood—merely because it possesses logical members (*avayava*) such as the proposition (*paṭijñā*) and so on, or words such as nouns (*nāma*), or the perfection of gender, number, case, tense, and grammatical function (*kāraka*). Even if it possesses such members and so forth...
For such speech is indeed ill-spoken because it brings harm to oneself and others.

However, if speech is endowed with these four factors, even if it is included in the language of foreigners or contained within the songs of a water-carrier girl, it is nevertheless well-spoken, as it brings mundane and supramundane welfare and happiness. For instance, [the case of] the crop by the side of the road...

While sixty or so insight-practicing monks were traveling along the road, they heard the sound of a Sinhalese slave-girl named Rakkhanti singing a song concerning birth, aging, and death; upon hearing it, they attained Arahantship.
Likewise, a monk named Tissa, who was engaged in insight practice, while walking near a lotus pond, saw lotuses being broken off in the pond and [thought]:
“Just as a full-blown *kokanada* lotus at dawn is shattered by the light of the sun,
so too are beings who have attained human status crushed by the force of old age.
Upon hearing this verse sung by the maidservant, he attained *arahantship*.
In another Buddha-interval as well, a certain man came from the forest with seven sons and saw a woman pounding rice with a pestle:
“This is worn out by old age, clinging to shriveled skin and hide;
This breaks apart through death—the baited morsel for the prey of Mortality.”
“This is an abode for worms, filled with various kinds of filth;
it is a vessel for impurity, equal to the trunk of a plantain tree.
Having heard this song and reflecting upon it, he attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha together with his sons. Thus, by these four...

Speech endowed with these factors should be understood as well-spoken even if it is included among the languages of barbarians or included among the songs of a water-carrier girl. Precisely because it is well-spoken,
it is blameless and irreproachable for the wise who seek the meaning and rely on the meaning, rather than relying on the letter.
"Sāruppāhi" means with what is suitable. "Abhitthavi" means he praised. "Na tāpaye" means he would not cause pain or affliction through remorse.
"Pare" means others; he would not overcome or harm them by causing dissension among others.
Thus, with this verse, he praises the Blessed One by way of non-slanderous speech. "Paṭinanditā" means beloved. "Yaṃ anādāya" means that which...
When speaking words to others, one does not take up evil or unpleasant harsh speech, but speaks only what is pleasant, sweet in both meaning and phrasing;
thus he praised [the Buddha] by way of his pleasant speech, saying, "one should speak such words.
"Amata" (deathless) means that, by virtue of its excellence, it is like the deathless nectar. For it has been said: "Truth is indeed the sweetest of tastes."
Or, they are "immortal" because they have Nibbāna as their condition for immortality.
"This Dhamma is ancient" means that this which is called true speech is an ancient Dhamma, a practice, and a tradition. For this alone was the habit of the ancients; they did not speak falsehood.
Therefore it was said: "The virtuous say they are established in truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma."
In this context, it should be understood that because they are established in truth, they are established in the welfare of both themselves and others;
and because they are established in welfare, they are established in the Dhamma. Alternatively, this is a qualification of "truth" itself. For what is meant is this:
established in truth—of what kind?—in welfare and in the Dhamma, since [that truth] does not deviate from the welfare of others.
Because it does not obstruct the welfare (*attha*) and because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it accomplishes that very welfare which is consistent with the Dhamma.
Thus, by means of this verse, he praised [the gift] by way of truthful speech.
"Security" (*khema*) means fearlessness and freedom from calamity. If one asks for what reason, it is for the attainment of Nibbāna and for the making of an end to suffering.
Because it leads to the extinction of defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*) and conduces to the making of an end to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*);

or alternatively, because the Buddha speaks words that are secure (*khema*) for the sake of attaining *nibbāna* and for the sake of the two elements of *nibbāna*—namely, the making of an end to suffering—he speaks those words which are indeed the supreme among all words. Thus, that speech is the best of all speech.

"Best" (seṭṭha)—this is how the meaning should be understood here. Thus, by means of this verse, praising the Blessed One through the expression of his wisdom, he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
The fifth [sutta]. 6. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta.
214. In the sixth [verse], "poriyā" means complete in its syllables and so forth. "Vissaṭṭhā" means unobstructed and unhindered.
For when the General of the Dhamma speaks, his speech is unhindered by bile or other humors;
it issues forth like the sound from a bronze gong struck with an iron rod. "Anelagalā" means without flaw, without impediment, and faultless.
And with words and syllables that are unerring. For as the Elder speaks, neither his word nor his syllable falters.
"Capable of making the meaning known" means capable of making the meaning understood. "To the bhikkhunīs" means to the bhikkhus. "Even in brief" means:
"Friends, there are these four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering... [and so on]."

"Friends, these are the four noble truths; therefore, friends, an application should be made thus: 'This is the noble truth of suffering. In this way he teaches in brief. "In detail as well" means that by analyzing those very truths according to the method beginning with, "Friends, what is the noble truth of suffering?
and so forth, he speaks in detail as well. This also applies to the teachings on the aggregates and so forth.
The same method applies. "Like the cry of a sāḷika bird":
just as the cry of a female sāḷika bird, who after tasting a sweet mango fruit, flaps her wings and utters a sweet sound, so too was the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma sweet-sounding.
"He uttered inspired eloquence" means that, like waves from the ocean, it was infinite.
Inspiration arises. "They lend an ear" means they listen. The sixth [chapter]. 7.
Commentary on the Pavāraṇā Sutta: 215.
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "on that day" (tadahū) means it occurred on that day; the meaning is "on that very day. It is called *uposatha* because they observe the fast (*upavasanti*) therein.
"Observing the fast" (*upavasanti*) means dwelling while endowed with either virtue (*sīla*) or fasting (*anasana*).
Furthermore, this Uposatha day is threefold, being divided into the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth; therefore, "on the fifteenth" is stated in order to exclude the other two.

"At the invitation" (*pavāraṇāya*) refers to the invitation after the rains-retreat (*vassaṃ-vuṭṭha-pavāraṇā*); "the invitation for purification" (*visuddhi-pavāraṇā*) is also a name for this very same [invitation].
"He was seated" means that in the evening, having taught the Dhamma at a time appropriate for the assembled multitude,
and having bathed his limbs at the water-pavilion, he put on his lower and upper robes, arranged his great robe of the Sugata over one shoulder,
and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared against the central pillar, facing the splendor of the moon-disk rising in the eastern direction.
He sat there, surpassing all in splendor. Whichever way he looked, he saw that they were entirely silent;
for not even a single bhikkhu had any fidgeting with hands or feet, and all sat in peaceful postures, free from agitation. "Having looked around" means with his five clearly visible faculties.
"Having looked around with a clear mind. *Handa* is a particle used in the sense of relinquishment (*vossagga*).

Regarding the phrase "and do not reproach me for anything," here *na ca kiñci* contains the negative particle *na* in the sense of a question. "Do you reproach me for anything? If you reproach me, speak;
I wish to allow you to speak—this is the meaning. By the words "whether bodily or verbal," he invites [criticism] specifically through the doors of body and speech.
Not the mind-door. Why? Because it is not manifest. For in the doors of body and speech, fault is manifest, but not in the mind-door.
Even when asked, "Though you are lying on the same bed, what were you thinking?", one knows the movement of the mind.

Thus, the mind-door does not invite [criticism] because it is not manifest, not because it is impure. For even when he was a bodhisatta, during his time as Bhūridatta, Chaddanta, Saṅkhapāla, Dhammapāla, and so forth—
The mind-door is completely purified; now there is nothing further to be said here.
"He said this" because, standing in the position of the General of the Dhamma (*dhammasenāpati*), he spoke these words while bearing the burden of the Saṅgha of monks.
"Indeed, venerable sir, we do not censure the Blessed One in any way," whether physically or verbally.
The Elder spoke this with reference to the four things that need no protection. For the Blessed One has four things that need no protection. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four things that need no protection for a Tathāgata. Which four? Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct is utterly pure;
there is no misconduct of body in the Tathāgata that he would need to protect."
“‘Let no one else know this of me,’ [one might think]. But, monks, the Tathāgata’s verbal conduct is utterly pure;
there is no verbal misconduct in the Tathāgata that he would need to guard against, thinking, ‘Let no one else know this of me.
Monks, the Tathāgata’s mental conduct is utterly pure; there is no mental misconduct in the Tathāgata.”
“That which the Tathāgata would need to guard, thinking, ‘Let no one else know this of me’—monks, the Tathāgata’s livelihood is pure;
there is no wrong livelihood in the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘Let no one else know this of me.
Now, speaking of the Blessed One’s qualities as they truly are, [the interlocutor] said, “For the Blessed One, venerable sir,” and so forth. Therein, “of what has not yet arisen” means:
"Never before produced by any other ascetic or brahmin since the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa.
"Unborn" (*asañjāta*) is simply a synonym for "unarisen" (*anuppanna*). "Unproclaimed" (*anakkhāta*) means not taught by another.
"Attained afterwards" (*pacchā samannāgatā*) means attained after the Blessed One had first gone [to that state]. Thus, since all [these qualities]... the Elder [said].
The Blessed One’s qualities, such as virtue and so forth, have arisen depending solely upon the path to Arahatship;
therefore, he spoke of the quality by depending upon that very path to Arahatship. By doing so, all the qualities are effectively spoken of.

And when the Elder said, "And I too, venerable sir," he spoke thus while extending an invitation for both bodily and verbal conduct on behalf of himself and the Saṅgha to the Supreme Person in the world with its devas.
"Set in motion by the father": when a wheel-turning monarch has passed away or gone forth into homelessness, the wheel disappears after seven days.
Then, for the son who sits fulfilling the tenfold or twelvefold duty of a wheel-turner, another wheel appears;
he sets that one in motion. However, because it is made of jewels, it is the same in terms of its essential nature.
Having performed his duty, it is said that [the wheel] was set in motion by his father. Or rather, because he said, "O King, you may remain at ease;
I shall provide instruction," he is said to have continued the wheel of authority set in motion by his father.
"He set it in motion rightly" means he set it in motion by way of the correct method, cause, and reason. For the Blessed One [taught] the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths...
The Elder speaks, and the other repeats exactly what he says; therefore, he spoke thus. "Liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) means liberated by two parts:

liberated from the aggregate of form (*rūpakāya*) through the formless-sphere attainments (*arūpāvacara-samāpatti*), and liberated from the aggregate of mind (*nāmakāya*) through the supreme path (*aggamagga*).

"Liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) refers to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) who have not attained the state of the three knowledges (*tevijja*) and so forth, but are liberated by wisdom alone.
