"Visuddhiyā" means for the sake of purification. "Saṃyojanabandhanacchidā" means having cut through the defilements known as fetters (saṃyojana) and bonds (bandhana), they remain [established].
"Vijitasaṅgāmaṃ" means one who has conquered the battle of lust, hatred, and delusion; it is also called "vijitasaṅgāma" because of having conquered the army of Māra.
"Satthavāhaṃ" means one who, having placed the caravan of those to be trained upon the chariot of the Eightfold Path...

He drives [the caravan] across the wilderness of *saṃsāra* and brings it to safety; thus the Blessed One is the Caravan Leader (*satthavāha*). To that Caravan Leader. "A fool" (*palāpa*) means one who is empty within and immoral.
"To the Kinsman of the Sun" (*ādiccabandhu*): he says, "I pay homage to the Teacher, the Kinsman of the Sun, the One of Ten Powers.
This is the seventh [verse]. 8. Commentary on the *Parosahassa-sutta*.
216. In the eighth [verse], "more than a thousand" (*parosahassa*) means exceeding one thousand. "Fearless from all sides" (*akutobhaya*):
since there is no fear from any quarter in *nibbāna*, or for one who has attained *nibbāna*, *nibbāna* is called "fearless from all sides.
"The seventh seer among seers" (*isisattama*): starting from Vipassī, he was the seventh seer among the seers.
"O Vaṅgīsa, what indeed [is this]?"—this the Blessed One spoke by way of a specific occasion. It is said that a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha:
"The Elder Vaṅgīsa has neglected his duties; he performs no work in recitation, nor in interrogation, nor in systematic attention;
he wanders about composing verses and creating collections of metrical words. Then the Blessed One reflected.
Thinking, “These bhikkhus do not know the perfection of Vaṅgīsa’s inspired eloquence;
they imagine that he speaks only after repeated reflection. I shall make them recognize his perfection of inspired eloquence,” he said, “What then, Vaṅgīsa? and so forth.

“The path of the abyss” (ummaggapatha) refers to the many hundreds of ways in which the defilements emerge; however, it is called a “path” because it is the path of the round of existence (vaṭṭapatha).
"Breaking through the obstructions" means that you move about having broken through the five obstructions, such as the obstruction of lust.
"Behold him" means behold that Buddha who moves about having thus overcome and broken them. "The maker of release from bonds" means the one who effects liberation from bondage.
"Unattached" means independent. "Distributing by way of parts" means analyzing the Dhamma according to its divisions, such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
Or the reading is *pavibhajja*; the meaning is: "having analyzed again and again by way of the divisions of the limbs and sub-limbs, behold.
*Oghassa* means "of the four floods. *Anekavihitam* means "of many kinds," by way of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
*Tasmiṃ ca amate akkhāte* means "in that deathless which has been proclaimed by him. *Dhammaddasā* means "seers of the Dhamma. *Ṭhitā*...
"Unshakable" means being established as one who cannot be shaken.
"Piercing through" means having pierced through. "Of all standpoints" means of all bases for views or stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).
"He saw the transcendence" means he saw Nibbāna, which is the state of transcendence. "The summit" means the supreme Dhamma. "The peak" (agge) [is used in the same sense].
Or the reading is *paṭhamataraṃ*, meaning "earlier. *Dasaddhānaṃ* means "of the five";
the meaning is that he taught the foremost Dhamma to the group of five, or he taught the Dhamma to the foremost among the group of five.

*Tasmā* means "therefore," because negligence must not be committed by one who knows that this Dhamma has been well-taught; therefore. *Anusik-kheyya* means one should train in the three trainings. The eighth [chapter].
9. Commentary on the Koṇḍañña Sutta 217.
Regarding the ninth [sutta]: "Aññāsikoṇḍañña" refers to the Elder who was given this name because he was the first to understand the Dhamma.
"After a very long time"—how long? After twelve years. During that period, where did he dwell?
At the abode of the Paccekabuddhas on the bank of the Mandākinī lotus pond in the Chaddanta forest.
Why? Because of his reverence for the monastery. For he was a wise Great Disciple;

just as in the case of the Blessed One, so too were his virtues spread throughout the ten thousand world-systems among gods and humans. Gods and humans, having gone into the presence of the Tathāgata...
Having performed worship with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they approached the Elder immediately thereafter, honoring him as "the disciple who has penetrated the supreme Dhamma.
Indeed, for those who have come into one's presence, such a discourse on the Dhamma or a hospitable welcome ought to be offered.
But the Elder was devoted to his monastery, and thus that [welcoming] appeared to him like an impediment. Thus, due to his devotion to the monastery...
Having gone there, he dwelt.
There is another reason as well: at the time for the alms-round, all the disciples go out according to their seniority.
But at the time for teaching the Dhamma, when the Teacher is seated upon the adorned Buddha-throne in the central place, the General of the Dhamma sits on his right-hand side.
On the left side of his hand sat the Elder Mahāmoggallāna; behind them, they prepared a seat for the Elder Aññākoṇḍañña. The remaining bhikkhus sat surrounding them.

Because the two chief disciples had realized the supreme Dhamma and because they were senior, they were full of reverence toward the Elders, regarding the Elder as if he were Brahmā, a mass of fire, or a venomous serpent.
Thinking as if they were [mere] imitations, they felt ashamed and abashed while sitting on the seats of honor. The Elder thought:
"For the sake of these seats of honor, these [beings] fulfilled the perfections for more than a hundred thousand aeons plus an incalculable aeon;
yet now, as they sit upon the seats of honor, they feel ashamed and abashed before me. I shall provide them with a comfortable dwelling. He [prepared] a suitable...
At that time, having approached the Tathāgata, he said, "Venerable Sir, I wish to dwell in the countryside," and the Teacher granted him permission.
The Elder, having tidied his lodgings and taking his bowl and robe, went to the bank of the Mandākinī in the Chaddanta abode.
Eight thousand noble elephants, who had previously been accustomed to serving the Paccekabuddhas, saw the Elder and—

Thinking, "The field of our merit has arrived," they leveled the walkway with their nails, removed the obstructing branches, prepared the Elder’s dwelling place, and performed the customary services. Then, having all gathered together, they deliberated:
"If we were to act by thinking, 'This one shall do what is to be done for the Elder; that one shall do it,' [the work would not be accomplished]."
"The Elder will go with his bowl as clean as when it was washed, as if he had gone to a village where he has many kinsmen;
we shall attend upon him by turns. However, on the turn of one person, the others must not neglect their duty. Thus they established a rotation.
Vārikanāga would set out water for the Elder's mouth and tooth-sticks every morning, and perform the customary services.
This lotus pond named Mandākinī is fifty yojanas in extent. In a space measuring twenty-five yojanas, there is no moss or aquatic weeds;

the water is the color of crystal. Beyond that, however, at a depth of water reaching to the waist, the remaining lotus grove stands encircling the lake for fifty yojanas, with a width of half a yojana.
Immediately after that was a vast grove of red lotuses; after that, a grove of red water-lilies;
after that, a grove of white water-lilies; after that, a grove of blue lotuses; after that, a grove of red lotuses;
after that, a grove of fragrant red rice; and after that, sweet-tasting climbing fruits such as cardamom, gourds, pumpkins, and so forth.
Immediately after that was a sugarcane grove one and a half *yojanas* in extent; there the sugarcane stalks were as thick as the trunks of coconut trees.
Following that was a plantain grove, where two people eating the ripe fruit would become exhausted.
After that was a jackfruit grove with fruits the size of water-jars, and after that a rose-apple grove, and after that a mango grove, and after that—
"Kapitthavana": In brief, it cannot be said that there was no fruit at all in that forest suitable to be eaten.
At the time when the flowers were blooming, the wind raised a cloud of pollen and deposited it upon lotus leaves;
there, droplets of water fell. Then, ripened by the heat of the sun, it remained like a ripe *payoghanikā* (a type of dried fruit).
This is called "lotus honey"; they bring it and give it to the Elder. The *muḷāla* is the size of a plowshare;
they bring that as well and give it. The lotus root (*bhisa*) is the size of a large drum or a lotus flower;
in one of its joints there is milk the size of a foot-jar; they bring that and give it. The lotus seeds are like honey-sugar.
Having prepared them, they give them. They place sugarcane on a stone slab and tread upon it with their feet.
Then the juice flows out, filling a vat; having been cooked by the heat of the sun, it remains like a mass of milk-stone, which they then bring and give.
As for the ripe jackfruit, plantain, mango, and other fruits, there is no need for further description.
On Mount Kelāsa dwells a son of the gods named Nāgadatta. From time to time, the Elder goes to the gate of his celestial mansion.
He fills a bowl with waterless milk-rice mixed with fresh ghee, lotus honey, and powdered rice, and gives it to him.
It is said that during the time of Buddha Kassapa, he had for twenty thousand years served milk-rice with fragrant ghee.

He gave it. It is because of that that this food has arisen for him. Thus the Elder, having lived there for twelve years, observed his own life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*), and knowing it was exhausted, thought, "Where shall I attain final Nibbāna? Having considered this, he thought:
"The elephant kings have performed a difficult service by attending upon me for twelve years; having obtained the Teacher’s permission, I shall [attain Nibbāna] right here."
“I shall attain final nibbāna in the presence [of the Buddha],” he said, and traveled through the air to the Blessed One’s presence. Therefore it is said:
“After a very long time, he approached where the Blessed One was.
And as for the phrase “and his name”: why does he announce his name? For some recognize the elder, while others do not. In that regard—

The Elder thought: “Those who do not know me and might think, ‘Who is this white-headed, bent-over, crooked-as-a-rafter old man exchanging greetings with the Teacher? will harbor defiled thoughts and will fill the states of misery.
But those who do know me will think: ‘He is a renowned and well-known Great Disciple, like the Teacher himself throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.’”

“They will clarify their minds and shall go to heaven”—thus, closing off the path to the states of woe for beings and opening the path to heaven, he announces his name. As for the term “awakened after the Buddha”:
first the Teacher awakened to the Four Truths, and afterwards the Elder; therefore, he is called “awakened after the Buddha.”
It is said: "One of intense exertion" means one who possesses powerful energy (*bāḷhavīriya*). "Of the three seclusions" refers to the three kinds of seclusion (*viveka*).

By saying "one possessing the three knowledges" and "skilled in the penetration of minds," he speaks of four of the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Although the other two are not explicitly mentioned, the Elder was nonetheless possessed of all six direct knowledges.
At the conclusion of this verse, the assembly sat down in silence. Knowing that the assembly was seated, the Elder—
Having exchanged greetings with the Teacher, he requested permission for the time of his final passing, saying: "Venerable Sir, my life-faculties are exhausted;
I shall attain final Nibbāna. "Where will you attain final Nibbāna, Koṇḍañña?
"Venerable Sir, my attendant noble elephants have performed a difficult service for me; it is in their presence that I shall do so. The Teacher granted him permission.
The Elder, having circumambulated the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, and while the great multitude was lamenting, "Venerable Sir, that was my first sight of you;
this is my last sight," paid homage to the Teacher, departed, and stood at the gateway, saying:
"Do not grieve, do not lament! Whether they be Buddhas or disciples of the Buddha, conditioned phenomena that have arisen..."
Having exhorted the great multitude, saying, "There is no one who can obstruct me," he rose up into the air right before the eyes of the people,
descended onto the bank of the Mandākinī, bathed in the lotus pond, put on his lower and upper robes, arranged his bedding,
spent the three watches of the night in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), and at the time of the powerful dawn, attained final nibbāna.
Immediately upon the Elder’s final passing away (parinibbāna), all the trees in the Himalayas became bent and bowed down with flowers and fruits.

The Nāga Vārika, unaware that the Elder had passed away, rose early in the morning, prepared water for washing the face and tooth-sticks, performed his duties, brought hard foods and fruits, and stood at the end of the walking path (caṅkama). He...
Until sunrise, not seeing the Elder emerge, he thought, "What can this be?
Previously, the Noble One would go for his walk at dawn and wash his face; but today he has not even come out from the leaf-hut.
Shaking the door of the hut and looking inside, he saw the Elder sitting right there. Reaching out his hand and touching him, he sought the signs of his breathing.
Knowing their state of non-occurrence [of movement], he thrust his trunk into his mouth and let out a great roar, crying out, "The Elder has attained Parinibbāna!

The entire Himālaya resounded with a single cry. Eight thousand elephants gathered together, seated the Elder upon the frontal globe of the senior elephant, and surrounding him while holding branches of trees in full bloom, they covered the entire Himālaya.
Having searched, they returned to their own place.
Sakka addressed Vissakamma: "Dear son, our eldest brother has attained final Nibbāna; let us pay him honor.
Build a gabled chamber nine yojanas in size, made entirely of all kinds of gems. Having done so, he [placed] the Elder there.
Having had them laid down, he gave them to the lordly elephants. They lifted up the gabled pavilion and repeatedly shook it across the Himalayas for three thousand yojanas.
From their hands, the sky-dwelling deities took it and performed a grand celebration.
Then, by this means, the rain-clouds, the cool-clouds, the warm-clouds, the Cātumahārājika gods, and the Tāvatiṃsa gods [participated].
The peaked pavilion ascended as far as the Brahma-world; then the Brahmā deities successively gave their own peaked pavilions to the elephant kings.
Each deity brought a sandalwood casket measuring four finger-breadths, and the funeral pyre became nine yojanas in size.
They placed the peaked pavilion upon the funeral pyre. Five hundred bhikkhus arrived through the air and remained throughout the entire night.
They engaged in recitation. The Elder Anuruddha preached the Dhamma, and there was a realization of the Dhamma for many deities.
On the following day, at the very moment of sunrise, they extinguished the funeral pyre and filled a casket with relics the color of jasmine buds.
When the Blessed One had departed and arrived at the gate of the Veḷuvana Monastery, [they offered them].
Having brought them, they placed them in the Teacher’s hand. The Teacher took the vessel for receiving the relics and extended his hand toward the earth;
having split open the great earth, a stupa resembling a silver bubble emerged. The Teacher deposited the relics in the stupa with his own hands.
It is said that even today that stupa still endures. This is the ninth [sutta].
10. Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta 218.
In the tenth [verse], *samannesati* means he seeks out and reflects upon. *Nagassa* means of the mountain.
*Munim* means the Buddha, the Sage. *Dukkhassa pāragum* means one who has gone to the further shore of suffering. *Samannesam* means while seeking out. Thus...
"Endowed with all factors" means thus endowed with all virtues. "Endowed with manifold aspects" means possessed of many qualities. The tenth [chapter].
11. Commentary on the Gaggarā Sutta.

219. In the eleventh [verse], *assudanti* means they weep; *assudam* is merely a particle. *Vaṇṇena* means by the color of the body. *Yasasā* means by retinue. *Vigatamalova bhāṇumā* means like the sun free from impurity.
This is the eleventh [chapter]. 12. Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta: 220.
In the twelfth [verse], *āyasmā* is a term of endearment. *Vaṅgīsa* is the name of that elder. It is said that formerly...
In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, having seen a disciple endowed with eloquence, he gave a gift and made an aspiration;

then, after fulfilling the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons, during the time of our own Blessed One, out of a desire to debate throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he carried a branch of the rose-apple tree (*jambu-sākha*).
Having engaged in a debate with a certain wanderer (*paribbājaka*), by the power of his victory and defeat in that debate, by that very [act]...
Having lived in association with a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka), a certain female wanderer gave birth to him; having reached maturity,
he wandered about after learning a thousand arguments— five hundred from his mother’s side and five hundred from his father’s side—
and he knew one spell (*vijjā*), by reciting which [he could raise] the heads of the dead.
Having struck with his finger, he knows: "He has been reborn in such-and-such a place.
Traveling by stages through villages, market towns, and other settlements, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī together with five hundred young brahmins and sat down in a hall at the city gate.
At that time, the city dwellers, having given alms before the meal, were afterwards dressed in clean upper robes, carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands.
They were going to the monastery to hear the Dhamma. Seeing them, the young brahmin asked, "Where are you going?
They replied, "To the presence of the One of Ten Powers to hear the Dhamma. He too, along with his retinue, went together with them;
having exchanged greetings, he stood to one side. Then the Blessed One said to him: "Vaṅgīsa, it is excellent..."
“Is it said that you know a craft? “Sir Gotama, I know many crafts.
Which one do you have in mind when you ask? “The craft of a corpse-despiser. “Yes, Sir Gotama.
Then the Blessed One, by his own supernatural power, showed him the head of one reborn in hell and asked, “Vaṅgīsa, where has this person been reborn? He [recited] the mantra...
Having recited the mantra and struck with his finger, he said, "In hell. "Excellent, Vaṅgīsa! Well spoken!

[the King] said, and he showed him the head of one reborn in the world of the devas. He likewise explained that one as well. Then he showed him the head of one whose taints were exhausted (a *khīṇāsava*).
Although he repeated the mantra again and again and struck with his finger once more, he could not see the place where that being had been reborn.
Then the Blessed One said to him, “Are you weary, Vaṅgīsa? “Yes, sir Gotama,” he replied. “Examine it again and again,” [the Buddha said].
Even though he did so, not seeing [the deity], he said, “Do you know, sir Gotama?
“Yes, Vaṅgīsa; it has gone because of me; I know its destination. “Do you know it by means of a mantra, sir Gotama? “Yes, Vaṅgīsa, by one...”
“I know it only through my own incantation. “Sir Gotama, give this incantation to me.
“My incantation, Vaṅgīsa, is without a root. “Give it to me, Sir Gotama. “It is not possible to give it to one who has not gone forth in my presence.
He addressed his pupils: “Sirs, the ascetic Gotama knows a superior craft; I [shall go] into his presence.”
"Once I have gone forth, I shall learn a craft; then there will be no one in the whole of Jambudīpa who knows more than I.
Until I return, you must wander about without becoming weary.
Having dismissed them with these words, he said, "Ordain me. The Teacher ordained Nigrodhakappa. The Elder led him to his own dwelling place.
Having led him away, he ordained him. Once ordained, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood before him, requesting, "Teach me a craft.
The Teacher said, "Vaṅgīsa, when you learn a craft, you must first perform the preliminary service by means of eating food without salt, sleeping on the bare ground, and so forth.
There is also a preliminary service for this craft; perform that first. "Very well, Bhante," he replied.
Then the Teacher explained to him the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects.
As he attended to it in direct and reverse order, he developed insight and gradually attained Arahantship.
"Experiencing the bliss of liberation" means that having thus attained Arahantship, he was experiencing the bliss of liberation. "In verses" means...
Intoxicated by poetry and the composition of verses; he taught the Dhamma, elucidating these aggregates, bases, and elements.
"Those who have entered the path and see the path" means those who have both entered the path and possess vision of the path. "Welcome" means a good arrival.

By the phrase "I have attained supernormal power," the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*) is included. By the phrase "skilled in the penetration of minds" (*cetopariyāyakovida*),...

The knowledge of penetration of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*). Furthermore, the divine ear (*dibbasota*) is indeed included even though it was not explicitly mentioned. Thus, it should be understood that this Great Disciple has attained the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). The twelfth [chapter].
Thus ends [the section] from the *Sāratthappakāsinī*.
The commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta of the Saṃyuttanikāya-ṭīkā is finished. 9.
Vanasaṃyutta (The Connected Discourses on Forests).
1. Commentary on the Vivekasutta 221.

Regarding the first sutta of the *Vanasaṃyutta*: “He was dwelling among the Kosalans” means that, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, he went to dwell there because alms-food was easily obtained in that country.
“Desiring to stir [him] up” means [to stir him up] toward seclusion (*viveka*).
"Desirous of making [others] practice. "One desiring seclusion" means one who aspires to the three kinds of seclusion. "It issues forth externally" means it wanders among external, manifold objects.
"Person to person" means: you, as a person, should subdue desire and lust toward other persons.
"Abandon" means: give up. "Become" means: come to be. "We shall remind that mindful one" means: that wise person endowed with mindfulness.

"We too shall remind him" means "we shall remind him of that Dhamma of the virtuous. "Dust of the underworld" (pātālaraja) refers to the dust of defilements (kilesaraja), so called because it is without foundation.
"Do not let the dust of sensual desire take it away" means: do not let this dust of sensual lust carry it off;
do not lead it to the states of misery (apāya). "Dusty" (paṃsukunthita) means smeared with dust. "Shaking" (vidhunanti) means shaking off. "The dust of the cold" (sitaṃ rajaṃ).

"The dust clinging to the body. "He attained a sense of urgency" means that he entered into seclusion, thinking, "Even a deity is thus admonishing me," or else, having exerted supreme energy, he set out upon the path of ultimate seclusion itself. First.
2. Commentary on the *Upaṭṭhāna Sutta*.
222. Regarding "he sleeps well in the second watch": it is said that this one was an arahant. Having gone to a distant village for alms and returned, he put away his bowl and robes in the leaf-hut.
He then descended into a nearby lake, bathed his limbs to take up the coolness, and swept the daytime resting place.
There, having prepared a low couch, he lay down without falling into sleep. Even for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), [sleeping]...
"Indeed, there is bodily fatigue"—it was said "he sleeps well" with reference to that [fatigue] for the purpose of its removal. "He addressed him" means:
thinking, "This bhikkhu has taken up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence of the Teacher and yet sleeps by day;
and this daytime sleep, when indulged in, destroys welfare both in this present life and in future lives," she thought, "I shall reprove him," and so she spoke.

"Of one who is afflicted": there are three kinds of affliction—the afflicted by old age, the afflicted by disease, and the afflicted by defilements. It is with reference to the one afflicted by defilements that he said this. "Of one pierced by arrows":
like being pierced in the heart by a poisoned spear-arrow, so it is for one pierced by the arrow of craving, which is smeared with the poison of ignorance.
"Of one who is suffering": of one who is being struck.

Now, speaking of the danger in sense pleasures, he says "impermanent," and so forth. In that context, "unsupported" means not supported by craving or views. Why does it not distress one who has gone forth? He asks: why does such a one whose taints are destroyed not distress him during the daytime sleep, and why would it not distress one such as him? Or perhaps this is the Elder’s own statement; therefore, this is the meaning here: *Asitaṃ taṃ namassantā, asitaṃ taṃ namassatha;* *Asitaṃ taṃ namassantā, sabbadukkham upaccagun ti.* "Worshipping him who is unattached, worship him who is unattached; worshipping him who is unattached, you have transcended all suffering. —Why should daytime sleep afflict one like me, who am liberated among the bound, who has drunk [the nectar of truth], and who has gone forth as one whose taints are destroyed?
It will not afflict him. This same method applies to the remaining verses. For according to the side of the deity’s argument, the meaning is:

“Such a one who has gone forth with taints destroyed is not afflicted by daytime sleep; how much less, then, will one such as this be afflicted? He will certainly not be afflicted. Regarding the Elder:
Regarding the phrase *vacanapakkhe*: “Why would one such as me, who has gone forth with taints destroyed, be scorched by daytime sleep? He is certainly not scorched”—this is the meaning.
This, however, is the commentary on the words not [yet] explained (*anuttānapadavaṇṇanā*). *Vinayā* means by means of discipline (*vinaya*).

*Samatikkamā* means by means of the transcendence of ignorance rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). *Taṃ ñāṇaṃ* means that knowledge of the Four Noble Truths. *Paramodānaṃ* means supremely pure.
"One who has gone forth" means one who has gone forth and is endowed with such knowledge as this. "By clear vision" means by the clear vision of the fourth path.
"One who has aroused energy" means one whose energy is exerted and whose energy is perfected. The second [sutta].
3. Commentary on the Kassapagotta Sutta.

223. "In the third [case], they kill one deer-hunter. Regarding "he exhorted": it is said that this deer-hunter, having eaten his morning meal, entered the forest with the intention, "I shall kill deer.
Seeing a red deer, he pursued it, thinking, "I shall strike it with my spear," and came near the Elder who was seated for his midday rest in the manner described in the first sutta.
He departed. Then the elder said to him, “Lay follower, this act of taking life leads to the states of misery and leads to a short lifespan.
It is possible to support one’s wife by other means, such as farming or trade; do not perform such a cruel deed.
Out of respect, thinking, “The great elder MahāPaṃsukūlika is speaking,” he stopped and began to listen.
Then, thinking, "I shall arouse his desire to hear," the Elder set fire to his thumb. He saw even with his eyes and heard even with his ears;
but his mind thought: "The deer must have gone to such-and-such a place, or descended to such-and-such a ford;
having gone there, I will kill it, eat as much meat as I desire, and take the remainder on my carrying-pole."
"Having gone, I will bring back my little son"—thus he runs after the deer, following its very tracks.
This was said with reference to the Elder who was teaching the Dhamma to one whose mind was thus distracted: "He admonishes. "He addressed him" means:
"This elder is like one carving wood that is not wood, or sowing seed where it is not a field; he ruins his own work as well. I shall reprove him too," thinking thus, he spoke.
"Appapañña" means devoid of wisdom. "Acetasa" means lacking a mind capable of understanding causes.
"Mandova" means like a blind fool. "Suṇāti" means he hears your discourse on the Dhamma. "Na vijānāti" means he does not understand its meaning.
"Āloketi" means he gazes upon your thumb as it blazes with the supernormal power of an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*). "Na passati" means here—
"He does not see this reason: 'There is neither oil, nor wick, nor lamp-stand;
yet this burns by the power of the Elder. 'Ten lights' means ten lamps on the ten fingers. 'Forms' refers to causal forms (*kāraṇarūpa*).
'The eye' is the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). 'He attained a sense of spiritual urgency' means [thinking], 'What use have I for this? and, exerting his energy, [he attained] supreme seclusion."
He entered upon the path to arahantship. Third. 4.
Commentary on the Sambahula Sutta. 224.
In the fourth [sutta], "a number" (sambahulā) refers to many masters of the Suttas, masters of the Abhidhamma, and masters of the Vinaya. "Dwell" (viharanti) means...
Having received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the Teacher, they dwelt there. Regarding the phrase "they departed":
it is said that when people saw them approaching a certain village in that district, their hearts were filled with faith;
they prepared rugs and coverings in a rest-house, offered rice gruel and solid food, and sat down nearby. The Elder [addressed] one preacher of the Dhamma, saying: "The Dhamma..."
“Tell us,” he said. He (Citta) gave a discourse on the Dhamma.
The people, having gained confidence, offered him choice food at the time of the meal. The Great Elder delivered a pleasing expression of gratitude for the meal.
The people, becoming even more devout, requested him to stay right there for the three-month rains retreat, and [they provided him with] excellent means of travel for coming and going.
Having had dwellings constructed in that place, they attended upon him with the four requisites.
On the day of the entry into the rains retreat, the Elder exhorted the monks: "Friends, you have received a meditation subject in the presence of the Teacher, who is so venerable;
indeed, the appearance of a Buddha is rare. Having listened to the Dhamma for eight days of the month, abandon socializing in groups and be diligent."
“Dwell [thus]. From that time forth, they applied themselves and strove. Sometimes they held all-night sessions for hearing the Dhamma;
sometimes they answered questions; sometimes they engaged in exertion.
On the days when they heard the Dhamma, the dawn would break while they were still preaching the Dhamma. On the days when they answered questions, a learned bhikkhu [would explain] the question...
"The wise one answers when asked" refers specifically to those who engage in the practice of asking questions and providing answers.
"On the day of striving, having struck the gong at sunset, they descend to the walking path and undertake the exertion" refers specifically to those who do so.
Having spent the rainy season in this manner and performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), they departed; it is with reference to them that this was said. "Lamenting" means...
Having said such things as, "Now, where shall I obtain such a sweet hearing of the Dhamma and discussion of questions?", she wept.
*Khāyati* means it is perceived, appears, or manifests. *Ko me* means "where are these?
*Vajjibhūmiyā* means they have gone toward the Vajji country. *Magā viya* means just as deer, wandering here and there on various mountain slopes or in forest thickets...

—“This belongs to our mother, this belongs to our father, it has come down through our lineage”—without grasping at such things, they wander wherever there is a comfortable range for their alms-gathering and where there are no obstacles.

In the same way, monks who are homeless and without a house, without grasping at the thought, “This, friends, belongs to our teachers and preceptors; it has come down through our lineage,” wherever...
For them, a favorable climate, suitable food, a favorable person, a suitable dwelling, and a favorable opportunity to hear the Dhamma are easily obtained;
they dwell there. This is the fourth [simile].
5. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta.
225. In the fifth [chapter], "Ānanda" refers to the Elder Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika. "Ativelan" means past the proper time.
"Gihisaññattibahulo" means frequently admonishing householders both by night and by day. After the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa said to the Elder [Ānanda]:
"Friend, having entered the rains retreat at Rājagaha, we shall recite the Dhamma; go..."
“Having entered the forest, you should exert yourself for the sake of attaining the three higher paths. Taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, he went to the kingdom of Kosala;
after staying in a certain forest dwelling, on the following day he entered a village.
When the people saw the Elder, they said, “Venerable Ānanda, formerly you used to come with the Teacher. Today you have come alone.”
They arrived and lamented at length, saying: "Where have you come from, leaving the Teacher behind? Whose bowl and robes will you now take and wander with?
To whom will you give water for the mouth and tooth-sticks? Whose cell will you sweep, and whose duties and services will you perform?
Then the Elder said: "Friends, do not grieve; do not lament. All conditioned things are impermanent. And so forth.
Having spoken thus and consoled them, he would go to his own dwelling place at the conclusion of the meal.
People also went there every evening and lamented in the same manner. The Elder likewise exhorted them in that way. It was with reference to this that it was said:
"He addressed [them]"—meaning that having heard the discourse of the Saṅgha of monks, the Elder thought, "I shall perform the duty of a recluse."
"Having entered the forest, he now dwells as if instructing householders;
the Teacher’s dispensation remains like a heap of flowers that has not been gathered, and he does not perform the compilation of the Dhamma. I shall reprove him," thinking thus, he spoke.
*Pasakkiya* means having entered. *Hadayasmiṃ opiya* means having placed [the matter] within the heart both by way of its function and its object.
“One who exerts energy with the thought, ‘I shall attain Nibbāna,’ is said to apply Nibbāna to the heart by way of function (*kicca*);

whereas one who sits having entered a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) that has Nibbāna as its object applies it by way of object (*ārammaṇa*). It is with reference to both of these that he speaks.
‘A meditator’: one who meditates by means of two jhānas. ‘Chatter’ (*biḷibiḷikā*): this is idle chatter with householders. The fifth [chapter].”
6. Commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta 226.

In the sixth [verse], "former wives" (*purāṇadutiyikā*) refers to those who were chief queens (*aggamahesī*) in a previous existence. "She shines" (*sobhasi*) means she shone in the past and she shines now as well.
"Ill-fated" (*duggatā*) does not mean ill-fated in terms of a miserable rebirth (*gati-duggati*); for they are established in a happy destination (*sugati*), possessing prosperity.
They experience [suffering], yet they are miserable due to the miserable course of practice. For when they pass away from there, they are reborn even in the hells;

thus they are "miserable. As for "established": one who establishes himself in identity-establishment (sakkāya) establishes himself by way of eight causes—being lustful, he establishes himself through lust;
being corrupt, through hatred... being deluded, through delusion... being bound, through conceit...
It is established through being grasped by way of views; it is established through being made firm by way of latent tendencies;
it is established through being led astray by way of doubt; it is established through being distracted by way of restlessness. Those [afflictions] too are established in this very manner.
"Of gods and men" means of gods and humans. "There is none now," she said; for that goddess was possessed of powerful affection for the Elders and was unable to return. At that time...
Having arrived, he swept the courtyard, and provided water for rinsing the mouth, tooth-sticks, drinking water, and water for washing.

The Elder consumed these without even looking at them. One day, as the Elder was wandering for alms with a tattered robe seeking scraps of cloth, someone placed a divine garment upon a rubbish heap and departed. Seeing it, the Elder picked it up and looked at it.
Seeing the cloth, he recognized, "This is a fine cloth," and thinking, "That will suffice," he took it.
With that very material, his robe was completed. Then three people—the two Chief Disciples and the Elder Anuruddha—wove the robe.
The Teacher, having prepared a needle, gave it to him. When his robe was finished, as he went for alms, deities provided him with almsfood.
Sometimes she came to the Elder alone, and sometimes with herself as her second;
but on that occasion, having come with herself as her third, she approached the Elder at his daytime resting place and said, "We are called Manāpakāyikā (the 'Pleasant-Body' goddesses);
we can fashion any form we desire in our minds. The Elder thought, "These women say this; I shall test them. Let them all become blue."
Knowing the elder’s intention, they all became blue-colored; likewise, they became yellow, red, and white.
Then they thought, “The elder delights in seeing us,” and they began to perform a concert:
one sang, another danced, and another snapped her fingers. The elder withdrew his senses. Then [they thought], “It is not for us...”
Knowing that "the Elder relishes this vision," and finding neither affection nor intimacy [therein], they became disenchanted and began to depart.
The Elder, perceiving their intention to leave, spoke this verse while declaring his attainment of Arahatship, so that they would not return again and again.
Therein, *vikkhīṇo* means "exhausted. *Jātisaṃsāro* means the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of births here and there. This is the sixth [chapter].
7. Commentary on the Nāgadatta Sutta 227.

Regarding the seventh [case], "at too early a time": having slept through the entire night, he enters at the very break of dawn after sweeping a little with a broom made of *koṭi* grass, washing his face, and seeking alms for rice-gruel. "At too late a time" means: having taken his rice-gruel...
Having gone to the sitting hall and drunk water, he lay down in one place and fell asleep.
Thinking, "I shall receive choice almsfood at the mealtime of the people," he rose when midday was approaching;
having taken water with his water-strainer and wiped his eyes, he went for alms, ate as much as he required, and when midday had passed—
He steps back. "And having arrived during the day" means that by one who has entered too early, other monks ought to have arrived earlier;
however, you have come at far too late in the day—this is the meaning. "I am afraid of Nāgadatta" means that I am afraid of that Nāgadatta. "Suppagabbha" means exceedingly shameless.
"In families" refers to the families of supporters, such as those of the kṣatriya caste and so forth. This is the seventh [chapter].
8. Commentary on the *Kulagharaṇīsutta* 228.
In the eighth [verse], "one who has reached deep immersion" (*ajjhogāḷhappatta*) means one who has attained penetration.

It is said that he, having received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the presence of the Teacher, entered that forest grove and on the following day went into the village for alms with inspiring qualities such as being "excellent" (*abhikkanta*) and so forth.
A certain family, having gained confidence in his deportment, paid homage with the fivefold prostration and gave him almsfood.
Having heard his expression of gratitude after the meal, they gained even greater confidence and invited him, saying, "Venerable sir, please accept alms here always.
The Elder consented, and while consuming their food, he exerted his energy.
Having gathered [the requisites] and striving, he attained arahantship and thought: "This family has been very helpful to me;
what would be the point of going elsewhere? Experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), he remained right there.
Regarding the phrase "he addressed [her]," it is said that she, not knowing the Elder’s state of having destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), thought: "This elder does not go to another village..."
"He goes nowhere else; he does not sit at the foot of a tree or in a sitting-hall and so forth, but enters the house and sits there at all times.
Both of these have reached a secure footing and found a firm foundation. Perhaps he might corrupt this family;
I shall reprove him. Therefore, she spoke.
*Saṇṭhāne* means at a resting place near the city gate where people have set down their goods.
*Saṅgamma* means having come together. *Mantenti* means they speak. *Mañca tañcā* means they speak this and they speak that.
*Kimantaraṃ* means for what reason? *Bahū hi saddā paccūhā* means there are many such discordant sounds in the world. *Na tena* means not by that.
For that reason, or by that ascetic, one should not be dejected.
"Not indeed by that" shows that a being is not defiled by the words spoken by others, but rather is defiled only by the evil kamma committed by oneself.
"Just like a deer of the wind" means just as a deer of the wind in the forest becomes agitated by the sound of leaves and other things stirred by the wind.
Thus, the meaning is: "he who is one who relies on the protection of the Dhamma. "His vow does not succeed" means that for him, whose mind is light, the vow does not come to fruition.
However, the Elder should be understood as one whose vow is fulfilled because he has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
The eighth [sutta]. 9. Commentary on the Vajjiputtaka Sutta.
229. Regarding the ninth [story], the son of a king in the Vajji kingdom, known as Vajjiputtaka, renounced the world after casting off his royal parasol.
"The all-night festival" refers to the festival celebrated by proclaiming the Kattika constellation, during which the entire city is adorned with banners, flags, and the like.
For this constellation remains connected [in splendor] as far as the realm of the Four Great Kings. "The sound of the resonance of musical instruments, cymbals, and percussion" means...
The sound of the resonance of beaten drums and other instruments, as well as played lutes and the like. He spoke thus:
it is said that in Vesālī there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings, and an equal number of their subordinate officers, generals, and so forth.
When they had adorned themselves and descended onto the street for the purpose of a festival celebration, [he spoke] at the Great Walkway (mahācaṅkama) measuring sixty cubits.
While walking back and forth, having seen the moon situated in the midst of the sky, he stood leaning against a wooden plank at the end of the walkway and spoke.
"Like a piece of wood cast away in the forest"—this is because, being devoid of clothing, wrapping cloths, and ornaments, he has become like a log discarded in the woods.
"Pāpiyo" means there is someone else even more wretched than we are. "Pihayanti" means they long for.
The meaning is: "Many desire for you who are an elder, a forest-dweller, a wearer of rag-robes, an alms-food eater, one who goes on a continuous round for alms, one of few wishes, and contented.
"Leading to heaven" means for those going to heaven and for those who have already gone there. The ninth [chapter].
10. Commentary on the Sajjhāya Sutta.

230. In the phrase *dasame yaṃ sudanti*, *yaṃ* is merely a particle. *Sajjhāyabahulo* means one who recites for a greater length of time because of his frequent recitation, both for the sake of mastery and for the sake of deliverance.
It is said that after he had swept the teacher’s daytime sitting place, he would stand waiting for the teacher.
Then, seeing him approaching, he would go out to meet him and receive his bowl and robe.

Having fanned him with a palm-leaf fan while he sat on the prepared seat, and having asked for water, washed his feet, anointed them with oil, and paid homage, he stood by and received the recitation; then, until sunset, he engaged in the study of the texts.
He prepared water at the bathing shed and kindled a fire on a charcoal brazier. When the teacher had finished bathing and returned—
Having wiped his feet with water, performed back-massage, paid homage, and received the recitation (uddesa), he practices recitation during the first watch;
during the middle watch, he rests his body; and during the last watch, having received the recitation, he practices recitation until the rising of the dawn.
Then, he contemplates the cessation of sound as its destruction. Thereafter, [he contemplates] the remaining derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Having developed insight into the five aggregates as "name-and-form" which is the true nature of reality, he attained Arahantship.
"Appossukka" means one who is free from anxiety regarding the memorization of texts and the performance of recitation. "Saṅkasāyati" means:

"Now that the purpose for which I was performing recitation has reached its fulfillment, what need have I now for recitation?"—thus [he speaks] due to the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"He passed away. "He addressed [him]" means: "What indeed has become unwell for this elder, or perhaps for his teacher?
For what reason does he not recite with his sweet voice as before? Having approached and standing nearby, she spoke.
“Dhammapadāni” (Verses of the Dhamma): here, the entire word of the Buddha is intended. “Nādhīyasi”: you do not recite;
or rather, the reading is “nādiyasi,” meaning you do not take up [the teachings]. “Pasaṃsanti”: they praise;
the preacher of the Dhamma receives praise, and those who are experts in the Abhidhamma, the Suttas, and the Vinaya become his praisers. “Virāgena”: by means of the Noble Path.

"Having known" means having understood. He explains that "the wise say 'laying down' refers to the relinquishing of what has been seen, heard, and so forth," but this does not apply to the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*).
To this extent, it is not the case that one must always be engaged in recitation simply because "an elder does not cause the Buddha’s word to be laid down";
rather, after having recited—[one reflects]: "Of such-and-such a meaning or doctrine..."
"Or is it capable of being a support? Having understood this, one should practice for the sake of bringing an end to the suffering of saṃsāra.
The Tenth. 11. Commentary on the Discourse on Unwholesome Thoughts (Akusalavitakkasutta). 231.
In the eleventh [discourse], "unwholesome thoughts" refers to the three great types of thought, beginning with sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*). "Inappropriate attention" (*ayoniso manasikāra*)...
"By way of unskillful attention. "He" refers to you yourself. "Relinquish that which is improper" means: avoid this unskillful attention.
With the verse beginning "The Teacher," he explains the meditation subject of the "Inspiring One" (Pāsādika).
"Without doubt, rapture and bliss"—you will certainly attain powerful rapture and bliss. This is the eleventh [section].
12. Commentary on the *Majjhanhika-sutta* (The Midday Discourse). 232.
Regarding what ought to be said concerning the twelfth discourse, that has already been stated in the *Devatāsaṃyutta*, in the *Nandana-vagga*. This is the twelfth. 13.
Commentary on the *Pākatindriya-sutta* (The Discourse on the Unrestrained Faculties).
233. The thirteenth [sutta] in the *Devaputtasaṃyutta*, the *Jantu-devaputtasutta*, is already explained in detail. This is the thirteenth. 14.
Commentary on the *Gandhatthenasutta*: 234.
Regarding "he addressed him" (*ajjhabhāsī*): having seen that bhikkhu holding a stalk and smelling a lotus, he spoke to him.
“This bhikkhu, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, has entered the forest to practice the duty of a recluse, yet he gazes intently upon the object of fragrance.
Since he has smelled it today, he will smell it tomorrow and the day after;
thus, that craving for fragrance will increase and destroy his welfare both in this life and in the lives to come. Do not—”
"Let it vanish while I am looking on; I shall rebuke him," she thought, and having approached, she spoke. "This is one part of theft":
among the five categories of objects to be stolen, such as visible forms and so forth, this is one part; the meaning is that it is one portion.
"I do not carry away" means I do not go taking it with me. "From afar," having taken hold of the stalk from a distance, she bent it.
"Standing at a distance, I smell [it]," he says. "By its color" means by its cause. "Yvāyaṃ" means "this one who.
It is said that while he was conversing with the deity, a certain ascetic descended and began to dig for lotus roots and so forth;
it is with reference to him that he spoke thus. "One whose work is crowded" means one whose activity is thus impure. It may also mean "one whose work is not yet exhausted."
The meaning is "a harsh occupation. It is not called [a thief of fragrance] or "a thief of flowers"—why is it not so called?
It is called "one who is crowded with cruelty," meaning one who is very wicked or intensely wicked; therefore, it is not so called.
"Smeared like a nurse’s garment" means just as a nurse’s worn-out garment is smeared with excrement, urine, dust, mud, and the like, even so...
"Stained by lust, hatred, and so forth. "I am worthy to speak" means "I am fit to speak. It is said that the exhortation of a deity is like the instruction of a Sugata;
it is not obtained by those who are base, of inferior disposition, or who have entered upon a wrong path.
However, in that particular state of existence, those individuals who are capable of attaining the paths and fruits obtain it; therefore, he spoke thus.
"Seeking purity" means seeking purity in virtue, concentration, and wisdom. "As large as a cloud" means like the mass of a rain-cloud.
"You know" means you know that "I am pure. "You might say" means you would speak thus. "We do not depend on you" refers to what the deity thought:
"This bhikkhu thinks, 'There is a deity who desires my welfare; she will reprove and remind me.'"
“Even if he should indulge in negligence, I will not accept his word. Therefore he spoke thus.

“You yourself” means you alone. “You would know” means you would know. “By which” means by whatever action you would go to a happy destination—that action you yourself would know. The fourteenth [chapter].
Thus ends the commentary on the Vanasaṃyutta (Forest Chapter) in the Sāratthappakāsinī,
the commentary on the Saṃyuttanikāya.
10. *Yakkhasaṃyutta* 1.
Commentary on the *Indakasutta* 235.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the *Yakkhasaṃyutta*: "Of Indaka" refers to the yakkha who dwells at Indakūṭa. For from among the yakkhas...
The name was obtained from a *kūṭa* and from a *yakkha*. "They do not say that form is the living being":
if the Buddhas do not say that form is the living being, the meaning is that they do not say that form is a sentient being (*satta*) or a person (*puggala*).
"How indeed is this? means how is this so? "Whither does this lump of bones and sinews go? refers to the lump of bones and sinews of that sentient being.
"From where does it come? Here, by the mention of "bones," three hundred bones are included; by the mention of "lumps of flesh," nine hundred pieces of flesh are included.
[The questioner] asks: "If form is not the soul, then from where do these bones and these pieces of flesh come for it?
"How indeed does this settle in the womb? By what cause?"

“Does this being cling, adhere, and remain within the mother’s womb? This was likely a *puggalavādin* (Personalist) spirit (*yakkha*), who, having grasped the view that “the being is born in the mother’s womb all at once,” claimed that the mother of the being lying in the womb eats fish, meat, and so forth;
yet all these [foods], having been digested in a single night, dissolve away like froth.
He spoke thus because of the view that "if form were not a living being, it would simply dissolve away in this very manner.
Then the Blessed One, showing that "it does not arise all at once in the mother's womb, but rather grows gradually," said:
"First there is the *kalala*," and so forth. Therein, "first" means together with the first rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*).

There is no name such as "Tissa" or "Phussa"; rather, at the tip of the thread spun from three fibers of wool, there is a *kalala* the size of a drop of oil on a surface, with reference to which it was said:
"Just as a drop of sesame oil, or a pure essence of ghee."
“Thus, resembling in color, it is called *kalala*. From the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*;

therefore, after seven days have passed, from that *kalala* there arises what is called the *abbuda*, which has the appearance of water used for washing meat, and the name *kalala* disappears. And this has been said:
“For seven days it is *kalala*; when fully developed and gathered together,”
"As it turns, that state becomes what is called the *abbuda* (the bubble).
From the *abbuda*, the *pesī* (the mass) is born; thus, after the lapse of seven days from that *abbuda*, there arises what is called the *pesī*, resembling a dissolved drop of honey.
This should be illustrated by the example of pepper and molasses. For instance, when village girls take well-ripened peppers and [place them] at the edge of their garments...
Having made it into a bundle and squeezed it, they take the essence, place it in a potsherd, and set it out in the sun;
as it dries, it exudes from all sides. Such is the *pesi*; the name "*abbuda*" disappears. And this has been said:
"For seven days it is an *abbuda*; when fully matured, it is removed."
“Turning back into that state, it produces what is called *pesī*.

From the *pesī*, the *ghana* is produced: after seven days have passed, there arises from the *pesī* a lump of flesh called the *ghana*, shaped like a hen’s egg, and the name *pesī* disappears. And this has been said:
“For seven days it remains as *pesī*; when fully matured, it becomes the *ghana*.”
As it turns, it comes to possess that state and is called a "solid mass" (ghana).
"Just as a hen’s egg is perfectly round all over,
so too is the shape of the solid mass produced by the condition of kamma."
Regarding the statement, "Thick branches arise," on the fifth week five swellings arise for the sake of the two hands, the two feet, and the head;
it is with reference to this that it was said: "Monks, on the fifth week, five swellings are formed through kamma."

From this point on, having passed six, seven, and so forth, up to seven days, and having abbreviated the teaching, he says "hair" and so forth to show that the time of full development is reached in forty-two days. In that context, it is said:
"Hair, body hair, and nails as well"—these grow during those forty-two days.
"He sustains himself there by means of that" means that the tube arising from his navel is connected as one with the mother's abdominal wall;
it is perforated like the stalk of a lotus. Through it, the essence of food flows and produces the material form originated by food (*āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).
In this way, he sustains himself for ten months. "A person gone into the mother’s womb" means gone through the side of the mother’s womb.
The meaning is: "one who has gone inside the womb. Thus the Blessed One shows:
"In this way, O yakkha, this being grows gradually in the mother's womb; it does not arise all at once. First. 2.
Commentary on the Sutta Named after Sakka.
236. "In the second [verse], 'the one named Sakka' refers to a certain *yakkha* of that name; it is said that he was a *yakkha* belonging to the faction of Māra.
'Of the one completely liberated' means of the one liberated from the three realms of existence (*bhava*). 'Whatever other' means whatever else. 'By way of appearance' means by way of reason.
'Association' means dwelling together; the meaning is the quality of a witness and the quality of a friend. 'The wise one' means the Supremely Wise One, the Sambuddha. This is the second [section]."
3. Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta 237.
Regarding the third [sutta]: "At Gayā" means in the village of Gayā; the meaning is that it was situated in dependence upon a village established not far from Gayā.
"A spiked couch" (*ṭaṅkitamañca*) refers to a long couch made by boring holes in the middle of the legs and inserting cross-pieces (*aṭani*). Of that...
"There is no such thing as 'this is above' or 'this is below'; even when turned over, it remains the same, and they place it in the position of a deity.
A house built by spreading a stone over four other stones is called a "stake-bed" (*ṭaṅkitamañca*).
"Of Sūciloma" means of one whose body hair resembles the needle of a *kathina* cloth. He, it is said, [lived] during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Having gone forth, he had come from a distant place with his limbs covered in sweat and grime;

he lay down upon a well-prepared couch belonging to the Saṅgha without showing respect or spreading a mat over it. Although his moral conduct was pure, that deed appeared to him like a black spot on a clean cloth.
Being unable to produce any spiritual distinction in that very existence, he passed away.
At the gateway to Gayāgāma, he was reborn as a *yakkha* in a heap of refuse.
As soon as he was reborn, his entire body became as if pierced all over by stiff needles.
Then one day, at dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world, [perceived] that *yakkha* with his very first act of attention.

Seeing him come into his range of vision, [the Buddha] thought: "This man has experienced great suffering for the duration of one *buddhantara*. What means of safety might there be for him now that he has come to me?
As he reflected, he saw that the man possessed the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for the first path.
Then, desiring to show him favor, he put on a well-dyed inner robe, draped himself in the Great Robe of the Sugata, and [assumed a form] like a celestial mansion.

Leaving the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), he went to a rubbish heap smelling foul with the carcasses of elephants, cattle, horses, humans, dogs, and so forth, and there he sat as if in a great fragrant chamber.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma.
He was "rough" (khara) because his body was rough like the back of a crocodile or like the uneven surface of a roof covered with tiles.

It is said that during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, there was a lay follower endowed with virtue who one day, on the ground of the monastery covered with rugs and such, lay down without spreading his own upper robe over the property belonging to the Sangha.
Without dividing the oil belonging to the Sangha and without spreading his own upper robe, he lay down upon the property of the Sangha. The property of the Sangha...
Some say that, instead of dividing the oil, he smeared his own body with it using his own hands.
Because of that deed, being unable to be reborn in heaven, he was reborn as a *yakkha* at a rubbish heap by the gate of that very village.
As soon as he was reborn, his entire body became of the aforementioned appearance. Thus, those two were born as companions.
Thus the harsh nature of the harsh one is to be understood.
"Passing by not far away" means they travel in a nearby place while seeking pasture or going to a meeting place.
Among them, Sūciloma did not see the Teacher; however, Kharaloma saw him first and [informed] Sūciloma.
He said this to the yakkha: “This is a recluse, my friend; this one who has entered and is sitting in your abode is a recluse.
“This is no recluse, he is a sham-recluse (samaṇaka),” [the yakkha replied].
It seems he calls one a “sham-recluse” who, upon seeing him, flees in fear, whereas one who does not fear is a true recluse. Therefore, thinking, “Seeing me, he will flee in fear,” he spoke thus.
"He drew his body near" means that, having manifested a terrifying form, opened his great mouth, and caused the hairs on his entire body to stand erect, he drew his body near.
"He drew it away" means that he drew it back slightly, as one would a hundred pieces of precious gold.
"Wretched" means base and unpleasant; he was like excrement, like fire, and like a black snake.
"He should be avoided; he must not be accepted on account of this golden-colored body.
When this was said, Sūciloma, thinking "My touch is indeed wicked," became angry and spoke that question beginning with "O ascetics...
[and so forth]. "Or I shall throw your mind into confusion" means that for those non-human beings who wish to cause the mind to waver, their face is white and their belly is blue.
Having manifested a terrifying physical form with reddened hands and feet, a massive head, and blazing eyes, they show it;
or they let out a terrifying sound; or, while they are still speaking, they thrust their hand into the mouth and crush the heart.
Because of that, those beings become insane and deranged. It was with reference to this that he said: "Beyond the Ganges."
"Having seized you by both feet and dragged you along, I shall hurl you to the other shore of the Ganges so that you never return," he said.
"Sadevake... and so forth; the meaning is exactly as previously stated. "Ask whatever you desire":
"Ask anything at all you wish, and I shall explain it all to you without remainder"—thus he offers an invitation to question his omniscience.
"Of what cause, of what origin? means "What is their cause, what is their condition? "They let go of the mind like boys letting go of a crow":
just as boys catch a crow and let it go—release it—so he asks: from where do these evil thoughts arise and let go of the mind? "Of this as their cause" (*itonidānā*):
this personal existence (*attabhāva*) is their cause; thus they are "of this as their cause. "Born from this" (*itojātā*): born from this personal existence.
"Arising from this, thoughts of the mind": just as boys, having tied a crow's foot with a long string, wrap the end of that string around their finger and let it go;
although it flies far away, it falls back again at the very feet of those boys—just so, thoughts of evil arising from this selfhood let the mind go forth.
"Born of affection" means born from the moisture of craving (*taṇhāsineha*). "Self-born" means born within oneself.

"Like the growth of a banyan trunk" means like the aerial roots (*pāroha*) that grow from the trunk of a banyan tree. "Numerous" means many and of various kinds, referring to evil thoughts (*pāpavitakka*) and the defilements associated with them.
"Entangled" means stuck or clinging. "In sensual pleasures" means in objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*). "As a *māluvā* creeper spreads through the forest" means as follows:
Just as the māluvā creeper in the forest, having grown by depending on a tree, stands entwining and overspreading it repeatedly from its base up to its top, and from its top down to its base;

even so, the manifold *kilesa-kāmas* (defilement-desires) are attached to the manifold *vatthu-kāmas* (object-bases), or rather, the manifold beings are attached to the *vatthu-kāmas* by means of those *kilesa-kāmas*. Those who...
"Knowing" means they know the personal existence (*attabhāva*) mentioned here as "arisen from self.
"From whatever source" means they also know that which is the source of this personal existence.
"They dispel it" means they dispel, by means of the truth of the path, the truth of the origin which is the source of the truth of suffering known as personal existence.
"Those who cross the difficult-to-cross": those who extract the truth of the origin [of suffering] cross this flood of defilements (*kilesogha*) which is so hard to cross. "Never crossed before":

even in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), it has never been crossed, not even in a dream. "For the sake of non-becoming": for the sake of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*), which is designated as non-becoming.
Thus, by means of this verse, he elucidates the four truths, culminating in Arhatship.

He brought his teaching to a conclusion. At the end of the discourse, Sūciloma, standing in that very place, directed his knowledge according to the teaching and was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

Since those who have attained stream-entry do not remain in a defiled state of existence, at the moment he obtained the fruit, all the white scabs, pustules, and needles on his body fell away. He stood there clothed in celestial garments.

Wearing a divine, excellent *dukūla* upper robe, wrapped in a divine turban, and adorned with divine ornaments, perfumes, and garlands, he became golden-hued and obtained the honors due to a terrestrial deity. This is the third [sutta].
4. Commentary on the Maṇibhadda Sutta.
238. "In the fourth [verse], 'happiness increases' means he attains happiness. 'Better day by day' means better every single day; the meaning is that it is always better.
'He is not released from enmity' means that merely by thinking 'I am mindful,' one is not freed from enmity. 'Of whom' refers to which Arhat.
'Through non-violence' means through both compassion and the preliminary stage of compassion. 'The essence of loving-kindness' refers to that very loving-kindness."
And he develops loving-kindness as a preliminary stage. Alternatively, "aṃsa" means a portion. One for whom loving-kindness is a portion is "mettaṃsa.

This is what is meant: for that Arahant whose mind at all times delights in non-violence, and who possesses the portion of loving-kindness toward all beings, there is no enmity whatsoever with any person.
“A *yakkha*. The fourth [section]. 5.
Commentary on the Sānu Sutta.
239. Regarding the fifth: “He was seized by a *yakkha*”; it is said that he was the only son of that female lay follower (*upāsikā*). Then him...
She ordained him while he was still very young. From the time of his ordination, he became virtuous and perfect in his conduct;
he performed his duties toward his teachers, preceptors, guests, and others with great care.
Rising early on the eighth day of the month, he would prepare water in the water-shed, sweep the assembly hall for the hearing of the Dhamma, light the lamps, and [proceed] with a sweet voice...
He would announce the time for hearing the Dhamma. When the bhikkhus recognized his strength, they would request of him, "Sāmaṇera, recite the *sara-bhāṇa*.

Without offering any refusal, such as saying, "I suffer from heart trouble" or "Coughing afflicts me," he would ascend the Dhamma-seat and, as if pouring down the celestial Ganges, deliver the *sara-bhāṇa* while descending [from the seat], saying: "To me..."
"He says, 'My parents also have a share in this recitation. However, the people do not know that his parents have been given a share.
Yet in his immediately preceding existence, his mother had been reborn as a female spirit (yakkhinī).
She came along with the deities, and having heard the Dhamma, she said, 'I rejoice in the share given by the novice, dear ones!'"
Since monks endowed with virtue are beloved by the world including its devas, the deities felt shame and reverence for that novice, regarding him as they would Mahābrahmā or a mass of fire.
Out of respect, they looked upon that yakkhinī with gravity. At assemblies such as those for hearing the Dhamma or gathering of yakkhas, they would say, "Sānumātā! Sānumātā!"
They gave the yakkhinī the first seat, the first water, and the first alms-food. Even powerful yakkhas, seeing her, stepped off the path and rose from their seats.
Then the novice, having reached maturity and with his faculties fully developed, being oppressed by a lack of joy, sought to dispel that lack of joy.
Unable to do so, with his hair, beard, and nails grown long, his robes soiled, and having told no one, he took his bowl and outer robe and went to his mother’s house all alone.
When the laywoman saw her son, she paid homage to him and said:
"Dear son, formerly you used to come here together with your teachers, preceptors, or young novices. Why have you come today all alone?"

“Have you returned? he asked. He then expressed his state of longing. The laywoman Saddhā, having shown him the various dangers of the household life and admonishing her son, was unable to convince him; yet, thinking, “Perhaps he will reflect upon it by his own nature,” she urged him on, saying:
“Wait, dear son, until I have prepared your rice gruel. [She then brought] the rice gruel.
Having said, "After you have finished your meal, I will bring out some pleasing garments and give them to you," she prepared a seat and offered it.
The novice sat down. In a mere moment, the laywoman prepared rice gruel and solid food and gave them to him.
Then, sitting not far away with the thought, "I shall prepare the meal," she began washing the rice. At that time, that female spirit—
“Where is the novice? Has he obtained any alms-food, or not? While reflecting thus, she perceived through her supernormal knowledge that he was sitting with the desire to disrobe.
Thinking, “Lest this cause shame for me among the deities, I shall go and create an obstacle to his disrobing,” she approached, took possession of his body, and twisted his neck.
He fell to the ground. With his eyes rolling and saliva trickling from his mouth, he writhed upon the earth.
Therefore it is said: "He was seized by a yakkha. She spoke:
having seen that distress of her son, the laywoman went in haste, embraced her son, and [placed him] on her thighs.
She had [the body] laid down. All the inhabitants of the village came and performed the offering rites and other duties. The female lay devotee, lamenting, spoke these verses.

Regarding the "miracle fortnight" (*pāṭihāriyapakkha*): thinking, "We shall perform the welcoming and the sending-off of the eighth-day Uposatha," people undertake the Uposatha factors on the seventh or the ninth day as well; likewise for the welcoming and sending-off of the fourteenth and fifteenth days.
Even on the thirteenth or the first day of the month, they undertake [the observance], thinking, "We shall perform the non-observance of the rains residence.
For half a month between two *pavāraṇā* ceremonies, they remain fixed in the *uposatha*. It is with reference to this that it is said, "and the fortnight of miracles (*pāṭihāriyapakkha*).
"Well-endowed with the eight factors" means well-endowed with, or associated with, the eight factors.
The meaning is as follows: "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means the supreme conduct. "Those *yakkhas* do not play" means that the *yakkhas* do not seize them and torment them.
Furthermore, with this verse beginning "On the fourteenth day," a female *yakkhinī* obsessed with the body of a novice monk said:

"Whether openly or in secret" means either in the presence of someone or behind their back. "Desiring release" (*pamutyatthī*) means there is a desire for release. "Even having approached" (*uppaṭṭhāpi*)... [text fragment].
"Even by flying up. He said, "Even if you fly away like a bird, there is still no escape for you.
Having spoken thus, he released the novice. The novice opened his eyes; his mother, with her hair disheveled, gasping and staring, wept.
He did not know that he had been seized by a non-human being, but looking about—
“I was previously sitting on a seat; my mother sat not far away from me and was washing rice.
But now I am sitting on the ground, and my mother sits weeping, gasping and sighing, while all the inhabitants of the village have gathered together.
What could this be? Even as he lay there, he spoke the verse beginning with “O mother, you have died.”

"Having abandoned sensual pleasures" means having relinquished both kinds of sensual pleasure. "She comes back again" means she returns by way of disrobing. "He who was dead lives again"—even though he has disrobed and is now living, he is as good as dead; therefore, she says they weep for him too.
Now, showing the danger in the household life, she spoke the verse beginning with "The pit of embers.

In this context, it is said that the household life is called a "pit of embers" (kukkuḷa) in the sense of its heat. To whom should one complain?—"Run after him, O blessed one!"... [text fragment] ...abhidhāvatha, bhaddaṃ.

Having said, "Let them be yours," he speaks thus: "To whom shall we complain, grumble, or report this misconduct of yours—this state brought about by the yakkha because you wished to disrobe? "Do you wish to burn again?

means that, like goods brought out from a burning house, having been led out of the home and gone forth in the Buddha’s teaching, one [desires to return] again to the household life, which is like a great conflagration.

The meaning is: "Do you wish to burn? As his mother spoke thus again and again, he took note of her words, regained a sense of shame and moral dread (*hiri-ottappa*), and said, "I have no need for the state of a householder.
Then his mother, delighted, saying, "Excellent, dear son," fed him choice food and asked, "How many years old are you, dear son? He replied, "I am of full age."
“Laywoman,” he said. “In that case, my dear, receive the full ordination. He gave him a set of robes.
Having had the three robes made, he was ordained; and while learning the Buddha’s word, he became a master of the Three Piṭakas.

Filling each respective requirement for virtue and the other qualities as they occurred in the texts, he attained Arahantship before long and became a great preacher of the Dhamma. For one hundred and twenty years—
Having stood [there], he caused the entire Jambudīpa to tremble and then attained final Nibbāna.
This is the fifth. 6. Commentary on the Piyaṅkara Sutta (240).
Regarding the sixth [sutta], "at Jetavana": there was a hut called Kosambaka-kuṭi on the outskirts of Jetavana; it was there that he dwelt.
*Dhammapadāni* refers here to the collection consisting of twenty-six chapters that was compiled separately; this is the text intended.
At that time, the Elder, sitting within the monastery, recited the *Appamādavagga* (Chapter on Heedfulness) in a sweet voice by way of *sara-bhañña*.
"Thus he gladdened" means that, it is said, he took his dear son Piyaṅkara on his lap from the western part of the Jeta Grove.
Having set out in search of food, she gradually made her way toward the city;
seeking excrement, urine, spittle, snot, and poor-quality food, she reached the Elder’s dwelling place and heard a sweet sound.
That sound, piercing through her skin and other layers until it struck the marrow of her bones, remained fixed within her heart. Then, while she was searching for food—
Not even the thought of listening arose in his mind; with his ears inclined, he stood listening only to the Dhamma.
However, because the young spirit was so small, he had no interest in hearing the Dhamma.
Oppressed by hunger, he said again and again: "Mother, why do you stand like a stump wherever we go? Are you not seeking any food or sustenance for me?"
She urges her mother on. Thinking, "She is creating an obstacle for my hearing the Dhamma," she comforts her son, saying, "Do not make a sound, Piyaṅkara.
In that context, "do not make a sound" means do not produce a noise.
In the verse beginning with "And among living beings," she shows the five precepts she has undertaken by her own nature. Therein, "I shall restrain myself" (saṃyamāmase) [means...]
"Let us restrain ourselves; let us be self-controlled. By this, abstention from taking life is included; by the second phrase, abstention from false speech;
and by the third phrase, the remaining three abstentions. "May we even be released from the realm of the *pisācas*":

may we indeed, having abandoned the five enmities that arise in the world of *yakkhas*, and having practiced with wise attention (*yoniso*), escape from this birth as a *pisāca* or *yakkha* during this time of drought and famine.
"Let us be released, dear father," he says.
This is the sixth [sutta]. 7. Commentary on the Punabbasu Sutta (241).
Regarding the seventh [sutta], "Now at that time": at what time? At the time when the sun was setting.
At that time, it is said, after the Blessed One had taught the Dhamma to the great multitude following his meal and dismissed them,
he bathed in the bathing pavilion and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber, gazing toward the eastern world-system. Then,
the monks who were rag-robe wearers and alms-collectors— those who wandered alone or in pairs and so forth— [arrived] from their respective dwelling places.
Having gone out and returned, they paid homage to the One of Ten Powers and sat down as if surrounding him with a red curtain.
Then, having understood their inner disposition, the Teacher delivered a discourse on the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna.
Thus he gladdened them. It is said that she, taking her daughter on her lap and holding her son by the finger, [sat] on the back of the Jeta Grove.
Searching for excrement, urine, spittle, and snot near the enclosure wall of the rampart, they eventually reached the gateway of Jeta’s Grove.
And as the Blessed One was saying, “Ānanda, bring the bowl; bring the robe;
give alms to those who eat leftovers,” his voice reached only about twelve cubits all around him. But when he taught the Dhamma, [it reached much further].

Even if the assembly were to sit extending as far as the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), the sound would follow the assembly and not go even a single finger’s breadth outside the assembly, lest the sweet voice be lost for no reason.
There, this female spirit (*yakkhinī*), standing outside the assembly, did not hear the sound; however, for her standing at the gatehouse, there was the great "Buddha-road" (*buddhavīthī*).

The Perfume Chamber appeared standing directly before him. Seeing the assembly motionless—free from nervous fidgeting and the like out of reverence for the Buddha, like the flame of a lamp in a windless place—he thought:

"Surely there must be some precious object here to be distributed, since even a little of the ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, trickling from the bowl or from my hand, falls upon the ground."
Thinking, "Or else I shall obtain one that has fallen [of its own accord]," she entered the interior of the monastery.
A protective deity stationed at the gateway to ward off those who were blocking the entrance saw the yakṣiṇī’s underlying disposition and did not stop her.
