As she and her retinue became one, her sweet voice pierced through the skin and other layers until it reached the marrow of the bones. This—
While she stood motionless for the sake of hearing the Dhamma, her children urged her as before.
Thinking, "They are creating an obstacle to my hearing the Dhamma," she pacified her children by saying, "Be silent, my little ones.
In this context, "until" means "as long as I am listening to the Dhamma, remain silent until then. "Liberation from all bonds" means...
By resorting to Nibbāna, one is released from all fetters; therefore, it is called "the release from all fetters.
*Ativelā* means exceeding the limit, exceeding the measure. *Piyāyanā* means seeking or longing for. *Tato piyataraṃ* means:
"this seeking and longing for this Dhamma is dearer to me than that"—this is the meaning. *Piyatarā*...
Or rather, there is another reading. "Of living beings" (*pāṇinaṃ*) means that he liberates them from suffering.
Who liberates them? One should say, having supplied the word "of living beings" (*pāṇinaṃ*). "The Dhamma which he has fully awakened to" means the Dhamma which the Blessed One has fully awakened to.
"This sister Uttarā is silent too" means he says: "It is not only I who am silent; this sister of mine, Uttarā, is also silent. "Without knowing the True Dhamma" (*saddhammassa anaññāya*).
"Mother, previously too, because we did not understand this very True Dhamma, we now experience this suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth;
thus we lead a life of suffering and dwell in suffering.
"Possessed of eyes" means being possessed of eyes by way of the five kinds of eyes. While teaching the Dhamma, the Blessed One was observing the assembly.

Seeing the underlying potential for the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) in both that female spirit (*yakkhinī*) and her young son, he turned back his discourse and elucidated the teaching on the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard it, while remaining in that very place, the female spirit together with her son was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
However, her daughter also possessed the underlying potential; yet, because she was too young, [he did not teach her].
However, she was unable to accept the teaching.
Now, that female spirit (yakkhinī), offering words of appreciation for her son, said, "Excellent indeed is the one named Wise," and so forth.
"Today I have risen up" means: today I have risen up from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), or I have risen up within the Dispensation (*sāsana*); and you too—
"May you be happy. "Seen by both" means seen by both myself and you.
"May my daughter Uttara also hear this of mine" means she says, "May my daughter Uttara also hear of our state of penetration into the Four Noble Truths.
Simultaneously with the penetration of the Truths, she too—just like Sūciloma—abandoned all her white leprosy, scabies, and other ailments, and obtained divine excellence.

Together with her son. As for her daughter, just as in the world when parents have attained sovereignty, their children likewise possess it, so too did she obtain prosperity solely through the power of her mother.
From that time forth, having obtained a tree near the Gandhakuṭī to dwell in along with her two children, she received the sight of the Buddha morning and evening.
Listening to the Dhamma, he resided right there for a long time. [End of] the seventh [sutta].
8. *Sudattasuttavaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Sudatta Sutta) 242.
In the eighth [sutta], the phrase "on some business" refers to the work of trade. And Anāthapiṇḍika was a merchant-prince from Rājagaha.
And they were mutual brothers-in-law. Whenever there was expensive merchandise for sale in Rājagaha, the merchant of Rājagaha would take it and travel to Sāvatthī with five hundred carts;
having stopped at a distance of one *yojana*, he would let it be known that he had arrived. Anāthapiṇḍika would go out to meet him and pay him great honor.
Having loaded [the goods] onto a single vehicle, he enters Sāvatthī. If the merchandise can be sold quickly, he sells it;
if not, he leaves it at his sister-in-law’s house and departs. Anāthapiṇḍika does exactly the same.
He (the merchant) also went on that occasion for that very business; it was with reference to him that this was said.
On that day, however, the merchant of Rājagaha did not hear the letter sent by Anāthapiṇḍika—standing at a distance of one *yojana*—to inform him of his arrival;
instead, he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma.

Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, for the following day’s meal, and [ordered] the preparation of stoves, the carving of wood, and so forth at his own house.
[The Buddha] had [the hall] constructed. Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "Now he will come out to meet me;
now he will come out to meet me," did not receive a reception even at the door of his house, and having entered the inner house, he received no great welcome.
"What is it, Great Merchant? Is all well with your children? Are you not weary from the road?"—only this much was said.
There was a hospitable reception. Seeing his great preoccupation, [the monk] asked, "Householder, will there be a wedding for you?
Having conversed with him in the manner recorded in the *Khandhaka*, he heard the word "Buddha" from his mouth and attained five-colored rapture (*pañcavaṇṇa-pīti*).
That rapture rose from his head down to the soles of his feet; rising from the soles of his feet, it...
As far as his head went, he rose from both sides and descended into the middle; rising in the middle, he went out to both sides.

Being continuously suffused with rapture, he asked three times, "Householder, do you say 'Buddha'? Householder, I say 'Buddha'! Then [the householder] said, "Even this sound 'Buddha' is rare in the world."
He said: "It was with reference to this that it was said: 'The householder Anāthapiṇḍika heard: "It is said that a Buddha has appeared in the world. Then it occurred to him:
'Today is not the right time. He asked that merchant: 'Where, householder, does the Teacher dwell? Then he [the merchant] replied to him:
'Buddhas are difficult to approach, like venomous serpents; the Teacher is staying in the charnel ground.'"
"It is not possible for those like you to go there at this hour," he was told. Then this thought occurred to him:
"He lies down with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha. It is said that on that day, his mind did not turn even toward his merchandise carts or his attendants;
he did not even take his evening meal. Instead, having ascended a seven-storied palace, he lay upon a well-prepared and exquisitely adorned excellent couch.
Reciting the meditation formula “Buddho, Buddho,” he lay down and fell asleep. Therefore it is said: “He lay down with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha.
Indeed, he rose three times during the night, thinking it was dawn. Thus, when the first watch had passed, he rose and recollected the Buddha;
then a powerful faith arose within him, and there was a radiance of rapture, and all darkness vanished.
The darkness vanished, and it became as if a thousand lamps were lit, like the rising of the moon or the rising of the sun.
Thinking, "I have indeed fallen into a precipice; the sun has risen," he rose and looked up at the moon standing in the vault of the sky.
Seeing that "only one watch of the night has passed, two others remain," he entered again and lay down. By this same method, even at the end of the middle watch—
"At the end of the last watch as well," he said, and he rose three times.
Then, at the end of the last watch, rising right at the powerful dawn, he came out onto the roof-terrace and stood facing the great gate; the seven-storied gate opened of its own accord.
He descended from the palace and set out upon the street.
They opened [the gates] thinking: "This great merchant set out with the intention, 'I will go to attend upon the Buddha.

At his very first sight, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry; having become the foremost attendant of the Three Jewels and having built an incomparable monastery for the Saṅgha, he will be one who leaves the doors open for the Noble Assembly from the four quarters. It is not fitting to close his door."
Having reflected, they opened [the door]. Regarding the phrase "it disappeared": it is said that Rājagaha was crowded with people—nine *koṭis* within the city and nine outside the city;
thus, eighteen *koṭis* of people lived depending on that city.
Being unable to carry out the dead at the proper time, they would stand on watchtowers and throw them over the outer gate. The Great Merchant [departed] from the city...
As soon as he had gone outside, he stepped on the wet body with his foot and struck it again with the back of his foot.
Flies flew up and swarmed around him. A foul stench assailed his nostrils. His devotion to the Buddha waned.
Consequently, his light vanished and darkness appeared. He let out a cry: "The merchant’s enthusiasm..."
"Let me give them away," he proclaimed with a sweet voice, as if striking a golden bell.
The preceding phrases, "a hundred thousand maidens," and so forth, are also to be connected with this word "hundred thousand.
For just as there were a hundred thousand maidens, so too there were a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, and a hundred thousand...
"Thousands of chariots"—this is the meaning here. Thus, each hundred thousand is illustrated. Regarding "the stride of a step":
the "stride of a step" (padavītihāra) refers to a space of one fist's breadth between two feet when walking together. "They are not worth a sixteenth part":
having divided that single stride of a step into sixteen parts, and then further dividing one of those portions into sixteen, [the former] does not equal even a fraction of it.
"Then one [part] of sixteenfold"—thus, when divided sixteen times into sixteen parts, one such portion is called a "sixteenth part" (*soḷasikala*).
These four hundred thousand do not equal the value of that sixteenth part. This is what is meant:
a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, a hundred thousand chariots, and a hundred thousand maidens.
And indeed, even those daughters of the kings of the entire Jambudīpa, adorned with necklaces and earrings, do not equal these gains for one going to the monastery;
rather, the volition that arises in that place known as the "sixteen-fold" (soḷasikala) is far superior. But by way of what is this "going to the monastery" understood?
It is understood by way of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) without obstacle after having gone to the monastery.

It is indeed permissible even for one who goes with the thought: "I shall perform worship with perfumes, garlands, and so forth; I shall pay homage to the shrine; I shall listen to the Dhamma; I shall perform a lamp-offering;
I shall invite the Saṅgha and give a gift; or I shall establish myself in the training rules or in the refuges.
It is likewise permissible for one who is actually establishing themselves [in these practices].
"The darkness has vanished"—he thought, "I perceive myself to be alone, yet there are those devoted to me;
why should I fear? and he became courageous. Then, a powerful faith in the Buddha arose within him; therefore, the darkness vanished.
This same sequence applies to the remaining sections as well. Furthermore, as he proceeded further and further into the terrifying...
On the way to the cemetery, he saw various kinds of corpses, such as skeletons, those with flesh and blood, and so forth.
He heard the sounds of dogs, jackals, and other creatures. Overcoming all those dangers by repeatedly increasing his serene confidence directed toward the Buddha, he continued on his way.
"Come, Sudatta," he said. It is said that as the merchant was departing, he thought:
"In this world there are many sectarian teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others who say, 'We are Buddhas, we are Buddhas. How indeed might I know whether the Teacher is truly a Buddha?
Then it occurred to him: "The great multitude knows my name as it arose on account of my own virtues."
"But as for my name, 'Kuladattiya,' no one other than myself knows it. If he is to be a Buddha, he will address me by the name Kuladattiya.
The Teacher, knowing his thought, spoke thus:

"Parinibbuto" means extinguished through the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*). "Āsattiyo" refers to the cravings (*taṇhā*). "Santi" refers to the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa-vūpasama*).
"Attains" means having reached. Having said this, the Teacher delivered a gradual discourse to him and proclaimed the Four Truths at the conclusion.
Upon hearing the Dhamma teaching, the merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry;
he then invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, and began giving a great almsgiving starting from the following day. Bimbisāra and others...
They sent a message to the merchant: "You are a newcomer; whatever you do not have, please have it brought from here.
He replied, "Enough, you are all very busy," and having declined them all, he gave a great almsgiving for seven days with the wealth brought by five hundred carts.
At the conclusion of the gift-giving, he requested the Blessed One to accept the rains retreat at Sāvatthī.
Having given one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for every league between Rājagaha and Sāvatthī, and while having forty-five monasteries built,
he went to Sāvatthī, had the Great Jetavana Monastery constructed, and dedicated it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
This is the eighth [story].
9. Commentary on the First Sukkā Sutta 243.
Regarding the ninth [case], "from street to street": having taken one street and proceeding from there to another, one is said to be "approaching from street to street.
The same method applies to the crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*) as well. And here, "street" (*rathikā*) means a carriage road.
*Siṅghāṭakaṃ* means a crossroads. *Kiṃ me katā* means "What have these done?"—the sense is, "What are they doing?
*Madhupītāva seyare* means they lie down as if having drunk fragrant honey-wine. It is said that one who has drunk fragrant honey-wine is unable to lift his head;
becoming unconscious, he simply lies there. Therefore, he spoke thus.
"And that which is not to be repudiated": he teaches that Dhamma which is not to be repudiated.
For even very delicious food, when eaten again and again by an outsider, no longer pleases him; one must reject it, saying, "Take it away! What is the use of this?
It becomes something to be repudiated and removed. But this Dhamma is not like that. For wise people, even for a hundred years or a thousand years, [delight in] this Dhamma...
They do not reach satiety while listening. Therefore he said, "irresistible. "Unadulterated and nutrient-rich" means it is not mixed with anything else and is full of nutritive essence (*ojas*).

For just as external things like unmixed rice-porridge become sweet and nutrient-rich only when mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar, this Dhamma is not like that. This [Dhamma], by its own inherent nature...
It is both sweet and nutritious, not having been infused with anything else. Therefore he said, "unadulterated and nutritious.

"The wise seem to drink" means that learned persons drink as it were. "Just as travelers [drink] from a cloud" means just as travelers scorched by the heat drink the water issuing from within a cloud. Ninth.
10–11. Commentary on the Second Sukkā Sutta, etc. 244.
In the tenth [verse], "Merit indeed he has produced in abundance," means "he indeed produces much merit.
The tenth is finished. 245. The eleventh is self-evident. The eleventh is finished.
12. Commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta 246.
Regarding "in Āḷavī" (*āḷaviyaṃ*): *Āḷavī* refers to both that kingdom and that city.
And his dwelling was situated about a *gāvuta* from the city. While the Blessed One was staying there, he dwelt in dependence upon that city, in Āḷavī.
"He dwells" is what was said. Regarding the phrase "in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka," this is the sequential account:

it is said that King Āḷavaka, having abandoned his various theatrical entertainments, went out on hunting expeditions every seventh day for the purpose of warding off thieves, resisting rival kings, and exercising his physical prowess; one day, together with his army...
He made an agreement with him: "Whichever side the deer escapes to, that side shall bear the responsibility.
Then the deer escaped on his very side; the king, endowed with great speed, took up his bow and pursued the deer on foot for three *yojanas*.
Deer of the *eṇi* species possess a speed of exactly three *yojanas*. Then, when his speed was exhausted, he was like water [that has run dry].

Having entered [the forest] and stood there, he killed [a deer], cut it in two, and—though he had no need for the meat—to avoid the reproach that he "could not catch the deer," he took it on a carrying-pole and was returning.
Not far from the city, seeing a great banyan tree with thick foliage and leaves, he approached its base to dispel his fatigue. And in that banyan tree lived the yakkha Āḷavaka.
Having obtained a dwelling from the great king, he lived there, devouring living beings whenever they entered the area shaded by that tree at midday. Seeing him, the king approached to be eaten.
The king made an agreement with him: "Release me, and I shall send you a person and a meal of boiled rice every day."
The yakkha said, “You, being intoxicated by royal luxury, will not remember;
however, I am not permitted to eat anything that has not entered my abode or been granted to me, so I might even devour you. He would not let him go.
The king, consenting, said, “On whichever day I do not send [food], on that day take me and eat me,” and he was released by him.
Having been released, he went toward the city.
The army, having established its camp on the road, stood waiting; seeing the king, they said, "Why, Great King, are you so distressed out of fear of a mere disgrace?
As they spoke, they went out to meet him and received him. The king, however, did not report that matter to them.
Having gone to the city and eaten his morning meal, he addressed the city guardian and reported this matter to him.
The city guardian asked, "Sire, has a time limit been set? "No, it has not been set," he replied. "That was poorly done, sire, for non-human beings will receive only what is limited;
however, if no limit is set, there will be affliction for the entire country."
"Let it be so, Your Majesty; even though you have acted thus, remain at ease and enjoy the pleasures of kingship, while I shall do what must be done here.
Rising early in the morning, he stood at the gate of the prison and, addressing those who were condemned to death, said:
"Whoever desires life, let him go out! Whosoever went out first—him...
Having led him home, bathed him, and fed him, she sent him off with the instruction: “Give this *thālipāka* to the *yakkha*.
As soon as he had entered the foot of the tree, the *yakkha* manifested a terrifying form and devoured him like a root or a tuber.
It is said that by the power of the *yakkha*, the entire body of humans—from the hair down—is like a lump of fresh butter. To the *yakkha*...
The men who had gone to fetch alms, seeing him, were terrified and reported it to their friends as they had seen it.
From that time forth, thinking, "The king seizes thieves and gives them to the yakṣa," people desisted from committing acts of theft.
Subsequently, due to the absence of new thieves and the exhaustion of old ones, the prisons became empty.
Then the city guard informed the king. The king had his own wealth scattered along the city streets, thinking, "Perhaps someone might take it out of greed.
Yet no one even stepped on it with their foot. Not finding the thief, he informed the ministers.
The ministers said, "We shall send each person in turn from the families of the elders; he is already on the path of death by nature."
They said, "He is coming. The king said, "If we send our father and our grandfather, people will become agitated;
do not let this please you," and he forbade it. They replied, "In that case, Your Majesty, let us send the infant lying on its back;
for one such as that has no affection [thinking], 'This is my mother' or 'This is my father. The king gave his permission. They...
They did exactly so. In the city, the mothers of young children took their children, and pregnant women fled;
they raised the children in other countries and brought them back. Thus twelve years passed.
Then one day, having searched the entire city and not finding even a single child, the ministers reported this to the king.
“There is no boy in the city, O King, other than your son Prince Āḷavaka in the inner palace.
The king said, “Just as my son is dear to me, so he is to the whole world; yet there is nothing dearer than myself.
Go, give him up and save my life! At that time, Āḷavaka’s mother had bathed her son...
Having adorned her, placed her on a pillow of fine linen, and laid her upon his lap, he sat there.

By the king’s command, the royal officers went there and, while she was still lamenting, took her away along with sixteen thousand queens and her nurse, saying, "Tomorrow he shall be food for the yakkhas.
And on that very day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One—
Having risen and entered the Great Compassion Samāpatti within the Gandhakuṭī in the Jetavana monastery,
he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and saw the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for the young Āḷavaka to attain the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*),

and for the Yakkha to attain the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*); and at the conclusion of the teaching, he saw that eighty-four thousand beings would obtain the Eye of Dhamma (*dhammacakkhu*).

Thus, when the night had brightened, having performed his morning meal duties and completed his post-meal tasks, on the day of the Uposatha during the dark fortnight, after the sun had set, he went alone without a companion, taking his bowl and robes, and traveling thirty *yojanas* by foot from Sāvatthī, he entered the abode of that *yakkha*.
Therefore it is said: "In the abode of the *yakkha* Āḷavaka."
But did the Blessed One dwell at the foot of the banyan tree where Āḷavaka’s abode was, or rather within the abode itself?
It was indeed within the abode. For just as the *yakkhas* see their own abode, so too did the Blessed One.
Having gone there, he stood at the door of the abode. At that time, Āḷavaka had gone to a gathering of *yakkhas* in the Himālayas. Then...
The yakṣa named Gadrabha, the doorkeeper of Āḷavaka, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said, "Why, venerable sir, has the Blessed One come at an improper time?
"Yes, Gadrabha, I have come; if it is not troublesome to you, may I stay for one night in the residence of Āḷavaka.
"It is not troublesome to me, venerable sir, but that yakṣa is harsh and cruel."
"He does not even perform such acts as saluting his parents; let it not please the Blessed One to dwell here.
"I know his nature, O camel; no obstacle shall come to me. If it is not troublesome to you, might we dwell together for one night?
A second time the camel-yakṣa said this to the Blessed One: "Bhante, he is like a bowl heated by fire."
“Āḷavaka does not recognize ‘mother and father,’ nor ‘ascetics and brahmins,’ nor even ‘the Dhamma.
Yet, he causes those who come here to lose their minds, he rends their hearts, and having seized them by the feet, he hurls them across the great ocean or beyond the world-system.
A second time the Blessed One said: “I know, jackal; if it is not troublesome to you, let us dwell together for one night.”
“Venerable sir, it is not that I am reluctant to tell you; however, if that *yakkha* were to deprive me of life even while I was giving my consent without first informing him, I would have been lost.
Therefore, Venerable sir, I inform you. “As you please, Gadrabha, inform him.
“In that case, Venerable sir, you yourself shall know,” he said, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he set out toward the Himālayas. He even reached the door of his dwelling.

He himself opened a passage for the Blessed One. Having entered the inner palace, the Blessed One sat upon that very same divine jewel-encrusted couch where he used to sit on specially marked auspicious days and other such occasions to enjoy his glory;
sitting there, he emitted a golden radiance. Seeing this, the female spirits of the *yakkha* approached, paid homage to the Blessed One, and—

They sat down surrounding him. The Blessed One addressed them with a miscellaneous discourse on the Dhamma, beginning: "In the past, you attained this prosperity by giving gifts, undertaking moral discipline, and honoring those worthy of honor;
now, act in the same way, and do not dwell overcome by mutual envy and avarice. As he spoke, they [listened to] the Blessed One’s sweet voice...
Having heard this, they gave a thousand shouts of "Well done! and sat down surrounding the Blessed One.
The donkey, too, went to the Himālayas and announced to Āḷavaka: "O sir, you should know that the Blessed One is seated in your celestial palace.
He gave the donkey a sign, saying: "Be silent; having gone there, I shall do what must be done."
It is said that he was ashamed because of his manly pride; therefore, he acted thus so that "no one might hear it in the midst of the assembly.

At that time, Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One right there at Jetavana, were traveling through the air with their retinues in various vehicles, thinking, "We shall go to the gathering of the yakkhas. And in the sky, there is no path for yakkhas anywhere.
Having bypassed the celestial palaces situated in the sky, the road remains right on its course.
However, Āḷavaka’s palace was built upon the earth, well-guarded, surrounded by a rampart, with well-arranged gates, watchtowers, and gatehouses;
it was covered above with a network of bronze and resembled a casket, being three yojanas in height. The road passed over the top of it. Having reached that place, they—
They were unable to go. For no one is able to pass above the place where the Buddhas sit, even as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).

Reflecting on what this was, they saw the Blessed One; like a clod of earth thrown into the air, they descended, paid homage, listened to the Dhamma, and after performing a circumambulation, said, "Blessed One, let us go to the assembly of *yakkhas*," and departed three times.
Praising those sites, they went to the assembly of yakkhas. When Āḷavaka saw them, he stepped aside and gave them space, saying, "Sit here.
They informed Āḷavaka: "It is a gain for you, Āḷavaka, that the Blessed One dwells in your abode;
go, friend, and attend upon the Blessed One. Thus, the Blessed One was right there in the abode.
He dwelt at the foot of a banyan tree where the abode of Āḷavaka was located; it was not at the tree itself. Therefore it is said:
“On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka.
Then Āḷavaka... [as above] ...said this: “Come out, ascetic! But why did he say this? Out of a desire to provoke him.
In this regard, the connection should be understood as follows from the beginning: since a discourse on faith is ill-suited for one who lacks faith—
just as a discourse on virtue and so forth is ill-suited for those who lack virtue and so forth— the Yakkhas, upon hearing the praise of the Blessed One from them,
felt their hearts seethe with internal anger like salt-grit thrown into a fire.
Having made the offering, he said, "Who is this one called 'Bhagavā' who has entered my abode?
They replied, "Friend, you do not know our Teacher, the Bhagavā, who, while dwelling in the Tusita heaven, performed the five great observations," and so on,
speaking in this manner up until the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, [describing] the thirty-two [marks] from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards.
Having described the preliminary signs, they reproached him, saying, "Friend, did you not see these wonders as well?
Although he had seen them, out of anger he said, "I did not see them. "Friend Āḷavaka, whether you saw them or not, what is it to you?
What does it matter to us whether you saw them or not? What can you do against our Teacher, compared to whom you are [but a trifle]?"
Like a calf born that very day in the presence of a great bull with swelling humps; like a young bee in the presence of a rutting elephant whose temples have just split in three ways;
like an old jackal in the presence of the king of beasts, whose shoulders are adorned with a magnificent mane of long, shimmering hair;
and like a young crow with clipped wings in the presence of the king of birds, whose body has increased to one hundred and fifty leagues.

"Eat! Go and do whatever you must do. When this was said, the wicked Āḷavaka rose up, stood upon the floor of emerald with his left foot, and said, "Behold now whether your Teacher is of great power, or I!
With his right foot, he kicked the peak of Mount Kelāsa for sixty yojanas. It was as if struck by an iron mace.
Like a mass of glowing embers being rubbed together, it emitted sparks; standing there, it proclaimed, "I am Āḷavaka!
The sound pervaded the whole of Jambudīpa.
It is said that four sounds were heard throughout the entire Jambudīpa: [the first was] when Puṇṇaka, the general of the yakkhas, [challenged] King Dhanañjaya Koravya...

Having won the game and clapped his hands, he proclaimed, "I have won! And furthermore, when the Blessed One Kassapa’s teaching was declining, Sakka, lord of the devas, transformed the divine son Vissakamma into a dog and made him proclaim:
"I devour all the wicked bhikkhus, the wicked bhikkhunīs, the laymen, and the laywomen—all those who speak what is contrary to the Dhamma! And furthermore...

In the *Kusajātakaya*, when the city was besieged by seven kings for the sake of Pabhāvati, the Great Man mounted Pabhāvati upon his own back on the elephant, departed from the city, and proclaimed, "I am Sīhassara, the great King of Kusa.

And likewise, standing upon the Kelāsa mountain, he proclaimed, "I am Āḷavaka. For at that time, it was as if he were proclaiming himself while standing at the gates throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
The Himālaya mountain, extending for three thousand yojanas, also trembled through the power of the yakkha.
He stirred up a whirlwind, thinking, "By this very means I shall drive the ascetic away.
Those winds, distinguished as eastern and so forth, having arisen, shattered mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas in size.

Having uprooted forests, groves, trees, and so forth, those winds rushed toward the city of Āḷavī, pulverizing old elephant stables and other structures, and scattering roof-tiles and bricks through the air.
The Blessed One resolved, "May no harm come to anyone.
When those winds reached the One of Ten Powers, they were unable to move even the hem of his robe. Then, a great rain fell.
He raised [the clouds], thinking, "I shall kill the ascetic by overwhelming him with water.
Through his power, clouds consisting of layers of hundreds and thousands of petals arose one above the other and rained down. By the force of the torrential rain, the earth was split open.
A great flood came over the forest trees and other things, yet not even a drop the size of a dew-droplet fell upon the Blessed One’s robe.
He was unable to terrify him. Thereupon, he raised a rain of stones.
Gigantic mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came through the air and, upon reaching the One of Ten Powers, were transformed into divine bouquets of flowers.
Then, he raised a rain of weapons: single-edged swords, double-edged swords, spears, javelins, arrows, and so forth, all smoking and blazing.
Blazing forth, they came through the air and, reaching the One of Ten Powers, became celestial flowers.
Then he raised a rain of glowing coals. Coals the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers came through the air and, having become celestial flowers, scattered at the feet of the One of Ten Powers.
Then he raised a rain of hot ashes (*kukkuḷa*). Exceedingly hot ashes came through the air...
They fell at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers (Dasabala) as sandalwood powder. Then he raised a rain of sand;
the exceedingly fine sand, smoking and blazing, came through the air and fell at the feet of the Dasabala as divine flowers.
Then he raised a rain of mud; that rain of mud, smoking and blazing...
Having come through the air, it descended at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, transforming into a divine fragrance.
Then, thinking, "I shall terrify the ascetic and cause him to flee," it produced a darkness endowed with four characteristics.
Upon reaching the One Possessed of Ten Powers, that darkness—which resembled [the usual] darkness—vanished like darkness struck by the radiance of the sun.
Thus, when the yakkha was unable to drive the Blessed One away with these nine showers of wind, rain, stones, clubs, embers, glowing coals, sand, and pitch-black darkness,

he himself approached the Blessed One with a fourfold army crowded with hosts of spirits of various forms, each holding diverse weapons in their hands. Those hosts of spirits displayed many kinds of transformations.
Having resolved thus, they seemed as though they were coming upon the Blessed One shouting, "Seize him! Strike him!
Nevertheless, like flies on a red-hot iron ball, they were unable to even cling to the Blessed One.
Even so, unlike Māra at the seat of enlightenment who turned back at the very moment he arrived, these did not turn back and caused a disturbance for about half the night.
Thus, being unable to move the Blessed One even by displaying many kinds of terrifying sights for the duration of half a night, Āḷavaka thought:
"What if I were to release a weapon that cannot be defeated by anyone?
For it is said that there are four weapons supreme in the world: Sakka’s thunderbolt weapon, Vessavaṇa’s club weapon, [Kuvera’s sword weapon, and Yama’s noose weapon].
Yama’s weapon is his eye, and Āḷavaka’s weapon is his robe.
For if the wicked Sakka were to strike Sineru’s summit with his thunderbolt weapon, it would pierce through the one hundred thousand and sixty-eight thousand yojanas and pass beneath it.
When Vessavaṇa is provoked to anger, the club weapon he hurls destroys many thousands of yakkhas.
Having caused his head to fall, he returns to hand’s reach and stands there.
At the mere glance of the wicked Yama with his eye-weapon, many thousands of *kumbhaṇḍas* perish, bursting like sesame seeds in a hot pan.
If the wicked Āḷavaka were to release his cloth-weapon into the sky, it would not rain for twelve years; if [he were to release it] upon the earth...
He might release it. All trees, grasses, and so forth would wither away and would not grow again for twelve years.
If he were to release it upon the ocean, all the water would dry up like a drop of water on a hot pan.
If he were to release it even upon a mountain as large as Sineru, it would shatter it into pieces and scatter them. Such was the great power of that weapon of cloth.

He cast off his upper robe and took hold of it. For the most part, the deities of the ten-thousandfold world system gathered together with great speed, thinking, "Today the Blessed One will subdue Āḷavaka; we shall hear the Dhamma there.
Deities who desired to witness the battle also gathered. Thus, the entire sky became completely filled with deities.
Then Āḷavaka, having paced back and forth near the Blessed One, released his garment and weapon.

Like a thunderbolt wheel, making a terrifying sound in the sky, smoking and blazing, it reached the Blessed One and fell at his feet, becoming a foot-wiping cloth for the purpose of crushing the pride of the *yakkha*. Seeing this, Āḷavaka was like a bull with its horns broken.
Like a snake whose fangs have been pulled out, devoid of luster, free from pride, and with the banner of his conceit cast down, he thought:
"Even my weapons do not overcome this ascetic. What could be the reason? "The reason is this: the ascetic is devoted to dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettā*);
well then, having provoked him, I shall separate him from that loving-kindness. It is with this connection that it was said: "Then indeed, Āḷavaka..."
The yakkha approached the Blessed One... [and said: "Come out, ascetic! The intended meaning here is this:
"Why, without my permission, have you entered my abode and sat in the midst of my harem like a master of the house?
Is this not unbecoming for an ascetic—namely, the enjoyment of what is not given and association with women? Therefore, if you, O ascetic, in the ascetic's duty..."
“Stand still, ascetic, come out! Some, however, say: “Having spoken these and other harsh words, he then said this.
Then the Blessed One thought: “Since one who is stubborn cannot be disciplined by means of stubbornness—for he [remains] in that state of stubbornness—”
"If he is being dealt with in this way, it will be just as if one were to apply bile to the nose of a fierce dog;
it would become even more fierce and even more stubborn. However, he can be disciplined through gentleness.
Knowing this, and having accepted his words with the affectionate address "Very well, friend," the Blessed One departed. Thus it is said: "‘Very well, friend,’ the Blessed One departed."
Then Āḷavaka thought: "This ascetic is indeed easy to speak to; he has departed at a single word.
It was truly easy for me to wage war against this ascetic all night long for no reason. With a softened heart, he reflected again:
"Even now it is not possible to know whether he has departed because of his easy-to-speak-to nature, or rather—"
"He is angry. Come now, I shall test him. Then he said, "Enter, ascetic!

Then the Blessed One entered, addressing him with kind words once more—"Excellent, sir"—in order to establish that he was indeed "easy to speak to" and to demonstrate that his mind had become softened.
Āḷavaka, repeatedly testing that very quality of being easy to speak to, said a second and a third time, "Come out! Enter! The Blessed One did likewise. If...
He should not do so; for the mind of one who is already naturally stubborn would become even more obstinate and thus would not become a fit vessel for a discourse on the Dhamma.

Therefore, just as a mother appeases a crying child by giving it whatever it desires or by doing what it wants, so too did the Blessed One act to appease the yakṣa who was crying with the wailing of the defilements. Whatever he...

He spoke, and the Blessed One did so. Just as a nurse, in order to give milk to a child who will not drink from the breast, satisfies him by giving him something else and coaxes him before nursing him, so too the Blessed One, wishing to make the yakkha drink the milk of the supramundane Dhamma, acted in this way while coaxing him by having him fulfill his own request.
And just as a man desiring to fill a gourd with the four sweet substances would first [cleanse] its interior...

He cleanses [it]. In this way, the Blessed One—desiring to fill the yakkha’s mind with the fourfold sweetness of the supramundane—performed the act of exiting and re-entering up to three times in order to cleanse the stain of anger within him.
Then Āḷavaka thought: “This ascetic is easy to speak to; when told ‘exit,’ he exits, and when told ‘enter,’ he enters.”
He entered [the city]. “What if I were to exhaust this ascetic right here throughout the entire night and, seizing him by the feet, throw him across the Ganges?
Having conceived this evil thought, he spoke for the fourth time: “Come out, ascetic!
Knowing that, the Blessed One said: “I am not that. When this was said, [Sujāta], seeking something further to do, [continued].
"He will think that he must ask a question; knowing that this will serve as the opening for a discourse on the Dhamma," [the Blessed One] said, "Indeed, I shall not [go out].
In this context, *na* is a particle of negation; *kho* is a particle of emphasis; *aham* indicates the self;
and *tam* is a word expressing the reason. Therefore, it means here: "Because you have thought thus, therefore, friend, I shall certainly not go out."
"Whatever you must do, do that"—this is how the meaning should be understood.
Then Āḷavaka, because he had previously, at the time of traveling through the air, thought: "What indeed is this golden mansion?
Is it one of the silver or jewel mansions? Come now, let us look at it," thus approached his own mansion.
Having asked questions of the ascetics and wanderers possessed of psychic power, he would harass them with mental derangement and other means when they were unable to answer;
therefore, thinking, "I shall likewise harass the Blessed One," he spoke the question beginning with "Tanti.
But from where did he get this question? It is said that his parents, having attended upon the Blessed Kassapa, [attained] the eight...
They learned the questions together with their answers. In their youth, they had Āḷavaka master them; however, with the passage of time, he forgot the answers.
Then, thinking, "Let these questions not be lost," he had them inscribed with vermilion (jātihiṅgulaka) upon a golden plate and placed them within his palace.
Thus, these questions posed were indeed within the domain of the Buddhas. The Blessed One [addressed] that—
Having heard this, because no one can cause an obstruction to the gains of the Buddhas, nor an obstruction to their life, nor an impediment to their omniscience,

their fathom-wide radiance, and so forth, he spoke the words beginning with "Friend, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas... in order to demonstrate that unique majesty of the Buddhas which is not shared by others in the world.
Thus the Blessed One, having restrained his intention to cause him distress and inspiring him with the desire to ask questions, said:
"Moreover, friend, ask whatever you wish. The meaning of this is: "Ask, if you so desire; there is no burden for me in answering your questions.
Or alternatively: "Ask whatever you wish; I shall answer everything for you"—this is the invitation of the Omniscient One (*sabbaññu-pavāraṇā*).
He invited [the Buddha] to accept an offering that was not shared even with the peerless disciples and great disciples of the Paccekabuddhas.
Thus, when the Blessed One had been invited by this invitation of omniscience, the yakkha Āḷavaka then addressed the Blessed One in verse.
In that context, "What indeed is wealth here? means: what indeed is wealth (*vitta*) here? "Wealth" (*vitta*) refers to riches; for it is that which is designated as joy.
It makes one find (vittiṃ karoti), therefore it is called "find" (vitta). "Well-performed" (suciṇṇa) means well-done. "Happiness" (sukha) is bodily and mental pleasure.
"Brings" (āvahāti) means it brings, leads, gives, or causes to settle. "Have" is a particle used in the sense of emphasis.
"More delicious" (sādutaraṃ) means exceedingly sweet. There is also a reading "sādhutaraṃ. "Of tastes" (rasānaṃ) refers to those phenomena designated as tastes. "How? (kathaṃ) [is the question].
In what manner? What is the life of one who lives thus? "What is the life of one who lives thus" (*kathaṃjīviṃ jīvitaṃ*).
It is pronounced with a nasal vowel (*sānunāsika*) for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse. Alternatively, there is the reading *kathaṃjīviṃ jīvanti*, the meaning of which is:
"What is the life of those who are living? Thus, by means of this verse [it is asked]: "What indeed is the best wealth for a person here in this world? What indeed is well-practiced?"
"What brings happiness? What is the sweetest of tastes? How does one live so that their life is called the best? He asked these four questions.
Then the Blessed One, answering him according to the very method explained by the Dasa-balas Kassapa, spoke this verse: "Faith is wealth in this world...
Therein, just as wealth such as gold and bullion brings the happiness of enjoyment and [removes] the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth...
It wards off [suffering], it pacifies poverty, it becomes a cause for obtaining treasures such as pearls, and it brings about the continuity of the world;
likewise, mundane and supramundane faith also brings about mundane and supramundane resultant happiness as appropriate.
For those who have practiced with faith as their primary guide, it wards off the suffering of birth, aging, and so forth, and it pacifies the poverty of virtuous qualities.
It is the cause for obtaining the jewels of the factors of enlightenment, beginning with mindfulness.
As it is said: "The person endowed with faith and perfected in virtue, possessed of fame and wealth—whatever region they frequent, there they are honored."
It is called "wealth" (*vitta*) because it brings about the continuity of the world through speech.

Furthermore, because their wealth of faith (*saddhāvitta*) is enduring, not shared by others, and is the cause of all success—and is even the source of worldly wealth such as gold and bullion—it is so designated.
For it is only through faith that one performs meritorious deeds such as giving and thereby acquires wealth; however, for one lacking faith...
Wealth leads only to disadvantage; therefore, it is said to be "inferior. "Of a person" is a teaching intended to set the upper limit.
Therefore, it should be understood that not only for a man, but for women and others as well, the wealth of faith alone is superior.
"Dhamma" refers to the ten wholesome states, or the dhamma of giving, virtue, and mental development. "Well-practiced" means well-performed or well-conducted. "Brings happiness" means...
It brings about human happiness, such as that of Soṇa the merchant’s son, Raṭṭhapāla, and others; divine happiness, such as that of Sakka and others;
and ultimately, the happiness of Nibbāna, like that of Mahāpaduma and others.
Regarding the word *sacca*: this term *sacca* is seen in many senses. For example: “One should speak the truth... [and so forth].

In such passages as “one might be angry,” it refers to truth in speech (*vācāsacca*). In such passages as “Samaṇas and Brāhmaṇas are established in truth,” it refers to truth as abstinence (*viratisacca*).
In such passages as “Why do they speak various truths, these skilled speakers who proclaim [their views]? it refers to truth of view (*diṭṭhisacca*).

In such passages as “These four, monks, are the truths of the Brāhmaṇas,” it refers to the truths of the Brāhmaṇas (*brāhmaṇasacca*). And in such passages as “For there is but one truth, no second exists,” it refers to—
In the context of ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*). In such passages as, "Of the four truths, how many are wholesome? it refers to the Noble Truths (*ariyasacca*).
However, here what is intended is the truth of speech (*vācasacca*), which includes within itself both Nibbāna—the ultimate truth—and the truth of abstinence (*viratisacca*).
It is by the power of this [truth of speech] that water and other elements obey one's will, and one crosses to the further shore of birth, aging, and death. As it has been said:
“By truth one runs through water;
by truth the wise destroy even poison;
by truth the rain-god pours down his showers.”
If, while standing, they aspire to Nibbāna:
“Whatever flavors there are on this earth,
truth is the sweetest of those flavors.”
“Monks and brahmins established in truth cross to the further shore of birth and death.
“Sweeter” means more sweet, more refined. “Of tastes” refers to those such as the “taste of roots,” the “taste of stems,” and so forth.
According to the method [of the suttas], there are qualities conducive to rest:

by way of such passages as, “Bhikkhus, I allow all fruit-juices,” “The venerable Gotama is one who lacks taste,” “Those things which are the taste of forms, O Brahmin, and the taste of sounds,” “There is no offense regarding the taste of tastes,” “This Dhamma and Vinaya has a single taste, the taste of liberation,” and “The Blessed One partakes of the taste of meaning and the taste of Dhamma”; thus, there are offenses regarding the taste of physical conduct.
The remaining factors, such as the syllables (*byañjana*), are called the "flavors of the Dhamma" (*dhammarasa*). Among those flavors, truth (*sacca*) is indeed the most sweet;
truth alone is the most sweet. That is to say, it is the more excellent, the superior, and the most sublime.

For while the flavors of roots and so forth nourish the body and bring about defiled pleasure, the flavors of truth—namely, the flavor of truth in abstinence and the flavor of truth in speech—[lead] through serenity, insight, and so on...
It cultivates the mind and brings about undefiled happiness. It has the flavor of liberation because it is permeated by the flavor of the ultimate truth;
and it has the flavors of the goal and the Dhamma because it proceeds in dependence upon the goal and the Dhamma which serve as the means for its attainment.
Regarding the phrase "the life of one who lives by wisdom," this refers to the person with two eyes among those who are blind, one-eyed, or two-eyed.
Whether as a householder, one lives having accomplished through wisdom the path of the householder—
consisting of the performance of work, going for refuge, giving, sharing, undertaking the precepts, the observance-day rites (*upoṣadhakamma*), and so forth— or whether as one gone forth,

one lives having accomplished through wisdom the path of the renunciant, which consists of the precepts that cause freedom from remorse and the further divisions such as the purification of the mind; the life of such a person living by wisdom is [true] life, or that [life] itself.
"The life of wisdom is supreme"—thus the meaning should be understood.
When the four questions had been thus answered by the Blessed One, the Yakkha, being delighted upon hearing them, asked the remaining four questions as well, reciting the verse:
"How does one cross over the flood? Then the Blessed One, in the same manner as before, [answered].
While explaining, he spoke this verse: "By means of faith one crosses over.

In that regard, although one who crosses over the fourfold flood also crosses over the ocean of saṃsāra, transcends the suffering of the cycle of existence, and is purified from the stains of the defilements—even so, because one who lacks faith does not leap forward, lacking conviction in the crossing of the flood, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure...
One who is negligent through the relinquishing of the mind does not cross the ocean of saṃsāra because of being attached right there;
the indolent person dwells in suffering, mired in unwholesome states; and one lacking wisdom, not knowing the path of purification, is not purified.
Therefore, this verse was spoken by the Blessed One to demonstrate the antidote to those [faults].
When this has been said, since the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is the proximate cause for the factors of stream-entry (*sotāpattiyaṅga*),
the phrase "by means of faith one crosses the flood" explains the crossing of the flood of views—

the path of stream-entry— and the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). Furthermore, because the stream-enterer, through diligence (*appamāda*) consisting of constant application in the cultivation of wholesome states, [proceeds...]

Having attained the second path and set aside the path of returning only once more to this world, one crosses the remaining flood of existence—the ocean of saṃsāra—which was not yet crossed by means of the stream-entry path;
therefore, by the phrase "crossing the ocean through heedfulness," he reveals the once-returner path and the once-returner himself. And because the once-returner...

Having attained the third path through energy, one transcends by means of the once-returning path the basis for the flood of sensual desire that has not yet been transcended, as well as the suffering of sensual desire known as the "flood of sensual desire.
Therefore, by the phrase "one transcends suffering through energy," he reveals the crossing of the flood of sensual desire, the non-returning path, and the non-returner.
Furthermore, because the non-returner possesses wisdom that is utterly pure due to the removal of the perception of sensual desire, [he is purified].
Having attained the wisdom of the fourth path, one abandons through the non-returning path the supreme stain known as ignorance (*avijjā*), which had not been abandoned previously;
therefore, it is said that "one is purified by wisdom. By this phrase, he reveals both the crossing of the flood of ignorance and the path to and the state of *arahantship*.
And at the conclusion of this verse, which was spoken with *arahantship* as its pinnacle, the *yakkha*—
He was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Now, taking up the word "wisdom" (paññā) as it was spoken here in the phrase "it is purified by wisdom," and asking a question—mixed with both mundane and supramundane matters—by means of his own inspired ingenuity, he posed this six-line inquiry: "How does one obtain wisdom? (kathaṃ su labhate paññaṃ).
He spoke a verse. In that context, the phrase "How indeed" (*kathaṃ su*) constitutes an inquiry regarding both the meaning and the logical justification (*yutti*) for all [the following terms].

For, having understood the meaning of wisdom (*paññā*) and so forth, he asks for its justification: "In what way, by what justification, and for what reason does one obtain wisdom? This same method applies to wealth and the other [terms].
Then the Blessed One, demonstrating the attainment of wisdom through four reasons, said: "One who has faith," and so on. Its meaning is as follows:
Having faith in that Dhamma— by which, through its divisions such as bodily good conduct in the prior stage and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the subsequent stage,
the Arahants, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples attained Nibbāna— one acquires both mundane and supramundane wisdom for the attainment of Nibbāna; yet this is not achieved by faith alone.

But because one who has conceived faith approaches [the teacher], and approaching pays respectful attention, and paying respectful attention lends an ear, and lending an ear listens to the Dhamma, therefore from the moment of approaching until the hearing of the Dhamma, one obtains the desire to hear.
What is meant? Even after having faith in that Dhamma, at the proper time toward the teachers and preceptors...
Having approached and waited upon him by performing the proper duties, when his mind has been won over by that service and he desires to say something,
then— having lent an ear through the desire to hear what has been attained— he gains [the teaching]. Thus, one who possesses a desire to hear,
being heedful through non-separation from mindfulness, and discerning through the knowledge of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, [attains success].
One attains it, not the other. Therefore he said: "The heedful one, the discerning.
Thus, because through faith one undertakes the practice that leads to the attainment of wisdom; through the desire to hear, one listens attentively to the means for the acquisition of wisdom;
through heedfulness, one does not forget what has been grasped; and through discernment, one [understands] without deficiency or excess.
Having grasped it without error, he makes it widespread. Or else, through the desire to hear, with attentive ears, he listens to the Dhamma that is the cause for the acquisition of wisdom;
through diligence, he retains the Dhamma he has heard; through discernment, he examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained;
and then, by means of this gradual process, he realizes the ultimate truth. Therefore, the Blessed One [bestows it] upon him.
Being asked, "How does one obtain wisdom? he spoke this verse, demonstrating these four causes.
Now, answering the three subsequent questions, he spoke this verse beginning with "one who acts appropriately" (*patirūpakārī*).

In that context, one is called "one who acts appropriately" because one employs a suitable means for attaining either worldly or supramundane wealth, without neglecting the place, time, and other such factors.
*“Dhuravā”* means one who does not lay down the burden by virtue of mental energy (*cetasika-viriya*).

*“Uṭṭhātā”* means one endowed with physical energy (*kāyika-viriya*), possessing exertion and unremitting effort in the manner described in such passages as: “He who regards cold and heat no more than blades of grass,” and so forth.
*“Vindate dhanaṃ”* (he finds wealth) refers to how, like the junior pupil (*cūḷantevāsī*), one soon acquires a sum of four hundred thousand [pieces of gold] through a single mouse.
He obtains both worldly wealth and supramundane wealth, like the Elder Mahā-Tissa the Aged. Having made a vow, thinking,
"I shall dwell in only three postures," at the time when sloth and torpor were about to come upon him, he moistened a pillow of straw,
placed it on his head, entered water up to his neck, and while warding off sloth and torpor, [he practiced] with the ten...

Within three years, he attained Arahatship. By means of truth—both through verbal truth in the sense of being "one who speaks truthfully and speaks what is real," and through ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) in the sense of being "the Buddha, the Paccekabuddha, or the noble disciple"—one attains such renown.
By giving whatever is desired or sought after, one binds friends; the meaning is that one accomplishes or establishes them. Or, by giving what is difficult to give, one binds them.
It should be understood that by means of "the door of giving" (dānamukha), all four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) are included; thus it is said that one makes friends by means of them.

Having thus answered the four questions by way of a method common to both householders and renunciants, consisting of a mixture of mundane and supramundane factors, he now addresses this fifth question, "How does one not grieve after passing away? by way of the householder.
Explaining this, he says: "Of whomsoever," and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows:
for one who is endowed with faith—that faith which was mentioned in the phrase "having faith in the Arahants" and which gives rise to all wholesome qualities;

for a householder seeking a home, that is, a layperson enjoying sensual pleasures who seeks and pursues the household life or the five strands of sense pleasure; [for such a person] "by truth, fame..."

In this context, there are four qualities: truth, as described in the phrase "he attains [truth]"; self-control, which is expressed by the term "wisdom" in the phrase "he gains wisdom through a desire to hear";
fortitude, which is expressed by the terms "burden-bearer" and "exertion" in the phrase "the one who bears the burden is an exertor";
and generosity, as described in the phrase "by giving, he binds friends. These are the four qualities that exist here.
“He indeed does not grieve after passing away” means that having gone from this world to the next world, he indeed does not grieve.
Thus, having answered the fifth question, the Blessed One, exhorting that yakkha, said: “Come now, ask others as well,” and so forth.
In that context, *iṅgha* is a particle used for the purpose of exhortation. *Aññepi* means: “Ask others as well—other teachings and many other ascetics and brahmins.”
Or rather, ask other numerous ascetics and brahmins who claim omniscience, such as Pūraṇa and others:

whether there is a cause for attaining fame greater than the kinds of truth we have described here under the phrase "one attains fame through truth," or whether there is a cause for acquiring mundane and supramundane wisdom greater than the "desire to hear" (*sussūsa*) mentioned here by way of the term "wisdom" (*paññā*) in the phrase "one acquires wisdom through the desire to hear."
Or else, it is something other than the kind of generosity described here as "giving binds friends," which serves as the cause for binding friends;
or it is something other than the patience— termed energy— that has reached a state of extreme exertion through its capacity to bear great burdens,
and which is designated by the names "burden-bearer" and "exertion" in the passage "the burden-bearer, the one who exerts himself" according to various specific purposes.

Or rather, it is the cause for finding both mundane and supramundane wealth; or, as it is said, "truth, self-control, fortitude, and generosity"—it is by means of these very four qualities that there exists here a further reason for not grieving when passing from this world to the next world.

This is the explanation of the meaning here, together with a brief analysis. In detail, however, each individual word [should be treated] by way of the extraction of the meaning, the extraction of the words, and the method of word-commentary.
It should be understood by way of analysis.
When this was said, since the doubt on account of which he might have questioned others had been abandoned, how could he now question?
Having said, "Many are the recluses and brahmins," he made known even to those who did not know the reason for his not questioning them.
"I, who today understand that which is for the sake of the future life"—this is what he said. In this context, "today" (*ajja*) means beginning from today; this is the intended meaning.

"I understand" (*pajānāmi*) means I know in the manner already described. By the phrase "that which is for the sake of" (*yo attho*), he shows the benefits pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) as stated in the sequence beginning with, "One who desires to hear gains wisdom.
By the word "for the future life" (*samparāyiko*), he indicates [the benefits] as stated in the verse beginning with, "He for whom these four qualities..."
The cause for the absence of sorrow after passing away in the future life has been stated. Furthermore, "benefit" (*attha*) is a designation for this cause.
For this word *attha* functions in the sense of a textual reading in such phrases as "meaningful and well-phrased" (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*).

It functions in the sense of a discernible object in such phrases as "I have need of gold and silver, householder. It functions in the sense of growth or prosperity in such phrases as "there is benefit for those who possess virtue."
In such passages as “The multitude resorts [to it] for the sake of wealth,” it refers to riches. In such passages as “He practices for the welfare of both,” it refers to benefit (*hita*).
In such passages as “When a matter has arisen, the wise man...,” it refers to a cause (*kāraṇa*). Here, however, it refers to a cause.

Therefore, that which is the cause for the acquisition of wisdom and so forth pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), and that which is the cause for the absence of sorrow hereafter pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*)—that which I today [have heard] from the Blessed One...
"I understand it myself according to the method already stated; how then could I now ask about it before the many ascetics and brahmins?"—in this way, the meaning here should be understood in brief.
Thus, having said, "I understand that which pertains to the future life," the Yakkha [acknowledged] that the source of that knowledge was the Blessed One.
“Indeed, the Buddha has spoken for my benefit,” he said. In this context, “for my benefit” means for one’s welfare and growth.
Regarding the phrase “where what is given bears great fruit”:

the meaning is that I recognize the Buddha as the supreme recipient of offerings—that one in whom giving is of great fruit, as stated in the verse beginning, “He in whom these four qualities exist. However, some say that he spoke thus with reference to the Saṅgha.
Having thus shown his own attainment of welfare by means of this verse, he now spoke the words beginning with "So I shall wander," illustrating his practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Therein, "from village to village" means from one divine village to another divine village; "from city to city" means from one divine city to another divine city.
"Worshipping the Fully Enlightened One and the well-enacted nature of the Dhamma" means: "Truly, he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One..."
Having praised the Buddha’s excellent awakening and the excellence of the Dhamma by way of the formula beginning, “The Blessed One is indeed the Blessed One;

well-proclaimed is the Dhamma of the Blessed One,” and—by means of the word *ca* (and)—having also praised the Sangha’s excellent practice by way of the formula beginning, “Well-practiced is the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples,” [the author] says:
“I shall wander about as a proclaimer of the Dhamma while paying homage. This is what is meant.

Thus, by means of this verse, the conclusion of the recitation, the breaking of the night, the arising of the sound of "well done," and the bringing of the youth Āḷavaka to the yakṣa’s abode all occurred at one and the same moment.
Hearing the sound of "well done," the king's men thought, "A sound of 'well done' such as this does not arise for anyone other than the Buddhas; has the Blessed One perhaps arrived?"

As they were searching, they saw the radiance of the Blessed One’s body; no longer remaining outside as before, they entered fearlessly within and saw the Blessed One seated in the abode of the yakkha, and the yakkha standing with palms joined in reverence.
Seeing this, they said to the yakkha: "Great yakkha, this prince has been brought here by you for the sake of a sacrificial offering."
“Come now, eat him, or consume him, or do with him as you see fit.
Because he was a stream-enterer, he felt ashamed, especially since he was being addressed in this way right in front of the Blessed One;
then, taking the boy with both hands, he presented him to the Blessed One, saying, “Venerable sir, this boy was sent to me; I give him to the Blessed One.”
“The Buddhas are compassionate for the welfare [of others]; may the Blessed One, O Venerable One, accept this boy for his welfare and happiness.
And he spoke this verse: “This prince, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits,”
“Endowed with all parts and complete in its features,
with an uplifted mind and a joyful heart, I give this to you;
O Visionary One, accept it for the welfare of the world.”
The Blessed One accepted the boy. While accepting him, for the sake of performing an auspicious rite for both the yakṣa and the boy, he recited a verse lacking one line.
The yakṣa, while taking refuge in the boy, completed it three times with the fourth line.
It was as follows:—
“May this prince be long-lived,
and may you too, O yakkha, be happy;
remain free from illness for the welfare of the world.”
“This prince goes for refuge to the Buddha;
this prince goes for refuge to the Dhamma;
this prince goes for refuge to the Saṅgha.”
Then the Blessed One gave the boy to the king’s men, saying, “Raise him up and give him back to me again.
Because he thus passed from the hands of the king’s men into the hands of the yakkha, from the hands of the yakkha into the hands of the Blessed One,
and from the hands of the Blessed One back again into the hands of the king’s men, he was named “Hatthaka Āḷavaka.”
He was born. When the king’s men returned with him and were seen, the farmers, forest workers, and others asked, "Is it a *yakṣa*? Frightened because the boy was so very young, they questioned them.
The king’s men said, "Do not fear! Safety has been established by the Blessed One," and they related everything.
Then, crying out "Excellent! Excellent! the entire city of Āḷavī broke into a single tumultuous roar.
It was facing toward the yakkha. When the Blessed One arrived at the time for his alms-round, the yakkha took his bowl and robe, followed him halfway along the road, and then turned back.
Then the Blessed One, having walked for alms in the city and finished his meal, stood at a secluded spot near the city gate.

He sat down on the Buddha-seat prepared at the foot of the tree. Then the king and the citizens, having gathered together with the great multitude, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down surrounding him, asking:
"Venerable sir, how did you tame such a fierce yakkha? To them, the Blessed One began by recounting the battle.
“Having rained down in this way for nine kinds of rain, he created such terrors and asked such questions;
and I answered him thus,” he said, and related that very Āḷavaka Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand living beings.
Then the King and the citizens [built a monastery] near the abode of the Great King Vessavaṇa.
Having established a dwelling for the yakkha, they offered a perpetual offering provided with flowers, perfumes, and other honors.
When that boy reached the age of discretion, they dismissed him, saying, "You obtained this life by relying on the Blessed One;
go and attend upon the Blessed One himself and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. He [then went] to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Attending upon him, he soon established himself in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), mastered the entire word of the Buddha, and came to be surrounded by a retinue of five hundred lay followers (*upāsaka*). And the Blessed One designated him as foremost among his disciples:
"Foremost, monks, among my lay disciple followers who gather assemblies by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) is Hatthaka."
“Āḷavaka. Thus ends the twelfth [chapter].
Thus concludes the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Sāratthappakāsinī.
The commentary on the *Yakkhasaṃyutta* is finished.
11. *Sakkasaṃyutta*, Chapter 1.
First Division.
1. Commentary on the Suvīra Sutta 247.
Regarding the first sutta of the Saṅkhyutta: "They have overcome" (*abhiyaṃsu*). When did they overcome? It was when they were powerful; it was then.
Herein, this is the sequential account: it is said that in the kingdom of Magadha, in the village of Macala, there was a young brahmin named Magha.
Having performed an offering and taken thirty-three men with him, he performed meritorious deeds and fulfilled the seven rules of conduct (*vratapada*).

Having passed away there, he was reborn in the world of the gods. Seeing him surpassing the other resident deities along with their retinue in ten respects by the power of his potent karma, the residents prepared perfumes and drinks, thinking, "New divine sons have arrived."
Sakka gave a signal to his own retinue: "Friends, do not drink the scented liquor; merely show the appearance of drinking.
They did so there. The resident deities, having drunk their fill of the scented liquor served in golden goblets, became intoxicated and fell here and there upon the golden ground to sleep. Sakka—
“Seize the sons of her whose sons were slain! he said; seizing them by the feet, he hurled them down to the base of Mount Sineru.
By the power of Sakka’s merit, all those who followed him fell right there. When they regained consciousness at the midpoint of Mount Sineru, they cried out, “Sirs, we did not drink liquor!
We did not drink liquor! From that time forth, they became known as *asuras*. Then...
Through the condition of their karma and the arising of the physical element, an Asura realm ten thousand yojanas deep was established at the base of Sineru.
Sakka, having turned them back, stationed a guard so that they would not return; with reference to this it was said:
"Between the two cities of Ayujjha..."
The protection established is fivefold:
water, a skull-bearer, a milk-stealer,
one possessed by madness, and four great beings.
Indeed, because they could not be captured by means of war, two cities became known as "cities beyond battle":
the city of the gods and the city of the asuras. For when the asuras were powerful, the gods would flee and enter the city of the gods, closing its gates;
even a hundred thousand asuras would then be unable to do anything to them. When the gods...
They become powerful, and then, having fled from the Asuras, even a hundred thousand Sakkas are unable to do anything once the gates of the Asura city have been closed.
Thus, these two cities are called Ayujjhapura.
Between them, at these five locations—beginning with water—protection was established by Sakka. Therein, by the term "water," the Nāgas are included.
For they are powerful in the water; therefore, their protection is on the first terrace of Sineru.
By the word *karoṭi*, the Supaṇṇas are included. It is said that their food and drink is called *karoṭi*, and by that they received their name.
Their protection is on the second terrace. By the word *payassahārī*, the Kumbhaṇḍas are included. They are indeed Dānavas and Rakkhasas. [Their protection is] on the third terrace.
Their protection [is provided] by the *madanayuta* spirits; by the word *yakkha*, the *yakkhas* are included. Those who act irregularly and are fond of combat are the *kiratas*.
Their protection is in the fourth gallery. By the phrase "the four great ones," the four Great Kings (*mahārājāno*) are meant.
Their protection is in the fifth gallery. Therefore, if the *asuras*, with minds agitated by anger, approach the city of the gods for battles, whatever...
The first terrace of Mount Meru is guarded by serpents (*uraga*); likewise, the others are guarded by the remaining classes of beings.
Those *asuras*, however, are equal to the Thirty-three (*Tāvatiṃsa*) gods in their perfection of lifespan, complexion, taste, and sovereignty.
Therefore, not recognizing themselves to be in between [the worlds] when the *pāṭali* tree was in bloom, they thought, "This is not the city of the gods; there, the *pāricchattaka* tree blooms."
"But here, Cittapāṭalī has been deceived by Jarāsakka after he made us drink liquor, and our city of the gods has been seized.

Let us go and fight with him! Having said this, they mounted elephants, horses, and chariots, took up shields of gold, silver, and jewels, prepared for battle, and sounding the drums of the asuras, split the waters of the great ocean in two.
They arise. When the rain has ceased, those ants begin to climb Mount Sineru just as they would a termite mound.
Then their first battle takes place with the Nāgas.
In that battle, however, neither the hide nor the skin of anyone is torn, and no blood is shed; it is merely like a game of wooden rams played by children.
It is merely a mutual intimidation of one another. Even hundreds of millions or thousands of millions of nāgas, having fought with them, enter the city of the asuras themselves and turn back.
But when the asuras are powerful, then the nāgas retreat to the second terrace along with the supaṇṇas.
Having gathered on one side, they fight. This same method applies to the Supaṇṇas and others as well.
But when the Asuras crush those five positions, then even the five forces combined retreat together.
Then the Four Great Kings go and report that situation to Sakka. Having heard their words, Sakka [prepares] his chariot, one hundred and fifty yojanas long...
Having mounted the Vejayanta chariot, he either departs himself or sends a son. On this occasion, however, desiring to send his son, he said, "Dear Suvīra," and so forth.
"Evaṃ bhaddantavā" means "Let it be thus; may there be prosperity for you. "Āpādesi" means he fell into negligence.

He did so. Surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs (accharā), having descended upon a great golden road sixty yojanas in width, he wanders through the Nandana Grove and other such places while sporting in the constellations; this is the meaning. "Anuṭṭhahanti" means not performing [tasks].
"Avāyāmanti" means not exerting oneself. "Alasvassa" means he would be lazy. "Na ca kiccāni" means and not his duties.
"Let him do"—that is, he would not fail to perform whatever task was required. "One who has all his desires fulfilled" means one who is successful in all his wishes.
"O Sakka, show me that boon"—Sakka, best of gods, he says this, meaning: "Show me, point out, and tell me of that boon, that supreme state or opportunity.
For that is the path to Nibbāna; [he speaks thus] because, without performing [worldly] deeds, he seeks a place of livelihood.
This is the path to Nibbāna. First. 2.
Commentary on the Susīma Sutta (248).
Regarding the second [sutta]: "Susīma" refers to one son among his own thousand sons who bore that very name. Second.
3. Commentary on the Dhajagga Sutta 249.
In the third [verse], *samupabyūḷho* means gathered together, formed into a mass. Regarding the phrase *dhajaggaṃ ullokeyyatha*:
it is said that Sakka’s chariot is one hundred and fifty yojanas in length. Its rear end is fifty yojanas long, and in the middle is the chariot-fence (*rathapañjara*).
It was fifty *yojanas* from the chariot’s axle to the chariot’s pole. By doubling that very measurement, they say it was three hundred *yojanas* in length.
Upon it was a couch (*pallaṅka*) one *yojana* in size; a white parasol (*setacchatra*) three *yojanas* high was placed above it.
To a single yoke were yoked a thousand thoroughbred horses (*ājanya*), while the remaining ornaments—
"There is no limit to it. Its banner, moreover, rises three hundred and fifty yojanas high;
when struck by the wind, it emits a sound like that of the fivefold musical ensemble. 'You should look at that,' he says.
Why? Because for those who behold it, the king does not come before them, but stands like a pillar planted at the edge of the assembly, [making them think], 'Of whom are we afraid?'"
There is no fear. Regarding "of Pajāpati": it is said that he, being equal in appearance and equal in lifespan to Sakka, obtains the second seat;
likewise Varuṇa and Īsāna. However, Varuṇa obtains the third seat, and Īsāna the fourth.
"He fled" means that, having been defeated by the Asuras, while standing on that chariot, he was of a nature to flee upon seeing even a tiny royal banner.
The phrases beginning with "Itipi so bhagavā" have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Idamavoca" means that the Blessed One spoke this, known as the *Dhajagga-paritta*, the power of which extends over a hundred thousand million world-systems within the sphere of his command.
Indeed, there is no end to those who are freed from sufferings such as the fear of *yakkhas* and the fear of thieves by reflecting upon this. Let alone the pacification of other forms of suffering—
For one who recollects this with a confident mind gains a foothold even in the sky.

Here is an account of this: it is said that while the whitewashing work was being done at the Dīghavāpi Cetiya, a young man fell from the foot of the head-railing and was crushed within the interior of the cetiya.
The Saṅgha of bhikkhus standing below [recited]: "Friends, the Dhajagga Paritta..."
"Recite [the protection]," he said. Terrified by the fear of death, he cried out, "May the Dhajagga-paritta protect me!
At that very moment, two bricks emerged from the belly of the cetiya and stood as a staircase;
those standing above lowered a vine-ladder for him. When he had stepped onto that ladder, the bricks returned to their original places. This is the third [story].
4. Commentary on the Vepacitti Sutta 250.
In the fourth [sutta], *Vepacitti* is said to be the eldest of all the asuras. *Yena* is merely a particle, as is *nanti*.
*Kaṇṭhapañcamehi* means by five bonds: namely, two hands, two feet, and the neck—thus by these five bonds.
