Furthermore, these [abusive words] come within the range of the eye like a lotus stalk or a spider's thread, obstructing one’s posture;
yet by means of the mind alone one is bound by them, and by means of the mind alone one is released from them. "He reviles" means: "You are a thief! You are a fool! You are deluded!
You are a rogue! You are a camel! You are an ox! You are a donkey! You are destined for hell! You are a beast!"—there is nothing [of substance] in you.
"‘A happy rebirth or indeed a miserable rebirth is to be expected for you’—with these ten grounds of abuse he reviles him.
‘He insults’ means, O Sakka, he threatens him by saying such things as: ‘You will not be victorious at all times;
when victory belongs to the asuras, we too shall bind you in this very manner, lay you down at the gate of the asura realm, and beat you.’"

Sakka, having achieved victory, did not take that to heart; rather, shaking off the great burden from his head, he entered and exited the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas. "He addressed him" means:
"Does this Sakka endure these harsh words out of fear, or because he is endowed with the patience of acceptance? Thus, while investigating, he spoke.
"By weakness" means by way of being weak. "Would connect with" means he would connect with or oppose. "They would break apart" means they would become alienated;
there is also a reading, "they would be angry. "The other" means the adversary.
"He who, being mindful, attains peace"—the meaning is that for one who, having become possessed of mindfulness, attains peace, I consider that very peace to be the warding off of the fool.
"When he conceives [himself as superior]" means because he conceives that [person]. "He overruns" means he overwhelms.
"Just as [cattle] more so when one has fled": just as in a fight between bulls, while two bulls are fighting, the herd of cattle stands looking on;
but when one flees, then the entire herd of cattle more fully overwhelms the one who is fleeing. In the same way, the dull-witted person [overwhelms] the one who is patient.
The meaning is that it "furthermore overwhelms.

"Supreme in one's own welfare" means supreme in one's personal interest. "Nothing is found superior to patience" means that among those interests which are supreme for one's own sake, no other purpose exists that is more excellent than patience. "That they call supreme patience" refers to that which is powerful.
He endures; they say that such patience of his is supreme. "The strength of a fool" means the strength of ignorance.

He explains that for one whose strength is that, it is indeed a weakness which they call "strength" when they speak. "Of one protected by the Dhamma" means of one guarded by the Dhamma, or of one protecting the Dhamma.
"An opposer" means one who speaks in opposition, or one who speaks in opposition [saying], "This is the strength of a fool."
One might even speak [thus], yet there is no one capable of shaking one who stands firm in the Dhamma.
"By that, he becomes worse off for him" means: by that anger, it is a misfortune for that very person. For whom? For the one who returns anger for anger.
"Those who desire to heal"—the plural is used for the singular; the meaning is "one who desires to heal. "People think"—[they think] of such a person, both themselves and others.
Ordinary worldlings who are blind fools think thus of that person who treats and accomplishes the welfare of both: "This one is a blind fool.
"Unskilled in the Dhamma" means they are not proficient in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Here" means in this teaching.
"Khu" is merely a particle. This is the fourth [section].
5. Commentary on the *Subhāsitajaya Sutta* 251.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "He said this to the Lord of Asuras": he said this because of his skill (*chekatā*). It is said that it occurred to him:
"It is a weighty matter to speak first after having released another from their grasp; however, it is easy to speak afterwards after following another's words."
"Let them speak. "The former gods" means those who have long resided in the world of the gods and were the former owners;

it means, "Speak what has come down through your own lineage. "Beyond the reach of punishment" means devoid of the application of punishment; the meaning is that there is nothing here to be seized as either punishment or a weapon. This is the fifth [section].
6. Commentary on the Kulāvakasutta 252.

Regarding the sixth verse, "He addressed [him]": it is said that when he was born facing toward the *simbali* grove, the sound of chariots, the sound of noble steeds, and the sound of banners were like the crash of thunderbolts on all sides. Having heard this in the *simbali* grove...

The powerful supaṇṇas fled; however, those who were aged and decrepit, those weakened by disease, and those whose winglets had not yet grown—unable to flee and terrified by the fear of death—they all cried out a great roar at once.
Hearing that, Sakka asked Mātali, "Whose sound is this, dear friend? "It is the sound of the chariot, O Lord," Mātali replied, "having heard it, the supaṇṇas..."
"Unable to flee, they cry out. Hearing this, his heart moved with compassion, and he spoke:
"By the front of the pole" means by the front of the chariot's pole. "Avoid them with this front of the pole so that the front of the pole does not crush them in their nest.
For that chariot was produced through the condition of merit; even if the Cakkavāḷa mountains or Mount Sineru were directly in its path, [it would pass through them].
It passes through, piercing right through, without clinging; it moves as if through the open sky.

If it had gone through that *simbali* grove, then just as when a great cart passes through the middle of a plantain grove or the middle of a castor-oil plant grove, the entire grove is shattered and crushed, so too would that *simbali* grove have been. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Nadubbhiya Sutta 253.
Regarding the seventh [verse], "He approached": Sakka was thinking, "Even if someone were my sworn enemy, I would not deceive him.
[The Buddha thought: "There is no one more of an enemy to him than I; I shall test him first."
Thinking, "Now, upon seeing me, does he feel resentment or not? he approached him. "Stop, Vepacitti!
You are caught!"—Vepacitti, he says, "Stop right there; you are caught by me.
With those very words, he became as if bound by five bonds, with the neck as the fifth. And [he said], "May my words be true," for the sake of ensuring that no resentment would arise toward him.
He says, "Take an oath. When he says, "The evil that comes from speaking falsehood," he refers to the evil of Cetiyarāja among the first beings of this eon.
"The evil of one who reviles the Noble Ones" refers to the evil of Kokālika.

"And the evil of one who betrays a friend" refers to the evil of one with a wicked mind toward the Great Being in the Mahākapi Jātaka. "The evil of one who is ungrateful" refers to one such as Devadatta.
The ungrateful commit evil. These, it is said, are the four great evils in this eon.
Seventh. 8. Commentary on the *Verocana-asurinda-sutta*. 254.
In the eighth [verse], "the eight" refers to those standing like door-keepers. "Nipphadā" means accomplishment; as far as...
"One should indeed strive as long as the goal is being accomplished," he says. This second verse belongs to Sakka.

In that context, "nothing surpasses patience" means that among goals already accomplished and made beautiful, there is no goal superior to patience. "Kinds of purpose" (*atthajāta*) refers to kinds of duties (*kiccajāta*).
For even creatures such as dogs and jackals are not called "beings" unless they possess some duty; even the mere act of going here and there [constitutes a duty].
It is indeed a duty. "But for all living beings, enjoyments have union as their ultimate" means that rice porridge and other such items are unfit for consumption when they are kept overnight;
however, once they have been reheated, roasted, and mixed with ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, they become fit for consumption.
Therefore he said: "But for all living beings, enjoyments have union as their ultimate. [The term] *nipphannasobhano*...
"Meaning": these meanings indeed shine forth when they have been fully accomplished. Furthermore, the fourth verse belongs to Sakka;
its meaning should also be understood according to the method already stated.
The eighth [chapter]. 9. Commentary on the Araññāyatana-isi Sutta.

255. In the ninth [chapter], it is said that they dwell in leaf-huts: they reside in leaf-shelters located in delightful forest regions of the Himalayan area, which are well-provided with night-quarters, day-quarters, walking-paths, and so forth.
Sakka, the lord of the gods, and Vepacitti—these two, being respectively son-in-law and father-in-law—sometimes quarrel and sometimes move about together; however, at this time, they were together.
They move about. *Paṭaliya* refers to sandals worn for walking from group to group. *Olaggetvā* means having slung the sword over the shoulder.
*Chattenā* means with a divine white parasol being held over his head. *Apabyāmato karitvā* means without making it wide.
*Ciradikkhitānaṃ* means those who have long undertaken their vows. *Ito paṭikkamma* means "depart from here; avoid this."
"Do not stand in the upper wind," they say. "For here, O gods" means that regarding the fragrance of those possessed of virtue, the gods do not perceive it as repulsive;
rather, they perceive it only as desirable, pleasing, and agreeable. This is the ninth [sutta].
10. Commentary on the Samuddaka Sutta.

256. "On the tenth ocean shore, in leaf-huts" means they dwell in leaf-huts of the aforementioned kind upon the sandy beaches, which have the color of silver plates, on the back of the great ocean that forms the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "It may be so, it may not be so for us" means:
"We shall ask for the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*). It is said that, for the most part, the battle between the gods and the asuras took place on the back of the great ocean.
It happens that the asuras do not always achieve victory; rather, on many occasions, they suffer defeat.
When defeated by the devas and fleeing, passing through the hermitages of the *isīs*, they become enraged, thinking, "Sakka has conspired with these men to destroy us!
Seize their children, you sons of a childless woman! Thus, in a fit of rage, they demolish the water jars, the walking-paths, the assembly halls, and other structures within the hermitages.
The seers, having brought fruits and roots from the forest, saw him and restored him back to his normal state by means of their suffering.
Yet they too were destroyed in that very same way again and again. Therefore, upon hearing that "now a battle has arisen between them," they thought thus:
"Kāmakaro" means one who does as he wishes. "Bhayassa abhayassa vā" means either fear or fearlessness. This is what was said.
"It is so—if you wish to grant fearlessness, you are able to grant fearlessness; if you wish to grant fear, you are able to grant fear.
But give us the gift of fearlessness. "The wicked" means those who are hostile.
"Planted" means established in a field.

"He became terrified three times" means that after eating his evening meal, having ascended to his bed and lain down, as soon as he had fallen asleep, he would rise up crying out like one struck all over by a hundred spears;
the entire asura realm, ten thousand *yojanas* in extent, fell into a state of agitation, wondering, "What is this? Then, they came to him and asked, "What is this?"
Thus he says, "Nothing at all. This same method applies to the second watch of the night and the others as well.
While the Asuras were thus consoling him, saying, "Do not fear, Great King," the dawn broke. From that time on, his mind became agitated due to the onset of illness.
For this very reason, another name for him arose: "Vepacitti" (the one of agitated mind). The tenth [chapter].
The First Chapter. 2.
The Second Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Vatapada Sutta.
257. In the first section of the second chapter, "vow-terms" (*vatapadāni*) refers to the constituent parts of a vow. "Completed" (*samattāni*) means fulfilled.

"Undertaken" (*samādinnāni*) means accepted. "Honoring the elders of the family" (*kule jeṭṭhāpacāyī*) means one who shows reverence toward the elders of the family, such as the maternal grandfather, the maternal grandmother, the paternal grandfather, the paternal grandmother, the maternal uncle, the wife of the maternal uncle, and so forth.
"Gentle in speech" (*saṇhavāco*) means one whose speech is affectionate, soft, and sweet.
"Relinquishing" (*muttacāgo*) means one who has abandoned [stinginess]. "Pure-handed" (*payatapāṇī*) means one whose hands are always washed for the purpose of giving gifts.

"Delighting in relinquishment" (*vossaggarato*) means one who delights in the act of letting go. "Devoted to being asked" (*yācayogo*) means one who is worthy of being requested by others; or alternatively, "devoted to being asked" means one who is engaged in the very state of being asked.
"Delighting in giving and sharing" (*dānasaṃvibhāgarato*) means one who delights both in giving and in sharing. First.
2. Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta 258.
In the second [verse], "become a human being" means he was born as a human being in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha.

"He gave a dwelling place" means that having constructed a lodging for the great multitude at the crossroads of the four great highways, he gave it away. "Even a thousand is not enough" means even a thousand [is not sufficient].

Even when a thousand people or a thousand voices declare, "This is the meaning of this," or "This is the meaning of that," he decides upon it while standing on a single word. This is the second [section].
3. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta.
259. "He approached in the third [case]" means: he approached thinking, "They say, 'Sakka is the king of the gods';
I shall ask the One of Ten Powers whether such a Sakka exists, by whom he has been seen before. "And I understand that" uses the singular for the plural;
the meaning is, "I understand those phenomena. It is said that in his immediately preceding existence, Sakka...
In the Magadha country, at the village of Macala, there was a young brahmin named Magha, who was wise and competent;
his conduct was like that of a Bodhisatta. Having gathered thirty-three men, he performed a meritorious deed.
One day, having investigated with his own wisdom, he took refuse-rubbish to a place in the middle of the village where a great crowd had assembled.
Having leveled both sides, he made that place delightful. Again, right there, he had a pavilion built.

Later, as time passed, he had a hall constructed. And having departed from the village, traveling for a *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, three-quarters of a *yojana*, or even a full *yojana*, he leveled the uneven ground together with those companions. All of them—
With one mind, they performed much merit by constructing bridges at various places where bridges were needed,
and by building pavilions, halls, lotus ponds, planting rows of trees, and digging wells in places suited for such works.
Having fulfilled the seven vows, Magha, upon the dissolution of his body, was reborn together with his companions in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
The Blessed One knows all that. Therefore he said: "I know those qualities by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the state of Sakka.
This is a brief account of Sakka’s attainment of the state of Sakka;
the detailed exposition, however, is stated in the *Sakkapañhavaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Questions of Sakka) in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*. Third.
4. Commentary on the *Daliddasutta* 260.
In the fourth [verse], "a poor human" (*manussadaliddo*) means one who lacks human wealth. "A wretched human" (*manussakapaṇo*) means one who has reached a state of human pitifulness.
"A miserable human" (*manussavarāko*) means one who is base among humans. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that place, or in that state of being outshone. "Lamenting" (*ujjhāyanti*) means...
They despise means they think of it as something base. They speak of it means they discuss and explain it.
They proclaim it means they discuss it here and there and elaborate upon it. Regarding the phrase "This, dear sir," this is the sequential narrative:
it is said that before the Buddha had arisen, he was the King of Bārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāsī, and [he saw] one who was well-adorned with various ornaments, including raised flags and banners.
He performed a circumambulation of the city while being gazed upon by the multitude of people whose eyes were drawn by his own splendor and success.
At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha, having come from Mount Gandhamādana, was walking for alms in that city;
he was one whose faculties were tranquil, whose mind was peaceful, and who was endowed with the highest self-mastery. The great multitude, too, directed their respectful attention toward the King.
Having abandoned [the king], he looked only at the Paccekabuddha. The king thought, "Now not even a single person in this assembly looks at me;
what could this be? While looking, he saw the Paccekabuddha. That Paccekabuddha was also advanced in years, standing in his final stage of life.
His robes were worn out, and the seams were falling apart here and there. To the king...

For two incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand more, while fulfilling the perfections, he had never experienced even a mere glimmer of faith upon seeing a Paccekabuddha, nor had he ever extended his hand in salutation. That king, thinking, "He has surely gone forth;
he does not look at me out of envy," became angry and departed, spitting and saying, "Where is this man who is clothed in the robes of a leper?"

As the result of that karma, having been reborn in the Great Hell, he came to the human world by means of the remaining residue of that maturation and took conception in the womb of an extremely destitute woman in Rājagaha.
From the moment he was conceived, that woman could not obtain even a mere measure of sour gruel to fill her belly; while he was still within her womb, his ears and nose dissolved away.
Having been born with scaly, white-tinged leprosy, he emerged from his mother’s womb. Parents indeed perform difficult tasks;
therefore, as long as his mother was unable to go about carrying an alms-bowl, she brought him sour gruel and water herself.
But when he reached the age where he was capable of wandering for alms, she gave him a bowl in his hand and said, "You shall become known."
"By one's own karma," he said, and departed.
From that time forth, pieces of flesh fell off his entire body one after another; his lymph flowed out, and great pains assailed him.
Whatever street he lay upon, he cried out with a loud voice throughout the entire night.
Because of the sound of his compassionate lamentations, the people throughout the entire street could not find sleep all night long.
From that time on, because he would wake those who were sleeping comfortably, the name "Suppabuddha" (Well-Awakened) arose for him.
Then, at another time, when the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagaha, the citizens invited the Teacher and [prepared] a great pavilion in the center of the city.
Having made their preparations, they gave the gifts. The leper Suppabuddha also went and sat down not far from the pavilion where the almsgiving was taking place.
As the citizens were serving the community of monks headed by the Buddha with various kinds of excellent hard and soft foods, they also gave him rice gruel and a meal.
When he had eaten that excellent food, his mind became one-pointed.
At the conclusion of his meal, the Teacher gave a blessing and illuminated the Truths.

While still seated in the place where he sat, Suppabuddha directed his knowledge according to the teaching and was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher rose and went to the monastery.
He, too, having mounted his cushion and taken up his bowl, leaning on his staff, departed for his own dwelling place.
While walking along, he deprived a stray cow of its life;

then, as if breaking an earthenware bowl and recovering a golden one, he was reborn in the world of the gods at the second moment of consciousness. By virtue of his own merit, he outshone the other gods.
To demonstrate this reason, Sakka, the lord of the devas, said: "This one, dear sir," and so forth.

"Faith" refers to faith that has come through the Path. "And whose virtue is beautiful" means that what is called "beautiful virtue" is the virtue dear to the Noble Ones (ariyakanta-sīla) belonging to a noble disciple.

Although there is not even a single aspect of virtue that is not dear to a noble disciple, in this context, the five precepts that have not been abandoned even in other existences are intended. This is the fourth [verse].
5. Commentary on the *Rāmaṇeyyakasutta* 261.

In the fifth [verse], "monastery shrines" (*ārāmacetyāni*) means monastery *cetiyas*. "Forest shrines" (*vanacetyāni*) means forest *cetiyas*. In both cases, it should be understood as a *cetya* in the sense of being honored or esteemed.
"Of the delightful state for humans" (*manussarāmaṇeyyassa*) means of the quality of being pleasing to humans. Now, by way of its being delightful to humans—
Showing the beauty of the land, he said, "In the village," and so forth. This is the fifth [verse].
6. Commentary on the *Yajamāna Sutta* (Sutta 262).

Regarding the sixth verse, "of those sacrificing" (*yajamānānaṃ*) means "of those performing sacrifices. At that time, it is said, people living in Aṅga and Magadha used to perform [sacrifices] every year.
Having taken the finest portions of clarified butter, honey, molasses, and so forth, they heap them into a pile about sixty cartloads of wood in one place and set fire to it.
When it is ablaze, they throw everything into it, saying, "We sacrifice to Mahābrahmā.
Their tenet is that "what is offered once yields a thousandfold fruit. Sakka, the king of the gods, [thinks], "All these..."
"Taking all the first-fruits, they burn them in the fire, saying, 'We sacrifice to Mahābrahmā. They make it fruitless.
While I look on, let them not perish; I shall act so that they produce much merit, just as they do when giving to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Having thus set the pile of wood ablaze while the people looked on, [he manifested] the form of Brahmā on the full-moon day.
Having performed this, he appeared as if he had burst through the lunar disk while the great multitude was looking on.

When the people saw him, they thought, "The Great Brahmā is coming to accept this sacrifice," and they knelt upon the ground, stood with palms joined in reverence, and paid homage. The brahmins said, "We were just discussing it among ourselves..."
“Think on this, now see it: here is Brahmā coming with his own hand to accept your sacrifice.
Sakka, having arrived and stood in the air above the wooden structure, asked, “To whom does this honor belong?
“To you, venerable sir; please accept our sacrifice. “In that case, come along; do not discard the scale and take it by hand!”
He deliberated: "This Teacher dwells in Dhuravihāra; we shall ask him, 'To whom does a gift given bear great fruit?
Taking inhabitants from both kingdoms, he went into the presence of the Teacher and asked, saying this.
In that context, *puññapekkhānaṃ* means "of those seeking merit," of those desiring merit. *Opadhikaṃ puññaṃ* means "merit with a substrate of rebirth" (*upadhivipāka*).
"Merit. What is given to the Saṅgha bears great fruit"—meaning that what is given to the Noble Saṅgha becomes expansive.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings drank the drink of the Deathless.
From then on, people gave all the finest gifts to the community of monks. This is the sixth [chapter].
7. Commentary on the Buddhavandanā-sutta 263.
Regarding the seventh verse: “Arise! means arise, strive, exert yourself. “Victors in battle” (vijitasaṅgāmā):

he addresses the Blessed One thus because of his victory over lust and the other defilements, as well as over the twelve-league army of Māra. “Those who have laid down the burden” (pannabhārā): those who have set aside the burden of the aggregates, the defilements, and volitional formations.
"On the fifteenth night" means on the night of the full moon of the fifteenth day. Seventh.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Homage of Householders (Gahaṭṭhavandanāsutta) 264.
In the eighth [discourse], "the various quarters" refers to the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions. "Dwellers of the earth" means those who inhabit the ground.

"Long-concentrated" (*cirarattasamāhita*) means one whose mind has been concentrated for a long time through access concentration (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*). "I revere" (*vandāmi*) means I pay homage.

"Devoted to the holy life" (*brahmacariyaparāyaṇa*) means one who practices the supreme conduct—the holy life—for ten years, twenty years, or even sixty years, until the end of life, observing such things as sleeping alone and eating only once a day. "Doers of merit" (*puññakara*) refers to the giving of the four requisites and the offering of *kusumbha* flowers and jasmine.

“An array of a thousand lamps”—such are those who perform meritorious deeds. “Virtuous” means being established in the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and endowed with either the five or the ten precepts.

“Supporting their wives according to the Dhamma” means supporting their children and wives not by engaging in activities such as breaking into houses, but rather through righteous occupations such as agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. “He mounted the chariot at the head” means he stood at the forefront of the gods.
The best man mounted the chariot. Eighth.
9. Commentary on the Satthāravandanā Sutta: 265.
In the ninth [verse], "he paid homage to the Blessed One" means that having arranged his upper garment (dukula) over one shoulder, he knelt with his knees raised as high as his head (brahmajāṇuko).
Having offered the sacrifice and placed his hands in añjali at his head, he pays homage. "He, the Yakkha" refers to Sakka.
"Of unsurpassed name" means that because there is no state of inferiority regarding all his qualities, he possesses an "unsurpassed name" derived from names indicative of all those qualities.

"By the transcendence of ignorance" means by the transcendence of the ignorance rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) which conceals the Four Noble Truths. "Learners" (*sekkhā*) refers to the seven types of learners (*sekkhā*).
"Delighting in diminution" means they take pleasure in the destruction of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "They train" means they practice. [This is] the ninth. 10.
Commentary on the Saṅghavandanā Sutta: 266.
Regarding the tenth verse, "he addressed": why did he speak thus repeatedly? It is said that this was because of Sakka, the king of the gods.
The sound is sweet; her lip-covering is well-proportioned, and at the time of speaking, it emits a sound like that of golden bells.
She speaks with the thought, "I shall hear this again and again.

She is called "one who lies on a putrid body" because she lies, having covered herself, upon the putrid body of her mother or upon her own body. She is "submerged in a heap of corpses" for ten months.
They are submerged in this carrion known as the mother’s womb. “I envy them this” means: I envy and long for this of theirs.
“They do not open up a granary for us” means they do not put their own grain into a granary;
for these people have no grain. “Nor a jar” means not in a jar. “Nor a basket” means not in a small wicker basket.
"Seeking what has been prepared by others" means seeking and searching for food cooked in another's house according to the practice of the alms-round.
"By that" means by what has been thus sought. "Of good conduct" means those who have well undertaken beautiful vows for ten, or even up to sixty years.
"Reciting and reflecting well" means: "We shall recite the Dhamma; we shall undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga); we shall partake of the Deathless."
"Those who speak such well-spoken words, thinking, 'We shall practice the duty of a recluse'—though they remain silent, they truly move in harmony.
Even while preaching the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night as if with the sound of a thundercloud, they are said to move in harmony while remaining silent. Why?
Because of the absence of useless speech. And 'many beings' means that many creatures are mutually opposed; they are intent on their own punishments."
"Extinguished" (*nibbutā*) means that among beings who have taken up sticks for the purpose of harming others, they have laid down the stick.
"Without grasping" (*anādānā*) means that among beings who possess grasping, they do not grasp even a single portion of the realms of existence, wombs, and so forth. Tenth.
Second Chapter.
3. The Third Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Having Cut Off. 267.
The first [discourse] of the third chapter has its meaning already explained. The first is finished.
2. Commentary on the Dubbaṇṇiya Sutta 268.
In the second [verse], "ugly" (*dubbaṇṇa*) means having the color of burnt wood or charcoal. "Okoṭimaka" means a hunchback with a large belly. "On the seat" refers to the Paṇḍukambala stone slab.
"Feeding on anger": this is simply the name he was given by Sakka. He was, however, a certain brahmā of the form realm; for it is said that "Sakka..."
Having heard that he was "endowed with the power of patience," [the yakṣa] came there for the purpose of testing him.
However, obstructive yakṣas are unable to enter a place where such protection has been arranged. Having heard from the gods, [the yakṣa] approached, thinking:
"It is not possible to move him by means of harshness; however, it is possible to drive him away by behaving humbly and remaining established in patience. Thus...

He approached desiring to revile him. "He disappeared" means that, having stood firm in patience and established a powerful mental resolve, he was unable to remain in his seat while being shown such humble behavior, and so he vanished. Regarding the phrase "I am not one whose mind is easily struck down":
here, *su* is merely a particle; he said, "I am one whose mind is struck down (*upahata-citto*). "Not by a turn of anger" means not by a whirlpool of wrath.
"I am not easily brought under the power of anger," he says. "Na vo cirāhaṃ" is merely a particle;
he means, "I do not become angry for long. This is the second [verse].
3. Commentary on the Saṃbarimāyā Sutta.
269. "In the third [case], 'afflicted with disease' means afflicted by the disease that arose at the time of being cursed by the company of seers.
'Recite it! he says, meaning, 'If you recite the *Sambarimā* for me, I will treat you as well.
'Do not recite it, dear sir,' [Sakka replies]. Even without the *Sambarimā*, Sakka already oppresses us; but if he should learn it, [it would be worse]."
"We are lost! Do not destroy us for the sake of one person alone," they said, and thus they restrained him.
"Just as Śambara was cooked in hell for a hundred years after employing his magic, so too does he cook [in hell].
You are indeed righteous; enough of your trickery," he says. But what can Sakka do against his anger?
“Would it be possible to cure him? “Yes, it would be possible. How? At that time, it is said, that company of seers was still present;
therefore, if he had been led into the presence of the seers and asked for their forgiveness, he would have found relief.
But because he had been deceived by him, he did not do so and departed instead. This is the third [section].
4. Commentary on the *Accayasutta* (Sutta 270).
In the fourth [case], "they engaged in dispute" means they quarreled. "He transgressed" (*accasāra*) means he overstepped;
the meaning is that one bhikkhu spoke words in excess of another bhikkhu. "He does not accept it according to the Dhamma" means he does not forgive it.
"Let anger come under your control" means: "Let anger come into your power; do not fall under the sway of anger. This is what it indicates.
In the phrase "And let there be no decay of your friendship," the word *hi* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*).

It means: "May what is called 'decay' not arise in regard to your duty toward friends. Alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative: "May decay not arise among your friends," that is, [may it not arise] from the state of friendship.
The meaning is: "May there be no change into something else. "Do not censure what is beyond reproach" means: do not censure the person whose taints are exhausted, who is beyond reproach.
This is the fourth [discourse]. 5.
Commentary on the Discourse on Non-Anger (*Akkodhasutta*).
271. "In the fifth [verse], 'May anger not overcome you' means: may anger not master you; rather, you yourselves must master anger. 'And do not be angry' means:
when others are angry, do not retaliate against those who are angry. 'Non-anger' refers to loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the preliminary stage of loving-kindness.
'Non-harming' (*avihiṃsā*) refers to compassion (*karuṇā*) and the preliminary stage of compassion. Furthermore, anger crushes an evil person, just as a mountain crushes [what lies beneath it]."
"Anger crushes a base person like a mountain. This is the fifth [sutta].
The third chapter is finished.
The commentary on the Saṅkhāra-saṃyutta is completed.
Thus ends the commentary on the Sagāthāvagga within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
This concludes the first volume of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* commentary.
